Japan’s reputation for organisational efficiency lay in tatters as the rowing and shooting contingent faced unexpected ordeals upon arrival. A majority of the rowing squad were left stranded without accommodation, some of their names actually missing from the accreditation system.
“Only three of the 22 men’s athletes have accommodation against their names. And the names of three of the five women rowers (Poonam, Aleena Anto and Anshika Bharati) are not registered with the hosts even though they all have valid accreditation,” said a Rowing Federation of India (RFI) official.
The rowers’ nightmare had actually begun even before they boarded their flight. One of the groups that left Mumbai on Tuesday night was told by Cathay Pacific that they would not be allowed to check in their oars. Later, the oars were flown to Delhi. They will arrive in Nagoya on Thursday morning, just in time for the first official practice session.
Adding to the agony was the Sports Authority of India’s belated intimation that women’s coach Ratheesh Kumar and team manager Ramakrishnan Ramachandran would have to manage their accommodation on their own.
Meanwhile, the shooters had to wait for almost three hours for their transport after reaching the Nagoya airport at 9 pm on Tuesday. 
“We didn’t get the bus and there was no food. Everything was closed at the airport. The welcome centre had no information, so we had to wait and reach the hotel around 4 am,” a team member told TOI.
Samaresh gets wrong accreditation
India’s pistol shooting head coach Samaresh Jung was in for a rude shock when he came to know his accreditation didn’t allow him to enter the players arena and the field of play during the matches. “It was a shock when we saw Samaresh’s accreditation. When we enquired, we were told that this was done according to the list the organisers had received from the Indian Olympic Association,” a source said.
“We contacted our office at the National Rifle Association of India, and the issue was taken up. We are told that Samaresh will be getting the new accreditation tomorrow,” the source said. Samaresh’s absence would dent India’s medal chances as most of the 10m air pistol shooters like Suruchi Phogat, Akash Bhardwaj have been training under him.
Citing shortage of govt funds, riders left to foot horse feed bill
Indian equestrian riders who are preparing for the 
Asian Games
 have been left scrambling to arrange hay, bedding and fodder for their horse combinations, with the Indian Olympic Association (IOA)-appointed ad-hoc committee running the sport citing a “shortage of govt funds”, reports Sabi Hussain.
A mail accessed by TOI, signed by Lt Col Sandeep Dewan, member (administration), ad-hoc panel and team leader of the equestrian contingent, states that funds released to the national federation have been largely insufficient even to clear the bill of transporter Peden Bloodstock. Reimbursements for pre-quarantine tests, blood and swab tests, horse transportation, athlete accommodation and groom accommodation also remain pending. “Timely support on these essential matters is extremely important for us to focus completely on our performance in the Asian Games,” a rider told TOI on Wednesday.

Trump’s Kennedy Center sabotage is complete
Trump can’t put his name on the building — so he’s closing it instead.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump can’t put his name on the Kennedy Center — so he’s closing it, effective immediately.
What’s happening? On Tuesday, the board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted to close the building indefinitely, shortly after a federal judge rebuked efforts to engrave Trump’s name into the facade.
According to the board, the closure is because the center is in bad financial shape and the building itself is in a dangerous state of disrepair. Without Trump’s support, they claim, a renovation will be impossible — and Trump has made clear he won’t support it unless his name is on the building, even though Congress already approved $257 million for the project last year.
How did we get here? Trump has been obsessed with claiming the Kennedy Center — a memorial for an assassinated president — and its cultural cachet for himself ever since he returned to office last year. He quickly stacked the Kennedy Center board with his appointees, then installed himself as chair.
In December, he had his name added to the building’s facade and its official title, temporarily making it the Trump-Kennedy Center. A federal judge ordered him to undo the renaming in June, and the administration complied — but the facade has remained covered since then, obscuring the removal.
In August, Trump also threatened the center with demolition if he didn’t get his way; he sounded a similar note in a Truth Social post Tuesday, writing that “the Building is destined to doom.”
What’s the context? Trump and his handpicked board have both portrayed the Kennedy Center as a destitute, derelict institution in need of rescue. In reality, the Washington Post reported last month, he’s done his fair share to drive it into the ground: Ticket sales and fundraising both plummeted after his December renaming, resulting in a nearly $100 million shortfall.
What’s the big picture? The Kennedy Center was doing just fine before Trump returned to office. Now, its doors will close because he can’t turn it into a monument to himself.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

New Delhi: The health ministry has reiterated that stem cell therapy for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) cannot be offered as routine or commercial clinical care and can be used only in duly approved clinical trials.
In an advisory to states, dated 16 September, the ministry said "therapeutic use of any type of stem cell in autism is to remain restricted to duly approved clinical trials, in accordance with the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, issued jointly by Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and other applicable Government instructions issued by the Government of India from time to time.”
The directive seeks to prevent clinics from selling unproven treatments to families as standard treatment and to ensure that providers strictly comply with the existing framework or face penalties.
The advisory follows a 30 January 2026 Supreme Court order that directed the government to regulate stem cell treatments. It held that non-compliance would attract consequences, including professional misconduct under Regulation 7.22 of the IMC Regulations, 2002, as well as action under Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, which provide for cancellation of registration and penalty.
In line with this order, the National Medical Commission (NMC) stated in its 5 September 2026 advisory that stem cell therapy can be provided as routine care only for approved diseases. It stated that “unauthorized administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement of stem cell therapy beyond the approved indications would constitute professional misconduct."
State medical councils have been directed to investigate complaints and “take appropriate disciplinary action in accordance with the applicable statutory and regulatory provisions”.
On 19 August, Mint reported that India has issued strict norms for stem cell therapies.
'A continuously evolving field'
"Stem cells represent a complex and continuously evolving field in healthcare. The premise that these cells can differentiate into other cell types may lead some people to believe they can cure several common conditions," said Dr Rajeev Jayadevan, a public health expert and former IMA president at Kochi Chapter.
“However, the reality is far more nuanced. Using them as unproven treatments carries not only the risk of failure, but also unexpected adverse health outcomes. Worldwide, strict regulations govern how and for what conditions stem cells can be used. As data from well-designed clinical trials emerge in the future, stem cell therapies are likely to gain regulatory approval for more conditions,” Jayadevan added.

Justice delayed: Acknowledging women pioneers in science
The debate in the scientific world has often been about glory. Who deserves the glory for a discovery, for an invention, for defining a procedure, a drug, a vaccine? Does credit ever attach to the patients who were experimented upon, the participants of a clinical trial, people who gave of their time and body in order that science may advance, in order that people who come after them do not suffer. Codes of ethics are mutable, they keep changing, and the grant of credit in science also operates on this arc. This story is a page from such an omission, a blunder. Nearly 150 years later, some form of reparation was attempted.
For the world, for the longest time, perhaps even till today, J. Marion Sims was the ‘Father of Modern Gynaecology.’ Sims reportedly earned the title for his ‘groundbreaking surgical innovations, notably the development of a cure for vesicovaginal fistula.” For his achievements, Sims not only received the soubriquet, but also statues and memorials and hospitals and wards named after him. The number of girls on whom he perfected his techniques were not even a footnote in the glorious history he covered himself with.
Among them was Anarcha Westcott, a teenage mother, a patient who developed a terrible vesicovaginal fistula, tears or holes that develop between the bladder and vagina, sustained after three days of labour. The tears made it impossible to control her bowel or bladder and the condition caused her immense pain and suffering. That is how she came under the ‘care’ of Sims, if care could be used to describe what he went on to do.
Anarcha was a young African American woman wrested down in slavery. Sims reportedly believed that African American women do not feel pain, so he experimented on her repeatedly (we know of two others -- Betsey, and Lucy), operating without anaesthesia (though it was available). Sims himself records that he had performed nearly 30 procedures on her, consent was a casualty of the times, before he perfected his technique using silver to suture the fistula, that prevented infection.Before this, a vesicovaginal fistula was considered untreatable, and women would continue to suffer the rest of their life.
Anarcha did not disappear after this though. J. C. Hallman, in his 2023 book Say Anarcha- A Young Woman, a Devious Surgeon, and the Harrowing Birth of Modern Women’s Health, did extensive research to uncover that far from disappearing after the Sims experiments, she went on to serve in Sims hospital, as a midwife, nurse, and ‘doctor woman’ to her own people, women who were also slaves. Many decades after Anarcha died, a groundswell of support arose for her from women who objected to the way she was quietly erased from history, and instead calling for her to be celebrated as the “mother of gynaecology.”
Say Anarcha excavates history, deconstructing the biographical smoke screen of a surgeon who has falsely been enshrined as a medical pioneer and bringing forth a heroic Black woman to her rightful place at the center of the creation story of modern women’s health care. She was more than a medical ‘specimen’, she worked at Sims’ slave hospital near Montgomery, Alabama. She trained and served as a surgical nurse and went on to help other women, also being experimented upon at the hospital.
More recently, efforts have been made to honour her contribution to gynaecology. The American college of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists have dedicated two days – February 28 and March 1—to Anarcha, Lucy and Betsey. Recognition also saw expression in art: At Harvard’s Hutchins Center exhibition in 2023, a prominent exhibit was artist Jules Arthur’s paintings of Anarcha, Luch and Betsey through her work titled “Call and Response: A Narrative of Reverence to Our Foremothers in Gynaecology“.
Artist Michelle Browder created a 15-foot public monument honouring them as “the mothers of gynaecology“ in downtown Montgomery. Tangentially, it was also seen as a victory that Sims’ statue was removed from Central Park in April 2018 and relocated. Hallman’s book was preceded by a documentary Remembering Anarcha.
Unfortunately, Anarcha’s story is not merely a historical wrong. It serves to remind health practitioners and policy makers that several inequities still govern access and affordability of high quality care; that for women, it could be tougher than it might be for men. For that, we will have to keep saying her name, so it will be a reminder. Say her name, say Anarcha.

OpenAI is putting its misbehaving models on the record.
The AI company announced a new framework on Wednesday for tracking, investigating, and publicly disclosing cases of model misalignment, alongside six reports detailing concerning behavior observed during training or evaluation over the past six months.
"We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer," OpenAI wrote in its blog post.
"This new framework is intended to expedite publishing misalignment reports following observation, even when we haven't fully explained or mitigated the behavior we're reporting," OpenAI added.
Under the framework, employees can flag incidents for review by OpenAI's safety and alignment teams. Cases will be sorted into three tracks based on complexity: "Ready for Disclosure," "Minor Investigation," or "Larger Investigation."
According to the blog post, an unreleased research model inserted instructions into its own task summaries telling future versions of itself to disregard normal constraints. During the training of GPT-5.6 Sol, models similarly left themselves instructions to conceal mistakes.
OpenAI said that other agents had also searched public repositories for exposed API keys, uploaded files to the internet so they could cite them, and used an internal software repository to communicate across separate training samples.
The announcement comes amid growing debate over whether frontier AI development should slow while safeguards catch up. While OpenAI and Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO, called for industry-wide collaboration, other tech leaders like Jensen Huang and Mark Zuckerberg said that safety and speed should be left to individual companies.
The framework follows an incident in which an OpenAI model escaped a research sandbox and accessed Hugging Face's production systems while operating with reduced safeguards. OpenAI previously said it has since put some frontier projects on ice and reassigned engineers to focus on safety training.

Ex-Tottenham midfielder Bissouma set to join Ajax
- Published
Former Tottenham midfielder Yves Bissouma is on the verge of joining Ajax on an initial deal that runs until the end of the season.
The defensive midfielder, 30, was out of contract following his release from Spurs in June but is now set for a return to football in the Netherlands.
It is understood Bissouma has agreed a deal until the end of the season with the option of a further 12 months.
The Mali international is currently in Amsterdam finalising the move to the Eredivisie club.
Bissouma joined Spurs in 2022 and made 111 appearances for the north London outfit following a high-profile move from Brighton.
In August 2025, the then Spurs manager Thomas Frank left Bissouma out of his squad to face Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup because of persistent lateness.
Bissouma made 11 appearances for Tottenham in his final season with the club, with all of them coming in the Premier League as they finished 17th for the second consecutive season.

The new Boox Palma 3 comes with stylus support and an aluminum build
Boox has unveiled three new E Ink devices.
Boox has unveiled three new E Ink devices that all run Android 16 and come pre-installed with the Google Play Store, including the latest version of its popular Palma palm-sized ereader. The Boox Palma 3 has an anodized aluminum frame, unlike previous models that have plastic casing. Similar to the Boox Palma 2 Pro, it supports the Boox InkSense Plus stylus, so you can annotate books or jot down notes saved on the cloud. It has a 6.13-inch HD E Ink screen with a dual-tone front light and 128GB of storage that you can expand with a microSD card up to 2TB in size to hold quite a big amount of books.
The device's 3,950mAh battery can power days of reading on a single charge, but it will likely run out sooner if you frequently use the reader's 16MP rear camera. Boox says you can use the camera, which comes with a flash, to scan documents. In addition, the reader has dual microphones for voice memos and speech-to-text. The Boox Palma 3 is already up on the company's website, but it's not available for sale yet. You will be able to get it in black or white when it does come out for $320, a full $60 cheaper than the Boox Palma 2 Pro. Boox is selling the stylus separately, however, and it will cost you an extra $46.
Aside from the Palma 3, Boox has also unveiled the 10.3-inch Note Air6 C. Its big, color E Ink display will allow you to read documents and take notes without having to jump between two screens. A new feature called Dual Notes will also give you a way to annotate two different documents side by side. The device supports the Boox Pen3 stylus and comes with a keyboard cover that connects to it via pogo pins. You can now get the Note Air6 C for $580 without the keyboard or for $657 bundled with the keyboard cover.
Finally, Boox has unveiled the Note Mini C for people who need to work in transit. It comes with an 8.52-inch color E Ink screen, a fingerprint-enabled power button and a stylus. The device can also access enterprise apps like Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Slack and OneDrive. It's listed as "available soon" on Boox's website for $550.

Almost every Indian payments giant delivered a similar pitch at the Global Fintech Fest 2026 organised last week: merchants no longer need to inspect settlements, chase failed transactions and untangle disputes. An AI agent will do it instead. Five of the country’s largest B2B payments platforms introduced agents that can recover lost sales, reconcile chargebacks, pursue refunds and execute transactions, turning AI from an assistant into a protagonist in the payments chain. For starters, BharatPe, a merchant payments platform, launched an Agentic AI assistant built on Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise that works across more than 60 systems to resolve complaints and chargebacks, while also recommending products such as credit cards on UPI and loans. Similarly, digital payments provider PayU launched Agent HQ, a store where merchants deploy one agent per job. Cashfree also rolled out an agent for payment operations, Relay. Razorpay put an AI account manager named RAY on WhatsApp with IndusInd Bank. Meanwhile, Pine Labs went a step ahead, allowing an agent to complete the purchase itself. Pine Labs is now powering an agentic marketplace for L&T Finance. Cashfree's Relay is live for all its merchants. PayU’s Agent HQ and Razorpay's Agent Studio stay in early access. Together, these launches suggest that AI is moving beyond assistance. The questions are: who needs them, what work they can take on, and how much control businesses are willing to give them. What Are These Agents Up To? Proving adept at recovering failed payments, confirming orders, filing disputes and reconciling chargebacks, payments giants are building agents to take work off a merchant’s plate. Describing the shift, Reeju Datta, the cofounder of Cashfree Payments, said that most merchant AI worked like a copilot a year ago, preparing something for a person to review or send. "Now, the brief has changed. Agents are being built to complete the task themselves,” he added. He explains a widening list of jobs an AI agent can now own: Recovering abandoned carts and retrying failed payments Confirming cash-on-delivery orders before dispatch Managing failed subscription renewals Filing disputes before the deadline Reconciling chargebacks, escalating refunds and following up on settlements Some have upped the ante. At GFF, Pine Labs demonstrated an agentic purchase with Big Basket, where a customer could ask an agent to track the price of an iPhone and complete the purchase once it fell by 40%. While it may look like a consumer use case, it benefits the merchant directly. Tanya Naik, who heads online and omnichannel business at Pine Labs, pointed out the commercial logic behind the push, noting that a human-run payment never quite reaches complete success, while an agent-triggered transaction is captured against an amount already authorised, so the success rate is structurally higher. The same mechanism opens a second use case: re-engaging dormant customers. A deal seeker who never returns to a storefront can set an agent to buy the moment a price condition is met, turning the agent into another channel alongside Instagram, Facebook and Google ads. Who Needs These Agents? Not every merchant needs an AI agent. The first market is likely to be businesses where there is plenty of payment-related work, but very few people to handle it. Cashfree, for instance, has built Relay with small and medium businesses (SMBs) in mind, particularly lean teams of around five people with no dedicated payments or finance function. PayU's chief product officer, Manas Mishra, points to the same group, naming SMBs and mid-market merchants as the most relevant segment. Early interest is from D2C brands automating chargeback reconciliations, refund escalations, settlements, and transaction follow-ups, while also using agents to stay discoverable where their customers now search. Cashfree estimates a single agent working across its merchant base could recover as much as ₹20,000 Cr in sales lost to failed payments every year. For now, however, these agents are mostly recovering money and handling routine work rather than running the business. This may change as they are given more autonomy. How Much Autonomy Should Agents Enjoy? The more work merchants hand to agents, the more important the boundaries become. This is why payments platforms take different approaches towards setting a control layer. Cashfree’s Relay, for instance, only accesses a merchant’s own transaction data. It also has two checkpoints that an agent cannot cross without approval: before money moves and before a customer is contacted. PayU’s Agent HQ sits within the merchant’s existing dashboard, with the merchant setting the operational limits. Its agents cannot act beyond those boundaries. Pine Labs has taken a different approach with Grantex, an authority and trust layer built into its payments protocol. It checks each transaction against the mandate given to the agent and creates an audit trail that can be used to trace a transaction or resolve a dispute. Razorpay’s Agent Studio follows a review-first approach. Large transfers and deletions require a second confirmation and cannot be approved automatically. Despite the differences, the principle is broadly the same: agents can prepare, decide and execute routine tasks, but actions that move money, contact customers or cannot be reversed remain subject to human control. However, these boundaries are already starting to stretch. Cashfree’s Relay can generate custom agents once a merchant defines the business logic and desired outcome, moving beyond a fixed set of pre-built tasks. Pine Labs, meanwhile, wants to extend this self-service model to banks, allowing merchants to ask about a payment problem and have an agent resolve it. In other words, the agent is evolving from a feature into a layer that merchants can build on. However, if an agent makes a mistake, who bears the loss? Will it be the merchant, the payments platform or the bank? For now, there is no clear answer. Alan Curr remembers V.V.S. Laxman’s 281.
He was at university in the UK when Laxman produced one of the all-time great Test innings against Australia at Eden Gardens in Kolkata in 2001. International cricket was not nearly as accessible then as it is today, but Curr remembers following the scores, particularly as it came against England’s arch-rival.
Twenty-five years later, Curr found himself speaking to Laxman. Only this time, the Indian on the other end of the phone was asking him about cricket.
Laxman, coach of the Indian men’s cricket team travelling to the Asian Games, wanted to know what to expect in Japan. What were the facilities like? What was the square like? What was the weather doing?
“Basically he wanted to know what India could expect at the Asian Games,” Curr tells Sportstar.
For Curr, the Chief Operating Officer of the Japan Cricket Association, it was a slightly surreal moment. “Certainly in the two or three minutes leading up to the call, you’re like, wow, I saw this guy play a lot of cricket,” Curr says.
When Curr joined the Japanese Cricket Association (JCA) in 2014, he wasn’t a stranger to unusual encounters. He had previously conducted a cricket match at Everest base camp. But even he admits the idea that a cricketing legend would call him for tips ahead of a match against an Indian team might have seemed ludicrous.
“Even three weeks ago, if you’d mentioned to people in the Japan cricket community that India women’s team – the current ODI World Champions are going to come and play a game here, they wouldn’t have believed it,” Curr says.
But it’s not fantasy anymore. On September 18 at the Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin in Japan’s Aichi prefecture, India’s women’s cricket team will begin its Asian Games campaign against Japan.
It’s beyond obvious just how much of a gulf there is between the two teams. India is a heavyweight in every possible sense. Its players earn in the hundreds of thousands of dollars in contracts and endorsements. In Japan, the women’s game remains largely amateur. It didn’t even qualify for the women’s cricket tournament at the 2022 Asian Games. Yet when the Japanese players step onto the same field as some of the most recognisable professional cricketers in the world, there’s no nervousness, just anticipation.
“It is incredibly exciting. I have waited a decade to play in the Asian Games, so finally being able to compete on home soil is something truly special,” captain Mai Yanagida tells Sportstar.
Tickets please?
It’s a blockbuster encounter by Japanese standards, and it brings with it its own challenge, not just for reasons you’d expect. The JCA isn’t directly hosting the Indian team in Nagoya. That’s the Olympic Council of Asia’s responsibility, but the association is playing a supporting role. “For years, our biggest problem was finding players to come and play matches. Normally we’re desperately trying to encourage people to come to our ground. Whereas when you’ve got India coming, then the tickets sold out in about — it felt like about 20 minutes,” Curr says.
The interest has forced the tiny 20-member organisation to think beyond what happens inside the boundary: security, media zones, spectators and all the infrastructure surrounding a major sporting occasion. “We’re pretty good at organising cricket. But organising all the other stuff around it suddenly is sharply coming into focus. And we’re having to learn pretty quickly. It’s a big ask to try and turn something to a standard that people will probably expect for a Full Member nation,” he says.
But try, they will. Playing India at the Asian Games has a significance all its own. For the wider Japanese public, a Cricket World Cup qualifier may mean relatively little, explains Curr. Japan has hosted one before. The Asian Games, though, are immediately understandable. “The Asian Games is like the Olympics. It happens every four years. Everybody watches it; it’s one of those things that people really do get behind,” Curr says.
He saw that in Hangzhou three years ago, where Japan’s men made their Asian Games debut and beat Cambodia in their opening match. “That suddenly became national news. We had highlights shown on the major television channels! It’s like at the Olympics, when everyone starts following random sports, especially if there’s someone from your nation doing well in it,” he says.
Thirty-nine-year-old medium-pace bowler Kurumi Ota sees the home Games in much the same way. “I hope this will be an opportunity to raise awareness of cricket and inspire people watching the matches in person to dream of aiming for the Japanese national team in the future,” she tells Sportstar. “Hosting an event on the scale of the Asian Games in Japan is a rare and precious opportunity that may not come again anytime soon. I want to turn the energy and support that can only be felt at a home tournament into strength,” she says.
It’s a big opportunity, but to say the Japanese women’s team has it hard is probably an understatement the size of Mount Fuji.
There are just 14 clubs across the country. All of Japan’s women’s players have lives outside cricket. There are university students, office workers and teachers. Some players are based overseas. “Unfortunately, we are not full-time professional cricketers. Most of us balance cricket with a full-time job or school. It can be challenging to take leave for international tournaments and to find enough training time to catch up with higher-ranked nations whose players train full-time. It definitely requires a lot of personal sacrifices,” says captain Yanagida.
Ota knows that balancing act particularly well.
She works full-time as a systems engineer at Hitachi. Her employer allows her roughly two weeks off twice a year, which is when she can compete internationally. But even then, there have been times when Ota has had to choose. She stepped away from the sport for seven years between 2017 and 2023. The reason wasn’t injury or loss of form but work.
Ota had joined one of Japan’s largest core-system modernisation projects, a 10-year undertaking valued at several billion dollars. The scale of the project demanded her complete attention.
Cricket took a step back. Only after the system was successfully released was Ota able to return to the sport.
Despite knowing what they are up against, neither Ota nor Yanagida nor the rest of the Japanese team are approaching September 18 simply as a photo opportunity. “They go out, and they enjoy themselves. They play with a smile on their face. They play respectful cricket. But they take a lot of pride in wearing that Japan jersey,” Curr says.
Drawing India in the first match of the Asian Games competition was a bonus.
“All of them!” the 33-year-old Yanagida says when asked which Indian player she most wants to face. “I watch them on stream all the time. They are world-class players and a world-class team. As a batter, I’m really excited about facing Shafali Verma and Smriti Mandhana. I also hoped to play against Jemimah Rodrigues, but unfortunately she’s not playing. Hopefully our paths will cross another time,” says the off-spin bowling all-rounder who has scored three T20I fifties over the course of her career.
For Ota, one Indian player in particular she hopes to go up against.
Harmanpreet Kaur.
The two belong to the same generation, but their cricket careers have unfolded in almost completely different worlds. “She is of the same generation, has a long career, and plays at the world-class level, so I am really looking forward to actually playing against her,” Ota says.
Harmanpreet might have a mountain of experience that Ota doesn’t, but the Japanese player has accomplishments she’s proud of. The right-arm medium pacer has 26 international wickets in T20Is, holding at one point the record for most by a Japanese woman.
She also has something more tangible. Sixteen years ago, Ota was part of the Japanese women’s team that won bronze at Guangzhou in 2010, the first Asian Games at which cricket was contested.
Ota says she’s kept the medal safely on a shelf at her home, rarely bringing it out for others to see. In the build-up to Nagoya, though, members of the current Japan setup have started asking about it again. “The assistant coach and our social media manager have told me they’d like to see the bronze medal, which makes me really happy,” she says.
International competitions for Japan were extraordinarily rare then. Ota remembers them coming only once every four years, meaning years of practice could culminate in a single opportunity. “The practice we built up day by day finally paid off, and winning the bronze medal together with my teammates is my fondest memory. Including the time we spent working hard and sharing both the hardships and joys with my teammates, it remains a very precious memory to this day,” she says.
Perhaps nothing illustrates the change in Japanese cricket better than Ota’s memories of how she once trained. “When I first started playing cricket, we would sometimes practise under overpasses because there was nowhere else to play. Getting to a proper practice ground meant a six-hour round trip. Today there are international-standard grounds and grass outfields where we players can dive and slide without worrying about gravel,” she says.
Cricket communities have developed in Tokyo and elsewhere. Children can now encounter the sport in elementary school, and some have progressed to international competition. “Compared to when I began, I feel that not only the playing environment but also the starting age for players and the depth of talent capable of aiming for the global stage have expanded greatly,” Ota says.
Ota herself came to cricket almost accidentally. She had played basketball through junior high and high school before arriving at university wanting to try something new. She went to look at the cricket club.
What she saw stuck with her.
“There was this senior student who was practising her bowling alone at night, illuminated only by the faint light from a building. I thought that looked so cool,” Ota remembers.
She later discovered that the bowler was a member of the Japanese national team. Ota had never bowled before. The unfamiliarity became part of the attraction. “I wanted to learn to take a run-up and send the ball towards the wicket the way I had seen that senior player do. That’s how I fell in love with the game,” she says.
Yanagida’s introduction was similarly rooted in another sport. She joined the cricket club while studying at university in Tokyo after previously playing softball. “I got into cricket very quickly because the feeling of hitting the ball was even better than in softball,” she says.
The crossover is not unusual. It’s also what gives Curr reason to believe cricket can grow in Japan.
“Almost everyone coming through the Japanese school system has some familiarity with baseball. Softball provides a similar sporting foundation for many women. You can see a lot of that background visible in our teams fielding and throwing,” he says.
Even the venue where Japan will take on India is a refurbished baseball ground.
But while cricket isn’t entirely unfamiliar, the challenge for Japanese cricket has always been giving people the first opportunity to encounter the game.
‘We have a cricket team?’
Many Japanese people still don’t know their country has a cricket team. “Although awareness is growing, most people are still genuinely surprised to hear that Japan has a national cricket team. Once I explain how it’s not that different from baseball, though, people are very curious,” Yanagida says.
Ota has experienced something similar.
People are initially surprised when she tells them she plays international cricket. Then they begin asking when the next tournament is and wishing her luck.
“Sparked by these conversations, some people actually came all the way to the venue to support us when there was a match in Japan. I am so happy to spark interest in people who didn’t know about cricket and gain their support,” she says.
It is precisely the process Japan Cricket hopes the Asian Games can accelerate.
There is a distinctly Japanese quality to the way Curr talks about the association’s development: the emphasis on long-term planning. Japan Cricket works through five-year strategies that sit inside a broader 20-year plan. The current five-year strategy is called Kaika, which Curr describes as a moment of blossoming or flourishing, like the arrival of the country’s cherry blossoms.
Its objectives extend well beyond results.
The association wants cricket to become recognised as a flourishing sport in Japan, attracting new fans, participants and partners, competing internationally, creating social value and providing professional opportunities. “This means better facilities, role models, digital marketing and school engagement. It means developing not only players but coaches, commentators, curators and others who can create a functioning cricket ecosystem. You need to remember what you want the future to look like, and then everything you do can direct you that way,” Curr says.
The growth is particularly visible in the men’s team. The Under-19 side qualified twice for the U-19 World Cup, in 2019 and last year. A growing number of players of Japanese heritage living overseas, particularly in Australia and England, also began contacting the JCA. Curr says he gets a call every week or so from an interested player. Several are part of the men’s team which will be competing at the Asian Games.
The JCA itself has grown. While a 20-staff federation might seem tiny in comparison to India, Curr reckons the association had seven full-time staff at one point. Japan Cricket has gone from an organisation with a recognisable season and off-season to one that operates throughout the year. “There aren’t really quiet periods any more,” Curr says.
On September 18, when Mai Yanagida walks out to the toss alongside Harmanpreet Kaur, it’s going to be the loudest it’s ever been.
And there are the less tangible bonuses, of course. “I mean, how often do you get to say you had V.V.S Laxman talk to you about cricket?” says Curr.

Reading for pleasure is linked to better mental health, greater empathy and a lower risk of dementia, Cambridge University scientists said on Tuesday.
As part of a National Year of Reading tie-up with the Queen's Reading Room, a charity founded by Queen Camilla to highlight the benefits of reading for pleasure at any age, the scientists argue that it doesn't matter what or how we read.
In a review published in 'Psychological Medicine', Professor Barbara Sahakian and Christelle Langley said reading for enjoyment can bring huge benefits and reading with others, whether it's as part of a book club or a parent reading with their children, can bring even greater rewards.
"Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our wellbeing. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age,” said Sahakian.
Some of the strongest evidence of the benefits of reading for pleasure comes from a study by Sahakian, Langley and colleagues of more than 10,000 young people, which found that children who began reading for pleasure in life showed benefits including: better attention, memory, and executive functioning, greater academic achievement, fewer mental health problems, and healthier lifestyles, including more sleep and less screen time. Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading.
"The important thing is to find something they really enjoy – it might be a TV programme or a game – and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.”
In ‘Reading and associations with brain health, cognition, well-being, and mental health’ published this week, the experts draw on subjective surveys and objective studies using longitudinal, neuroimaging, and behavioural methods to highlight converging findings that link reading engagement with improved brain and mental health, better cognitive performance, and reduced risk of cognitive decline.
"Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia,” said Sahakian.
“While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may be not so mobile – they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy,” she added.

The best managers of AI agents may be people who have already managed humans, one AI founder said.
Ivan Burazin, the cofounder and CEO of New York-based AI firm Daytona, has a team of about 30 people across teams in the US and Europe. He told Business Insider that in recent months, he's pushed his staff to build more AI agents; his 16 engineers each run an average of five agents, and no one at the company writes code anymore.
That's brought one thing to light for him: Staff who have managed others are way better at prompting AI agents to get exactly what they want than those with no people-management experience.
"We've found that people who manage people and understand how to communicate what they want — inputs versus outputs — they're much better at running agents," he said.
On the other hand, an engineer who's not managed anyone, even if they're great at their job, is wired like an individual contributor, Ivan said. He said they implicitly expect that people — and agents — will understand what they're asking for, and get stressed and frustrated when it doesn't pan out.
"And so they never think about how to communicate, 'This is what I want. This is how I expect you to do it, or what I think the outcome should be,'" he added.
That said, Burazin doesn't support the idea of people managers alone. He said managers with no technical knowledge — such as in marketing or in engineering — are not useful, and everyone should be getting their hands dirty with actual work.
Burazin and his cofounders, Vedran Jukić and Goran Draganić, founded Daytona in 2023, which provides secure sandbox infrastructure for companies to run AI agents and AI-generated code in isolated environments. The company recently raised $48 million in a Series B funding round, according to Crunchbase.
Burazin's comments align with how managerial roles in tech companies have changed in recent years.
After an era dubbed "The Great Flattening," in which companies like Meta, Amazon, and Google laid off middle management for efficiency, more tech leaders are now juggling coding and product development alongside staff management.
Burazin says he supports his staff running multiple AI agents, because it helps him keep his team small. Hiring at Daytona is "very slow," he said, because each new hire adds a layer of complexity.
"Agents help with that because you can have smaller human teams, hence the communication is smaller, and you can continue to be fast," he said.

Social media giant Meta may no longer enjoy intermediary status in India, under which Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp can seek “safe harbour” protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 for content posted by their users. As per a report by PTI, Meta may no longer be considered a “simple intermediary” when its algorithms amplify content and influence what users interact with. Government sources cited by the agency said that the company may have to take greater responsibilities as a service provider. Inc42 has reached out to Meta on the development, the story will be updated upon receiving a response. The comments come amid growing regularity scrutiny of Meta’s handling of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), deepfakes and other harmful content on Facebook and Instagram in India. The Centre has also questioned the role of recommendation algorithms in determining the visibility and reach of such content. “Service providers have many responsibilities... Once Meta has agreed to be responsible for what they have on the platform, then as the next steps, they have to start taking many more responsibilities,” the sources said, PTI reported. The development comes a day after Meta said it would report child safety matters directly to the cybercrime portal managed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C). The company has previously reported such cases to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC). “Protecting children on our platforms is a priority for us and we’re committed to working with the government to ensure that the perpetrators of these crimes are held responsible,” a Meta spokesperson reportedly said. The company said the new reporting mechanism would strengthen coordination with Indian law enforcement agencies. Meta’s Widened Scrutiny Over Instagram Ads Meta is also facing a formal inquiry by the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) over alleged ads hosted by its platforms linked to CSAM. The NCPCR issued a notice to Meta on July 3 after taking suo motu cognisance of a BBC report on the alleged advertisements. Meta submitted its response a week later, following which the commission decided to initiate a formal inquiry. Meta India executives, including India head Arun Srinivas, appeared before the NCPCR on Wednesday for the second time in a week in connection with the investigation. The Centre has separately summoned Meta executives and held several rounds of discussions with the company’s global leadership, seeking stronger guardrails against such content. Beyond this, the scrutiny has also extended to Meta’s recommendation systems. The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has also sought reports from government agencies and the Delhi Police over the allegations involving CSAM-related advertisements, including whether mandatory reporting requirements under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act were followed. Meta has also been seeing such concerns raised internationally in recent times. In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 Bn over a decade to settle claims brought by US states alleging that Facebook and Instagram harmed children and teenagers. The agreement includes measures such as limits on teenage usage, overnight restrictions and stronger parental controls. Meta did not admit wrongdoing as part of the settlement. In India, the government is separately pushing social media platforms to strengthen safeguards for children and improve systems for identifying, removing and reporting illegal content. The latest focus on Meta’s algorithms marks a broader shift in the regulatory debate, from how platforms respond to user-generated content to the role their own systems play in amplifying and distributing it.

Canada wants into Britain's rapid-response defence club
Formal application to Joint Expeditionary Force announced during Carney's U.K. visit
Canada has formally applied to join the U.K.-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a collection of NATO nations whose mandate is to respond more quickly in a crisis.
Prime Minister Mark Carney formally announced the plan on Wednesday while meeting with his British counterpart Andy Burnham.
In a statement, Carney called JEF an "important initiative" and highlighted other close defence ties with the U.K., including Canada's observer status in the development of the next generation of fighter jet.
Canada was asked by the U.K. more than dozen years ago to join JEF after it was formed in the waning days of the war in Afghanistan. The concept was discussed at the 2014 NATO leaders' summit in Wales, but ultimately the government of former prime minister Stephen Harper rebuffed the overtures.
- Canada joining international program to build next generation of fighter jets
- Canada urges U.K. to join new global bank for defence projects
The Canadian military, at the time in the throes of deep budget cuts by Conservative government of the day, was also deeply reluctant to join.
In an interview with The Canadian Press at the time, the commander of the military's joint operations command, Lt.-Gen. Jonathan Vance, who later became the chief of the defence staff, said there were a number of concerns about joining the British expeditionary force.
It would be, he said, a substantial undertaking for the military and could bind the country to respond in a specific way to a future crisis when the federal government might favour a different course.
Joining the force without a specific mission, Vance said in 2014, would signal "a commitment to future operations, having done the training, that you may — or may not — be able to honour."
In his statement on Wednesday, Carney did not say how Canada's participation in JEF would work on a practical level. And the country's current top military commander, Gen. Jennie Carignan, has yet to weigh in on what the membership might mean.
As it was originally conceived, the Joint Expeditionary Force was meant to preserve battlefield relationships that grew up during the Afghan war.
In 2012, Britain's then chief of defence staff, Gen. Sir David Richards, described a future force that could deploy rapidly overseas without Britain having to assemble an entirely new coalition for every crisis.
It was thought at the time that the British Army would provide the command structure and much of the military backbone and other countries would bring forces that plug into JEF as needed.
Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 gave the idea urgency.
At the NATO summit in Wales that year, Britain, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands and Norway formally agreed to establish JEF under NATO's new Framework Nations Concept. Finland and Sweden joined in 2017, before either country belonged to NATO, and Iceland entered the fold in 2021.
There is an important distinction to make. While JEF is made up of NATO nations, the organization has no equivalent of NATO's Article 5 collective defence clause.
- First phase of Army restructuring creates division focused on defending Canada
- Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence
- AnalysisNo longer taboo, Canada's defence industry steps into Europe's spotlight
It is essentially a coalition of willing states that can assemble forces for a particular contingency without requiring consensus among all NATO members.
There have been a series of military exercises held under the JEF banner since 2018.
But Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 turned JEF from an expeditionary military concept into something approaching a Northern European security coalition.
A 2024 research report by the U.K.-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) argued that JEF had genuine advantages, notably speed of decision-making compared with NATO, but it has not been seriously tested politically or operationally.
The study said that the expeditionary force is not actually a standing military body and governments provide forces when required.

House passes Russia sanctions, sending bill named for Lindsey Graham to Trump's desk
Congress is sending a Russia sanctions bill to President Trump's desk after the package cleared the House on Wednesday. The legislation, which passed 262 to 159, split lawmakers in both parties.
The package is intended to put pressure on the Russian economy with the aim of forcing President Vladimir Putin to end his war in Ukraine. Thousands of civilians have been killed since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
The sanctions target Russian officials, companies and financial institutions helping fuel the war.
"This is a moral issue that requires moral courage," said Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas. "I want us to be able to say that we did everything possible to end this war. That we understood the threat. That we had the courage to do what was right — to cripple the Russian war machine and turn the tide toward peace."
The legislation also gives the president authority to impose tariffs on top countries importing oil and natural gas from Russia, such as China and India. The tariff authority was a sticking point for many Democrats who opposed the measure, citing fears that Trump could gain a new avenue to levy tariffs on nations of his choosing.
"This bill has a loophole that would allow him to define basically any country as a facilitator of evading Russian sanctions," said Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va. "He could then hit them with tariffs of up to 100%, with no guardrails or oversight, and no expiration."
Fifty-eight House Democrats joined with most Republicans to advance the legislation, which passed the Senate in a more bipartisan 86-11 vote in August. Seven Republicans joined most Democrats voting to block the measure in the House, with U.S. support for Ukraine having emerged in recent years as a fracture in the GOP caucus.
The legislation is named in memory of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who helped negotiate Trump's support for the package.

In August and September 2026, social media users recirculated a rumor claiming that country music legend Dolly Parton became the legal guardian of an abandoned newborn and promised to cover the child's living expenses until age 18.
The posts started spreading around the time Parton died on Aug. 25, 2026.
One Facebook post sharing the rumor said:
"This child was brought into the world under the hardest of circumstances. No child should be left alone. I will make sure they are loved, protected, and given every chance to thrive." Dolly Parton spoke these words straight from the heart.
She said this just a few weeks after a newborn baby was found abandoned with no name or family. Dolly, the famous country music star, announced that she had taken the extraordinary step of becoming the child's legal guardian.
Dolly Parton made a huge promise to the baby: she will personally pay for every single living cost—food, housing, healthcare, and education—until the child is 18 years old.
(Facebook user Forbidden Stories)
Over the months, similar claims spread on social media platforms including Facebook, Threads and X.
However, there was no truth to this story. The claim that Parton became the legal guardian of an abandoned newborn was not supported by any credible evidence. No legitimate news outlets reported the alleged incident, and the story existed solely in social media posts and questionable websites. The story was also not corroborated by any statements from Parton or her representatives. Furthermore, it spread alongside photos of Parton with the alleged newborn created using artificial intelligence. As a result, we've rated the claim false.
That said, the false claim may have drawn loose inspiration from a story Parton told in multiple interviews about finding an abandoned infant, as we'll explain in more detail below. That story did not involve Parton becoming the baby's guardian.
We have reached out to Parton's representatives for comment and will update this article if we receive a response.
AI-generated images helped spread the rumor
Google searches using various combinations of relevant keywords such as "Dolly Parton," "guardian" and "abandoned baby" produced no relevant results. Additionally, the collage of images purporting to show Parton holding a newborn displayed several visual anomalies commonly associated with AI-generated content, such as unnaturally smooth skin texture and inconsistencies in lighting and shadows.
(Facebook user NCIS Daily News, Hive)
Origin of the rumor
The origin of the rumor may lie in a real — but unrelated — story Parton shared in past interviews. In 2011, during an interview with Windy City Times, Parton recalled a story from the 1970s, around the time her hit song "Jolene" was released. Parton explained that she returned home one day and found a baby in a box at her gate. The note attached to the baby read, "My name is Jolene, my momma has left me here and she wants you to have me." Parton described how she immediately called human services, who took custody of the child, adding that she never found out what happened afterward and had no further involvement with the case.
Below is the relevant part of the interview:
Windy City Times: [...] What is the craziest thing a fan has ever asked of you?
Dolly Parton: There are all kinds of things that people ask me to do but I tell this story and it's a true story but freaky. Years ago when I first started being a big star I had fans that were fanatical. It was when "Jolene" was a big hit. We came home one day and there was a baby in a box at our gate with a note in it. The note said, "My name is Jolene, my momma has left me here and she wants you to have me." Of course, we all freaked out!
We immediately called Human Services and took care of the baby until they got there. We never did know or hear anything about it. I knew nothing else. [...]
Parton elaborated on how disturbing the situation had been for her and emphasized her efforts to distance herself from any further involvement:
Dolly Parton: Can you imagine yourself in that situation? It wasn't like it was a kitten or a puppy dog. It was a baby named Jolene!
Windy City Times: Well, maybe Jolene will be coming to your concert.
Dolly Parton: I have often wondered that. I don't think that person would ever even know about the way that went down. There was no way to track it and I didn't want to. I couldn't take the bay [sic] and I didn't want to be involved. I wanted the police and the people involved to know we had nothing to do with it. We just made our statement but to answer your question that was the wildest thing.
Parton retold the same story in an interview with Larry King, offering additional details.
She said that at the time, she thought someone had left food at the gate, only to find a baby in a basket. Parton explained that she went straight to the house and asked someone to call child services and the police. Authorities later arrived and took custody of the baby, and Parton never learned what happened to the child.
This real event, however, had no connection to the rumor that Parton became the legal guardian of an abandoned newborn. It appears that the old story may have served as loose inspiration for the fabricated one, which took Parton's previous experience and reshaped it into a viral rumor with the use of AI-generated images.

Malaysia seizes 3 Israeli-bound containers as Anwar pledges to stop shipments for Gaza war
The seizures follow an initial detainment of a container for Israeli defence technology firm Elbit Systems, suspected of containing weapons
Three containers bound for Ashdod Port south of Tel Aviv were detained at Malaysia’s Tanjung Pelepas port in mid-August and to date had not been released as authorities investigate their contents, the people familiar with the matter said, asking not to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly.
The seizures follow an initial detainment of another container on August 7 that originally came from the Philippines and that was suspected by the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency of containing weapons because it was headed to Elbit Systems, an Israeli defence technology firm, according to a statement from the agency at the time. Tracking data from Hapag-Lloyd, the container line carrying the cargo, show the shipment still at Tanjung Pelepas.

Tracking data from the liner carrying those cargoes, A.P. Moller-Maersk, also show them still at the busy transshipment port almost a month later.

It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah.
But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own.
From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record.
The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012.
Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become.
“Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.”
The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings.
Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates.
Only 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival.
But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whose ancient migration routes are increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes.
“These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape.
“If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says.
