The Toronto International Film Festival is a place to go to see the future of film, but this year it also provided a glimpse at what is coming very soon in the realm of streaming. Four different streamers — Peacock, Netflix, Amazon, and AMC — all premiered early looks at upcoming horror-adjacent series that are dropping very soon. And by doing it at TIFF, they showed just how important the month of October has become in the realm of streaming.
The streamers are fighting over Halloween
Crystal Lake, Carrie, Below, and Yaga are all competing in a very busy October.
Perhaps the most high-profile is Carrie, which is coming to Prime Video. An adaptation of the classic Stephen King novel, which has already been turned into no fewer than three feature films, this version of Carrie is notable in particular because of who is helming it. Mike Flanagan has done a handful of King adaptations in the past — including Doctor Sleep and The Life of Chuck — but the director is perhaps best-known for his work on limited series for Netflix. That includes the likes of The Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass, and The Fall of the House of Usher. Those series came out on a near-annual basis between 2018 and 2023, making Flanagan’s particular blend of dramatic horror a staple of Netflix in October.
Then, in 2022, Amazon poached Flanagan to work on projects for Prime Video. The first of these is Carrie, which starts streaming on October 7th. It still tells largely the same story as its predecessors — a young girl’s destructive psychic powers awaken after getting bullied in high school — but it updates it in a few ways. For starters, the story has been thoroughly modernized, with much of the bullying happening in cyberspace. But since it’s a series instead of a movie, Carrie also stretches out the story, which gives it the space to explore the teen drama a little, and also adds plenty of opportunities for Flanagan’s trademark lengthy monologues. I’ve only seen the premiere episode so far, but early on it’s a combination of flavors that work really well together.
Netflix, meanwhile, has filled in the gap with a new series called Below, which premieres on October 8th, just a day after Carrie starts streaming. I saw the first two episodes earlier this week — there will be six in total — and while it’s a different kind of story compared to the likes of Hill House, it has a similarly dark and mysterious energy. Below is about what seems to be an ancient sea creature that begins terrorizing a small fishing village in Newfoundland, on the east coast of Canada. From what I’ve seen, the show does a great job of steadily building the terror of the creature’s reveal, while also mixing the scares with a healthy dose of family drama, led by Josh Hartnett as a struggling fisher who is struggling to keep his family together.
Then there’s Peacock, which is joining the fray with a prequel series. Fans of Friday the 13th will know that Jason’s mom plays a pivotal role in the very first film, and the new show Crystal Lake explores how she got to that point. It stars Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees, a single mother who is thrown into a pit of despair and disbelief when her young son drowns to death.
I went into the show thinking that I didn’t really need to know much more about the backstory of Jason’s mother, but the first two episodes that premiered at TIFF — and Cardellini’s performance in particular — have me second-guessing that. Crystal Lake is surprisingly tense and dramatic, but, given its connection to Friday the 13th, it also has slasher-movie levels of gore and gross-out deaths, ones that are so brutal they approach comedy. If nothing else, it gets off to a very strong start. All episodes of Crystal Lake hit Peacock on October 15th.
Rounding out the list is Yaga, a supernatural detective series that’s coming to AMC Plus on October 23rd. Unfortunately I wasn’t able to catch the premiere screening for the show, but it does seem promising, with a cast that includes Carrie-Anne Moss and Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams, and a very intriguing trailer:
What has become abundantly clear in 2026 is that horror is big business. The likes of Backrooms and Obsession have exploded at the box office, while Widow’s Bay had a dominating night at the Emmys. So it only makes sense that streamers are continuing to capitalize on the trend, and using TIFF as a showcase event. October is going to be a very busy month for horror fans.

Ed Sheeran reportedly donating $2M to 'aid in the region' amid Macklemore fallout
Macklemore pledges $1M to pro-Palestinian causes after tour ouster over comments
The billionaire stadium owner who allegedly led efforts to remove Macklemore as Ed Sheeran's opening act over his pro-Palestinian comments onstage is now donating $2 million US to "aid in the region."
The news came shortly after Macklemore announced plans Wednesday to donate $1 million US from his net earnings from the tour to six organizations helping Palestinians — including the UN agency for Palestinian refugees — and challenged Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft to do the same.
While Kraft did not specify in his statement where his funds would be going, and a spokesperson did not clarify, he said Sheeran had asked him to match a $2 million US donation from Sheeran "before Macklemore challenged me."
He also said that he wanted people to know that "for decades, I have supported efforts that create opportunity for Palestinians and have brought young Palestinians and Israelis together to build businesses, create jobs, and forge relationships."
Benjamin Hammond Haggery, better known as Macklemore, opened for Sheeran for the first two U.S. shows on the Loop Tour on Sept. 4 and 5 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. He was slated to open for the remaining eight of Sheeran's 10 U.S. shows, but announced in a lengthy Instagram post on Monday that he'd been dropped from the tour.
Macklemore's onstage remarks at MetLife — including chanting "Free Palestine" and expressing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank — drew criticism from pro-Israel groups, including a petition calling for his removal.
Macklemore blamed his removal on Kraft, claiming Kraft said Macklemore would not be allowed onstage and rallied other stadium owners to threaten to cancel scheduled concerts if he was not taken off the bill.
Sheeran released his own statement on Tuesday, defending his choice not to take a public stance and saying he is "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine."
In the statement, Sheeran said, "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine. Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me."
In response, Sheeran's remaining supporting acts all quit the tour.
The Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe were scheduled to replace Macklemore as the opening acts on Sheeran's remaining U.S. tour dates. Finneas, the American singer and close collaborator of his sister Billie Eilish, was scheduled to open for Sheeran on four of his South American dates. Beoga, an Irish folk band, had been performing with Sheeran for part of his set since the tour began in January in New Zealand.
"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas wrote.
Graham also appeared to take a veiled shot at Kraft, writing: "Money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody's bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we're allowed to acknowledge."
Sheeran hasn't posted since those supporting acts left the tour, and his representative didn't respond to an emailed request for comment. The promoter, Messina Touring Group, also hasn't responded to requests for comment.

Pending regulatory approval, SpaceX said today it intends to launch its 14th Starship mission as early as September 22. This flight is notable, as it will be the first time that SpaceX attempts to launch the experimental vehicle into orbit.
The company set a target liftoff time of 7:15 am local in Texas (12:15 UTC), with a 75-minute launch window. Sunrise in Brownsville, Texas, is 7:17 am CT, so the launch could make for some striking imagery.
The super heavy lift rocket will be carrying 26 of the larger V3 Starlink satellites into an orbit 275 km above the Earth. In an update on its website, SpaceX said the Starship upper stage will seek to complete six orbits around the Earth before completing its mission after about 10 hours.
Reaching orbit would mark a significant milestone in the company’s Starship development campaign, which conducted its first test flight on April 20, 2023, and has since made progress in fits and starts. With the upcoming mission, SpaceX continues to make modifications to the Starship vehicle as it seeks to improve the third iteration of the Super Heavy booster and Starship upper stage. After recent successes, the company appears to be closer to developing a fully reusable, super heavy lift rocket.
First-stage modifications
During the most recent Starship test flight on July 24, the vehicle’s first stage performed nominally during ascent. However, after a successful boostback burn, the vehicle experienced problems during the return through Earth’s atmosphere.
“In the terminal phase of the burn, the three center engines showed signs of ice clogging, which triggered an early end to the maneuver,” SpaceX said in its update on Tuesday. “The booster went on to attempt a landing burn, with 8 of the 13 planned engines reigniting before the booster made a hard splashdown in the Gulf. The Super Heavy on this upcoming flight has hardware modifications to improve filtering to the engines and software changes to enhance relight reliability.”

Kosovo's ex-President Thaci convicted of war crimes, sentenced to 25 years in prison
THE HAGUE, Netherlands — A European Union-backed court on Wednesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of four counts of war crimes committed during his country's war for independence from Serbia and sentenced him to 25 years in prison.
Thaci, 58, who resigned from office nearly six years ago to face the charges, was convicted by a panel of judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers of murder, torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention.
Wearing a suit and tie, Thaci stood in silence as Presiding Judge Charles Smith read out the sentence.
Thaci faced multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity including murder, torture and persecution alongside three other former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army who fought Serb forces in the 1998-99 war. They are widely regarded as national heroes in their homeland.
Thousands of people rallied in Pristina, Kosovo's capital, over the weekend in support of the four men. The protesters filled a central square in the capital, many carrying red and black Albanian flags.
Portraits of the four former KLA fighters have been plastered across the city along with a huge digital clock counting down to Wednesday's verdicts.
"In the name of the people, declare them innocent," one banner read.
Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers court in The Hague have asked for a maximum 45-year prison sentence for Thaci and the other defendants, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi. They have all denied the charges against them.
"Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice," Thaci told judges in February at the end of his nearly three-year trial.
According to prosecutors, the men targeted political opponents and civilians perceived as collaborators and traitors during their time in the KLA.
The staff at the European Union-backed court are largely international due to fears about witness safety and security. In 2022, the court convicted two leaders of a Kosovo war veterans' association for intimidating witnesses by publicizing leaked confidential documents.
Thaci also faces a separate trial on charges of intimidating witnesses that will begin later this month.
He was a student who returned from what he described as political exile in Switzerland to join Kosovo's struggle for independence. He earned the nickname "the Snake" for his ability to evade Serb forces during the conflict.
He was embraced by Western leaders, who invited him to the 1999 peace talks in France in his role as political director of the Kosovo Liberation Army, and was seen as a leader who could guide the country toward independence.
Thaci rose to political power after the war but resigned as president to defend himself before the court in The Hague.
Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians. A 78-day campaign of NATO airstrikes against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About 1 million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes.
In 2008, Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia, a move that Belgrade refuses to recognize. Ties between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense, despite years of negotiations mediated by the European Union and supported by the United States.

The US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald Trump’s administration continues to claim that South Africa’s government racially discriminates against white minority Afrikaners.
The announcement did not specify individuals who were barred from the US. Trump has spent his second term falsely claiming there is a “white genocide” in South Africa and railing against its affirmative action policies.
Since the start of last year, the US has cut aid to South Africa, barred it from this year’s G20 summit in Miami and set up a refugee programme for Afrikaners and other South African racial minorities. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been dismantling refugee and asylum programmes for people fleeing war and persecution.
“The South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said in a post on X.
“The South African government has consistently failed to adequately address rural crime, violent and dehumanising rhetoric, and race-based discriminatory policies against Afrikaners and other minority populations.”
The US visa restrictions would target “foreign nationals who enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”, Rubio added.
The US ambassador to South Africa, the conservative media activist Leo Brent Bozell III, said on X: “As has been made absolutely clear, the time for endless ‘dialogue’ has run its course … This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter.”
Spokespeople for South Africa’s presidency and foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Afrikaners, who are descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime discriminated against and repressed the country’s black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.
Since Nelson Mandela took office as South Africa’s first black president in 1994, South African governments have tried to redress the country’s racial inequality, including through Black economic empowerment policies and buying land to redistribute.
These efforts have had limited impact. White South Africans typically have 20 times the wealth of Black people, according to a 2023 article in the Review of Political Economy, an economic journal.
Nonetheless, some white South Africans claim they are now the victims of racial discrimination, allegations that US conservatives have long promoted.
Rubio’s visa restrictions announcement criticised land expropriation without compensation. South Africa introduced a law last year that allows the government to seize land without paying for it in specific circumstances, including if it is abandoned or only held for speculation. There is no large-scale expropriation of land.
Among white South Africans who think they are discriminated against, many cite the far-left opposition leader Julius Malema’s repeated use of apartheid-era chant “Kill the Boer”, Boer being another word for Afrikaner. A video featuring the chant was played by Trump when he met South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, in the Oval Office last year.
The ruling African National Congress party has disavowed the chant, which South African courts have ruled is not meant literally and therefore not hate speech.

“I hope they all work, I need money bro,” Coluzzi told one of his co-offenders.

The agreed facts of the case state that, by the end of the scheme, Coluzzi was worried about changes to Australia Post procedures that would stop him from accessing new cards.
“It’s only gonna be parcels bro, and I can’t fucking touch parcels,” he said to an unnamed person.

Coluzzi is estimated to have gambled millions of dollars throughout his life and the excessive losses put repeated strain on his marriage, Kiely said.
For 15 months, the Australia Post employee and his accomplices systematically stole dozens of cards from secure mail and obtained more than $100,000 in cash and fraudulent purchases.
The men bought perfume, a night out in Darling Harbour, scented candles and more than a dozen phones and tablets.
Thousands of cigarettes, phone recharge cards, groceries and Roblox gift cards were also in the haul.

The legal notice was issued by Satish Salian, who alleges that public statements made by key political figures damaged his reputation and integrity.

Actor Sushant Singh Rajput, for whom Disha Salian had worked as a celebrity manager, died six days later on June 14, 2020.

For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley have argued that the US is locked in an AI arms race with China, and that the consequences of losing would be disastrous. But over the past week, those same executives have started emphasizing a different message. AI has the potential to become so dangerous, tech leaders say, that the two countries urgently need to work together to slow the race down.
“Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post published Saturday titled “We Must Pace the Frontier.”
China’s government and AI companies have made it clear that they’re deeply skeptical of Amodei’s proposal, but not because they want to keep blindly racing ahead or don’t believe the technology poses serious risks. The problem the Chinese government and Chinese AI companies see is far simpler. They think they’re being offered a bad deal.
“The AI safety community in China is growing and shares many of the same concerns that American labs do,” says Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under President Barack Obama. “The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it’s being treated from a position of equals.”
Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring that the US and other democracies maintain “as large as possible” a lead in AI development over autocracies like China. To do that, he urged the US to take steps including cracking down on chip smuggling and preventing unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies.
“His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional to increasing the lead over China," says Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, “which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.”
Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic: He argued that weakening China’s AI industry would somehow give the US more leverage and make “an agreement more likely in the future.” How, exactly, that is supposed to entice Beijing to come to the negotiating table is left unexplained. (To Amodei’s credit, he later admitted in a television interview that he has “no idea how to negotiate with China.”)
The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators in China who responded to Amodei haven’t argued that AI poses no risks. But many of them clearly resent the idea that their country should simultaneously be treated as an essential governance partner and a competitor that needs to be constrained.
When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference, Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, didn’t mince words: He described the proposal as “fear-mongering, confrontation, and vicious competition” that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts. The next day, the ministry also stressed that “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI.”
The mixed comments are reflective of another reason that Beijing may be less receptive to the Anthropic CEO’s warnings than other audiences. Unlike many of the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China’s leaders are not primarily concerned about so-called existential risks from AI, such as the possibility that a rogue agent could kill everyone on Earth. Like in many other policy areas, Beijing’s prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on power.
“Beijing finds it difficult to take these calls at face value partly because it’s skeptical of the possibility of achieving AGI and doubtful of the narrative that AI poses extreme risks to humanity,” says Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow at the Center for a New American Security focused on national security and artificial intelligence. “Although Beijing is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks, the risk that Beijing seems most worried about is the threat AI could pose to CCP rule.”
In a recent essay, China’s minister of state security Chen Yixin warned that AI could fuel political disinformation, cyberattacks, espionage, social unrest, and new military threats. He spent far less time on the kinds of doomsday scenarios that frequently preoccupy people at US frontier AI labs.
“Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies’ calls for AI safety as instrumental,” says Nie. “They believe that US companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down their competitors, which are primarily Chinese companies at this point.”
That skepticism is also shared by many people who work in China’s AI industry, which has broadly focused on releasing lower-cost, open-weight models. In a widely shared essay published on Sunday, a researcher at DeepSeek said he believes AI could move human society to one of two extremes. In the first, powerful AI is broadly available and raises living standards. In the second, a handful of tech companies control the most advanced systems and the resources that come with them, making it even harder for everyone else to catch up.
“That is why I still believe the most advanced intelligence should be made available to everyone in an open and inexpensive way,” the DeepSeek engineer wrote. “I do not trust Anthropic or OpenAI to do that. And I especially do not want Anthropic to control the most advanced artificial intelligence or AGI.”
None of this means that US-China cooperation on AI safety is doomed. Preliminary negotiations between the two countries are reportedly already underway ahead of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s planned visit to Washington later this month to meet with US President Donald Trump.
There are plenty of reasons to be hopeful that these discussions will result in some progress, even though it may be incremental. Both governments have expressed worries about some of the same things, including cybersecurity threats, the misuse of powerful models, and the possibility that increasingly capable AI systems could behave in unexpected ways.
“There are people who genuinely care about AI safety on both sides, and there’s a possibility they could engage in good-faith discussion in narrowly scoped issues,” says Nie. What might move the needle most, she says, is designing a credible way for each country to verify that the other is abiding by its commitments.
Still, others worry that rhetoric from Amodei and other US tech leaders about weakening China could erode the fragile trust that diplomatic talks depend on. Kristy Loke, a research fellow at the AI safety nonprofit MATS Research, says that Amodei’s missive may ultimately backfire. “Dario is undermining one of the few available levers for reducing the very risks he professes to take seriously,” she says.

What to know about the deaths of 8 women in South Africa that have sparked fear and anger

The discoveries have sent shock waves around the country, sparked a high-level investigation and highlighted the scourge of femicide and high levels of violent crime.

On stage at Davos in the Swiss Alps earlier this year, Bill Gates, before an audience of the global do-gooding elite, announced a $50 million partnership between his foundation and an unlikely new ally, OpenAI, aimed at improving healthcare in Rwanda.
Can AI save global health? Bill Gates is betting $1 billion that it can.
AI can’t fix all the infrastructure aid cuts broke. But maybe it can help.
Just a month earlier, the Gates Foundation had released a harrowing report about widespread global health cuts and collapsing foreign aid infrastructure, documenting a rise in child deaths for the first time this century. But at Davos, even as the US hemorrhaged funding for vaccines, maternal healthcare, and HIV treatment, the Microsoft co-founder struck an optimistic tone.
“Using innovation, using AI,” Gates told Reuters, “I think we can get back on track.”
As it turns out, the partnership was just an opening salvo for what’s become a wholesale embrace of AI by the world’s largest global health philanthropy. A $200 million partnership with Anthropic came just a few months later. And then, on Tuesday, the Gates Foundation announced a plan to dole out a jaw-dropping $1 billion over the next two years for scaling up AI interventions across healthcare, education, and agriculture around the world.
The sense that AI will soon change everything, and mostly for the worse, has perhaps never felt so pressing and alarming as it does right now. But this hefty new commitment is premised on the idea that AI could eventually make our lives much better too. In a country like America, AI requires massive investments and buildout — in the grid, in power, in technology, in water. In many parts of Africa, already infrastructure-poor, the foundation is effectively betting that AI can compensate for some of the infrastructure that isn’t in place or that has been lost — and offer a new layer that can help in education, in delivering healthcare, and more.
The Gates Foundation’s new commitments include projects to improve how farmers analyze their crops, how doctors diagnose patients, and how students learn. Some have already proven to be quite effective, according to the foundation, with one tool improving the accuracy of medical diagnoses by 16 percent across several Kenyan clinics. “In poorer countries with enormous health worker shortages and lack of health systems infrastructure,” Gates wrote on his blog earlier this year, “AI can be a game-changer in expanding access to quality care.”
Last year’s foreign aid cuts were unfathomably destructive for some of the world’s poorest countries, shuttering thousands of clinics and perhaps hundreds of thousands of classrooms in places where critical workers and supplies were already stretched thin. No, AI cannot deliver a baby, administer a vaccine, or manage a classroom — not yet, at least — but it can, the Gates Foundation hopes, help ease the burden and augment the quality of care for nurses and teachers now tasked with serving far more people than any one person should.
“This is the most transformative technology of our lifetime,” Mark Suzman, CEO of the Gates Foundation, told me, and while there are “very real risks and challenges” surrounding AI, it also presents genuine opportunities to tangibly improve many people’s lives.
It is a tantalizing premise: We can’t afford to build clinics, hire teachers, or lay new power lines, but perhaps AI could create the digital infrastructure needed to help billions of people do more with what they have — or rather, with what’s left. The question is, can the right layer of innovation help bolster a buckling system, even as the physical and logistical infrastructure surrounding it crumbles?
Is AI really what global health needs right now?
Most Americans have yet to see AI improve their lives in meaningful ways, much less those living in poverty or in countries where only a sliver of the population has ever used ChatGPT.
But those numbers in the developing world are slowly changing, a shift enabled in part by other global health funders convinced that as foreign aid dries up, AI could soon help the world do more with less. The Trump administration itself is on board with this thinking, so long as it benefits American tech companies. Last year, the State Department announced a $150 million partnership with the drone company Zipline to transport medical supplies in several countries.
To Zipline’s credit, an NPR reporter in Rwanda last month found that the company’s drones were already saving lives in places with poor road infrastructure, where driving to the nearest hospital can take hours on winding hills, but where drones can deliver crucial blood transfusions within minutes.
And yet, for Rwandans to benefit fully from these high-tech deliveries, they need staffed clinics to visit. As a result of foreign aid cuts, some of those literal landing spots are now on the verge of closing in some of the nation’s most vulnerable rural corridors. “Without the underlying infrastructure, like roads, energy and power and unless there is accessibility, rural and otherwise,” Enoh Ebong, president of the global development department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told NPR, “then all of these solutions will stop short.”
But just as medical delivery drones still need a clinic to fly to, most of these interventions require some layer of physical infrastructure — roads, schools, power, and quite obviously, broadband — to function. Satellite imagery shows that some rural communities in sub-Saharan Africa quite literally went dark in the aftermath of USAID cuts. It will be much harder for their kids to prompt an AI math tutor, or for a local farmer to download a weather app.
“We’re seeing this very much as a both/and,” Suzman told me, calling more traditional funding for education and healthcare “the bedrock for long-term economic growth,” which AI is meant to supplement, not replace. But, in practice, foreign aid cuts have left serious cracks across much of that bedrock, which could make it harder for state-of-the-art solutions to function as intended.
It is obviously not incumbent on the Gates Foundation to pay for all of this alone – nor would it even be feasible for them to do so. And for the record, plenty of the foundation’s other grant programs are not AI-related at all. But this tension does speak to a broader question that may be felt most acutely in a context like global health, but ultimately one that touches us all: Do we spend our scarce resources on the digital infrastructure of the future at the peril of our needs right now? Could you justify buying the new $1,999 folding iPhone if you can barely afford to buy groceries?
The answer is not actually always an easy one. It is not for us to say, for example, that just because a community lacks reliable running water, its people should be excluded from the benefits (and encumbrances) of the smartphone, especially if that smartphone can connect them to health advice they could never access otherwise, or guidance that could help them survive a drought.
In some parts of the world, digital forms of banking arrived long before local brick-and-mortar branches did, instantaneously connecting countless people to a cheap and secure way to save and send their cash to family and friends in need. It is certainly possible that AI, or at least the kind of applications the Gates Foundation funds, could one day have a similarly transformative effect on how people access personalized levels of care, education, and other services in places without the resources to do so otherwise.
That is the hope, but it is also hard right now to believe uncritically in a technology that, as Gates himself blogged just last month, “will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice,” ushering in “one of the most turbulent times in human history.”
In an interview with the New York Times soon after, he seemed convinced that AI will likely do more harm than good. “I don’t like bringing bad news to people, and I don’t like saying that innovation may be a net negative,” he said. “But that’s where we are.”
Now he wants billions of people around the world to use it? Yes, Suzman said, because if not, then inevitably the best parts of AI — the potential for exponentially better cancer treatments, for example — will go only “to those who can pay for it,” while the worst parts of it will fall, as they so often do, on those who benefit the least. “These decisions are being made now,” he said, “and the decisions being made now will then probably shape the following two decades.” Here’s hoping they’re good ones.

Paris Saint-Germain has announced the return of judo legend Teddy Riner, who has signed a new deal keeping him with the club until 2028. Riner, a five-time Olympic champion and 11-time world champion, first joined PSG in 2017 and was central to reviving its judo section.
This comeback comes just over 18 months after his last appearance in PSG colours at the 2024 Judo Champions League.

He also won Olympic gold in the +100kg at London 2012 and Rio 2016 (having taken bronze in Beijing 2008), added team gold and individual bronze at Tokyo 2020, and capped Paris 2024 with two more golds (individual and mixed team), bringing his Olympic tally to five.

Pushpa Rana: Time for this bunch to make its own history; reputation is motivation not pressure
As the Indian women’s Kabaddi team gears up to represent the country at the upcoming 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, captain Pushpa Rana and Pooja Kajla believe the responsibility of defending India’s gold medal comes with confidence and motivation, with the team firmly setting its sights on the top spot.
Rana, who has been handed the responsibility of leading the 12-member squad, said the team has been preparing extensively by analysing opponents and working on areas of improvement identified by the coaching staff. “First of all, we practice according to the situation. We also analyse the videos of the upcoming matches. Our coaches also tell us about the shortcomings of the past and what needs to be improved. And now we are working on that. I think our team is well prepared,” said Rana.
Kabaddi has traditionally carried immense expectations at the Asian Games, with India having won 11 gold medals in the sport, including three in the women’s event. The Indian women’s team will look to defend the gold medal won in Hangzhou, where they edged Chinese Taipei 26-25 in the final. The Indian women’s team also clinched the gold medal at the World Cup in November last year and Rana believes that expectation to win again is a source of confidence rather than pressure. “Yes, I feel that motivation. When our seniors have already done a good job, they have made their own history, so it is upto us to maintain that momentum. So, we see it as motivation, we don’t see it as pressure. We are also working hard to maintain that momentum,” she said.

Having previously served as vice-captain, she said she continues to rely on the guidance of senior players such as Ritu Negi and Sonali Shingate to strengthen team bonding. “I rely a lot on the seniors because they are already captains like Ritu Negi and Sonali Shingate. Trump administration plans ideological warning signs for Smithsonian
The Trump Administration says it is preparing a dozen signs for its Washington, D.C., museum sites that will warn visitors about the Smithsonian Institution in general, and the National Museum of American History in particular.
In letters to U.S. Senators Lisa Murkowski and Jeff Merkley, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote that a "commitment to public transparency" and "academic honesty" required the administration to advise visitors that "the leadership of the Smithsonian and NMAH have altered the museum's role from accurately and coherently telling America's story to using the museum as a tool to advance personal, radical ideologies."
Murkowski, a Republican from Alaska, and Merkley, a Democrat from Oregon, are the top members of the Senate Appropriations committee, which oversees Smithsonian funding.
The signs, which the administration says are temporary, will be placed on National Park Service land and will reflect President Trump's July executive order, called "Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution."
The Sept. 3 letter from Burgum outlines several grievances, including that Anthea Hartig, the director of the American History museum, "has stated that history is 'a prime tool of social justice'," and that the museum seeks "to legitimize illegal immigration and open borders." It charges that several exhibits "present ideological viewpoints inconsistent with biology, including ideologies that sex is not binary."
The letter also says that "visitors should be aware of Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch's history of invidious discrimination and anti-white animus."
The Smithsonian declined to comment on Burgum's letter. Bunch, however, in a letter addressed to Smithsonian staffers in July, responded forcefully to a report that detailed the administration's accusations of bias: "At the Smithsonian, our work is driven by scholarship, accuracy and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America's story.
Bunch, who is highly respected in the worlds of academia and museums, announced on Sept. 8 that he would retire at the end of the year. He told NPR that the timing was not connected to attacks from the Trump Administration.
The Interior Department letter said the text for the signs is not yet finalized, and estimated they would cost $7,000 each, or about $84,000 total.
NPR has reached out to Murkowski for comment.
The Trump Administration and Congressional Republicans have been pressuring the Smithsonian through executive orders and hearings as part of an effort to change the culture of Washington, D.C. institutions and monuments. The proposed changes to the city have included renovating the Kennedy Center, and renaming it after Trump, and a proposed triumphal arch.
"This is another step in a well-planned pressure campaign by the Trump Administration to undermine the integrity and independence of the Smithsonian Institution," Sen. Merkley said in a statement about the letter emailed to NPR. "I'll fight like hell to protect the Smithsonian's independence so that the Institution can continue to tell all of America's story for generations to come."

Pressure for quick VAR decisions obvious in rushed derby review
- Published
"Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!"
The words of video assistant referee Matt Donohue as he rushed through the review to award Erling Haaland's winning goal in the Manchester derby.
No doubt Donohue was simply trying to be as efficient as possible, but it led to one of the most catastrophic VAR errors the Premier League has seen.
Donohue and his assistant VAR, Blake Antrobus, inexplicably failed to notice that Enzo Fernandez was three yards offside before he tried to head the ball.
The goal was given, and Manchester City beat Manchester United 1-0.
Refereeing has always been a goldfish bowl of scrutiny and pressure, heightened by the introduction of VAR.
The Premier League made a "more efficient application of VAR to reduce delays" one of its football principles for the season.
Has the game tried to prioritise speed over accuracy?
Rushed and chaotic rather than calm and collected
The urgency in Donohue's voice was all too apparent.
"Let's go, let's go, let's go, let's go!"
It was a panicked exchange between the VAR and the replay operator. Not calm, collected and methodical. Rushed and chaotic. The opposite of how a video official should operate.
Officials hear repeatedly - from fans, pundits, radio phone-ins and newspaper columns - that VAR has to be quicker. That delays are not acceptable.
In the Premier League stakeholders' survey - which includes managers, coaches and supporters - the key theme for improvements to VAR was the speed of decisions.
This has to create pressure - but it is no excuse for such an error.
City boss Enzo Maresca had some sympathy speaking on Wednesday, though he was of course the beneficiary of the gaffe.
"To make a decision in 10, 20 seconds is not easy for them," said Maresca.
"Sometimes they make mistakes. I make mistakes, players make mistakes. It's part of our job."
Referees' chief Howard Webb has taken the desire for quicker reviews on board, but it is still a balancing act.
There has been a positive impact, as far as the stats go.
VAR delays - including the referee making an announcement to the crowd - have been reduced, from an average of 46 seconds per game to 36 seconds season-on-season.
Yet the only other VAR mistake, the failure to award a penalty to Arsenal at Aston Villa, also arguably came about because the incident was cleared too quickly.
Crucial failure in process a key cause
Completing a VAR review in the shortest possible time is not about skipping steps. And it was a critical mistake by Donohue and Antrobus.
Speed is a factor, but the most serious error in process came before Donohue tried to rush through the attacking phase.
Donohue asked the replay operator to stop the video on the first replay when Josko Gvardiol touched the ball to cross into the area. He then went immediately into the semi-automated offside technology.
This should not have happened.
The VAR team should have assessed the full picture, from the playing of the cross to the head of Haaland. This would have provided awareness of Fernandez's position and impact.
They did not, and the events inside the penalty area were not considered until the attacking phase was looked at.
By then, all that mattered to Donohue and Antrobus was whether Fernandez touched the ball. This would have created a new phase and placed Haaland offside.
Donohue has received much of the criticism, but arguably Antrobus' involvement, or lack of, was just as influential.
The AVAR's contribution to the entire review was to utter "no, yeah" about the potential touch by Fernandez. This was one second before Donohue uttered the words "final decision is goal, check complete".
Antrobus' role is to provide the checks and balances, to make sure the VAR has not missed anything. This fell short.
There has been only one lengthy VAR delay this season, in the game between Brentford and Sunderland. A Dan Ballard goal was ruled out for a subjective offside against Kevin Danso.
Antrobus was the AVAR in this game, too. There was a great deal of criticism in some parts of the media for that delay, which took over four minutes.
Could that have played on Antrobus' mind on Sunday? We cannot know for sure.
Ironically, Antrobus played a crucial role in steering VAR Tim Wood to the correct offside decision against Danso.
There is also the role of the support VAR, who sits in the operations room next to the match hub at Stockley Park and can intervene on points on protocol.
Aware of what was unfolding with the review, no action was taken.-
It would still have been salvageable in the period between the goal being scored and the kick-off.

Dedicated VARs not seen as the answer
Pro Ref has placed a huge level of training and resources into VAR in an attempt to make it as efficient and accurate as possible.
But when an error of this magnitude happens, no amount of investment can mask the failure.
There have been calls to appoint VAR specialists, yet this is exactly what Donohue is - in the Premier League's definition.
Three seasons ago, Pro Ref asked for candidates interested in becoming video officials.
All those who applied were put through aptitude tests. About 15 made it through to the final stages of training, of which 10 have officiated games in the Premier League.
One of those is Donohue, who on Sunday was the video official for the 65th time.
Such as been Donohue's development that he is now on the international list, appointed to Uefa club competition qualifying ties over the summer.
Donohue has made mistakes, in fact very few do not. It shows how difficult the role is.
The only two VARs to have a clear record over the last two seasons are Nick Hopton and Neil Davies, both graduates from the same accelerated programme.
Persuading referees to hang up their whistles and spend their professional lives in the VAR room is not easy, nor does it guarantee success.
Lee Mason and Mike Riley, the Premier League's only full-time VARs appointed after retirement, were both dismissed by Webb just a few months into his tenure because of a catalogue of errors.
One of the only leagues which has a full team of officials who only act as VARs and never go out on the pitch is Spain's La Liga and second division - yet one glance at the headlines there will tell you the controversy is no different to that in England.
At the start of last season the VAR completely missed that a player who scored a goal was in an offside position when the ball was played.
Pro Ref will have questions to answer over its processes and why a VAR is rushing so desperately over a review in one of the biggest games of the season.
That did not happen when West Ham's stoppage-time equaliser against Arsenal was ruled out last season. It took over four minutes - but the VAR came to the correct outcome.
The obsession with speed threatens to undermine all the work behind the scenes.
But that feels like a football problem and not one caused solely by the actions of the VAR.

The 18th BRICS Summit was held on 12 and 13 September 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, bringing together leaders from BRICS member countries and several partner nations. Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, and other heads of state and government attended the summit. During the summit, Prime Minister Narendra Modi proposed a new agenda for BRICS for the next 20 years, focusing on strengthening cooperation among member countries and shaping the bloc’s future priorities (here, here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Prime Minister Narendra Modi presenting his own portrait to Chinese President Xi Jinping during the BRICS Summit. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows Prime Minister Narendra Modi presenting his own portrait to Chinese President Xi Jinping during the BRICS Summit.
Fact: The video does not show Prime Minister Narendra Modi presenting his portrait to Chinese President Xi Jinping at the 2026 BRICS Summit. The visuals are from the 2019 second informal summit between PM Modi and President Xi in Mamallapuram, Tamil Nadu. During the gift exchange, Modi gifted Xi a handmade silk shawl, while Xi gifted Modi a porcelain memento featuring Modi’s portrait. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, here, and here) published in 2019, featuring the same visuals. According to these reports, the visuals were captured on 12 October 2019 during a meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu. Prime Minister Narendra Modi gifted Xi Jinping a handmade silk shawl; in return, Xi Jinping gifted Modi a porcelain memento featuring his portrait.
We also found a post shared by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting on Facebook on 12 October 2019, which described Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping exchanging gifts in Mamallapuram, Tamil Nadu. The post included photos from the meeting, including an image of the memento presented by Xi Jinping.
The Press Information Bureau (PIB) also shared photos of the two leaders meeting on the concluding day of the summit on 12 October 2019.
The same photo was also found in a magazine released by the Chinese Embassy in New Delhi in 2020 to commemorate 70 years of India-China relations. The caption below the photo states that the Chinese President presented the memento featuring PM Modi’s photo to him during the second informal summit in 2019.
The Press Information Bureau’s fact-checking wing also debunked the claim, clarifying that the video is from 2019 and that the porcelain memento featuring Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s image was gifted to him by Chinese President Xi Jinping in Mamallapuram on 12 October 2019.
To sum up, this video shows Chinese President Xi Jinping gifting PM Modi a porcelain memento featuring Modi’s portrait in 2019.

The Best Android Phones
Featured in this article
The best Android phone means something different to everyone. It's hard to find one that caters to every need, but chances are there's a new smartphone that comes close to what you're looking for. From the bottomless pit of phone choices, my favorite Android handsets include the Google Pixel 10a, Pixel 11, and Galaxy S26 Ultra. The phones we've selected have specific advantages, and I've laid them out here based on extensive testing.
See our other mobile buying guides for more, like the Best iPhones, Best Cheap Phones, Best Samsung Phones, Phones With a Headphone Jack, Best Pixel Phones, and Best Folding Phones.
Updated September 2026: We've added the Motorola Razr Ultra (2026), Google Pixel 11 series, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8, and Fairphone (Gen. 6+), alongside other options like the Galaxy S26 FE, Nothing Phone (4a) Pro, and Motorola Edge 2026.
Is Now a Good Time to Buy?
Yes. All the major smartphone makers have released their devices for the year. Prices will dip during major sale events like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, so those are often the best times to upgrade if you're hunting for a bargain.
Buy an Unlocked Phone
We recommend unlocked phones in this guide. When a phone is sold unlocked, it means you can use it on multiple wireless carriers and networks. When you go into a carrier store and buy a phone, usually on a payment plan, it often comes locked to that network, and they'll try to get you to pay for a host of unnecessary accessories and features.
Carriers are legally required to unlock a phone upon request so you can switch networks, but it's a big hassle, and they may have terms about how long you have to wait to ask. Try to pay full price for your phone, or make sure it specifically says it's unlocked. Buy it from the manufacturer or an authorized third-party retailer, or check your carrier's unlocking policy if you bought a device on a payment plan that requires you to use its network. An unlocked phone is also less of a hassle when you travel and want to switch to an international SIM card or eSIM.
Android Specs to Look For
If none of the smartphones in this guide strike your fancy and you want to continue searching, keep these specs in mind.
Display: Gone are the days of shoddy phone displays—almost every smartphone uses an OLED panel now. Cheaper phones still use LCD, which won't have as deep blacks and poppy colors, but even phones under $300 can sport OLED. You'll see some variations, like AMOLED or Dynamic AMOLED 2X, but that's mostly marketing jargon.
Screen size: You hold a smartphone all the time, so make sure whatever you pick fits your palms. Most small Android phones are around 6.1 to 6.3 inches (measured diagonally), whereas larger phones typically top out at 6.8 or 6.9 inches. Foldable phones will have a smaller outer screen and a larger display when opened. For example, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 we recommend has a 5.5-inch screen when closed and a 7.6-inch display when unfolded, but sizes vary by manufacturer.
Processor: Most smartphones use a Qualcomm or MediaTek processor. Google phones use the company's in-house Tensor chip, and some Samsung phones utilize Samsung's Exynos processor in select markets. It's hard to say how reliably a processor will perform without looking at reviews and benchmark results, so do your research. For reliable performance, try to stick to Qualcomm's Snapdragon 7 series or higher, or MediaTek's Dimensity 7000 series or higher. The 2026 flagship chip is the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5.
RAM: You'll want at least 8 GB of RAM, though 12 GB is better. This lets you juggle multiple apps more seamlessly and run more intensive AI tasks.
Cooling: High-performing phones can be ruined if they get too hot because the processor throttles, causing slowdowns. This mostly applies to folks who game a lot, but it's worth checking whether the phone has a dedicated cooling system. You'll want to look for language like “heat pipes” or “vapor chamber cooling.”
Refresh rate: Most phones used to come with 60-Hz refresh rates, meaning the display refreshes at 60 frames per second. Nowadays, even cheap phones offer 90- or 120-Hz screens. The more frames refreshed in a second, the more fluid everything looks and feels. It might sound small, but it can make a big difference in whether your smartphone feels buttery smooth. We have a broader guide that explains this technology. Flagship phones have screens with variable refresh rates ranging from 1 to 120 Hz, which often makes them more battery-efficient (look for LTPO or LTPS).
Battery capacity: Smartphone batteries are measured in milliampere-hours (mAh). A big battery doesn't necessarily mean better battery life, because it depends on screen size and other technologies the phone is powering. Most phones should have 4,000-mAh cells or higher, and you typically won't see much above 5,500 mAh. Some phones now use silicon-carbon batteries, a new technology that allows them to be denser but thinner.
Charging speeds: Most Android smartphones can charge fast, but certain companies offer shockingly fast recharge times. That's usually because they require a proprietary charging brick. You can find charging speed information on a phone's product spec page. Just remember that these days, most smartphones do not come with a charging brick, just a cable. We have more details in this fast-charging guide.
Software updates: Software support is crucial. Your phone stays secure longer, and you'll get new features over time. Even if you trade in your phone, it may end up in someone else's hands, and a long update policy means the phone will continue to be supported. The gold standard in Android is seven years right now, thanks to Samsung and Google. However, if you replace your phone every two or three years, the shorter update policies of other Android makers might not be a deal-breaker.
Cameras: Camera specs are very misleading. A phone with a 108-megapixel (MP) sensor doesn't mean it will take better photos than a phone with a 50-MP sensor. The only way to know for sure is to read reviews. If the camera matters to you, check whether it has a versatile system. The best camera phones offer a primary wide camera, an ultrawide, and a telephoto zoom (usually 5X). Cheap phones tend to come with a lot of cameras, many of which are useless.
Extra features: Don't overlook the secondary features. Does the phone have a near-field communication sensor (NFC) so you can make contactless payments? Does it have a good IP rating that can survive a drop in the pool? (You'll want IP67 or IP68!) What about wireless charging (Qi2 or Qi)? Or a microSD card slot, dual-SIM tray, or headphone jack? Vet the phone's specs if you're after something specific.
5G service: Nearly all smartphones support 5G, the current generation of network connectivity. 4G LTE isn't disappearing, and you may still fall back to LTE when 5G isn't available. Avoid smartphones that don't offer 5G at all.
How to Switch Between Phones
The best way to switch phones is to follow the setup prompts when you first boot up your new device. Make sure you transfer data from an old phone via a cable. It's much faster than doing it wirelessly, though that's an option too. Some manufacturers, like Samsung, will suggest you download a proprietary data transfer app on your old device, like Smart Switch, and you should. It means less work for you—whether it's fewer apps you need to sign into or fewer icons you need to rearrange. If you're coming from an iPhone, you can use Google's official Android Switch app, though Apple and Google have improved the transfer process to make things smoother.
Check out our tips on setting up your new Android phone, and our steps on backing up an Android and how to factory reset it.
How We Test Smartphones
I put my personal SIM card in every smartphone I test and use it for at least a week, if not two or three. I stress-test performance by playing mobile games and running benchmark tests, like Geekbench and Antutu, while also monitoring thermals. I make calls to test the smartphone's microphone quality, since, you know, it's still a phone.
I often test the cameras by bringing a competing phone along and analyzing photos side by side on a larger, more color-accurate screen. I've been reviewing smartphones for close to a decade—not just flagship devices either. I'm always testing cheap phones to see what innovations are trickling down.
Other Phones to Consider
We test a ton of Android phones. We like the ones below, but you'll be better off with one of the options above. Check out our Best Cheap Phones and Best Folding Phones guides for more.
Nothing Phone (4a) Pro for $499: This midrange phone from Nothing (7/10, WIRED Recommends) strikes a good balance of features and price, and you won't find another smartphone that looks this distinct. You may have some carrier compatibility issues on AT&T and Verizon, and I don't love that it's only IP65 dust- and water-resistant and lacks wireless charging. Still, performance is good, the screen is bright, and battery life is reliable. There's a triple-camera setup with a 3.5X zoom telephoto, and the Glyph Matrix display on the back is weird, light-hearted fun that will surely be a conversation starter.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE for $700: Like most consumer electronics, Samsung has hiked the price of its midrange Galaxy S26 FE (6/10, WIRED Review), which stands for “Fan Edition.” Some features have even gotten worse, like how it now only supports USB 2.0 instead of USB 3.2. Still, if you want a Samsung but don't want to spend big bucks on the flagship S26 range (the Galaxy S26 doesn't cost significantly more, so look for the S26 FE on sale), the FE is a capable handset with a good triple-camera system, a great screen, and good battery life.
Motorola Edge 2026 for $600: Are phones too heavy for you? You might appreciate the Edge—it has an amazingly lightweight 160-gram frame and a fairly compact 6.3-inch screen. It's great to use one-handed. Performance is more than capable, and there's even a handy triple-camera system, though it doesn't quite match the quality of our recommended picks above. Disappointingly, Motorola only promises two Android OS upgrades and three years of security updates, which is hard to accept at this price. Buy it on sale!

'What kind of language': Congress slams US senator's warning to India over Russian oil
The remark by US senator, who took a stern tone against countries buying oil from Russia, did not go down well with Congress.
Congress took strong exception to a US senator's warning to India over its oil trade with Russia on Thursday. Party MP Pawan Khera flagged the language used after Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal asked India to "clean up" its act.
The remark by US senator, who took a stern tone against countries buying oil from Russia, did not go down well with the opposition party. "What kind of language is being used for our country," asked Khera in a post on X.
Deep Dive
What US Senator said on India
After the US House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, Blumenthal sounded a warning to India and other countries, saying, “To China and India: You better clean up your act. Buy your oil and gas somewhere else. Appeasement is not a strategy."
The bill, which was cleared by a 262-159 vote, will now go to President Donald Trump for his signature.
ALSO READ: US Congress clears Russia sanctions bill, hands Trump new tariff powers: What it means for India
US bill threatens 100% tariffs on India
The new legislation would give Trump the power to impose up to 100 per cent tariffs on five major buyers of Russian oil and gas — China, India, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan.
The bill would also target companies and foreign actors supporting Russia's military and extend sanctions involving Iran.
The legislation provides exemptions for European allies, citing their efforts to reduce Russian energy dependence. India has no such exemption.
How India responded to Russia sanctions bill
As US tariffs loom ahead, India said on Thursday that it would continue buying oil "through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics".
India said it will take all necessary steps to protect its trade and economic interests after the US Congress passed the sweeping sanctions bill on Russia.
In a statement, the ministry of external affairs said the issue has been discussed at high levels with various US interlocutors. "Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side,” it said.
“The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” the ministry said without divulging details of the proposed steps.

Former Haptik CEO Aakrit Vaish-led VC firm Activate has announced the final close of its maiden fund at $105 Mn (around ₹1,000 Cr). The fund, which was closed within a year of its launch, comprises an $85 Mn flagship early-stage fund and $20 Mn deployed through dedicated growth investment vehicles. Activate said the flagship fund closed at 125% above its original target. Activate's LP base includes more than 50 founders and AI researchers, around a dozen global VC general partners and more than 50 family offices, enterprises and corporates. Notable backers include Vinod Khosla, General Catalyst, Raghu Raghuram, Vijay Shekhar Sharma, Lalit Keshre, Harsh Jain, Bhavin Turakhia, Ronnie Screwvala and Ranjan Pai, among others. Founded in December 2025 by Vaish and former Together Fund partner Pratyush Choudhury, Activate aims to back AI-native startups at the pre-seed or idea stage. It is targeting to back 25-30 startups operating across AI applications, foundational models, physical infrastructure and related areas, with initial equity investments in the range of $500K-$3 Mn. The fund reported its first close at $75 Mn in December, and has since made 10 investments. Through its early-stage strategy, called Inception, Activate has backed seven startups across consumer AI, AI-led services and frontier technology. All seven remain in stealth. The firm said it works with founders from as early as the ideation stage, including in some cases before incorporation, and supports them across product development, technical architecture, hiring, go-to-market and subsequent fundraising. Beyond early-stage investments, Activate has also backed Sarvam AI, ElevenLabs and Wispr Flow. Activate’s investment in Sarvam came amid the Bengaluru-based AI startup’s ongoing $300 Mn Series B round. Vaish had said the investment was the firm’s largest capital commitment to a company at the time, although the exact amount was not disclosed. In February, Activate partnered with NVIDIA to provide its portfolio founders with access to the chipmaker’s Nemotron family of open-source models, along with technical training, compute resources and support. Beyond capital, the firm said its ecosystem includes a GenAI community of more than 15,000 technical practitioners across over 40 groups. It has also forged partnerships with NVIDIA, OpenAI, Anthropic, ElevenLabs, AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Notion, with portfolio companies eligible for up to $1 Mn in credits and other benefits. AI Emerges As A Major VC Theme In India AI has become one of the fastest-growing areas of venture investment in India, with startups in the segment raising $676 Mn across 57 deals in the first half of the year, an over 4X YoY jump, according to Inc42's Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, H1 2026. Amid this growth wave, institutional investors are also sharpening their AI focus. For instance, Bajaj Finserv chairman and MD Sanjiv Bajaj said earlier this year that the firm is planning to launch a dedicated ₹450 Cr fund focused on AI ventures. Prominent startup investors are also doubling down on the nascent tech as of now. Accel recently closed a $550 Mn fund to back AI and deeptech startups while Elevation Capital launched its $500 Mn AI-focused Fund IX in July. Alongside, there is an emergence of dedicated AI and deeptech investment vehicles. For instance, Fundamentum cofounder Ashish Kumar launched Fundamentum Frontier Advisors, which is targeting consumer, enterprise and physical AI through its investment vehicles.

In September 2026, a series of images circulated online that social media users claimed (archived) showed Iranian damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East.
For example, one X user shared a video consisting of six photographs that appeared to show a damaged aircraft, vehicle and structures, and wrote:
BREAKING: Troops leaked photos of their wrecked bases to CBS, saying they're "standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face"
Active service members sent the images anonymously.
The images also circulated on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived).
The images came from an exclusive CBS News report that said its reporter Jonah Kaplan had received the photos from "active service members on condition of anonymity because of rigid media restrictions within the military."
It wasn't possible for Snopes to independently verify the authenticity of the images. We don't rely on anonymous sources. Therefore, in order to independently verify them, we would need to speak to the people who took the images and verify their metadata (information about where and when a photo was taken). This did not appear possible given the sources told CBS News they didn't want their names published alongside the images. Therefore, we leave claims about the authenticity of the images unrated.
We contacted Kaplan to ask how he verified the authenticity of the photos. We also contacted U.S. Central Command, which directs U.S. security operations across the Middle East, to ask about the authenticity of the images. We await replies to our queries.
What we know about images
The CBS News report included six photos. The first claimed to show a damaged plane at the Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. The image resembled photos verified by the BBC in March 2026 after Reuters and The Wall Street Journal reported that Iranian strikes damaged an E-3 sentry aircraft and injured 12 troops at the base.
Snopes could not verify the exact location of the plane at the base, though CBS News' image did show a sign reading "35L S2." 35L is the name of one of the runways at the Prince Sultan Air Base, suggesting the damaged plane was parked on or near that runway when Iranian strikes hit. The image showed what appeared to be a drain or tunnel under the runway. Google Earth imagery showed identical structures along the 35L runway.
A report about Operation Epic Fury (the U.S. government's name for the war in Iran) that the lead inspector general submitted to Congress in September 2026 found one E-3 aircraft had been "damaged on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian strikes" during the conflict (Table 5).
The next two images in the CBS News article claimed to show damage to a large tent structure and several trailers at Camp Buehring in Kuwait. According to the Institute for the Study of War, a public policy research organization that analyzes military and foreign affairs, Iran has claimed to have struck Camp Buehring at least five times since the start of the war.
One of the images, which showed a burned-out vehicle, also showed a mural that included a hand grasping three lightning bolts. This was the same imagery used by the 136th Expeditionary Signal Battalion. That battalion has previously been deployed to Camp Buehring. The unit was deployed to Central Command's area of operation, which includes the Middle East, around April 2026.
Another image appeared to show damage to the Unaccompanied Officers Quarters at Camp Arifjan, Kuwait. The ISW reported that Iranian forces had struck Camp Arifjan at the start of March 2026. CNN reported on March 3 that six U.S. service members had been killed in strikes on the Port of Shuaiba, which is around 18 miles north of Camp Arifjan, suggesting the Iranian military had targeted the area.
The sixth image claimed to show damage to a large tent structure at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. Snopes could not independently confirm the location or date of that image.
Foreign base damage difficult to confirm
Verifying damage to U.S. bases or equipment overseas is difficult because U.S. authorities generally do not publicly confirm such strikes so as not give away equipment locations or military capabilities. For example, in April 2026, the Pentagon declined to comment on reported damage to U.S. bases in Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq and Saudi Arabia for operational security reasons.
The September 2026 report to Congress about Operation Epic Fury included damage estimates only for diplomatic facilities such as embassies and consulates (Page 19), not military bases.
U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said (at 32:57) on March 3, 2026, that the six people killed near Camp Arifjan in early March 2026 died because a "squirter" passed through U.S. air defenses and hit a "tactical operation center."
Hegseth said such incidents happened "every once in a while."
Speaking to CBS News about the September 2026 images, a service member reportedly refuted that characterization of the alleged damage caused to U.S. bases in the Middle East, instead saying, "We're not defending these bases. We're just watching them get destroyed."
For further reading, Snopes has investigated a number of claims related to the war in Iran.
