Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Some of the most widely used private torrent trackers for pirating movies suspect that a banned user may have posed as a filmmaker protecting copyrights in a failed attempt to seek revenge.
TorrentFreak has been tracking this story closely, reporting last September that an alleged independent filmmaker named Matthew Schneider sued six private trackers for infringing copyrights on some films that he supposedly made. Trackers targeted include PassThePopcorn, BroadcasTheNet, and HDBits. For months, the filmmaker sought to get Cloudflare to unmask operators of the trackers through a copyright fight, which went on until trackers alerted the court last month that Schneider appeared to be an impostor.
In a sworn declaration, the actual filmmaker behind the movies cited in the complaint wrote that he had no association to the plaintiff in the case. “I am not involved in, nor have I ever appeared in, this case,” Schneider wrote.
To keep the copyright fight alive, the plaintiff swore, “I’m a different Matthew Schneider.” He then claimed to have coincidentally made three films with the same exact titles as the other filmmaker’s movies, Split: A Film Anthology, Do Us Part, and Orlando Gloom, Always the Same.
For the judge, Andrea R. Wood, this unusual turn in what could have been a major case was unexpected. TorrentFreak noted that this was the first copyright case to target “multiple prominent private torrent trackers,” and the judge warned that the plaintiff could face sanctions if the private trackers’ allegations were true and he filed a frivolous claim with intent to deceive the court.
As pressure mounted on the plaintiff to clarify his complaint, he abruptly decided to voluntarily dismiss the claims, TorrentFreak reported Tuesday. But that last-minute move might not save him from being sanctioned.

Later today, Max Verstappen will strap on his helmet and take to the track at the Silverstone circuit in England for a rather unusual race. The four-time Formula 1 world champion is recognized as the leading talent of his generation, but unlike some of the legends that have preceded him, Verstappen’s passion for motorsport extends beyond just the rarified world of F1. With apologies to Midweek Motorsport, but if it has wheels and they keep score, odds are good Verstappen’s down to race it. So at noon Eastern Time (5 pm BST) today, September 16, Verstappen will slip into something a little more basic: a kart.
It’s one of 101 identical karts that have been sourced from Eastern Europe for the event—the other 100 will be driven by a mix of content creators and Red Bull athletes, all of whom fancy their chances at beating one of the world’s greatest drivers at his own game. They get a bit of an advantage, all starting ahead of Verstappen. Once he passes another karter, they’re out of the race, and Verstappen has 30 laps of a purpose-designed layout at Silverstone to get through them all and win.
Other F1 drivers have attempted slightly similar challenges in the past—Alex Albon raced 25 kids last year, and last month Oliver Bearman raced 50 amateurs. But neither is as high-profile as Verstappen, and neither is facing as much competition.
It might have been many years since Verstappen traded his kart for things larger and faster, but that’s no reason to doubt his abilities.
“Max is pretty unique in comparison to the other Grand Prix drivers in that he’s already done the Nürburgring 24 hours in his GT3. He’s out testing those cars often. I saw his quote saying that it’s been a while since he did karting; do we honestly think that he hasn’t gone and done a little test? It’s Max Verstappen! He’s a serial winner, and therefore he’s not turning up here to shine a spotlight on some other individual. He’s going to go for it, and he’s going to try and achieve this target,” said David Coulthard, a Grand Prix winner and one of Red Bull Racing’s first factory drivers.

India’s ubiquitous UPI payment system is set for a significant change from October 15, with the introduction of a merchant discount rate (MDR) on select transactions. Under the new framework, merchants will be charged an MDR of 0.4% on person to merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000. The charge will be capped at ₹300 for transactions worth ₹75,000 or more. The October 15 change does not necessarily make UPI a paid service for consumers. Instead, it introduces a commercial layer on the merchant side. With a 0.4% MDR for regular P2M transactions above ₹2,000 and a ₹300 cap for transactions of ₹75,000 and above. The framework keeps P2P payments free, protects P2PM merchants from MDR and provides lower flat rates for sectors such as fuel, insurance and utilities. The broader shift is from an entirely zero-MDR merchant model towards a threshold-based system intended to create a more sustainable financial model for India's UPI infrastructure. Payments Council of India's chairman and AvenuesAI CEO Vishwas Patel believes that the introduction of the charges is a key step to build a viable economic model while keeping UPI free for consumers. "At the same time, sustainability must not come at the cost of financial inclusion. The continued zero-MDR protection for eligible small and micro merchants, along with support for expanding digital acceptance in Tier III, IV centres, will help preserve UPI’s accessibility," Patel said. So, what exactly changes next month and who will actually have to pay? UPI MDR: What Is Changing From October 15? The new MDR framework will come into effect on October 15, 2026. For regular P2M transactions above ₹2,000, merchants will pay 0.4% of the transaction value as MDR. Transactions of ₹2,000 or below will continue to attract zero MDR. For high-value payments, the MDR will be capped at ₹300. This cap applies to transactions of ₹75,000 and above. In practical terms, the structure will look like this: Transaction value ₹2,000 - ₹0 MDR Transaction value ₹3,000 - ₹12 MDR Transaction value ₹50,000 - ₹200 MDR Transaction value ₹75,000 - ₹300 MDR Transaction value ₹1 Lakh - ₹300 MDR The MDR is a charge on the merchant side. Consumers will continue to pay the listed price of the product or service. P2P transactions, including transfers to friends, family or between a user's own bank accounts, will continue to remain free. UPI apps won’t be allowed to charge a platform fee or any other fee for payments made through UPI. There are also no monthly quotas under the framework that would result in consumers being charged after a certain number of UPI transactions. The new MDR is a merchant-side charge and not a consumer-facing UPI fee. Merchants onboarded under the framework cannot pass the MDR on to customers while accepting UPI payments, the NPCI said. What About Small Merchants? Not every merchant will be subject to the 0.4% MDR. Small merchants operating under the Person-to-Person-Merchant (P2PM) framework will continue to enjoy zero MDR. The framework defines these as small vendors receiving up to ₹1 Lakh per month through UPI QR codes directly into their accounts. This means a small vendor does not automatically become liable for MDR simply because a customer makes a payment exceeding ₹2,000. Acquiring banks and payment service providers will monitor the monthly inward transaction threshold. Merchants receiving more than ₹1 Lakh through UPI for three consecutive months will be transitioned to the P2M category, effectively making the Existing QR codes will continue to work and small merchants will not have to replace their QR stands or soundboxes because of the MDR changes. How Are MDR Charges Bifurcated Among Sectors? Several sectors will not be charged the standard 0.4% MDR. Instead, they will have a flat MDR of ₹5 for transactions above ₹2,000. These include categories such as railways, telecom, insurance and fuel. For example, an insurance premium or fuel payment of ₹10,000 would attract a ₹5 MDR rather than the ₹40 charge that would apply under the standard 0.4% rate. Utility payments, including electricity, water and piped natural gas, will also fall under the designated industry programme category, with a ₹5 MDR for transactions above ₹2,000. Payments below ₹2,000 in these categories will continue to remain free of MDR. What About Mutual Funds And Stock Market Payments? Capital market transactions will have a separate MDR structure. Payments involving mutual funds, securities, stockbrokers and dealers will attract an MDR of 0.02%, with a maximum cap of ₹300. The category covers regulated capital-market entities, including asset management companies, SEBI-registered stockbrokers, securities dealers and investment platforms. The lower rate is intended to distinguish investment-related payments from routine retail and commercial transactions. Will Credit Card Payments On UPI Be Affected? The new MDR framework applies specifically to direct account-to-merchant UPI payments. Credit-linked UPI transactions, such as payments made using RuPay credit cards linked to UPI or pre-sanctioned bank credit lines, operate under separate credit product rules. As a result, the MDR won't apply to these transactions in the same manner as direct bank-account-to-merchant UPI payments. How Will The MDR Revenue Be Divided? The 0.4% MDR paid by the merchant will flow through different parts of the UPI ecosystem. In effect, the ₹0.40 MDR is split as 0.28% for the issuer bank, 0.08% for the TPAP and 0.04% for the acquiring bank. For every ₹100 eligible UPI transaction, the merchant will pay ₹0.40 as MDR to the acquiring bank, which is the bank handling the merchant’s UPI account. Of this ₹0.40, ₹0.28 (0.28%) will be paid by the acquiring bank to the customer’s issuing bank as interchange. A further ₹0.08 (0.08%) will go to the UPI app provider, paid by the payer-side payment service provider (PSP). This leaves ₹0.04 (0.04%) with the acquiring bank. Why Is UPI Introducing MDR Now? The move comes as UPI has scaled to become one of India's primary digital payment systems. UPI processed 24.51 Bn transactions worth ₹29.82 Lakh Cr in August 2026 alone. The policy framework argues that operating a payment system at this scale requires significant spending on server infrastructure, bandwidth, fraud prevention, cybersecurity and banking technology. Industry estimates cited in the framework put the annual cost of maintaining UPI operations at around ₹20,000 Cr. Until now, government incentives and subsidies have helped support the ecosystem. The new framework argues that these were intended as short-term support rather than a permanent mechanism for covering payment infrastructure costs. The MDR revenue will be retained within the UPI ecosystem and is intended to support infrastructure resilience, innovation, cybersecurity and customer service. It will also What Happens To The MDR Money? A dedicated fund for small merchants is also proposed under the framework. The fund will be used to support digital payment infrastructure in Tier III to Tier IV centres, including the northeastern states, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. It will also cover notified government schemes in Tier I and Tier II centres. The fund is expected to provide financial assistance to acquiring banks and payment aggregators for merchant onboarding and incentivise UPI transactions among small merchants. The detailed framework for the fund is expected to be finalised in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India within three months. Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

Trump specifically called 40 Wall Street the tallest building on downtown Manhattan, not all of Manhattan or New York City. Whether Trump's comments amounted to bragging, as some people online claimed, is open to interpretation.
Around the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. President Donald Trump, then a New York City real estate developer, said after the attacks that he now owned the tallest building in downtown Manhattan or New York City.
For example, one X user posted a clip from an alleged TV news interview with Trump captioned, "Here is Trump on 9/11 bragging that Trump Tower is now the tallest building in Manhattan."
Here is Trump on 9/11 bragging that Trump Tower is now the tallest building in Manhattan pic.twitter.com/Fy5ZW85tZc
— FactPost (@factpostnews) September 11, 2026
Similar claims that Trump had said his building was the tallest in Manhattan or even New York City after the Twin Towers fell circulated on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers also contacted us to ask about the claim.
Trump did tell (time code 2:05, archived) a reporter soon after the 9/11 attacks that 40 Wall Street, which the Trump Organization still owns, was "the tallest" building in downtown Manhattan (not Manhattan as a whole or New York City). As such, we've rated this quote as correctly attributed to Trump.
Whether Trump's comments amounted to bragging, as some people online claimed, is open to interpretation.
Fox 5 New York posted a video of Trump's phone interview with WWOR-TV reporter Alan Marcus on YouTube in 2016. Trump made the claim about owning the tallest building in downtown Manhattan after Marcus asked if 40 Wall Street had sustained any damage during the attacks. The exchange went as follows (at 1:43 — emphasis ours):
MARCUS: Donald, you have one of the landmark buildings down in the financial district, 40 Wall Street, did you have any damage or did you know what's happened down there?
TRUMP: Well, it was an amazing phone call I made. 40 Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan. And it was, actually before the World Trade Center, was the tallest. And then when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second-tallest. And now it's the tallest.
During the 2001 interview, Marcus also asked Trump how he would have handled 9/11 if he were president given that he had considered running for the office the year before (at 4:14). Trump said he would have taken a "very, very tough line" against "the group of people that did this."
In an interview with Politico in 2016, Marcus reportedly said that Trump's remark about 40 Wall Street was "Donald being Donald." Marcus added, "He is the brand manager of Trump, and he is going to tout that brand, and he does it reflexively."
Trump's claim that 40 Wall Street was the tallest building in downtown Manhattan following the attacks was incorrect. The nearby 952-foot tall 70 Pine Street skyscraper, which was also part of the Manhattan skyline in 2001, is 26 feet taller than 40 Wall Street.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Trump attacked the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York for telling him he would not be allowed to speak at its 25th-anniversary commemoration.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

Gordie Howe bridge vehicle traffic tops 340,000 in first full month of operation
New bridge traffic was nearly on par with nearby Ambassador Bridge
Traffic at the new Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit topped 340,000 in its first full month of operation, according to new data.
There were 343,507 crossings at the bridge in August, the first full month it was open, per fresh figures from the Bridge and Tunnel Operators Association.
It was nearly the same as traffic at the nearby Ambassador Bridge, which saw 345,445 crossings last month.
But the composition of the traffic on the competing spans was different. The majority of crossings at the Gordie Howe bridge were passenger vehicles: Nearly 270,000 vs. roughly 74,000 trucks.
At the Ambassador, truck traffic was around 150,000, compared to 196,000 passenger cars.
- ExclusiveAmbassador Bridge 'aggressively' pursued trucking clients amid Gordie Howe delay: industry rep
- New bridge, same traffic: Why is the road to the Ambassador Bridge still packed with trucks?
Jason Miller, a supply chain management professor at Michigan State University, says he believes many trucking companies have toll price contracts with the Ambassador Bridge.
"So what's happening is they are probably locked in for this year," he told Windsor Morning on Wednesday. "So it does not make as much sense for them to shift trucks over to Gordie Howe until they would have some type of renegotiated contract or they themselves have a contractual price with Gordie Howe."
The Windsor-Detroit Tunnel still had the highest volume of passenger vehicles, with approximately 280,000 crossings in August.
StatsCan data offers different look
Recently released numbers from Statistics Canada offer a more detailed look at the origin of the people crossing the various ports of entry in the Windsor-Detroit corridor.
"In August, the Gordie Howe International Bridge was used for 134,900 Canadian-resident return trips from the United States by automobile, 56.7 per cent of which were same-day," the federal agency said Friday. "It was also used as a port of entry for 101,000 US-resident trips to Canada by automobile, 52.2 per cent of which were same-day.
"During the same period, 348,000 Canadian and US residents entered Canada by automobile at Windsor's Ambassador Bridge and the Windsor-Detroit Tunnel, down 35.4 per cent from August 2025."
The agency also said that 34,800 commercial transport trucks entered Canada using the Gordie Howe Bridge last month.
"Commercial transport truck entries at Windsor's other ports increased by 0.4 per cent from the same period one year earlier to total 87,400," it added.
Miller said traffic volumes at the three crossings are likely to shift in the months ahead as the "novelty effect" of taking the brand new Gordie Howe bridge wears off.
In any case, he said the traffic volumes at the new span being nearly as high as those at the Ambassador Bridge show "the need for that second crossing."

Argentine judge orders halt to Falklands oil project as tensions with Britain rise
An Argentine judge has ordered British and Israeli companies to stop developing an oilfield off the British-controlled Falkland Islands
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- An Argentine federal judge on Wednesday ordered British and Israeli companies to stop developing an oilfield off the Falkland Islands, opening a new legal front in the decades-old sovereignty dispute between Argentina and Britain that Argentine President Javier Milei has revived in recent weeks.
The injunction by Judge Mariel Borruto, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, targets the Sea Lion oil project 220 kilometers (140 miles) north of the British-controlled archipelago in the South Atlantic, barring drilling, offshore installations and port construction until Argentine authorities can conduct an environmental review and issue a decision.
But in practice, Wednesday's order is unlikely to halt progress on the project. Judge Borruto acknowledged that enforcement “depends on international cooperation and the conduct” of the two companies, Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration, which have already vowed to press ahead with the project despite Milei's threats of tougher sanctions against them and other companies operating around the islands.
Rockhopper declined to comment, and Navitas did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the injunction.
With its commercial oil production expected to start in 2028, Sea Lion has raised the stakes of a territorial dispute that led Britain and Argentina to a short and bloody war in 1982.
For the territory’s roughly 3,500 residents, the oilfield promises to transform an economy long dependent on fishing. For Argentina, which calls the islands the Malvinas, the project would allow foreign companies to extract oil riches it regards as its own. Its claim to the archipelago, roughly 480 kilometers (300 miles) off its coast, is enshrined in the constitution and woven into national identity, drawing support across the country’s political divisions.
U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Argentina's radical libertarian leader, has brought new uncertainty to the dispute in recent weeks. Citing Britain’s lack of support for his war against Iran, he has suggested that Washington could change its historically neutral stance on the islands’ sovereignty.
Speaking to reporters in Dublin on Saturday, Trump again expressed skepticism that Britain would be able to retake the Falklands as it did after Argentina's military dictatorship invaded in 1982, saying, “I don’t know if they’re going to be willing to travel that far."
Milei seized on what he called “winds of change” following Trump’s comments earlier this month, using a Sept. 3 national address to announce measures against companies developing oilfields around the islands. He warned that the projects posed a “clear and urgent danger” to Argentina’s sovereignty claim and pledged to use all “diplomatic, economic, judicial and legal tools” to defend it.
His administration is now preparing legislation to broaden sanctions against companies involved in oil projects around the islands and filed three criminal complaints against Tel Aviv-listed Navitas and nine other companies and their executives, accusing them of violating Argentine law by pursuing oil operations without the country's authorization. It's unclear what impact the charges have on the project.
Britain has responded to the Argentine government’s legal campaign with defiance. It argues that the people who live in the Falklands should determine its status, citing the results of a 2013 referendum in which islanders overwhelmingly voted to remain a British territory.
“Argentine domestic law does not apply within the Islands,” the British government said Tuesday in guidance aimed at reassuring businesses operating there.
Wednesday's ruling issued by the federal court in Argentina's southernmost province of Tierra del Fuego stems from a separate civil lawsuit brought by environmental lawyers and veterans of the 1982 war seeking to prevent environmental damage from the project. The complaint cites ecological threats ranging from chemical pollution and underwater noise to ship traffic and potential oil spills.
Borruto warned that allowing drilling and construction to proceed could alter the marine ecosystem in ways that would be difficult to reverse.
“The risk is neither hypothetical nor remote,” she wrote, noting that work on the project’s infrastructure had already begun.

Associated Press writer Débora Rey contributed to this report.

Virender Sehwag-hosted reality series “Rise & Fall Season 2” is heading to Prime Video this September, with the first four of 15 contestants set to compete across the 42-day run confirmed.
The Banijay Asia production will be available free of charge on Prime Video and the MX Player Android app – the latter now operating under its refreshed identity as MX Player by Prime Video – with new episodes releasing daily. The four names confirmed are Swara Bhasker, Shehzad Poonawalla, Priyanka Chahar Choudhary and Karan Patel, with the remaining 11 yet to be announced.
The series, adapted from the hit U.K. format originally created by Studio Lambert, is built around a shifting hierarchy in which players move between Ruler and Worker positions, with their standing shaped by in-game decisions rather than scripted outcomes.
Popular on Variety
Chahar Choudhary, who has prior reality-television credits, said: “I’ve experienced reality television in different forms, but ‘Rise & Fall Season 2’ brings a whole new dimension to the game. The idea of going from being a Ruler to a Worker and having your position shaped by the choices you make, makes this experience especially exciting for me. Reality shows have taught me to trust my instincts, stay true to myself and play every moment as it comes, but this time, the power dynamics add an entirely different layer. I’m ready to step into the game, take on whatever position comes my way and see how far I can rise.”
Bhasker said: “I’ve always been someone who wears her opinions on her sleeve, so entering a game like ‘Rise & Fall Season 2’ is going to be quite an experience. The show brings together personalities with very different perspectives, and when power and strategy come into play, I’m sure those differences will make for some fascinating dynamics. I’m excited to see how it all unfolds.”
Patel, known for a long run in Indian television drama, said: “People have seen me play different characters and tell stories through television all these years, but ‘Rise & Fall Season 2’ gives me the chance to enter a completely different arena as myself. What excites me is the competitive side of it having to make a move, back your decision and keep pushing yourself when the game shifts. I’m looking forward to embracing that challenge and giving this game everything I’ve got.”
Poonawalla added: “My life and journey has been synonymous with rise and fall. Literally this show espouses my journey and even as one chapter ends – a new chapter in life begins with its own set of challenges and opportunities. ‘Rise & Fall Season 2’ feels like a particularly interesting innings for me. I’ve always enjoyed spaces where there is room for a strong point of view and this game brings together people with very different perspectives and ways of looking at things but they must know by now I have zero tolerance for those who try to belittle Bharat and its history. It will be interesting to see how absolute strangers walk into a situation where they have to ally at times or be on opposite sides at other times. On a lighter note – I’m glad I don’t have to pay rent for the next six weeks.”
“Rise & Fall Season 2” streams free from Sept. 26 on Prime Video and the MX Player Android app.

New Delhi, December 1975. It was love at first sight when a Swedish hippy called Lotta von Schedvin sat down to be sketched by an Indian street artist, Pradyumna Kumar Mahanandia, known to everyone as PK. In the 10 minutes it took PK to complete her portrait, everything clicked into place for the pair. They were swept headlong in a whirlwind romance, and PK took Lotta to his village in the east of India to meet his family. But soon after, the time came for Lotta to pack up her VW campervan and head back home with her friends.
Heart-stricken PK promised to follow, but a plane ticket to Sweden was an impossible dream. Determined not to lose the love of his life, PK bought a secondhand Raleigh bike, and with $80 sewn into the waistband of his trousers, set off to cycle 6,000 miles to Lotta. He knew the sun set in the west, so that was the direction he took. His plan was to follow the hippy trail, cycling through India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, crossing Europe, finally arriving in Sweden.
Actually, he was heading to Switzerland until a fellow backpacker pointed out that Switzerland and Sweden were two different countries. In a new Netflix documentary, The Cycle of Love, PK jokes that his strength was his fuzzy grasp of European geography. Watching the film, you wonder if his superpower might have been his smile – warm and joyous, it lights the room. Either way, he made it to Sweden. The journey took 123 days, and ended up involving a flight or two, and a couple of trains. In May 1977, PK knocked on Lotta’s door in Borås, Sweden. They have been together ever since.
Documentary-maker Orlando von Einsiedel first heard about the story when he gave a talk in Sweden. “At the end, two young people came up and handed me a book,” he says. “They said: ‘This is about our parents’ story. We know your work. Would you be interested in this as a film?’” The book was The Amazing Story of the Man Who Cycled from India to Europe for Love by Swedish journalist Per J Andersson.
The two young people were PK and Lotta’s grownup kids Emilie and Karl. Von Einsiedel politely took the book but didn’t think too much about it. “Normally in my experience, when somebody approaches you and says ‘I’ve got a brilliant story’, it doesn’t work out.”
A couple of months later, Von Einsiedel picked up the book as a holiday read, opening it on the flight out of London. “The moment I started I thought, ‘Oh my God, you idiot Orlando! This is extraordinary.’” It wasn’t just the against-all-odds, 6,000-mile cycle ride, PK’s story was a tale of fate and destiny. When he was born, the astrologer in his village made four predictions about his future wife: she would be a Taurus, born outside India, musical and own a jungle. So naturally the first question he asked Lotta was: “Are you a Taurus?” Her answer was yes. She was also a gifted musician, and – most bonkers of all – her family owned land with a forest in Sweden.
“When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true,” says Von Einsiedel, cheerful and chatty on a video call from New York. The previous night he attended the US premiere of The Cycle of Love with PK and Lotta, who have been happily married for nearly 50 years. The pair have been getting the celebrity treatment wherever they go. “Everybody in the cinema stands up for them, people are weeping when they come on stage.” What do the couple make of the film? He grins. “I know they like it, because whenever they go to a festival, they watch every single screening from beginning to end.” How many times have they seen it? “A lot.”
The film tells their story with enormous warmth. It includes a dramatisation of the epic ride, with PK played by the British-based Indian actor Chirag Lobo, and Mina Dale as Lotta. Everybody else is non-professional, explains Von Einsiedel. “Our producers would go out and street-cast people on the morning of filming.”
What about the script, I ask? There are gorgeous, heartwarming scenes as PK shares his story with people he meets on the road, who in return tell him about their life and loves. How were those scenes scripted? “No script. Everything is improvised. When PK interacts with everyday people he meets along the way, those are just normal conversations about love and hopes and dreams.”
Wasn’t that a bit risky – getting a plane to India with two actors, no script and trusting that deep and meaningful conversations would materialise from conversations with ordinary people? “Massively risky, except I tested if it might work in Lewisham town centre,” Von Einsiedel says, grinning. “I have a friend who’s an actor. We went to Lewisham with a bike.” Armed with a notepad, his friend told people that he was cycling from London to Cape Town for love. “He pretended to draw portraits. What was extraordinary is the first person he sat down to draw turned around and said: ‘I love your story. I’ll buy you a plane ticket immediately.’”
It’s the kindness of strangers that makes the documentary so uplifting. When PK cycles out of Kabul, he stops to help an Austrian backpacker, Linea, who crashed her car, knocking out most of her teeth. He stays with her for several days at hospital, even though it means his visa expiring and further delay. Later, when he arrives in Istanbul and checks his post, there is a train ticket to Vienna – a thank you from Linea for his kindness.
What struck Von Einsiedel when he met the real-life PK was that his story about love went beyond boy-meets-girl. “For me, it’s not just about romantic love. It’s about self-love and love for all the people that we share this planet with.” PK was born into a dalit family, the marginalised group in India formerly known as “untouchables”. At school, he was made to sit outside during lessons and not allowed to play with the other children. Even after he won a scholarship to study fine art in Delhi, he experienced periods of homelessness and isolation.
“From the moment I started talking to PK it became clear what a difficult and traumatic childhood he’d had,” Von Einsiedel says. “He spoke so movingly about being on the journey and how it was the first time that strangers would touch him and hug him. That it was key to him starting to believe in himself and love himself. He said: ‘How can you love anybody if you can’t love yourself?’ I get emotional just saying that.”
PK explained how he felt accepted on the journey, hanging out with hippies and locals in the villages and towns he passed through. People with very little offered him hospitality, a meal or a roof for the night. In the documentary, this warm feeling of togetherness thuds to the ground when PK arrives in Europe, grilled by hostile and overtly racist German border officers. “That was his first experience,” says Von Einsiedel. “He travelled through all these countries, Afghanistan and Iran, and everybody treated him with respect. Then as soon as he got to Europe he immediately experienced racism.”
Von Einsiedel grew up in south London. At university he studied social anthropology and in his 20s was a professional snowboarder. “I learned the craft of film-making making snowboard films,” he says. “When I knew how to do that, I segued into making films about social issues I believed in.” He started working with Al Jazeera, travelling to conflict zones.
In 2015, he was nominated for an Oscar for his first full-length documentary, Virunga, about the battle to save a national park in eastern Congo, home to some of the world’s last mountain gorillas. His documentary short, White Helmets, following Syrian volunteers rescuing civilians, won an Oscar. Next he made Evelyn, an incredibly moving film in which Von Einsiedel turned the camera on his own family. His brother Evelyn took his own life aged 22 over a decade earlier. In the film, Von Einsiedel and his two surviving siblings hiked the routes their brother loved to walk with friends and family. “I was very emotionally closed for a long time after my brother died,” he says. “I used to think being emotionally open was a sign of weakness. I was terrified of my own emotions. I see the opposite now. I think being emotionally open is a sign of strength.”
When it comes to picking a subject for a new documentary, he says he is attracted to people who inspire him. “I’m drawn to stories that show the better side of human beings. That’s a thread that runs through the work I like to make.” The Cycle of Love is by far the sunniest film he has made to date. What’s that all about, I ask? “I wanted to make an optimistic film that’s about joy and human connection. The world is difficult. Love is one of those things that all of us can agree on. This story just felt so important to tell.”

For over a month and a half, residents of Chitpur Jyotinagar Colony in Cossipore, North Kolkata, have been without regular water supply after five public taps serving the colony ran dry following pipeline work in the area. Home to around 5,000 people, the 200-metre-long stretch is largely inhabited by people belonging to the Muslim community, and from lower-income backgrounds.
Residents, whose daily lives and livelihoods have been disrupted, alleged that water supply has been deliberately cut off by the state’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government to target them on the basis of their identities and force them out of the slum.
It is worth noting days after the election results were declared, local BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari had pledged not to do anything for Muslims in his constituency. “Today, in front of Baba Bholenath, I swear, I will not do one job for them (Muslims) in the next five years. Will not issue any certificate for them. I am saying this live. I do not care about what anyone else says or thinks,” he had said.
Residents of Jyotinagar this colony, around 95% of them Muslims, depend on informal jobs for their sustenance. While women manage household chores in the morning before working at nearby factories in the afternoon, where they clean glass bottles and break glass panels into shards, most men work as daily wage labourers, masons, drivers, rickshaw pullers, or at factories.
How Did Water Supply Stop?
Alt News visited the water-deprived area, located a few meters from the over 200-years-old Cossipore Gun and Shell factory. The colony has five taps, which used to supply water from 5 am to 11 pm daily. Since July 29, after water supply was cut off, all five taps have been dry, locals said.
Locals said that water supply was perfectly normal and no complaints from the neighbourhood was made to the local civic body or any authorities, and yet, pipeline work was carried out in the area by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) from July 26-28.
“Pipeline work was happening, they had dug two pits, one at the beginning of the slum and another at the end, marking the slum. On July 28, the water supply stopped around 11 pm. The next morning, we were waiting for the water supply to return. It has not been restored since,” said a resident, Mohinudeen Sheikh.
Sheikh, along with other residents, alleged that the pipelines were shut during the night while the roads were being repaired. “They used the cover of midnight to close the pipelines and mend the streets. We had no water from the early morning onwards,” he claimed.
‘They Also Took Away Electricity’
Residents said the water crisis was accompanied by a disruption in electricity supply as well. “They took away both water and electricity,” one youth said.
“They thought we were drawing electricity illegally from the main line, so they stopped the supply,” said a resident, Pinki Bibi. “All our houses have separate electricity connections and we receive separate bills. Then how can they say we are drawing electricity illegally?”
Residents claimed that electricity was restored after more than a week, following an incident during the Kanwar Yatra when poor visibility allegedly led some Kanwariyas to fall into the pothole-ridden lane. Alamgir Biswas, secretary of the Jyotinagar Colony, said that the supply was restored 10-15 days after the Basti Unnayan Samiti protested against the disruption.
Locals alleged that Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation (CESC) said the main-road connection had been shut to verify whether allegations of illegal electricity tapping were true. However, electricity supply remained available in the lanes branching off the main road. After seven days, CESC was able to verify that no illegal tapping was taking place and restored the connection, they added.
‘They are Trying to Evict Us’
Residents alleged that the disruption of these essential services was a part of a concerted attempt to evict the slum dwellers. Alamgir alleged: “The plan was to cut off the basic needs of water and electricity so that we leave the area. In this area, there is absolute communal harmony. Hindus and Muslims live harmoniously together. However, this government is trying to create a rift between us.”
Morjina Begum, who works at the glass factory, also alleged, “They are trying to evict us from this colony and therefore employing these tricks of cutting off the water supply. We are not new to this place. I was born here. My grandfather had settled here years ago,” while asserting, “We are not going to leave this place so easily. We will fight.”
Begum said residents had also approached the local councillor, Suman Singh, but has received no meaningful assistance as of yet. Alt News tried to speak to Singh, but he did not answer our calls till press time.
Saraswati Biswas, a 60-year-old Hindu resident, alleged that Tiwari, the newly elected MLA, had referred to the residents as “Bangladeshis and encroachers”. “He is calling us Bangladeshis and encroachers. How am I a Bangladeshi? My forefathers used to live here. I have proper documents proving that I am an Indian. I voted this year,” she said.
Legal Entanglement With Kolkata Port
While investigating the possible reason behind the elongated water supply disruption, Alt News found an intricate legal entanglement between the residents of the colony and the authorities of the Kolkata port.
As per legal records, the entire colony is built on a parcel of land measuring approximately 3478 square metres officially belonging to the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata. On February 23, the estate officer of the port issued an eviction order for the colony.
Alt News accessed the order, and found that it was issued based on the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. The notice terms the residents of Jyotinagar Colony as ‘unauthorised occupants and/or trespasser to the port property’. The estate officer ordered the residents to vacate the land within 15 days of date of publication of this notice. Before the eviction order was passed, a hearing took place, wherein, port authorities submitted that ‘there is potential threat to communal unrest’ due to the existence of the colony.
According to legal documents accessed by Alt News, the residents of the colony came to know about the existence of this eviction order on June 9. The residents alleged that after the change of government in West Bengal, local BJP supporters started to campaign for the demolition of the slum. The locals claimed that they began deeming the colony as “a den of illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators”.
In order to seek legal protection from the eviction drive, residents appealed before the chief judge of the city civil court, Calcutta, however, on August 18, the court declined to grant any immunity from eviction to them.
The Port authorities in their submission before the city civil court had mentioned that ‘unlawful activities’ were ongoing in the colony. They described the premises as congested and unsafe for human habitation, citing the presence of inflammable materials and several uninsulated electrical wires that could potentially cause a fire. They also lodged two police complaints at the North Port police station on September 9, 2020 and July 25, 2022.
On August 19, the residents appeared before the Calcutta high court, seeking protection from eviction. The court granted an interim stay order on the eviction process till September 18. In the meantime, the water and electricity disruptions happened, which residents believe was done to purposely disrupt their lives to expedite the eviction.
Nine residents of the colony: Alamgir Biswas, Pinki Bibi, Mafajel Gazi, Sk Mainuddin, Rahima Bibi, Saraswati Biswas, Anita Prasad, Lima Bibi and Bonani Bibi appeared as petitioners before the high court. In their appeal, the residents had informed the HC that although the proceedings recorded before the estate officer of Kolkata Port mentioned two persons: Hafizul and Tarcina Bibi as respondents from the colony, the order does not record that any notice for eviction, under section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, was issued publicly.
It was also submitted before the HC that the order issued by the Kolkata Port does not record that the petitioners were called upon to show cause against the proposed eviction, were afforded an opportunity to produce evidence or were given an opportunity of personal hearing.
According to Section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, all concerned persons, that is all persons who are in occupation of the public premises, have to be given the opportunity to show cause why they wouldn’t be evicted.
Section 4(3) of the Act clearly mentions: The estate officer shall cause the notice to be served by having it affixed on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the public premises, and in such other manner as may be prescribed, whereupon the notice shall be deemed to have been duly given to all persons concerned. However, the order issued by the estate officer makes no mention of any such notice being issued or served. This issue was also raised in the petition before the high court.
A team of lawyers including Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya, Samim Ahammed, Md Nasirul Hoque and Ivi Banerjee represented the residents legally. Speaking to Alt News, Ahammed said, “The Port authorities are claiming that the land in question is their property. But in reality, it is public property. Therefore, a government body like the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, must ensure the fundamental rights of the public, in this case, their right to shelter.”
The State has the power to regulate and make sure people follow the law and cannot occupy public property illegally. They are exercising this power through the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. But while doing this, the State cannot treat people unfairly or take away someone’s home and leave them without shelter. Having a place to live and being able to live with dignity are part of a person’s inalienable rights protected by the Constitution, he explained.
Simultaneously with the HC appeal, another appeal was submitted by the residents before the chief judge of the city civil court seeking the restoration of water connection. This prayer, however, is still pending.
According to the port authorities, the total damage incurred due to the existence of the colony, starting from 1990, has reached approximately over Rs 61 crore. As per the legal records, the estimated monthly damage amount is calculated to be more than Rs 19 lakh rupees, and the port is losing more than Rs 2 crore annually in terms of revenue due to the colony.
Questions Of ‘Communal Targeting’
The geographical location of the water disruption has become a point of contention for residents, who have alleged that this is a form of communal targeting.
When one walks along Khagendra Chatterjee Lane towards the Ganges, with the Gun and Shell Factory on the right, the road turns left towards the river after two temples, and becomes Chitpur Strand Road. The Cossipore Jetty is on the right, followed by Jyotinagar Colony.
Residents showed Alt News the two points where pipeline work had been carried out. They said the entire stretch between the two points had remained without water. They also alleged that the points where the road was dug up correspond to the boundaries of Jyotinagar Colony, which has a predominantly Muslim population. According to the residents, taps immediately before and after this stretch, located in predominantly Hindu residential areas, continue to receive water.
Alt News checked the taps inside the colony and found them dry. Taps located immediately before and after the stretch where the pipeline work had been carried out, however, had water supply. We found that the tap directly opposite a temple, just before the first point where the road had allegedly been dug up, had water supply. The tap at the other end, near the second point where digging had taken place, also had water. In between, however, an approximately 150-metre stretch, had no water supply.
‘A Basic Need’
For residents, the suspension of water has led to tremendous daily struggle. “Water is a basic need. There are so many people in our colony, and there is no water. People have to stand in queues to fetch water from the taps that are present in the nearby areas. Though people are sharing their taps, they prioritise their own needs. This affects our work,” a resident said.
A woman in her mid-twenties, while cleaning utensils, showed buckets filled with water fetched from the river. “Look at the condition of the water we are using to clean. It is so muddy and filthy. At this point, all we can hope is we don’t fall ill,” she said.
The monsoon season has made it more difficult. “The water level is very high in Ganga now, so it becomes dangerous to bathe in the river or fetch water. The river water is muddy and unfit for consumption. But we are left with no option,” an elderly woman said. “We are scared that our children will develop skin infections. There are already a few cases,” said a woman in her thirties, while standing in queue to bathe her children.
Residents have to walk some distance from their colony to a functioning tap to fill water, which they then transport back on vans.
Locals Allege Administrative Apathy
Alamgir elaborated that after water and electricity supply was cut off on July 29, the following day, locals reached the corporation office and complained. “They took my number and told us that they would look into the matter. But nothing happened. On the following day, we submitted a written complaint at the main corporation office in Hatibagan. They also told us they would try to look into it. However, as everyone can see, nothing has changed as of yet,” he said.
Several residents had approached the local police station, the councillor, and MLA Tiwari, seeking their intervention, but no official visited the colony to inspect the reality so far, they lamented. Residents also said that when a group of women approached Tiwari, he dismissed them stating he was not responsible for the disruption of water supply and refused to restore it.
Further, Pinki Bibi alleged that Tiwari had used communal slurs and threatened the locals with eviction. “While talking to the people, he threatened them, ‘If I want, I could demolish the mosque that was built in the colony. And evict the entire colony with it,’” she said.
Morjina Begum told Alt News that residents believe they are being purposely treated this way because of their Muslim identities. Asked why they felt this was the case, she referred to speeches by chief minister Suvendu Adhikari and the local MLA following their election victories, in which they said they would not work for Muslims because Muslims had not voted for them. “Where are we supposed to go? There are so many of us?” she asked.
Also Read: I swear I won’t do anything for Muslims, says Bengal BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari
Burdened by the uncertainties of their future in the colony, an elderly woman in her 70s, sitting on the threshold of her house, said, “I pray that in my next life I am not born as a Muslim in this country.”
On September 9, Minakshi Mukherjee, CPI(M)’s central committee member, visited the locality along with other workers and leaders, and expressed her solidarity with the residents and protested against the eviction drive. At the initiative of the party, a water tanker visits the colony every two to three days to provide residents with an alternative source of water.
MLA Ritesh Tiwari Responds
When Alt News asked Tiwari about the predicament of people in his constituency, he distanced himself from the issue, saying, “The plot belongs to the Port. The people have a feud with the Port. The Port had ordered them to vacate. Later, the high court ordered them to refrain from taking temporary coercive action. The water supply is provided by the KMC. So, what role do I play here? What can I say here? The matter is sub judice, and it is better for political leaders to refrain from making any comments.”

The Himalayas are melting faster - and India's economy is 'at risk'
- Published
The Himalayas are approaching a dangerous threshold as glaciers melt faster, glacial lakes grow more unstable and the mountains face a widening gap in monitoring, according to new research.
The findings come in the aftermath of devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, which killed more than 1,300 people and caused widespread destruction, highlighting the growing risks from a rapidly changing Himalayan environment.
Himalayan glaciers are now losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, the report by global consultancy Systemiq, produced with the Integrated Mountain Initiative and with technical contributions from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and GB Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment, says.
Yet only about 21 of the estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Himalaya-Karakoram region are being monitored in detail and on a sustained basis, according to the report.
That monitoring gap matters because the physical landscape is changing rapidly.
As glaciers retreat, they can leave behind expanding lakes held back by unstable deposits of rock and ice. At the same time, warming is destabilising permafrost - permanently frozen ground that can thaw as temperatures rise - and high mountain slopes, increasing the possibility of cascading hazards, the report says.
India already has evidence of the scale of the risk.
Some 18% of Indian land is Himalayan, yet the region accounts for about 35% of disasters, according to the report.
The government told parliament in July that 56 glacial lakes had been classified as "very high risk", external following a 2025 scientific assessment of 189 high-risk lakes in the Indian Himalayan region. The Central Water Commission is monitoring 2,485 glacial lakes larger than 10 hectares across India's Himalayan river basins, the government said.
The Himalayas have already seen devastating examples of what can happen when glacial lakes burst their natural dams.
In 2023, a glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim killed at least 70 people and caused widespread damage to roads, bridges and hydropower projects. In 2021, a similar disaster in Uttarakhand killed more than 200 people after a massive flood swept through the Rishiganga and Dhauliganga valleys.
But the danger is not confined to spectacular floods.
The Himalayas are a vast natural water system feeding rivers that sustain hundreds of millions of people across South Asia. ICIMOD says "peak water", external is expected around mid-century in most Hindu Kush Himalayan river basins - the point at which glacier runoff reaches its maximum before declining as glaciers lose mass.
The new research puts an unusually large economic number on that dependency.
It estimates that Himalayan water underpins roughly 20% of India's GDP, sustaining wheat, rice, tea, hydropower and pilgrimage economies. Yet the mountain states capture only about 5% of that value, it says.
"The Himalayas are the Third Pole," said economist Lord Nicholas Stern, chair of the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the London School of Economics. "Unlike the Arctic or Antarctic, this pole has hundreds of millions of people living beneath it."
"This is national and international infrastructure," he said, warning that the ecological system underpinning it is "approaching a tipping point".
Not all the forces driving glacier loss are beyond the region's control.
The Systemiq research estimates that roughly a third of Himalayan glacier melt is driven by black carbon, much of it originating from brick kilns in the plains. Soot deposited on snow and ice absorbs more sunlight and accelerates melting.
Unlike global greenhouse-gas emissions, black-carbon pollution is a lever that India and its neighbours can act on directly, the report argues.
"The Himalayas are approaching a tipping point, with millions of lives and livelihoods hanging in the balance," said Arushi Chopra, Systemiq's senior director and lead author. "Glaciers are melting faster than they were a decade ago."
The report proposes 10 priority transitions, ranging from reducing black-carbon emissions and expanding glacier monitoring to improving disaster early-warning systems and changing the way tourism is developed in the mountains.
One priority is to strengthen disaster preparedness, with governments agreeing in advance what action to take when hazards emerge - from evacuation to protecting vulnerable infrastructure.
Another is to rethink tourism. The Indian Himalayan region receives roughly 400 million tourist visits a year, according to the report, and researchers argue that the objective should shift from maximising visitor numbers towards generating value that is retained and reinvested locally.
Pema Gyamtsho, director general of ICIMOD, said the risks were becoming increasingly complex.
"Glaciers are retreating, permafrost and high-mountain slopes are becoming increasingly unstable, and communities and infrastructure downstream face growing risks from complex and cascading hazards," he said.
And those risks do not stop at the borders drawn across the Himalayas. Such hazards, Gyamtsho said, "do not respect national borders, and no single country can address them alone".
That makes cross-border monitoring, shared risk information and early-warning systems, and joint investment in resilience increasingly urgent - not just to save lives, but to protect the livelihoods and economies of hundreds of millions of people who depend on the mountains.

Amazon Prime Day events are some of the most confusing shopping occasions in existence: It’s not even a single “day" anymore. Amazon promises “millions of deals”—but the displayed discounts are often misleading, and while it’s advertised as a members-only event, some deals are available to people who don’t subscribe to Prime. Add in the frenzy of limited-time Lightning Deals and you’ve got a perfect recipe for spending too much money on stuff you don't even really want.
Fear not! I've been covering deals for over a decade and am here to help. WIRED’s Reviews team is familiar with common shopping pitfalls, and we closely track the best Prime Big Deal Days prices. What time do sales start and end? How do you tell whether a deal is actually a deal? We pooled our collective expertise to get you prepared for the latest Amazon Prime Day Event, which is technically dubbed “Amazon Prime Big Deal Days” and will be on October 6 and October 7 this year.
When Is Amazon Prime Day?
Amazon Prime Day has a main sale in the summer and a secondary sale—called Prime Big Deal Days—in the fall. This year, Prime Big Deal Days will take place on Tuesday and Wednesday, October 6 and October 7.
When Do Prime Day Deals Start?
The event kicks off at 3:01 am Eastern time (midnight Pacific) and runs for 48 hours. New deals will drop three times each day of the event, at 3 am, 11 am, and 4 pm ET, with Lightning Deals going live sporadically as well. WIRED will cover the best deals from both Amazon and retailers that have competing sales.
Are Prime Day Deals Only for Prime Members?
That's the official line: You need to be an Amazon Prime member to shop Amazon Prime Day deals. There is a free 30-day trial available for eligible new accounts. (Prime membership comes with a lot of perks, and we've rounded up all of them here.) The trial will let you get in on the sale—just remember to cancel your membership to avoid any subsequent $15 monthly renewal charges.
However, there are usually plenty of discounts available if you're not a subscriber. Other major retailers like Best Buy, Target, and Walmart typically hold competing sales during Prime Days. The prices are often close to what Amazon is offering on the same products, and sometimes the competing sales match the Prime Day price exactly. This is a good way to save even if you object to shopping on Amazon.
Is Prime Day Worth It?
It depends. For some items, Prime-exclusive event prices tend to be among the lowest we see all year. That's especially true for Amazon hardware, like Kindles, Fire tablets, Fire TV sticks, and Echo devices. The kicker is that prices on nearly everything fluctuate throughout the year, and some products are discounted on a frequent basis. Even if the price is good, a deal on a product that goes on sale all the time diminishes the overall quality of that offer.
The sheer volume of deals promoted by Amazon during sales like Prime Day is a blessing and a curse. The truly standout discounts can be difficult to pinpoint—there's so much stuff on sale that just browsing the site can feel overwhelming. But if you're in the market for something specific, there's a good chance the item you want will be discounted. We've seen some fantastic Prime-exclusive discounts in the past, ranging from dirt-cheap Kindles and video doorbells to elusive price drops on gaming consoles and office furniture. The tricky part is finding the diamonds in the rough.
WIRED covers legitimately good deals all year long, including during Prime Day. Our policy is to only cover deals on products someone from our team has personally used and would buy or has bought themselves, to avoid promoting cheap junk. Maybe it'll be a product we've reviewed or an item we use in our day-to-day lives. We also only cover actual deals—if the price isn't lower than it normally is, we don't include it. We aim to provide pricing context as well. Our tips below will help you find those great discounts on your own—in the same ways that we would. No gatekeeping here.
How Do I Know Whether a Deal Is Good?
ABC: Always be checking (prices, that is). Researching an item's price is the most important aspect of determining the quality of a discount. Don't fall prey to deceptive marketing language and inflated MSRP prices. The easiest step is to take a second to Google the items you're considering so you can see the price across multiple stores. Amazon product pages now feature a Price History link to see up to 365 days of pricing history, though it may not always be accurate.
One tool we use is CamelCamelCamel, which tracks Amazon's prices over time. Paste the Amazon link or ASIN (found in the Product Information section on the Amazon product page) into CamelCamelCamel's search bar to see the item's lowest recorded price and its average price, and how frequently the price fluctuates. Some deals, such as Lightning Deals, are excluded from the pricing history, but this works for most items. It's useful to see what an item has sold for in the past. And while Amazon's Alexa for Shopping chatbot has price history information, it isn't always reliable and often misses context (as evidenced by our personal testing). We also like Keepa, which has an extension (available for multiple browsers) that shows the recent price history for products directly on the Amazon page so you don't have to open a new tab. When in doubt, check multiple sources.
Keep in mind that these services may not work all the time. But being able to see how much a product costs right before the sale starts (and whether the MSRP happened to increase) can be helpful. Putting these tools together can help you deduce whether a deal is worth your money.
WIRED always fact-checks deals to determine their quality. Of course, I'm biased, but you can check out our ongoing deals coverage to find roundups of the best discounts available—during Prime Big Deal Days and beyond.
What Are Lightning Deals?
Lightning Deals are limited-time deals that Amazon runs for only a few hours. They're not restricted to Prime Day, but they're especially prevalent during major sales events. Once an item sells out, you may be able to join a wait list, but not always.
Put bluntly, the Lightning Deals selection is often full of impulse buys, like makeup, skin care products, or toys. Prime members can browse upcoming deals on Amazon's website and in the mobile app. The app can also alert you before a Lightning Deal begins. We'll share some of our favorite Lightning Deals in a live blog during the event this year.
Be sure to also keep an eye on Amazon Haul, Amazon's discount page featuring novelties, fashion accessories, and gadgets starting at $1. Additional discounts are rumored to be dropping on holiday decor and tailgating items.
Are There Other Ways to Make Sure a Deal Won’t Sell Out?
If you know what time a deal begins, make sure to pay attention to the product page around the starting time. You may also be able to add an item to your cart before the sale starts, so you can refresh the page and snag it right away. With the Amazon app (Android, iOS), you can set up personalized deal alerts to get notified when items you have searched for recently are on sale, but only if you're a Prime member.
It's smart to create an account at trusted retailers so you can save your credit card information and shipping details ahead of time. This will make the checkout process as fast as possible. It's also a good idea to clear your web browser cache before you start shopping during sales events like Prime Day. Just be sure to log back in to those retailers afterward.
If a deal does sell out, there's a high chance another store will be offering a similar or matching discount. Check other stores, especially big-box merchants like Walmart, Target, and Best Buy. Sometimes expired deals can come back in stock, too.
You may also be able to use Amazon's Alexa for Shopping AI assistant to set deal alerts. But keep in mind that sometimes the notification system is dodgy. It can be useful, but if you're set on getting something specific, you should keep a close eye on it regardless of any AI tools you use.
Should I Buy It?
It's easy to fall into a trap during events like Prime Day. You might see a great deal on a product you don't really need. Don't do it. Make a list of items you've actually been wanting to buy ahead of the event and save those links. When Prime Day begins, take a look around to see whether they're on sale, and use the aforementioned practices to make sure it truly is a good deal. Don't buy a product just because it has a nice price.
This isn't your last chance to score a great deal this year—there's always Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which take place around Thanksgiving weekend. You might see even bigger price drops then.

Philippines' Duterte seen in person at International Criminal Court for first time
- Published
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte has appeared in person at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, where he is due to be tried for alleged crimes against humanity.
He is facing charges over his bloody war on drugs, which saw tens of thousands of small-time drug dealers allegedly executed summarily.
The 81-year-old wore a dark suit and white shirt on Wednesday, which marked the first time he has been seen in person since his arrest in Manila 18 months ago. He did not speak but waved at family members in the public gallery when proceedings ended.
Until now he had appeared before the court by video link and then skipped multiple hearings.
The ICC called a status hearing on Wednesday after Duterte's lawyers argued the former leader's deteriorating health had made him unfit to stand trial .
The first trial date is scheduled for 30 November.
The war on drugs was the centrepiece of Duterte's presidency, which ran from 2016 to 2022. He argued peace and order was necessary to grow the economy.
The ICC is looking at killings from 1 November 2011, when Duterte was mayor of Davao, a sprawling southern metropolis, until 16 March 2019, when he withdrew the Philippines' membership in the ICC.
Duterte's lawyer Peter Haynes recently told the court his client was suffering from "significant memory impairment", making him unable to engage with his legal team. Prosecutors argued otherwise.
Judges are deliberating whether Duterte is mentally fit to be tried and have ordered a medical assessment by three specialists.
That assessment has not been made public but according to AFP, defence lawyers say it shows Duterte thinks he is living in 2007 or 2008, that he is 84 or 85 years old, and was found to be unable to recall Donald Trump's name.
Relatives of those killed in Duterte's brutal anti-drugs campaign watched the proceedings over a livestream in Manila.
Llore Pasco, who lost two sons, told Reuters: "We're happy that he has finally appeared and that he looks OK. In fact, he looks like he has put on weight."
Randy Delos Santos, who lost his teenage nephew in 2017, told AFP he was happy to see Duterte in court, adding: "We hope that his being physically fit will help speed up the hearings."
In 2019, when he was still president, Duterte revealed he was suffering from myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune condition that causes nerve malfunction. At 71 in 2016, he was the oldest Philippine president at the time of election.
Duterte's family is currently caught in a high-stakes dynasty war for control of the Philippines. His daughter, Vice-President Sara Duterte, has feuded spectacularly with President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos.
The break-up of the Duterte-Marcos alliance, which helped them win the 2022 elections by a landslide, paved the way for the Rodrigo Duterte's arrest at Manila airport in March 2025.
Sara Duterte is a frontrunner to replace Marcos in the 2028 elections, where the incumbent is ineligible under the constitution to stand for a second term.
But she is also fighting for her political survival in an impeachment trial, where if convicted, she will be disqualified from running for public office.
She is charged with misusing public funds and threatening to have Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and Marcos' cousin, congressman Ferdinand Martin Romualdez assassinated.

Kolkata Police’s ₹89 lakh tender for orange T-shirts and caps for Durga Puja volunteers has triggered a political row, with TMC and Congress alleging “saffronisation”.
A political row erupted in West Bengal over a tender floated by the Kolkata Police to procure orange-coloured, full-sleeve T-shirts and peak caps for temporary volunteers during Durga Puja.
“An e-tender has been invited for the procurement of orange-coloured full-sleeve T-shirts and peak caps for temporary volunteers during the Durga Puja. The total estimated cost is ₹89 lakh,” a senior officer of Kolkata Police said.
Every year, the police recruit temporary volunteers for a 10-day period during Durga Puja to assist police personnel with crowd management at major intersections and arterial roads. National Cadet Corps (NCC) cadets, scouts, students and NGOs also serve as volunteers.
“While NCC cadets, scouts and students come in their uniforms, the full-sleeve T-shirts and caps will be given to volunteers recruited for a temporary period during the puja,” said the officer.
Around 20,000 such volunteers are deployed. “The colour will be changed this year from blue and white to orange. This will make the volunteers conspicuous and easily identifiable in the crowd,” another officer said.
This, however, triggered a political row in the state, with the Trinamool Congress (TMC) and the Congress alleging that it was an attempt to “saffronise” the police force.
“The BJP treats saffron as its party colour. The police are already behaving like BJP cadres and introducing saffron colour in uniform amounts to complete ‘saffronisation’. They have effectively put them in a ‘jersey’, and significant expenditure is being incurred to manufacture these new uniforms,” TMC spokesperson Kunal Ghosh said.
“They (BJP) are trying to mix administration and religion. They are trying to identify this government with a particular religious community. This government hasn’t done anything fruitful so far. The BJP is playing divisive politics,” Congress leader Soumya Aich Roy said.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), however, refuted the charges, saying that saffron is the first colour of the Indian flag from the top and symbolises courage and sacrifice.
“It doesn’t matter what the TMC or the Congress are saying. They always make baseless allegations. Saffron is the first colour on our National flag. It symbolises courage and sacrifice. UEFA remains on course to find a credible challenger to FIFA President Gianni Infantino and has not allowed its campaign for change to dissolve into wishful thinking, vice-president Laura McAllister said on Wednesday.
McAllister said the candidate for next March’s election need not be European but must be capable of defeating Infantino, uniting football’s confederations and delivering lasting governance reform.
Speaking to Reuters at the World Football Summit in Madrid after UEFA’s Executive Committee met in Thessaloniki, she rejected suggestions that opposition to Infantino had lost momentum despite the FIFA president appearing to retain enough support to win another term.
UEFA’s efforts were not about installing a European figurehead to lead a rebellion, she said, but building support for a candidate with a clear reform programme.
“I don’t think so,” McAllister said when asked whether Infantino’s opponents had overestimated the damage to his authority.
“We always knew that things wouldn’t just change overnight. That would be naive. We knew that there would be a resistance to change as well, of course.
“We’re taking things step by step, both legally in terms of the political context with an alternative candidate and in terms of the programme of governance reforms that we need to see.”

UEFA ‘UNITED AND VERY CONCERTED’
Swiss Italian Infantino, 56, faced the biggest challenge to his presidency following the collapse of his proposal to sell a stake of up to 20 percent in FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors.
The plan prompted fierce opposition, with UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF among those calling for change at the top of FIFA. Several European national associations have since withdrawn their support for Infantino’s re-election, with Greece becoming the latest on Tuesday.
McAllister said UEFA nations remained “united and very concerted” in their determination to change the way FIFA is governed, but stressed that the dispute went beyond Infantino.
“This was always about more than one person,” she said.
McAllister said UEFA had been working quietly on several fronts and regarded the reform platform as more important than the identity or nationality of the eventual candidate.
“There’s lots of prongs to any campaign to change something,” she said. “There’s tactics that you need to follow, but I feel very reassured that we’re on track, that we will try to find a candidate that can unite all of the confederations, because it’s not just UEFA; all of the confederations feel strongly about the need for change.
“And that candidate would then stand on a manifesto of reform and modernisation.”
Infantino has announced that he will seek another term at the election in March. McAllister said his opponents must find a candidate capable of doing more than mounting a symbolic challenge.
“If you’re in a position where you know the incumbent will be standing again, and Gianni Infantino has made it clear that he will be a candidate in the election unless something changes in the time before next March, then it’s incumbent on those who oppose him to get the right candidate,” she said.
“You don’t fight an election unless you can win that election.”
