According to The Information, Apple is planning to get back into the server game and might just pair up with NVIDIA to make it happen. Apple retired its Xserve line in 2011 and has largely left enterprise machines to other manufacturers since. But the growing demand for compute power as the AI industry continues to expand has apparently led the company to believe there is an opening for its powerful but efficient ARM-based M processors. Its Mac Mini and Mac Studio have proven popular with AI developers, which has led to shortages.
Apple might make servers again to cash in on the AI rush
The company could borrow tech from Nvidia to make it happen.
The server product, whether it’s called Xserve or something else, likely won’t debut until 2029. Word is that it will run on two or four (depending on the model) M8 Ultra chips. Apple only just announced the M6 in August, so the M8 line is a ways out.
It’s also rumored that Apple’s servers could incorporate Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion tech, which connects multiple chips together so they can operate as one. While the two companies have historically had a frosty relationship behind the scenes, recently Apple turned to Nvidia chips to power its revamped Siri servers. Incorporating NVLink could lead to further collaboration between the two, but plans could still change.

MindsEye developer Build A Rocket Boy is reportedly shutting down
Several employees have said they're leaving the studio.
Build A Rocket Boy (BARB), the developer of the widely maligned action-adventure game MindsEye, appears to be shutting down. Several employees wrote on LinkedIn that their time at the studio is "coming to an end," and Kotaku reported that BARB is set to close its doors for good.
"With a very heavy heart I raise my green banner, along with the rest of my colleagues at Build a Rocket Boy. I am 'Open to Work' actively looking for a new adventure," BARB's principal talent acquisition partner Dan Hawkins wrote, implying that all of the studio's employees are out of a job. "I will be seeing BARB through till the very end, helping wrap things up here in the HR department."
MindsEye had a disastrous debut in June 2025, with PlayStation said to have issued refunds to some players who checked out the game in its initial bug-riddled state. A round of layoffs followed soon after the Grand Theft Auto-esque game's release while BARB founder (and former GTA producer) Leslie Benzies reportedly blamed its woes on "saboteurs" inside and outside the company.
The studio released an expansion for MindsEye this spring. It contained a mission it claimed would expose some evidence of the purported conspiracy that ruined the game's chances for success. This had no juicy details about said "scandal" and was just a humdrum riff on a Hitman mission, according to Rock Paper Shotgun. The addition of multiplayer and a Rocket League-esque soccer mode this summer didn't exactly turn around MindsEye's fortunes either.
BARB became the sole publisher of MindsEye in March after parting ways with IOI Partners, an arm of 007 First Light developer IO Interactive. Further rounds of layoffs took place that month and in May.
Earlier this year, dozens of employees accused the studio of spying on them. According to the IWGB Game Workers Union, BARB "management installed invasive Teramind surveillance software onto their devices without their knowledge" and went beyond "monitoring workers' productivity or safeguarding the company's security by recording individuals in their homes and without their consent."

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

Fintech startup Lendingkart’s NBFC arm Lendingkart Finance has managed to trim its loss by 62% to ₹32.4 Cr for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 (Q1 FY27) from the ₹84.8 Cr loss incurred in the year-ago quarter. The loss also shrank dramatically on a sequential basis, down 73% from ₹121.9 Cr in Q4 FY26, signalling that the sharp deterioration seen through FY26 may be bottoming out. However, the topline also continued to shrink. Operating revenue fell 55% to ₹52.7 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹116.9 Cr in Q1 FY26. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, operating revenue rose about 15% from ₹45.9 Cr. Interest income declined 20% YoY to ₹38.9 Cr, while fees and commission income drag fell 78% to ₹15.3 Cr. Including other income of ₹1.8 Cr, total income for the quarter stood at ₹54.5 Cr, down 54.5% from ₹119.8 Cr a year earlier. The company also booked a net loss of ₹70 Lakh on fair value changes and a ₹80 Lakh loss on assignment of loans during the quarter. During the quarter, the NBFC transferred stressed loans worth ₹94.7 Cr in aggregate principal to an asset reconstruction company for a consideration of ₹2 Cr. Lendingkart Finance, founded in 2014 by Harshvardhan Lunia and Mukul Sachan, is a wholly owned subsidiary of Lendingkart Technologies and serves as the licensed lending vehicle for the group's MSME-focussed digital lending business. The company slipped into loss in FY25. Its net loss widened further through FY26, alongside a sharp pullback in disbursals and a leadership overhaul following Fullerton Financial Holdings' takeover — with former DBS Bank executive Prashant Prakash Joshi now serving as managing director and CEO. The company also remains party to a pending case before the NCLT Ahmedabad, filed by certain minority shareholders of Lendingkart Technologies alleging oppression and mismanagement. Zooming Into Lendingkart Finance's Q1 FY27 Expenses Total expenses for the quarter fell 58% to ₹97.5 Cr in the first quarter from ₹230.2 Cr in Q1 FY26, driven primarily by the narrower loss. Here is a breakdown of where the startup spent the most in the reported quarter: Impairment Of Financial Instruments: This fell the sharpest among expense heads, dropping 83%to ₹13.2 Cr from ₹78.5 Cr in Q1 FY26. Finance Costs: Spending under this head nearly halved, falling 53% to ₹26.3 Cr from ₹55.8 Cr. Employee Benefit Expenses: Expenses towards paying salaries, wages, gratuity fund and provident fund, came down 18% to ₹25.4 Cr from ₹30.8 Cr.

US accuses Russia of trying to kill Ukrainian allies overseas
- Published
The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has accused Russia of plotting to murder Ukrainian allies in the US and Europe.
In a statement on Tuesday, the DoJ charged five men allegedly connected to the Russian Intelligence Services (RIS). The men are accused of paying, or trying to pay, people in the US and overseas to target those "aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine".
"It is our job to stop America's adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil," Attorney General Todd Blanche. All those accused remain at large.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday Moscow will not comment until it hears or sees "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts".
It is not clear if the five accused are in the United States, or in a different location.
Washington has charged all five men with participating in a conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a maximum 20-year prison sentence.
Three of the defendants are "high-ranking members of the RIS network", the DoJ said.
Among them are Russian father and son Yuri Khrameev, 63, and Kirill Khrameev, 27. Khrameev senior was a colonel in the Russian intelligence services and his son is an officer in the Federal Security Service of Russia (FSB).
The third high-ranking suspect is Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a 35-year-old Cuban national who the US describe as "an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia who has coordinated attacks for the RIS network".
Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, are the other two defendants.
The pair are accused of recruiting or attempting to recruit US-based individuals to "surveil and attempt to murder a prominent US-based Russian dissident".
The FBI's James Barnacle said the group "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world".
One of the incidents is as recent as this summer. The DoJ described how the RIS network was able to recruit someone in the US to surveil and eventually murder a Russian dissident in the US.
Suarez allegedly sent the recruit to two locations linked to the victim with "explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance". In exchange, the recruit was offered between $1,000 (£743) and $1,500.
Suarez and Castro are said to have offered an additional $40,000 if the US resident could "eliminate" the dissident.
The DoJ said the RIS recruit did not go through with it, which led Suarez to try and recruit "multiple other individuals within the United States". He allegedly offered "substantial sums of money to carry out the targeting of US based victims".
The release by the DoJ goes on to list other instances in which the accused allegedly tried to recruit others to kill those who were a perceived threat to Russia.
It said that in 2025, Khrameev junior allegedly recruited a US citizen to surveil and murder someone in Lithuania who was "telling lies about Russia". The release quotes Khrameev as saying the purpose was to target "all the countries that are helping Ukraine".
His father, Khrameev senior, is said to have offered the recruit $25,000 to kill the individual in Lithuania for "spreading dirt about my country" and "distorting history".
Khrameev senior, Suarez and Castro are the only ones also charged with "participating in a conspiracy to commit murder for hire". If found guilty, this charge carries a maximum 10-year prison sentence.
It is not the first time authorities thwart threats of this kind.
Last month, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities had detained an individual allegedly working for the Kremlin and who was plotting to murder an American-Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw.
Tusk told reporters the American-Ukrainian citizen "was uncomfortable for the Putin regime", adding: "We have to accept the assumption that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons."
In 2024, German authorities were reportedly warned by US intelligence of a Russian plot to kill Armin Papperger, the head of Germany's biggest arms company Rheinmetall.
Moscow dismissed the accusation at the time, with Kremlin spokesman Peskov saying: "It's all presented in the style of another fake story, so such reports cannot be taken seriously."
The fresh accusations from the DoJ come at a time of closer relations between Moscow and Washington following US President Donald Trump's return to the White House in 2025.
A few weeks ago, the head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) visited Moscow for talks with figures from Russia's intelligence services - an unconventional move that led to speculation.
The Kremlin confirmed that talks between John Ratcliffe and the intelligence services had taken place. President Trump did not say what was discussed but described the meeting as "semi-routine".

S.N. Sasidharan Kartha, the managing director of Cochin Minerals and Rutile Limited (CMRL), had also submitted a retraction affidavit to the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in 2024 in connection with statements recorded in the Exalogic-CMRL pay-off case, it has now emerged.
CMRL’s former Chief Financial Officer and Chief General Manager P. Suresh Kumar, along with the current Chief General Manager, had similarly submitted retraction affidavits to the ED in 2024.
Mr. Kartha was interrogated by the ED at his residence on April 17, 2024. In his statement recorded under Section 50 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), Mr. Kartha allegedly admitted to transferring funds to vendors and withdrawing cash without genuine expenses. He also admitted to payments made to T. Veena, daughter of former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, and her now-defunct firm Exalogic Solutions Pvt. Ltd. without services rendered, citing personal relationships with Mr. Vijayan.
In an email to CMRL dated May 15, 2024, Mr. Kartha’s brother N. Ajith alleged that ED officials had forcefully recorded his brother’s statements. “I would like to inform you that in this connection, I had submitted a retraction affidavit, on behalf of my brother, to the Director, ED Delhi office on May 15, 2024,” the mail read.
On September 7, 2026, the ED sent a detailed report to the State Police Chief seeking registration of a separate FIR under the Prevention of Corruption Act and other relevant laws against Mr. Vijayan, former Public Works Minister P.A. Mohamed Riyas, and Ms. Veena, who is Mr. Riyas’s spouse. The report accused Mr. Vijayan of receiving a bribe of ₹3.28 crore through his daughter, based on the alleged admission of Mr. Suresh Kumar.
Mr. Kumar later submitted a retraction affidavit to the ED Directorate in Delhi, alleging “illegal and high-handed conduct of the officers of the Kochi office of the ED.”
“I felt intimidated and pressurised during the recording of my statements,” Mr. Kumar, who has since resigned from CMRL, said in a mail to the company dated May 15, 2024, the same day he submitted the retraction statement to the ED.
At a press conference held on September 11, 2026, following the ED’s report to the State Police Chief, Mr. Riyas, a CPI(M) State secretariat member, alleged that the investigative agency was intimidating individuals into issuing statements against him, Ms. Veena, and Mr. Vijayan.
Incidentally, Mr. Suresh Kumar, the current Chief General Manager of CMRL, also submitted a similarly worded retraction statement to the ED and mailed CMRL about the same on May 15, 2024.

India’s AI story is moving beyond models, and the next quest is about how AI is being deployed, integrated into workflows, governed and navigated to deliver measurable value. Last month, Inc42 reported that enterprise LLM adoption in India is taking a vertical turn, with companies such as Razorpay, Fractal, BharatGen and Tech Mahindra building models for payments, healthcare, agriculture and education rather than general-purpose chat. A fortnight ago, we reported that enterprise AI deployment was getting a reality check, with organisations imposing budget caps, approval gates and unit-economics scrutiny on AI features well before they reach production. This suggests that value is shifting towards the layer where AI is deployed, governed and measured, and away from the layer where it is merely demonstrated. The ecosystem data agrees. The Bharat AI Startups Report 2026, published by Inc42 with Google, put India's AI market at $126 Bn by 2030, led by enterprise AI growing from $11 Bn to $71 Bn, and noted that 47% of enterprises are already moving pilots into production. Capital is following the same logic. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, nearly four times the $162 Mn raised in the same period last year, according to Inc42's Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, H1 2026, even as overall startup funding slipped 9%. But the more telling signal is not how much capital is flowing into AI. It is which problems capital is being asked to solve. Against this backdrop, Inc42 returns with its monthly AI Startups To Watch series. The twelfth edition highlights five emerging startups building across AI operations, education, sovereign compute, financial services deployment and enterprise execution. These are not simply startups using AI as a feature. They are trying to build businesses at the point where AI stops being a demo and starts carrying consequences. With that said, here are the five emerging AI startups that caught our attention in September. Editor's Note: This is not a ranking. The startups featured here are a curated selection by the Inc42 editorial team and are listed alphabetically. Oppex AI | Helping Engineers Detect, Investigate, Resolve Production Incidents Faster Every time a company ships new code, something can break in production. Engineers get paged, often at night, then lose hours finding what went wrong. Clues sit scattered across logs, dashboards, customer complaints, and old fix notes, and alerts pile up faster than a small team can clear them. Oppex AI is trying to automate that work. Founded in 2025 by Prasun Kumar and Pranit Kumar, the Bengaluru startup has built an AI system that reads across a company’s monitoring tools, support tickets, cloud systems and internal notes, then points to the likely bug. The platform groups alerts describing the same issue into one incident, learns a company's setup so its answers improve over time, and remembers earlier fixes so nothing is lost when the on-duty engineer changes. Oppex says its agents resolve issues five times faster with half the on-call engineers. Within eight months of writing its first line of code, it deployed its platform across enterprises in India, the UK, the EU, and the US, targeting the global AIOps market, projected to reach $41.6 Bn by 2030 at a 30.3% CAGR. ProLearn | AI-Native Learning Companion Personal tutoring works. It has simply never scaled. Most Indian students preparing for board exams or entrance tests still learn from recorded lectures and static test papers, with little feedback on where exactly their understanding breaks down. ProLearn is trying to put that attention inside a phone. The Bengaluru startup was founded in April 2026 by Ravneet Singh, a former Vedantu executive. He is building an AI-native learning companion for K-12 students and aspirants preparing for JEE, NEET, UPSC and CAT. The companion is built for conversation rather than content delivery. It listens to how a student explains a problem, asks questions back, adapts to their pace and walks them through a solution step by step, the way a tutor would. ProLearn raised ₹30 Cr in a pre-seed round led by BEENEXT to build its AI and reasoning infrastructure and curriculum-aligned content ahead of a public launch. It is targeting India's AI tutors market projected to reach $1.2 Bn by 2031. Quantum Tiger | Sovereign AI Systems For Architectural Autonomy Most enterprises running serious AI workloads still do it on someone else’s infrastructure, sending sensitive data across borders to models and cloud services they do not control. For banks, hospitals, defence contractors and government institutions, that is becoming unacceptable, commercially and legally. Quantum Tiger wants to make the alternative smaller. The Kolkata-based startup was founded in 2025 by Rana Dutta and Manas Paul, and is building full-stack sovereign AI infrastructure that lets organisations train and run AI workloads within their own trusted boundaries, without depending on public cloud infrastructure. Its stack pairs an AI operating layer with purpose-built compute hardware designed to run large language models locally at predictable latency, doing training and inference on the same system so enterprises are not billed for every external call. The company says the system is engineered for data locality and continuous model adaptation across heterogeneous workloads. Quantum Tiger is targeting the sovereign AI infrastructure market, estimated at $15 Bn in 2025 and projected to reach $177.09 Bn by 2035. Vecton AI | Production-Ready AI For BFSI Financial services is where AI promises the most and delivers the least. Banks and insurers sit on decades of structured data and repetitive, high-volume processes, yet most AI pilots inside them never leave the sandbox, held back by regulatory requirements, legacy architecture and the cost of reworking core systems. Vecton AI is built to solve just that. Founded in 2025 by Himanshu Goyal and Gaurav Mandlecha, the Bengaluru startup positions itself as an AI transformation partner for banks, financial services and insurance companies. It works across AI consulting and strategy, process automation, custom-trained models and autonomous agent development, with a delivery model built on forward-deployed engineers who stay with the client through implementation. It ships production-ready, compliant agent systems and machine learning workflows aligned with BFSI regulatory standards, focussed on sales acceleration, customer engagement, document processing, and intelligent copilots. Vecton is targeting India's AI in BFSI market, estimated at $1,069 Mn in 2025 and projected to reach $9,425.2 Mn by 2034. Zenalyst | AI Workforce For Enterprises Every CIO says the same thing: dashboards everywhere, answers nowhere. Enterprise decisions still depend on numbers scattered across ERP, CRM, banking and document systems, stitched together by hand. By the time a finance team spots a variance, the quarter it belonged to is closed. Zenalyst is building agents that do the work rather than describe it. The Bengaluru-based startup was founded in May 2025 by Nagendra Singh, Sanketh Krishnappa and Vijay Jha, and its ZenForce platform connects to more than 150 enterprise systems across ERP, CRM and banking to run finance, procurement and legal workflows. Zenalyst is targeting the autonomous finance market, projected to reach $112.84 Bn by 2031. Its agents include ZenBank for treasury and money operations, ZenProcure for procurement and ZenCollect for order-to-cash and contract intelligence. Zenalyst positions ZenForce as deterministic rather than probabilistic: reasoning is gated through verification steps, queries are grounded in the customer's own schema, and customer data is never used to train external models. China’s rocket boom turns Hainan into a space hub. Can launches fuel wider growth?
Factories, supercomputing centres and satellite businesses are springing up in the province as officials push to build a fully fledged aerospace ecosystem
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the first part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Mia Nurmamat examine how Hainan province is betting on a growing aerospace cluster to rewrite its economic playbook beyond tourism.
On Hainan’s northeastern coast, launch towers rise abruptly from a flat landscape of coconut palms and open sky. At Pad 1 of the commercial spaceport in Wenchang, an 83-metre (272 feet) service tower stands surrounded by four slender, steel lattice towers, designed to protect the launch site from lightning during the island’s frequent tropical storms.
No mission is scheduled, but an orange flame flickers from a gas vent at one facility.
Long known for its coconuts, its namesake chicken and generations of emigrants who left for Southeast Asia in search of a living, Wenchang has been thrust onto the frontier of national development. Beijing’s space ambitions have turned the city into a showcase for rocket launches – and given Hainan an unexpected catalyst to reshape an economy long reliant on tourism and consumer services.

Three dead after NBC News helicopter crashes in Los Angeles while covering bus accident
Aircraft goes down between two commercial buildings in Chatsworth neighborhood
At least three people have died and another is injured after a local NBC News helicopter crashed in a Los Angeles neighborhood on Tuesday while reporting on a bus collision earlier in the day, according to officials.
The helicopter went down between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighborhood, a Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) spokesperson said.
Five patients were assessed, with one person transported to a local hospital in an unknown condition while three others were pronounced dead at the scene, according to the fire department.
NBC4 Los Angeles said it was their news helicopter, NewsChopper 4, that crashed in the city during a live broadcast. Several television news helicopters covering the bus collision were operating in the area, according to media reports.
"We've been telling you that we've been piecing it together here. We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received the confirmation that, in fact, NewsChopper 4 went down just before 7 o'clock tonight in Chatsworth," NBC anchor Colleen Williams said.
NBC said the helicopter was operated by Angel City Air, which is affiliated with the station.
The helicopter crash happened after a vehicle collision in the area in which a Los Angeles Metro bus and a passenger vehicle met with an accident, killing at least two people.
Footage from the scene showed two shipping containers and several vehicles burning and firefighters working to douse the blaze, which has been extinguished.
The Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) said the helicopter crashed at around 6:58 pm and its officers responded to the area of Lurline Avenue and Nordhoff Street in Chatsworth.
It said it was not confirmed how many people were on board.
At least one person killed in the helicopter crash was outside in the parking lot next to the commercial building, Capt Branden Silverman, a spokesperson for the LAFD, said during a news conference. It was unclear if the other two who were killed were on the ground or inside the aircraft.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said she was "devastated" by the loss of life in the helicopter crash and the bus collision in Chatsworth.
“I’m absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight. My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash,” she said, thanking emergency responders for their swift response.
California governor Gavin Newsom also shared his condolences and said "our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family".
At least four cars and two storage containers on the ground caught fire from the burning helicopter wreckage, which was quickly put out, according to officials. More than 50 firefighters responded to the helicopter crash, according to the Fire Department.
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration will investigate the crash, the Fire Department said.
About two hours before the crash, an SUV slammed into the middle of a city bus, killing at least two people and injuring six others. Photos and videos online showed half of the SUV lodged into the side of an MTA bus.
The helicopter crashed about a mile and a half from the bus crash.

Charlie Kirk's family alleges 'stunning failures' by Utah officials led to his shooting
- Published
Charlie Kirk's family has accused the Utah Valley University and state officials of "stunning failures and reckless decisions" that they say led to the conservative activist's 2025 assassination during a campus event.
In a legal notice, lawyers for the family say Kirk's Turning Point USA event at the university campus was not properly secured or monitored, making him an easy target.
Kirk, 31, was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus, when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof.
The university said it was aware of the claim but did not comment further on the allegations, according to a statement shared with the BBC's US partner CBS News.
"We are aware of the notice of claim. UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes, " the university said in its statement. "Our focus remains on supporting our campus community."
The legal notice was filed on 9 September, a day ahead of the one-year anniversary of Kirk's death, and is typically a precursor to a lawsuit.
It names Utah Valley University, local police, the state of Utah, and other university officials as parties who were allegedly aware of the threats against Kirk and did not take steps to protect him.
"Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie," the notice alleges.
"Placing a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event in the quad surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms is accurately described as walking him into a fishbowl," it says.
Kirk's family alleges the university failed to conduct a meaningful security assessment ahead of the event, failed to assign enough police officers, and did not have an ambulance available on site.
The family also alleges the university ignored warnings about securing the rooftops surrounding the courtyard where Kirk was speaking.
"The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk's close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," the family's attorney D Loren Washburn wrote in the court filing.
Tyler Robinson, a 23-year-old man from Utah, who has been accused of shooting Kirk from a roof, is due to appear in court next month to hear the date of his trial.
Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in the state, as well as six other charges.
Prosecutors have called for the death penalty.

Anime drew a larger monthly audience than any other genre on Asian streaming platforms between July 2025 and August 2026, and viewing on Netflix grew nine times faster than the service overall, according to a new report from Media Partners Asia (MPA).
“The Anime Economy” report draws on ampd audience panels MPA runs across eight Asian markets, on how MPA classifies Netflix’s engagement figures and public filings, and on additional research and interviews MPA conducted. Between 31% and 47% of premium-VOD users across those markets watched anime in any given month during the period, compared with 26% to 34% for the average of the other seven genres tracked. In Japan, the figures ran higher still, from 45% to 59% against 24% to 36%. Anime accounted for 15.6% of tracked premium-VOD hours in the second half of 2025 and 14.0% in the first half of 2026, with the Japan figure at 28%.
“Jujutsu Kaisen” ranked as the top anime title in seven of the eight markets tracked in the first half of 2026, MPA found, propelling MAPPA’s share of regional anime hours from 6.1% in the second half of 2025 to 17.3% in the first half of 2026. That put MAPPA just ahead of TMS Entertainment at 16.6%, with Toei Animation at 13% and titles mastered by Aniplex at 12%.
Popular on Variety
Netflix carried roughly half of the region’s anime viewing across the tracking period, holding 51% of anime hours in the second half of 2025 and 50% in the first half of 2026. Japan, the world’s largest anime market, has become a two-way contest between the two biggest global platforms: Prime Video held a 43% share of anime hours there in the second half of 2025, before Netflix pulled even with 42% each in the first half of 2026.
MPA’s classification of Netflix’s “What We Watched” disclosures shows the platform’s Japanese anime viewing climbing from 3.33 billion hours in the first half of 2023 to 4.64 billion hours in the first half of 2026, a 39% jump against 4.5% growth in Netflix’s total viewing over the same period. Anime rose from 3.6% to 4.75% of all Netflix hours in that window. Four-fifths of that viewing remains licensed library content, though MPA points to Netflix’s January 2026 partnership with MAPPA as a marker of the shift toward owned franchises.
YouTube has become both a marketing channel and a production base for anime: MPA counts 70 million people watching anime-related content there monthly in Japan alone, totaling 2.8 billion hours. Official channels including Aniplex, with 5.1 million monthly viewers, and Toho animation, with 4.8 million, now function as media businesses in their own right, while YouTube-native outfits like Plott are turning out franchises for a fraction of what a traditional TV production would cost.
MPA counted 21 anime transactions and alliances since 2021, 11 of them struck in 2025 and 2026. Sony took part in seven of those deals, building what MPA calls the industry’s only end-to-end anime operation. Crunchyroll, with 21 million paying subscribers, now sits alongside Sony Pictures, Sony Music and Aniplex within Sony’s portfolio, with the group also holding equity positions in both Kadokawa and Bandai Namco. Toei Animation, Toho, Bandai Namco and other broadcasters have separately bought up studios, distributors and pipelines to build their own capacity.
MPA projects worldwide anime spending will rise by some 10% annually through 2030, driven mainly by Asia outside Japan and North America, with the gains concentrated among a limited group of franchise-owning companies, studios and platforms. The firm’s base case for the next 24 months is a hybrid financing model in which platforms put up the money for production while studios keep hold of the rights.
“Anime’s scale is established; the question is where the next growth comes from and who captures it,” said Vivek Couto, CEO and executive director of Media Partners Asia. “The catalysts are streaming pushing deeper into new markets globally, theatrical events on the scale of ‘Infinity Castle’ [“Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba Infinity Castle”] becoming repeatable, and games and merchandise carrying franchises well beyond the screen. The direction is toward ownership: platforms financing production directly, Japanese IP groups buying studios, and the two learning to work together.”
“The constraint is capacity, not demand or capital,” he added. “The studios making the biggest hits are often the least able to invest, and the industry still leans on a handful of franchises. The companies that solve for capacity, and bring the animators with them, will be best placed for the next phase of growth.”

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

California is on the verge of accepting $1.86 billion in federal broadband grant funds, despite the Trump administration telling states they cannot enforce net neutrality rules on any Internet service provider that gets a piece of the grant money.
When the Trump administration overhauled the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program last year, it ruled that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive funding. This is particularly problematic for California, which previously won a yearslong court battle to defend its state net neutrality law.
Similar to federal net neutrality rules repealed during the first Trump administration, California’s law prohibits ISPs from blocking or throttling lawful traffic and says ISPs may not require fees from websites or online services to deliver or prioritize their traffic to Internet users. While the first Trump administration lost its attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws, the second Trump administration is trying to achieve a similar result by making federal broadband money conditional on whether states agree not to enforce net neutrality.
Trump’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) says each state participating in BEAD must exempt ISPs from net neutrality rules and price regulations in all parts of the state, not just in areas where the ISP is given funds to deploy broadband service. The exemption from state laws and rules would apply for up to 14 years.
Under BEAD, each US state and territory receives an allotment that it can distribute to ISPs in exchange for deploying broadband to unserved and underserved areas. California and Illinois are the only states that haven’t finalized their funding, according to the BEAD progress dashboard maintained by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA). Tomorrow, the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) is scheduled to vote on a resolution to ratify the state’s final BEAD plan.
Vote is “beginning of the end”
California could try to continue enforcing its net neutrality law even while accepting the federal funding, a strategy that would involve another long court battle over its right to regulate broadband providers. This would be difficult, as the Trump administration is requiring states that accept grant funding to commit that they won’t enforce net neutrality rules.
A CPUC spokesperson told Ars that tomorrow’s vote is a “procedural requirement” to ratify the state proposal submitted to the federal government in December 2025. But nearly 30 advocacy groups that focus on access to technology are treating the vote as a significant milestone and urged state leaders to defend California’s net neutrality law in a letter yesterday.
One of the letter signers is Paul Goodman, legal counsel for the Center for Accessible Technology. He told Ars in a phone interview that tomorrow’s CPUC vote is much more than a procedural step.
“It’s the beginning of the end,” Goodman said. Winning a court battle would become much more difficult after the state accepts the money, he said. Goodman said the CPUC should delay the vote and that California should file a lawsuit arguing that the NTIA-imposed condition is illegal.
In addition to net neutrality, Goodman said California may be giving up other regulatory authority over companies, like AT&T and Verizon, because the NTIA requirement forbids rate regulation and “utility-style rules on broadband Internet service” in general.
US forbids enforcement anywhere in the state
The advocacy groups’ letter was sent to Governor Gavin Newsom, Attorney General Rob Bonta, CPUC President John Reynolds, and the other CPUC commissioners.
“While our organizations recognize the significance of BEAD funding—and the role it will play in advancing critical broadband infrastructure buildout across the State—we strongly stand against allowing for the presumption of preemption of the State’s net neutrality laws in order to accept BEAD funds,” the groups said.
shall commit that it will not enforce any law, regulation, order, contracting requirement, or other enforceable obligation that directly or indirectly regulates the rates, terms, and conditions of broadband Internet service… or imposes net neutrality rules, open access, or other utility-style rules on broadband Internet service, against a Subgrantee or its affiliates anywhere it provides service within the State (i.e., both BEAD and non-BEAD locations), while that Subgrantee has any subgrant that is still within its period of performance, extended period of performance, or federal interest period.
The NTIA said the exemption from state laws must extend statewide, because “applying net neutrality and rate regulation at non-BEAD locations could raise compliance costs and threaten the overall financial viability of the Subgrantee, increasing the risk of default for the Subgrantee at BEAD locations and jeopardizing the success of the entire BEAD program.”
Goodman said the exemption from state laws would last for up to 14 years. This is because ISPs receiving grants would have four years to deploy the required broadband networks, and the extended period of performance lasts another 10 years.
Groups: Accepting US terms would set dangerous precedent
The letter to state leaders said the California decision to accept BEAD money under these conditions “would set a dangerous precedent for the federal government to use federal funding as a cudgel that forces states in line with its agenda… If California were to allow this funding to be used as leverage, there is no telling what other resources the administration would confidently seek to exploit.”
The groups urged California leaders to “defend the hard-won protections that have brought us this far” and pledged “to support California leadership in defending our state’s values and the progress it has made on closing the digital divide.”
Goodman told Ars that upon receiving BEAD money, AT&T could tell California that it can’t regulate the price of AT&T’s copper landline phone service or require AT&T to serve everybody who wants phone service, Goodman said. AT&T is already trying to get out of state obligations related to its basic phone service in California, as we’ve reported.
Goodman said the BEAD money could also jeopardize a merger condition that requires Verizon to offer $20-per-month broadband service to people with low incomes in California. Goodman said the savings for people with low incomes from those required Verizon plans would dwarf the money California is due to receive for BEAD.
Of the $1.86 billion in BEAD money for the state, California is slated to spend about $1.4 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.
Law professor: US is overriding Congress’ intent
The NTIA-mandated exemption to state laws throughout the country would also apply to any other ISP receiving BEAD funding, such as SpaceX’s Starlink satellite division.
“Roughly 69 percent of California’s BEAD funding flows to five large, national providers: Comcast ($400 million), AT&T ($331 million), Verizon/Frontier ($173 million), Amazon’s Kuiper satellite service ($55 million), and SpaceX’s Starlink ($22 million),” Stanford Law professor Barbara van Schewick wrote today.
According to van Schewick, another casualty of the BEAD restriction would be a 2019 California law that prohibits mobile providers from throttling first responders during emergencies. The law was passed after Verizon throttled an “unlimited” data plan used by Santa Clara County firefighters during a wildfire.
“Those protections exist for a reason: left to their own devices, Internet providers have put profits over public safety before. California is now being asked to sign away those protections for fourteen years,” she wrote.
California would have a good case because the federal BEAD law says funded providers must follow state and local laws, van Schewick wrote. “A federal agency can’t use fine print in a grant to override what Congress wrote into the statute,” she wrote, adding that Newsom “should refuse to sign away California’s net neutrality, affordability, and public-safety protections and go to court to get the money the way Congress intended: with every state protection intact.”
State agency: Vote is “procedural”
In a statement to Ars, a CPUC spokesperson said the resolution to be voted on tomorrow is a “procedural requirement to ratify the Dec. 19, 2025 CPUC draft California Final Proposal submitted to the Federal Government.” The NTIA approved the plan on July 17, 2026, after multiple rounds of revisions, the statement said.
“The Resolution adopts the now-approved California Final Proposal only. It does not address subgrantee agreements, or the conditions the NTIA requires be included in subgrantee agreements,” the CPUC told Ars.
We contacted the offices of the governor and attorney general yesterday afternoon and will update this article if we get any response. We also contacted Democratic State Senator Scott Wiener, who authored the net neutrality bill that was enacted by California in 2018, and haven’t heard back.
The BEAD law enacted by Congress and President Biden in 2021 requires ISPs that receive grants to offer “low-cost” plans to people with low incomes, but the Trump administration told states that they cannot set the rates of those plans. That means ISPs themselves get to pick the price of the mandated low-cost broadband offerings.
Last year, California Assemblymember Tasha Boerner proposed a bill requiring ISPs to offer $15 broadband plans to people with low incomes. But she dropped the proposal after Trump administration officials warned that setting rates would jeopardize the state’s access to broadband grants.
Suing US would be “enormously” difficult
Goodman said that once California accepts the money, the state attorney general would only be able to challenge the Trump administration’s requirements in the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. The DC Circuit court “can really only review that decision for basically fraud or corruption, which is a really high bar to prove,” he said.
Goodman said that if California takes legal action before finalizing the agreement with the Trump administration, it could sue the US in the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals.
“Right now, the California AG could sue saying, ‘Hey, these general terms… are illegal. You can’t require us to do that.’ [The state] could sue here in California and the Ninth Circuit has a sort of favorable view of that claim, so [the state would have a] pretty good view of success,” Goodman said.
In the DC Circuit, “it’s a much, much harder push,” he said. “Not impossible, but enormously more difficult.” He said the CPUC has a deadline at the end of this month to sign the agreement with the NTIA, but the state “can get a 30-day extension and then challenge the case in court.”
On the other side of the country, New York may have to stop enforcing an affordable broadband law that requires ISPs to offer $15- or $20-per-month service to people with low incomes. New York defended the law in court against broadband industry lobby groups and won that battle less than two years ago but has agreed to take $664.6 million of BEAD money from the Trump administration.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said in an April 2026 press release that closing the digital divide requires bringing broadband to every household in the state and ensuring “that it remains affordable when it gets there. New York is showing the rest of the nation that both are possible through its landmark Affordable Broadband Act and commitment to reaching the final 1 percent of unserved or underserved households.”
But with New York having accepted the BEAD funding, it may be unable to enforce the Affordable Broadband Act on ISPs that receive grants. We contacted the offices of Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James yesterday and will update this article if we get a response.
Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

NEW DELHI – India said Thursday that it remained firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its people and will continue to source supplies from diverse sellers based on market dynamics, hours after the U.S. made a new move to punish such buyers.
New Delhi also said that it had warned Washington any such new moves could impact ties between the two countries.
The statement came after the U.S. House of Representatives passed a sweeping sanctions and tariff bill intended to increase economic pressure on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine.
The legislation authorizes U.S. President Donald Trump to impose stiff tariffs of up to 100% on countries, including India, to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas, as well as to extend sanctions on Iran.
The bill will now be sent to Trump, who needs to sign it into law.
The Indian foreign ministry said that it had noted the passage of the bill, adding that New Delhi had raised the issue with various U.S. interlocutors in recent months, and had “very clearly articulated” the potential implications for the bilateral relationship and the international energy market.
“The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” it said in a statement.
The government would work closely with trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications of the legislation, it added.
India, the world’s third-biggest oil importer, is among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, which is seen as helping Moscow replenish its budget since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and was hit with sweeping Western sanctions.
New Delhi has repeatedly sought to resist pressure to scale back its oil trade with Russia, saying its large population and economy need secure, affordable and reliable energy supplies.

Versions of the rumor also spread on TikTok, Facebook and Threads, and readers contacted us to ask whether the elements of the claim were true.
In short, the claim contains a mixture of accurate, false and unconfirmed information.
In August 2026, Trump did expand a U.S. beef import quota by roughly 660 million pounds, and the European Union did adopt restrictions on Brazilian beef. Trump expanded beef imports in August 2026

Describing the imports as "tariff-free," however, is imprecise. Under a tariff-rate quota, a set amount of a product can enter at a lower tariff, while imports above that amount face a higher tariff. The White House said Trump's measure increased the amount of beef eligible for the lower tariff rate rather than eliminating duties for beef altogether.
Moreover, the proclamation did not explicitly say the beef would come from Brazil. It allocated the additional quota to "other countries or areas" and directed U.S. Customs and Border Protection to ensure that "all eligible countries have full access" on a first-come, first-served basis. JBS is also not mentioned in the proclamation.

JBS does have documented relationships with several companies named in the social media posts, but it was not possible to confirm that it is the primary beef supplier for all of them, as of September 2026.
For instance, a 2017 JBS report (Page 87) says its Seara division supplied 75% of McDonald's hamburger requirements in Brazil at the time and listed McDonald's and Burger King among its global customers. A 2020 JBS sustainability report (Page 76) also says Friboi, a JBS beef brand, received Burger King's Best Supplier Award that year.
There is also evidence of relationships with Sysco and Kroger. Sysco 
But those sources do not show that, as of September 2026, JBS was the primary beef supplier for all the companies listed in the social media posts. McDonald's, for example, 
Walmart also disputed the post's description of JBS as a supplier of its ground beef. Annie Walker, director of Walmart U.S. communications for food and U.S. manufacturing, said via email, "We do not source ground beef from JBS."
Snopes contacted JBS, McDonald's, Burger King, Sysco and Kroger to clarify their current supplier relationships. We will update this article if we receive responses.
EU did restrict Brazilian beef
The posts were also broadly correct that the EU restricted Brazilian beef. On June 4, 2026, the European Commission adopted a regulation changing the list of countries authorized to send certain animal products to the EU under rules concerning the use of antimicrobial medicines. The changes took effect Sept. 3, 2026.
The regulation says Brazil was previously authorized for bovine products, among other categories, but that the commission did not receive information guaranteeing Brazil had implemented the measures needed to comply with the antimicrobial requirements by Sept. 3. Brazil's authorization for bovine products was therefore removed.
Importantly, the regulation does not say Brazilian beef tested positive for unsafe antibiotic residues. Rather, it says Brazil did not provide enough information to show it met the EU requirements laid out above, which a European Commission spokesperson confirmed via email. The spokesperson said Brazilian exports could resume once the country meets those requirements.
Brazil's government also said the restrictions concerned new rules governing the use of antimicrobial medicines, adding that Brazilian authorities are continuing engagement with European officials.
Snopes contacted Brazil's Ministry of Agriculture for additional context on the restrictions and will update this story if we receive a response.
China case unrelated to Brazil
Chinese authorities did suspend (Page 1921) the export authorization of one Argentine beef plant, ArreBeef, after detecting the antibiotic chloramphenicol in a shipment in March 2026, as Snopes previously reported. 
As we previously reported, that incident was separate from Trump's August import plan. The president's Aug. 26 proclamation does not assign the additional 300,000 metric tons to Argentina, Brazil or any other individual country.

A post (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that a pregnant woman gave birth on the road in Unnao, Uttar Pradesh, after a government hospital refused her admission due to her inability to cover the medical expenses. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of a woman giving birth on the roadside in Unnao, Uttar Pradesh, after a government hospital denied her admission.
Fact: The visuals are from Rajbiraj, Nepal, where a woman gave birth on the street outside a government Hospital in September 2026 after being denied care over unpaid preliminary test fees. However, a similar incident took place in Uttar Pradesh in April 2026, when a woman delivered her baby on the roadside outside a government hospital in Shamli district after staff allegedly demanded a bribe and refused her admission. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of viral visuals directed us to Nepali news reports (here, here & here) covering the same incident. The event reportedly occurred in the town of Rajbiraj, Nepal. According to these reports, on 10 September 2026, Babita Kumari Paswan, a 30-year-old woman, delivered her baby on the pavement outside the state-owned Gajendra Narayan Singh Hospital in Rajbiraj, Nepal, after her family couldn’t get the money required for preliminary tests.
After a video of the incident went viral, six hospital staff were reportedly suspended pending an investigation. A Google Street View of the hospital’s location matching the area seen in the viral video can be viewed here. However, it is worth noting that in April 2026, a similar incident (here & here) did occur in Uttar Pradesh, where a 30-year-old woman gave birth to a baby boy on the roadside outside the Shamli District Combined Hospital after staff allegedly refused her admission and demanded money. Hospital authorities formed a committee to investigate the matter.
To sum it up, the viral video depicting a woman delivering an infant on the street is from Nepal, not from Uttar Pradesh.
