Assad regime planned US journalist's kidnap for weeks, BBC finds
- Published
US journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation which was more than a month in the planning, the BBC can reveal.
A member of the group which detained Tice has also claimed the abduction was sanctioned by Syria's leader at the time, President Bashar al-Assad.
Tice was seen getting into a car with a driver he knew and trusted. For years, many assumed they had stumbled upon a government checkpoint, and that the abduction of the journalist had been opportunistic.
But we have uncovered evidence that, in fact, his disappearance was anything but chance.
In a new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, we reveal the findings of a years-long investigation into what happened to Tice, who had been reporting on Syria's civil war at the time.
His case has been followed closely by international media and cited by successive US presidents.
Where is Austin Tice?
Josh Baker enters a dangerous world of fear, greed and betrayal as he uncovers what happened in one of the biggest missing-person cases of our time - the abduction of Austin Tice.
Georgetown University law student Tice, who had served as a US Marines captain, was last seen in a video - blindfolded and in apparent distress - posted more than a month after his capture.
As the regime fell 12 years later, tens of thousands of people emerged from the administration's prisons. Tice was not one of them.
We obtained co-ordinates from an intelligence source for multiple locations US authorities suspected he could have been held at, and searched for him for more than a month, but found no sign of him.
A former Syrian commander has said Tice was executed. Others have questioned this account and no remains have been found.
But in the aftermath of the regime's collapse, we did uncover secret Syrian intelligence files on Tice - hundreds of pages of internal records providing the first definitive proof that it was the regime that had held the journalist.
Two crucial questions remained unanswered, however: how exactly had Tice been taken in the first place? And, who was responsible for his abduction?
We have spoken to a number of men from the regime involved in Tice's detention, and have reviewed recordings of discussions about it. One man we spoke to, Abu Ali, is a former member of the National Defence Forces (NDF), a militia which was fiercely loyal to Assad.
He says the abduction operation began when Tice's driver - who multiple sources say had been passing the regime information for some time - told a senior NDF member that Tice was moving through rebel-held areas, reporting on the opposition.
Tice had pushed into areas most journalists deemed too dangerous and was writing front-page stories for the Washington Post. The Assad regime was cracking down on anyone highlighting its human rights abuses.
We have been told the NDF member Tice's driver spoke to was Sakr Rustom - not just any NDF militia contact, but nephew of Bassam al-Hassan, one of Assad's most trusted security figures and head of the NDF.
The information on Tice was passed up to Hassan, Abu Ali says, who is then said to have telephoned Assad.
"Bring him to us," Assad replied, claims Abu Ali.
Abu Ali says he was subsequently called into Hassan's office and told the president had approved the operation.
But Tice was not taken immediately. The driver, Abu Ali says, suggested that he and the NDF continue watching him, to uncover more about what he was doing.
"He trusts me," Abu Ali recalls the driver saying.
Some time later, the driver reported back that Tice's actions seemed suspicious, Abu Ali says.
Tice, as a trained marine, would sometimes share his military experience with rebel fighters - according to several people we spoke to - and would correct fighters on how they used their weapons.
To the men watching him, that behaviour made Tice look less like a journalist and more like someone from the CIA. The BBC has found no evidence to suggest this was the case, and a former senior US official responsible for part of Tice's case has denied he was an intelligence officer.
In the days before Tice vanished, the driver made one particularly brazen move while Tice was interviewing rebel fighters. He secretly took the American's backpack, containing his MacBook, a satellite transmitter and other personal items, for regime operatives to look through, multiple sources say.
On 11 August 2012, Tice celebrated his 31st birthday at a rebel safehouse on the western edge of Damascus, a few miles from Assad's presidential palace. There was a swimming pool, Free Syrian Army fighters, Taylor Swift music and whiskey, Tice revealed in what would become his final tweet.
"Hands down, best birthday ever," he wrote.
Then came the time for Tice to leave Syria. He had told various people he was planning to take time out in Lebanon.
But he was not heading to safety. He was heading to a state facility where Hassan had an office, in an area called Tahouneh on the outskirts of Damascus, according to several sources. Abu Ali was waiting there for Tice.
Abu Ali says Tice's driver told him that when he drew up to the gates, he pulled out a gun.
Tice laughed at first, Ali recalls the driver saying, apparently believing the man he trusted was joking. But the driver told Tice he was serious, Abu Ali says, and the journalist realised what was happening.
According to Ali, Tice pulled out his chequebook and pleaded with the driver to name his price, rather than go through with the kidnap.
NDF militia members then grabbed Tice, covering his eyes, Abu Ali says.
Another NDF member told us he would never forget Tice's expression as he realised he had been betrayed. Abu Ali says Hassan immediately called President Assad to tell him they had the American.
For years, the identity of Tice's driver has remained a mystery.
The BBC spoke to more than 20 people to discover who he was, with the trail eventually leading to the city of Homs, and the family of a man called Hamid Abu Obeid.
They confirmed he was the man who had driven Tice away, an account also supported by multiple NDF members. But by the time we identified him, Abu Obeid had disappeared.
His family say they do not know where he is, and fear for his safety. They say they were not aware of Hamid's involvement in Tice's case, and learned about it from him afterwards.
But they did give a motive for his betrayal of Tice.
The Abu Obeid family, Palestinian refugees from Gaza, live in poverty. Under Syrian law they are not entitled to Syrian citizenship and live under significant restrictions.
According to Hamid's brother, he had been promised a passport, Syrian citizenship, a house, and a weapon, in return for delivering Tice - life-changing rewards. But after the abduction, the family says all he got was a pistol.
Then, after Assad's regime fell, Abu Obeid's wife says her husband was called by a man who knew about his involvement in Tice's case and was threatening to tell the US embassy, hoping it might help him secure asylum.
Abu Obeid urged him not to. He then took some money, told his wife he was going shopping, and she says she has not seen him since. She does not know if he is in hiding, or if he has been detained or killed.
Not long after he disappeared, she says masked men - some dressed in military clothes - visited and took a number of Abu Obeid's possessions, including his laptop and other devices.
The wishes of Abu Obeid's wife now chillingly mirror those of Tice's mother and family. On opposite sides of a disappearance that began more than a decade ago, both families are searching for the same thing: a loved one who vanished, and an answer to where he went.

My favorite part of wearing the Specs, Snap’s new augmented reality glasses, was playing dominoes. Sitting across the table from a Snap employee wearing the same pair of chunky glasses, I could select a virtual domino with a pinch and then move my hand to drop it in place, watching the tile snap down in front of us on a real table. It was unlike anything I’ve tried in other VR headsets or smart glasses — the ability to sit with another person and have a shared digital experience.
I wore Snap’s $2,200 smart glasses
Snap has spent half a decade working toward its first consumer pair of AR glasses. They’re finally here — and they’re bold as can be.
I wore Snap’s $2,200 smart glasses
Snap has spent half a decade working toward its first consumer pair of AR glasses. They’re finally here — and they’re bold as can be.
Snap really believes in AR glasses. The company has spent more than half a decade developing the technology, producing two generations of glasses that only ever shipped to a small number of developers. The company seems to want to untether itself from the limitations of being just one app in a big store and instead pioneer the next great platform.
Now, Snap is nearly ready to launch its first pair of AR glasses for consumers, the Specs, sometime this fall. That suggests Snap thinks these meet its vision well enough for regular people to enjoy using the $2,195 glasses. They’re certainly full of big ideas. But after an afternoon of testing at Snap’s offices this week, I’m skeptical of whether they’ll be fully ready for primetime.
The Specs are big, black, bold glasses that come in two lens sizes, 47mm and 52mm. Part of why they’re so bold is almost certainly to make a statement — there’s no mistaking these for a regular pair of glasses, like you might with Meta’s Ray-Bans. (They’re a little too conspicuous for me personally; my glasses style is squarely “Elder Millennial Who Shops At Warby Parker.”) But they’re also so chunky because they house all the hardware necessary to let the Specs function as a standalone computer, meaning they don’t need to be tethered to a phone, compute puck, or external battery.
They may be chunky, but the Specs aren’t quite as heavy as they look. They’re heavier than my Warby Parker glasses, of course, which I can comfortably wear for most of the day. But the Specs didn’t drag on my face like a full-on VR headset. The Specs felt sturdy, too: I shook my head around and they didn’t fall off or even really slip. I wouldn’t suggest playing pickup basketball in these, but they’ll stay on your face while walking around. They made my ears sag just a little, though. And I wasn’t able to use the Specs enough to tell you if they’d start to feel uncomfortable over the course of a full four-hour battery cycle.
Actually using the Specs is kind of like using a hybrid of smart glasses and a VR headset. In front of your eyes, you can see menus, app windows, and elements of whatever app (“lens”) you’re using, like the digital dominoes. Those elements appear over whatever you’re looking at with your eyes through the lenses of the glasses, which have waveguide displays that can show “16 million colors” and “sharp, high-resolution visuals” (Snap hasn’t specified the exact resolution).
Thanks to hand-tracking tech in the Specs, you can pinch and drag to manipulate parts of the interface, such as resizing a window or moving a domino onto the game board, and Snap says you can even snap your fingers to take a picture in the Specs’ Snapchat app. Clever. You can also have windows follow along as you move your head, in case you want to keep a window in your vision no matter where you’re looking. You can access a home button, a Control Center-like menu, and status information like the time by holding up your palm in a setup that reminds me of the ill-fated Humane Pin.
In my limited testing, it was all rather finicky. I often had to pinch a few times or make sure my hand was placed in just the right spot to get something to work the way it should. I never quite nailed the two-part action of flipping my hand up and then using my other hand to press the home button. While standing in the sun, it was much harder to see the augmented reality graphics.
Snap has beaten competitors like Meta to shipping a pair of glasses with displays in both lenses, letting it deliver a true AR effect and not just another flat screen. But by putting the AR display dead center in your vision, the Specs’ 51-degree field of view becomes a major limitation. It meant that digital elements kept slipping out of sight during my demos, which ruined the illusion that they were actually in the real world. While watching Lanterns on HBO Max in a browser in a moving car, I had to shrink the window to make it easier to see in front of me. While playing dominoes, I had to keep physically turning my head to see my dominoes and the playing board and back again.
Because it’s 2026, the Specs also have a dedicated AI chatbot assistant, but in my limited experience it was slow and inconsistent. With a “Hey Specs” command, I asked it to show me funny cat videos on YouTube, as suggested by a Snap rep. I had to ask it twice because it didn’t pick up the command the first time. When the command worked, it then took about 15 seconds for the Specs to pull up a YouTube page with search results for funny cat videos.
Watching that video also revealed to me a bizarre social interaction that people will have to come to grips with if AR glasses gain any sort of traction. On that YouTube page, I picked some random cat video collection, and it played in the background while the Snap rep kept talking to me. Even though the Specs were playing audio through the onboard speakers, the Snap rep standing right next to me said they couldn’t hear anything.
That made me feel weird — these glasses theoretically let you watch and listen to a private video while staring somebody else straight in the eye. Even when I wasn’t watching the video, I found myself constantly distracted from the in-person conversations I was having during the demo because my eyes were caught up with what they were looking at while my hands were focused on arcane gestures for tasks that only I could see. I didn’t feel very present.
Like Meta glasses, which are currently grappling with a “pervert” glasses reputation, the Specs also let you take photos and record video. They too have a privacy indicator light, and it’s arguably more prominent than Meta’s take: Instead of a light that’s off to the side, the Specs’ light is right in the center of the glasses. But I don’t know if, given the growing pushback against Meta’s glasses, a blinking light is enough to deter concerns about potential unwanted recording.
In 2024, Snap CEO Evan Spiegel told The Verge that there is an opportunity for computers to evolve to “support the ways that humans have long interacted socially by looking at each other eye to eye with much more natural interaction.” Today, Snap has a simpler message: It says that its vision with Specs is to “make computing more human.” But even in my controlled demos, I found that Specs were actually more computer than other hardware; the glasses are unmissable on my head, and the digital content that only I could see was getting in the way of me interacting with the other people in the room.
Still, these headsets are coming. Meta is working on a pair, Google has a new glasses initiative, OpenAI has reportedly considered smart glasses, and Apple is apparently planning to announce Ray-Ban Meta-like smart glasses next year (and it’s worth noting that former Apple CEO Tim Cook has repeatedly praised AR in the past). It’s clear they all see the next frontier as glasses with tech like cameras and screens that sit on your head. Specs will be the first real test of what AR glasses can be. But even after Snap’s years of work, they still might be coming out too soon.

Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for using ants as garnish
- Published
A two Michelin-starred restaurant in Seoul has been fined for using ants as a dessert garnish.
The owner of Evett in the South Korean capital was fined 15 million won (£8,144; $10,965), while the company operating the restaurant was fined 10 million won for violating the Food Sanitation Act, local media report.
Ants are not among the 10 insect species approved for human consumption in the east Asian nation. The approved list includes grasshoppers, locusts and some silkworms.
Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the restaurant's owner, as well as a 20 million won fine - but the judge took the owner admitting the charge and having no prior criminal record into account.
However, the judge is reported as saying that, as well as violating food standards, the presence of heavy metals exceeding standards was detected in the ants when they were tested, meaning the "culpability is not light".
The owner was said to have been unaware that providing ants in food was prohibited in South Korea, as they are used as food elsewhere.
Their use as a topping for sorbets at Evett came to light after the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety found online reviews accompanied by photographs.
It said the owner had sprinkled three to five ants on certain dishes to give them a "sour taste", over a period of nearly four years - amounting to approximately 49,000 ants used as a garnish.
Most of the ants were imported from the US, while some came from Thailand, the ministry said.
The owner had argued that they were used in a "small part" of the restaurant's 15-course menu and that diners were told they could opt for a non-ant alternative topping.
Ants are eaten and sometimes even valued as a delicacy in several Asian, African and Latin American cultures. Weaver ants and their eggs are used in Thai and Cambodian cooking, while in Colombia, queen ants are as prized as caviar.
The Michelin Guide considers a two-star establishment as one that does "excellent cooking" and is "worth a detour".

Gender disparity in organ transplantation is a global problem affecting each step of the transplantation process, from organ donation, recipient listing, waiting times and access, to post-transplant outcomes. This inequality is most visibly expressed in the overrepresentation of women as living donors, while men continue to be the majority of transplant recipients.
What the data reveals
India’s case is a particularly striking example of this gender imbalance. Women constitute the majority of living organ donors, but men get the majority of transplants. As per recent data from the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organization (NOTTO), between 2019 and 2023, 63.8% of living organ donors were women and 69.8% of transplant recipients were men.
This is not a new divide. In 2019 and 2020, roughly two-thirds of living donors were women, but only about a quarter of recipients were women. A 2025 analysis found that women accounted for 36,038 of the 56,509 living donations over the five-year period studied, also highlighting the scale of the imbalance. Of these, however, only 17,041 were transplanted into women, as against 39,447 transplanted into men.
This gendered pattern raises a fundamental question: why are women expected to give and men positioned to receive in disproportionate numbers? The answer goes far beyond biology.
Behind the donations
Women’s decisions to donate organs are shaped by a complicated interaction between sociocultural expectations, economic conditions and family structures. In many Indian homes, women, particularly wives and mothers, are still expected to put the needs of their families before their own. The expectation can be particularly sharp in the case of a life-saving transplant for a close family member.
Studies have noted the role of women in familial organ donation. Mothers are, on average, 73% of all parental donations, and wives are 91% of donations between married couples. These figures are suggestive of a long-standing social tendency to assign the bulk of care work to women, and perhaps even to the final act of bodily sacrifice.
Psychological and experiential reasons may also play a role in women’s higher willingness to donate. Past experiences with the health care system, such as pregnancy and delivery, may increase familiarity with medical settings and trust in health care providers. But these explanations have to be discussed in the light of the strong influence of social conditioning. What seems like a personal choice can sometimes be influenced by expectations, emotional duties or an unspoken belief that a woman should make sacrifices for her family.
Patriarchal attitudes can also be a disincentive for men to become donors. Men are generally considered the primary breadwinner and economic provider for their families. Thus, the prospect of a man needing major surgery, a long recovery period or a temporary loss of income might be seen as an unacceptable financial risk. Such pressure can transfer the burden of donation to women.
This dynamic is particularly problematic when financial dependency is a factor. The costs of evaluation, surgery, recovery and the potential loss of household income may make male donation seem less feasible. In such cases, women may be subtly, and in more troubling cases, explicitly encouraged to donate, because they are seen as more expendable in the family’s economic structure. Thus, the line between voluntary altruism and coercion can become perilously blurred.
It is, therefore, the duty of healthcare providers to fully discuss these issues at every stage of the process, explain the ramifications of a donation and t ensure that they are indeed personal choices of women, and not influenced by other factors.
What needs to change
This has implications for more than just transplant statistics. Essentially, it’s a question of equity, autonomy and justice in healthcare. An organ donation system cannot be truly equitable when it is based on social and familial pressures about who is supposed to donate, and on socioeconomic or structural barriers about who gets the transplant.
Interventions are required at several levels to address this gap. Awareness must be the starting point, but awareness is not enough. Transplant services and community-based initiatives should be extended to rural, underserved and marginalised regions and not be confined to major urban centres. In particular, women should have equal access to information, evaluation and transplantation services.
Equally important is strengthening psychosocial assessment of potential living donors. Pre-transplant evaluation should not only include medical suitability and financial considerations, but also explore the wider social environment in which the donation decision is being made. Healthcare professionals should be trained to recognise warning signs of coercion, domestic abuse, threats, violence, manipulation and financial dependence. Donors must be provided with real opportunities to make informed and voluntary decisions, including the opportunity to withdraw without fear of repercussions.
Better and more comprehensive data collection is also needed in India. Good, disaggregated data on donors and recipients – disaggregated by gender, age, socioeconomic status, geography, relationship to recipient and other relevant factors, would enable policymakers to better identify disparities and design evidence-based interventions. Grassroots research is important because national averages can hide significant inequalities at the regional and community level.
The challenge is to move beyond the financial transaction of organ donation, and to acknowledge the quieter pressures that can exist within families. Sometimes coercion doesn’t take the form of an explicit threat. It could be the expectations of a wife, the responsibilities of a mother or the assumption that a woman should sacrifice herself for the family’s survival.
The bigger message is hard to miss: gender inequality does not stop at the hospital door. It can influence who gives, who gets, who waits and ultimately who gets a chance to live.
(Dr Shivakumar S. Patil is consultant, renal transplant surgery, Manipal Hospital, Hebbal. shivakumar.patil@manipalhospitals.com)

In early September 2026, people shared an alleged screenshot of an X post from the platform's Twitter era purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump posting on his @realDonaldTrump account, "Don't let Obama buy the election by handing out unlimited free money to states."
Users shared the image after Trump's pledge to give $5,000 to every U.S. adult should the Republican Party win the 2026 midterm elections. The president announced the pledge during the GOP midterm convention in Dallas on Sept. 10, calling the payments a "Trump dividend."
The screenshot of the alleged tweet spread on Bluesky, Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X and other platforms.
(Thomas Mohr accessed via Bluesky)
Some users drew direct comparisons between Trump's alleged remark in 2012 and the news of his $5,000 pledge. Others referred to the "dividend" as bribery and socialism.
(@mandyarthur accessed via X)
In sum, the 2012 Trump post is real. He tweeted (archived) it on Oct. 30 of that year, one week before the Nov. 6 elections.
Don't let Obama buy the election by handing out unlimited free money to states.
— Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) October 30, 2012
Snopes emailed the White House for its response to users comparing the 2012 post to the "Trump dividend." We will update this article if we receive further information.
The 2012 elections concluded with former President Barack Obama winning a second term. The Democratic Party picked up two seats to continue maintaining a majority in the Senate. Republicans lost eight House seats but continued their control of the legislative chamber.
For further reading, we previously published a collection of 24 things Trump actually posted on Truth Social, including, for example, an Easter Sunday post threatening Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz or be "living in hell," as well as a Memorial Day message addressing "scum" that spent years "trying to destroy our country."

Pennsylvania says an unvaccinated woman has died from measles-related complications
An official in Pennsylvania has confirmed the measles-related death of a 40-year-old woman. Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong told NPR that the woman, who died on Saturday, was unvaccinated.
"This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease," a statement from the coroner's office said.
Officials have not released the woman's identity, but said she was a resident of Jefferson County. This is the third death that Pennsylvania state officials have linked to measles this year. No other states have announced measles deaths in 2026.
On Friday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported 676 measles cases so far this year. It also reported 52 new positive cases from Wednesday to Friday.
Pennsylvania officials and the federal government have clashed over the number of measles-associated deaths in the state in recent weeks, as the U.S. faces a nationwide resurgence of the illness. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared that the highly contagious virus had been eradicated from the U.S. in 2000.
Last week, the CDC reported more than 3,200 confirmed measles cases in the country.
The agency said it was reviewing whether to count two measles-related deaths involving infants in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. After Gov. Josh Shapiro announced the state's first two deaths, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said on X the announcement appeared to have been "premature" and "may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor's hopeful staffers."
This clash is notable, as NPR's Rob Stein has reported. "The CDC usually defers to the state's determination" of cause of death in this kind of outbreak, "so the agency can alert the public, doctors and health officials around the country."
The CDC lists the number of measles cases reported in each state for 2026, as well as the number of hospitalizations. The agency has not listed the number of deaths for this year. Instead of giving a figure, there is an asterisk that explains: "The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause."
Kennedy has said on X that NCHS "will update as it receives and reviews submitted records."
The Jefferson County Coroner's Office also emphasized measles can lead to severe complications at any age.
"While cases of severe illness remain uncommon, this tragedy highlights that measles should not be taken lightly," said Chief Deputy Coroner and Public Relations Officer Jason Stiver in a statement. "Public health measures, early recognition of symptoms, and consultation with healthcare providers are important tools in protecting our community."
The county coroner's office is working with the Pennsylvania Department of Health on the case. Pennsylvania and South Carolina have the highest numbers of confirmed measles cases in the U.S., according to federal data.

Abundantia Entertainment, led by Vikram Malhotra, and Almighty Motion Picture, led by Prabhleen Sandhu, have joined hands to produce Heavy Metal, a feature film based on Ameer Shahul’s investigative book Heavy Metal: How a Global Corporation Poisoned Kodaikanal, published by Pan Macmillan. The film is currently in pre-production, with principal casting underway and filming expected to begin soon.
EXCLUSIVE: Abundantia Entertainment and Almighty Motion Picture join hands for Kodaikanal Mercury thriller Heavy Metal
The project will explore the mercury contamination controversy in Kodaikanal, Tamil Nadu, and the events surrounding a thermometer factory operated by Hindustan Unilever. The issue came into focus in 2001 following allegations related to the disposal of mercury-contaminated waste from the facility.
Over the years, the controversy developed into a prolonged campaign involving former factory workers, local residents, environmental activists and Greenpeace. The issue also attracted international attention, raising questions around worker safety, corporate accountability and environmental responsibility.
Based on Shahul’s investigative account, the film is being developed as a corporate-environmental thriller with an investigative narrative and a strong human element. The makers are looking to explore the events through the experiences of those affected by the controversy and the larger questions surrounding industrial practices and environmental impact.
According to those familiar with the project, the creative approach draws inspiration from films and series such as Erin Brockovich, Dark Waters and Chernobyl, while focusing on the specific events surrounding the Kodaikanal controversy.
For Almighty Motion Picture, Heavy Metal adds to its slate of projects inspired by real-world events, people and institutions. The production house recently backed the streaming series Made in India: A Titan Story.
The collaboration with Abundantia Entertainment brings together two production banners for a project that combines elements of a corporate thriller, investigative mystery and human drama.
The film is expected to go on floors shortly. Details about the director, cast and other members of the production team are expected to be announced in the coming days.

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.
City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.
Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.
In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.
Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.
“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.
BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.
Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.
He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.
“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.
“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.

Investment platforms Zerodha and INDmoney have flagged the cost impact of the new merchant discount rate (MDR) on UPI transactions, warning that they could incur charges on fund transfers without necessarily generating corresponding trading revenue. While Zerodha cofounder and CEO Nithin Kamath called for the charge on broking transactions to be capped at ₹5 or ₹10, INDmoney founder Ashish Kashyap used a hypothetical example to illustrate the potential cost for investment platforms under the new framework. The concerns came after the Centre introduced a new MDR framework that will end nearly six years of fully free UPI payments for certain merchant transactions. Under the new UPI MDR framework, which will come into effect on October 15, capital market transactions will attract an MDR of 0.02%, capped at ₹300. The category covers payments to stockbrokers, securities dealers, mutual funds, and investment platforms. Standard person-to-merchant transactions above ₹2,000 will attract a higher MDR of 0.4%, capped at ₹300. Person-to-person transfers and eligible transactions involving small merchants will remain exempt. The finance ministry has said MDR is a charge within the merchant-payment ecosystem and cannot be passed on to customers. In a post on X, Kamath said Zerodha currently does not charge brokerage on equity delivery trades because its economics allow it to offer the service for free. However, a charge on every UPI transfer could create an additional cost for the broker, irrespective of whether the customer ultimately executes a trade. “If every UPI transfer starts carrying an additional cost, irrespective of whether the customer actually trades, I don’t see how we can absorb this indefinitely,” he said. Broking’s UPI MDR Problem Kamath said the new structure does not account for the fact that transferring money to a stockbroker does not necessarily result in a transaction. Unlike a typical merchant payment, customers can deposit funds into their broking accounts without subsequently using the money to purchase securities. In such cases, the broker would bear the UPI cost without earning any revenue from the transfer. Illustrating the potential impact, Kamath said 10,000 customers could each make 50 UPI transfers of ₹2 Lakh in a month without executing a single trade, potentially costing the broker around ₹2 Cr without generating any business. Kamath also flagged the impact of SEBI’s periodic settlement requirement, under which brokers must return unused funds to clients every month or quarter. Customers who want to deploy the returned funds must transfer them back into their broking accounts. Kamath said more than half of these transfers take place through UPI, potentially leaving brokers to bear MDR on funds redeposited following the mandatory settlement, without generating incremental revenue. Kamath said MDR on UPI was “probably inevitable”, given the payments platform’s widespread adoption. However, he said the proposed structure does not work for use cases such as investing and broking. He proposed retaining the 0.02% MDR for broking transactions while reducing the cap from ₹300 to ₹5 or ₹10 per transaction. INDmoney Flags Potential Cost Impact INDmoney founder Ashish Kashyap also flagged the potential impact of the MDR on investment platforms. Using a hypothetical example, Kashyap said an investment app receiving ₹200 Cr through UPI each day for investments in stocks, derivatives, and mutual funds would incur ₹4 Lakh in MDR at the 0.02% rate. Assuming 24 trading days a month, this would translate into an annual cost of ₹11.52 Cr. Kashyap added that INDmoney would not pass the additional cost on to investors. PhonePe, which operates the stockbroking and investment platform Share.Market through its subsidiary PhonePe Wealth Broking, could also face MDR costs when customers transfer funds into their broking accounts through UPI. However, the group stands to benefit from the new framework through its much larger payments business, as UPI app providers will receive a share of the MDR generated from eligible transactions processed through their platforms. PhonePe founder and CEO Sameer Nigam highlighted that around 96% of merchant transactions would remain outside the scope of the new MDR, as they are either below the ₹2,000 threshold or covered by exemptions for small merchants. Nigam said the revenue would help the payments industry recover some of the operational costs it has absorbed while UPI remained MDR-free and support further investment in the ecosystem.

Vladimir Putin has arrived in India’s capital of Delhi ahead of an 11-member Brics summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
The Russian president and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, were due to hold talks with India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, while Chinese leader Xi Jinping was also expected to attend the two-day meeting.
Putin arrived at Palam air force Station in Delhi, where he was greeted by India’s minister of state for external affairs, Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia’s Ria Novosti news agency.
The summit will mark Xi’s first visit to India since 2019 and is seen as the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
On Friday posters of a beaming Modi lined streets in Delhi, along with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
Brics was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the Brics summit,” said Harsh V Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation. “What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of Brics – today looks like a big constraint on Brics”.
It will be Pezeshkian’s first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the [expanded] group’s cohesion,” said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the Brics foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025 but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, visited Kyiv this month, when the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

When I make my yearly trip to Denver, I always bring my road bike. It’s my annual chance to suffer on the kinds of gradients unavailable in the glacier-scoured lands of northeastern Illinois. In advance of this year’s trip, Specialized hooked me up with its new gravel bike, the Diverge 4 Pro, so I brought it with me to challenge it in ways not possible on the fastidiously groomed gravel trails of suburban Chicago.
In contrast to the Specialized Turbo Creo 2 we reviewed a couple of years ago, the Diverge 4 Pro is strictly human-powered. Specialized calls it “the ultimate getaway vehicle,” designed with input from off-road adventure riders, scientists, and racers. It’s marketed as the only gravel bike you need for racing, adventure, and distance rides. While I can’t speak to its racing performance, I can say the Diverge 4 Pro is a blast on any kind of gravel and does well enough on the road.
Priced at $8,249, the Diverge 4 Pro is designed for rough trails and technical descents, both of which unfolded below me at the summit of an is-it-gravel-or-is-it-single-track climb in Douglas County, Colorado. I took a deep breath, and down I went. The descent was rutted and slightly more technical than anything I’ll ever run into around Chicago, but I had enough time on the bike to realize that if I had trouble on the descent, it wouldn’t be the bike’s fault.
A “shocking” update
To understand what makes the Diverge Pro 4 stand out, I’ll start with my favorite feature. Future Shock 3.3 is Specialized’s suspension system, and it’s a significant upgrade over the earlier versions used on the Turbo Creo 2 and Diverge Pro 3. The mechanism lives between the head tube and stem. It isolates the rider from high-frequency impacts while adding relatively little weight and without changing the bike’s steering geometry or introducing brake dive—two compromises that can come with conventional suspension forks. The fork, head tube, and front wheel remain rigidly connected, with the stem and handlebars moving vertically relative to the rest of the bike.
Future Shock uses hydraulic damping to control the movement of the spring inside the head tube. A spring by itself will just compress and return the stored energy, which can lead to a pogo-stick-like experience on bumpy roads and gravel. The damper converts some of that energy into heat by forcing fluid through a controlled pathway. The result on nasty terrain is controlled vertical movement rather than a bouncy rebound. 20 mm doesn’t sound like much, especially to anyone accustomed to mountain bikes with 100 mm or more of suspension travel. But Future Shock isn’t trying to keep a wheel planted while you launch off a rock. Its job is to prevent a stream of smaller impacts from traveling through the handlebars, into your hands, arms, shoulders, and eventually your increasingly annoyed brain. And it’s very good at it.
Specialized says laboratory testing showed up to a 53 percent reduction in peak impact at the bars versus competing setups. That’s an impressively precise number generated under equally precise laboratory conditions, so don’t read it as “every bump feels 53 percent smaller.” But whatever the decrease, the underlying effect wasn’t difficult to detect, as I felt less arm and upper-body fatigue after long rides than I experience on my own gravel bike.
Compression damping can be adjusted on the fly with a dial at the top of the stem, changing how readily the system moves through its 20 mm of travel. At the firmest setting, Future Shock moves very little under normal riding loads; open it up, and the bars move much more freely over bumps. After some experimentation, I left it fully open on nearly every surface.
Specialized made a number of other changes from the Diverge Pro 3, all of which are positives in my book. The Diverge Pro 4 sports the bike maker’s mid-range FACT 9r carbon frame with reworked geometry that offers longer reach for better weight centering. With the bottom bracket sitting 5 mm lower, the rider’s center of gravity is lower, contributing to a more planted feel in corners. All told, the Diverge Pro 4 weighs in at 8.72 kg.

Although the Diverge 4 Pro comes with 45 mm tires, there’s more than enough clearance for 50 mm tires—in fact, the Diverge I reviewed came with a set of 50 mm Terra TLR Trail gravel tires mounted on the tubeless-ready Roval Terra CL carbon wheelset.
The Diverge 4 Pro’s drivetrain is the SRAM Force XPLR E1, which comes with a single 40t chainring; a 13-speed, 10–46 cassette; and programmable bonus buttons on the brake hoods. It’s a fantastic groupset, offering the same features as the pricier SRAM Red drivetrain in a slightly heavier, less-expensive package. The rear derailleur mounts to a replaceable Universal Derailleur Hanger, or UDH, which means a bent hanger is easier to replace than a proprietary one (which is better than finishing a long ride with limited shifting after you bit it on a corner because you didn’t see some loose gravel and bent your derailleur hanger… not that I’d know anything about that). I found the gear ratios to be more than adequate for anything outside of dropping the hammer on a flat segment of smooth tarmac, and I really appreciated the gearing on climbs while laboring up steep gradients on the big sprocket. I even had an occasion to take advantage of the massive 46t cog in back on a particularly steep stretch of road.
There’s also a Quarq Power Meter tucked away inside the spindle, which measures watts generated on the left side to calculate total power output.
The Diverge 4 Pro keeps the downtube storage area from the 3, and it’s larger. That means more room for a spare inner tube, CO2 cartridges, and tools for in-ride repairs. Or snacks, but I prefer a top-tube bag for gels, Skittles, and other on-bike munching.
A lesson in compliance
To make it to the nearest gravel trail, I need to ride a couple of miles of surface streets, so let’s briefly talk about riding the Diverge 4 Pro on pavement. It’s fine. With the DT350 hubs and bumpy 50 mm tires, the bike sounded like I was powering up a dynamo with each rotation of the pedals. The Diverge feels decidedly stolid on pavement, favoring comfort and stability over the liveliness of a road bike.

Gravel is where the Diverge 4 Pro shines.
It didn’t matter whether I was cruising down a smoothly groomed, crushed-limestone path winding along the Des Plaines River or barreling down a washboard of a gravel road in the foothills of the Rockies. The Diverge gobbled up every surface I threw at it, giving me more confidence to attack stretches of chunky gravel and a feeling of stability on descents—even the technical ones. Whether you’re on rough country roads, flowy singletrack, or bikepacking, the Diverge can handle it.
I’m not a fan of the MTB bottle cage, but the tool storage compartment is a nice feature.
Credit:
Eric Bangeman
I’m not a fan of the MTB bottle cage, but the tool storage compartment is a nice feature.

Eric Bangeman
There’s not much to dislike about the Diverge 4 Pro. The Quarq DUB-PWR meter estimates total wattage from the left leg alone; I’d prefer a spider-based meter that measures total power at the crank spider rather than extrapolating from one side. The cranks on the 56 cm Diverge are 172.5 mm, which is out of step with an industry trend toward shorter cranks. After my second right knee replacement, I swapped out the 172.5 mm cranks on my road bike for 165 mm. Getting into an aero posture is easier and more comfortable with shorter cranks, and since my knees don’t go as high at the 12 o’clock position, there’s less hip impingement, and I experience less discomfort overall. I’m also not a fan of the mountain bike-style S-Works Carbon Zee bottle cage with the openings on the side. I ride with one-liter bottles on hot days, and my leg would occasionally bump the bottle lid on the open side of the cage.
But those are truly minor quibbles. Ultimately, the Diverge 4 Pro is a fantastic gravel bike that is ideal for those who love rough gravel, long rides, or bikepacking through the wilderness. But let’s be frank: Not everyone needs to ride around on an $8,000 gravel bike—if you would be happy with a less-expensive aluminum bike or carbon setup with a mechanical groupset, this isn’t the bike for you. (And if your wallet is wide open, Specialized just launched the $12,500 S-Works Diverge 4 this week.) But if you’re more Unbound Gravel than groomed gravel, you can’t go wrong with the Diverge 4 Pro.
Eric Bangeman is the Managing Editor of Ars Technica. He lives in the northwest suburbs of Chicago, where he enjoys road cycling and plays bass in a band.

Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
- Published
Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way.
His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb.
But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta.
And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present.
"If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can."
Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society.
As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous. In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together.
That has made the service a target for Russia - which in recent months has stepped up not only its attacks on postmen and women but also sorting offices and logistical hubs. The Kremlin has claimed strikes like this are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian online retailers like Wildberries.
Speaking in his imposing Soviet-era office building that overlooks Kyiv's famous Maidan square, Smelyansky said: "If we don't go [to a village], we don't have basic supply. We don't have food. We don't have medicine. People will struggle. If we do go, they may delay a decision to evacuate from the areas they probably should have evacuated."
There are many risks. If a post van turns up unannounced, a crowd can form, creating a target for an opportunistic Russian drone operator. But if they call ahead, information could leak.
"Is it a danger?" Smelyansky said. "Absolutely. Because there are Russian sympathisers who can give them the location of the truck that's coming."
By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in
If Smelyansky chooses not to send a van in, he faces criticism. "You get messages from people from those villages: 'You betrayed us. You didn't come...' But if I go, I may risk the life of the driver."
Smelyansky says Russia is deliberately targeting his staff because of the vital role they play shoring up Ukraine's resilience, helping people stay alive in their homes through the fighting and bitter winters.
"It's not an accident, it's deliberate," he said. "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in." Russia denies targeting civilians.
Since 2022, hundreds of Ukrposhta branches and vehicles have been hit, and more than 50 staff have lost their lives, either on the frontline or on their rounds, according to Ukrposhta.
We travelled with Kateryna Marynych, a 38-year-old postmistress, near Zaporizhzhia - a city not too far from the southern frontlines.
She lost her home and her husband during the full-scale invasion, and came to the area to rebuild her life. She ran the post office in the village of Lukasheve for two years until it was destroyed in March by a Russian drone, targeting soldiers working nearby.
After her van drew up, a steady queue of elderly folk formed. She sat in the front passenger seat, window open, handing out cash, taking payments.
One customer, Nadiia, said she was grateful: "It's a long way for us to travel to Zaporizhzhia. Especially now, at a time when there are attacks all around us. The fact that they come here is really nice."
Oleksandrivna, 77, arrived wearing a purple dressing gown, walking with a crutch. When I asked her where she would be without Kateryna, she replied: "We would be stuffed! I am just out of hospital after a stroke. Where could I go for my medicine?"
But Mykola, 64, pointed to another service the post office provides to a largely elderly population. "It is very important," he said. "It's one of the few joys of the month: you come out, have a chat with people, collect your pension, and go home."
For many people in remote communities, Kateryna can be their last link with the Ukrainian state.
She says she hopes her customers are proud of her. "They love me, they need me," she said. "They are waiting for me. Sometimes they call me, especially after attacks on Zaporizhzhia and ask me how I am. We are like a big family. My attitude towards them is like a grandmother or grandfather."
The attacks on Ukrposhta form part of Russia's wider escalation of its war on Ukraine, stepping up fast drone attacks on civilian infrastructure including business infrastructure, energy facilities, transport networks and border posts. Analysts say that as Russia's invasion stagnates on the battlefield in the east, it is looking for other ways of putting pressure on Kyiv.
For safety, Kateryna always travels with her partner, Slava, who drives. While she sorts the cash, he works from the back of the van, taking and receiving parcels, delivering food and water. He also carries a side-arm in a holster, for personal protection; these vans carry a lot of cash.
Both wear body armour when close to the front line. And they have an antenna in the van that shows them the location of the small first-person-view drones that render the frontline so deadly. They have seen drones from the car but luckily have not yet been hit.
She accepted her job was dangerous but would never change it. "It is my work," she said. "If I can't, who will do my job?"
Ukraine's defence comes in many forms - and it's not always delivered at the barrel of a gun.

President Trump-splains economy to Fed in rant after first interest rate hike in 3 years
President conflates central bank’s interest rate with what a consumer would pay based on a credit score
President Donald Trump on Wednesday slammed the Federal Reserve after the central bank raised its benchmark rate for the first time in more than three years with a nonsensical rant in which he lectured the bank on how to run monetary policy, insisting interest rates "should be 1%, or less," hours
"Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR," Trump wrote. "Our Country is BOOMING with new Investment! If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year. The word 'Deficit' is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS. We are 'carrying' almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"
The president appeared to erroneously conflate the federal funds rate, which the Fed raises or lowers to manage inflation and employment across the entire economy, with the interest rate an individual borrower actually pays based on that borrower's own credit history — the kind of rate a bank quotes a homebuyer or a credit-card company quotes a customer, not something the government sets by decree because the country's credit is good.
And despite the president’s boast that the United States has the "Best Credit in the World," bond investors demand to hold U.S. government debt is going the opposite direction Trump wants, with the yield on 10-year Treasurys topping 5 percent this week.
Trump’s post came as Trump was leaving to campaign in North Carolina for Senate candidate Michael Whatley, just hours after the Federal Open Market Committee voted Wednesday to raise its target rate by a quarter point, to a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent — the first increase, rather than cut, in the federal funds rate since 2023.
The move was engineered not by one of the Fed governors Trump has spent years attacking as "boneheads," but by Kevin Warsh, the chairman Trump elevated to the job in May after months of bullying his predecessor, Jerome Powell, over interest rates that he considered to be too high.
The committee's statement gave little comfort to a president demanding rate cuts. "Inflation remains elevated," the Fed said, adding that "today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2% goal."
Projections released alongside the decision showed policymakers expect, on average, one more quarter-point increase before the end of the year, and none in 2027.
Warsh, who has said the Fed bears responsibility for "65 months of sustained, elevated inflation" and warned in an August speech that "we must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed" before easing up, offered no forecast of his own at Wednesday's press conference — an omission NPR attributed to his general reluctance to hand markets forward guidance that could "tie the Fed's hands."
The backdrop Trump did not mention in his post is a re-acceleration of inflation rather than the "BOOMING" economy he described. Consumer prices rose 3.4 percent over the year through August, driven in part by a surge in gasoline prices that the government has linked to the fallout from the U.S. war with Iran. Diesel hit an all-time high of $6.31 a gallon on Wednesday, according to AAA, and wages have trailed price growth since April.
Wednesday's post is only the latest entry in a fight Trump has picked with the Fed for years. He spent much of his first term demanding rate cuts from Jerome Powell, the chairman he himself had nominated, at one point complaining the Fed had gone "loco" and dismissing its rate-setters as "boneheads" for not cutting fast enough, and mused openly to aides about whether he had the legal authority to fire Powell outright.
The attacks on Powell went nowhere, with the now-former Fed chair stating publicly he would not resign if asked, and Trump's first-term attempts to stack the Fed's board with loyalists, including Stephen Moore and Herman Cain, both collapsed before confirmation.
He revived the pressure campaign in his second term, reviving the "Too Late" nickname for Powell, pushing a Justice Department investigation into cost overruns on the Fed's headquarters renovation that prosecutors ultimately dropped, and installing his own CEA chairman, Stephen Miran, on the Fed's board while he searched for a permanent successor. Warsh, the chairman he found, told senators at his confirmation hearing he would be "strictly independent" and would not cut rates simply because the president demanded it.

Meta is cooking up camera-free glasses, according to a new report. And why shouldn't they? After all, wearing a camera on your face has always been a tough sell — just ask Google.
Remember when Sergey Brin jumped out of a plane wearing Google Glass, recording grainy video of his sky dive? That was way back in 2012, and the bizarre-looking camera glasses flopped soon after.
The public did not take kindly to the idea of being filmed (even though, yes, smartphones with cameras had long existed). A former colleague of mine was even assaulted in a San Francisco bar while wearing them.
Meta has been re-testing the waters with its AI smart glasses. Meta's have proved far more popular than Google Glass thanks to AI, their more traditional look, and list of genuinely useful features.
(Meta's ad that aired during the US Open — where a woman records the back-and-forth of a tennis rally by moving her head, while the crowd around her films on their phones — was particularly effective at pointing out how they can help you stay in the moment.)
But Meta is still hitting the same wall of uneasiness that Google experienced more than a decade ago.
Now, there are signs that Meta is cooking up a simpler, but likely less controversial product. The Information reported this week that Meta is working on a camera-free variant of its AI glasses, though there's no sign that the company is throwing in the towel on camera glasses. The idea is that customers would just have more choices. (Meta declined to comment on the report when contacted by Business Insider.)
I think it's a good idea, and one I'm sure Meta considered years ago, back when they were first mapping out what their smart glasses would look like, and which tech to include. Mark Zuckerberg was no stranger to the Google Glass debacle.
But Meta decided to roll the dice with cameras when its glasses first went to market, and in many ways that's paid off. Sales have boomed in recent years, but so has the backlash, both of which Business Insider has reported on extensively.
With AI glasses, sometimes less is more
A camera-free design means trade-offs. It means no visual identification of what you're looking at (sorry, tourists), and a lot of compelling features go out the door. Say goodbye to recording that tennis bout without your phone.
But in return, there's the opportunity to side-step a lot of IRL controversy, too.
It's easy to suggest Meta should have done this out of the gate, but it's important to remember that Amazon did exactly that with its Echo Frame smart glasses, which plugged into Alexa, before the first pair of Meta Ray-Bans ever launched.
Alexa was pretty bad back then (it's gotten better after Amazon's big AI overhaul), and you probably have never heard of Echo Frames. Meta is the clear market leader in the smart glasses category. In many ways, that early bet paid off.
Introducing a camera-free version still offers compelling use cases. People love listening to music on smart glasses, since it's less isolating than putting in earbuds. You can still ask AI questions without taking out your phone. No cameras also undoubtedly means a sleeker design.
But I'd argue they'll still inherit the baggage of Meta's camera glasses. That's a much harder reputational genie to put back into the bottle. Meta is certainly trying, rolling out a PR campaign and doing some legitimately creative things to fight back against bad actors using its glasses to be creepy (though Business Insider has reported that its crackdown on harassing videos recorded surreptitiously on its glasses is off to a bumpy start). Shaking the "pervert glasses" rep isn't going to be easy.
Meta would be hedging its bets by introducing a camera-free model, five years after launching its first smart glasses. That's not altogether surprising, as the company offers various configurations of wearables with different levels of tech crammed inside (you can buy the pricier Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, which are bulkier but include an integrated screen). Selling a camera-free model could prove a savvy move to tap into a new customer base that isn't willing to risk a stranger grilling them about whether they're recording.
Social norms change. People balked at bringing Jeff Bezos into their bedroom with an always-listening Alexa. Amazon has since sold over half a billion Alexa-enabled devices. Even the famously privacy-focused Apple is now dipping its toe into always-listening territory with its controversial new Apple Watch features.
Will people en masse ever be comfortable with camera glasses? It's entirely possible. Google was met with a resounding "no" 12 years ago. Meta has pushed the needle to "maybe" — but it makes sense to cater to the "no" crowd, too.

It's that time of year: The weather's finally starting to cool off, Halloween decor has taken over most of the stores, and tech companies are dropping their fall launches. Last week was Apple's annual September iPhone event, and last night another tech launch hit the books, though this one's a little more niche. (Though I'd still say folding smartphones are in their early days.)
If you're a fan of e-paper devices that use E Ink, a technology that mimics the appearance of ink on paper, you've probably stumbled across Boox's wide range of E Ink digital notebooks and tablets. One of Boox's most popular models is the smartphone-sized Palma, and the company just announced its third-generation Palma along with two other new products.
Here are all three products released last night and what’s available to shop now (and which one I'm most excited to test as WIRED's resident E Ink device tester).
Boox’s New Generation
Boox launched three new E Ink products: the Boox Note Air6 C ($580), Note Mini C ($580), and the Palma 3 ($340).
The Note Air6 C is a new addition to the Note Air line I've previously tested for my guide to the best digital notebooks. These are essentially E Ink Android tablets that come with a stylus, making them an excellent choice for a powerful digital notebook. That remains true with the Note Air6 C, which will run on Android 16 for an even more tablet-style user interface and apps. The C stands for color, since this model has a color screen with a 10.3-inch Kaleido 3 color display. The Note Air6 C also has new firmware that adds Dual Notes so you can annotate two documents side by side. There are also several AI features, including a meeting and audio insights feature and a document summary. Out of the three devices announced, the Boox Note Air6 C is the only one available right now.
The Boox Note Mini C will cost the same as the larger Note Air6 C, but it has a smaller, 8.52-inch screen. It uses the same Kaleido 3 color display but is designed for more on-the-go work and for holding the device in one hand compared to the larger Air6 C. The Mini C and Air6 have fairly similar specs when it comes to power—both models have an octa-core processor, 6 GB of RAM, and 64 GB of storage. You can expand that storage on both devices up to 2 TB with a microSD card. Overall, it's more about size than it is power if you're choosing between them, but the Note Mini C is not on sale yet. Boox says it's coming soon.
Size also comes into play for Boox's final of the three launches. The Palma 3 is the device I'm most excited to check out, as it's the latest iteration of the beloved Palma line. It's another E Ink screen device with an Android 16 base, but it's shaped like a smartphone—“palm-sized.” Boox promotes this as a low-stimulation second screen, and we've liked it as an e-reader option before. The screen isn't color, but it is 6.13 inches with a dual-tone front light and ambient light sensor to adjust to your surroundings. You'll also get a rear camera (promoted for the Palma 2 as great for document scanning rather than photography), dual microphones, and a customizable smart button like the Palma 2 had before it. The Palma 3 also has an aluminum build, which is a new look after the plastic design of the Palma 2. It's due out simply “soon,” with no formal release date. I'm most interested in how it will compare against smaller models like the Xteink.

In late July, one of the world’s most famous mathematicians issued a warning to his field. Math is entering a “turbulent period,” the UCLA professor Terence Tao said in front of a packed lecture hall at the International Congress of Mathematicians. AI is getting so good at math, he said, that it’s causing a “crisis in our mathematical values and practices.”
Earlier in the same week that Tao gave his talk at math’s most prestigious conference, a researcher at Anthropic had used Claude to disprove an 87-year-old math conjecture. Still, when I asked mathematicians at the conference about their experiences with AI, most hadn’t thought deeply about the topic. Many seemed a little surprised that a journalist was asking them about it at all.
Now mathematicians are paying attention. Last week, OpenAI announced that its bots had cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems regarded as among the grandest challenges in the field. Navier-Stokes has stumped mathematicians since the 1930s: “It’s a career-killing problem—you can spend all your career doing it and never get the solution,” David Dritschel, a mathematician at the University of St. Andrews, told me. OpenAI said its swarm of 10,000 AI agents solved the problem in less than four days.
In the math world, the initial shock over OpenAI’s result has morphed into something of an existential reckoning for the discipline. Although OpenAI was able to solve the Navier-Stokes problem only by pulling from nearly a century’s worth of human efforts, academics are realizing just how much power the AI industry now has over math. “We’re seeing how swiftly an entire field can be ravaged by AI,” Max Weinreich, a math professor at CUNY Baruch, told me.
OpenAI’s breakthrough is as notable as how it was achieved. The night before OpenAI announced its solution, the NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster released a statement alleging that he had been scooped by OpenAI. With the heavy assistance of AI tools, Buckmaster and his collaborator, Levent Alpöge (who works at Anthropic), had made major progress toward solving the Navier-Stokes problem. Buckmaster implied that OpenAI might have copied their approach by accessing his messages with OpenAI’s agents. “Almost nobody else I know of was working on it,” he wrote.
In an announcement the next day, OpenAI said that it had tasked its AI systems to work on all of the Millennium Problems after hearing rumors that Anthropic had solved two of them. OpenAI claims that it focused on the Navier-Stokes problem only after finding promising partial results, and that it never looked at Buckmaster’s inputs. In any case, OpenAI poured incredible resources into solving this problem—expending millions of dollars in tokens—all because it heard an unfounded rumor of a solution. (OpenAI declined to comment.)
This drama has underlined concerns many mathematicians have about AI developments within the field. AI companies are encouraged to solve problems in a way that generates good headlines for their bots—marshaling resources that academics never could—but those solutions won’t necessarily aid further discoveries or help humans understand mathematics. On Friday, 25 winners of the Fields Medal (sometimes called the Nobel Prize of mathematics) released a statement called “A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics.” “The push by AI companies to solve mathematical problems as a benchmark is detrimental to the science of mathematics, and to the mathematical community,” they wrote.
All of this can seem obtuse. Isn’t the point of mathematics to solve problems? But there’s more to a problem than just knowing whether it’s true. Solving a major problem in pure mathematics is often like getting a man on the moon: symbolically meaningful but with little direct value. Even though the Navier-Stokes problem deals with one of the most important models in fluid dynamics—a topic of great interest to airplane designers, climate modelers, and many other scientists—knowing the actual result is basically useless.
However, with both a math problem and the moon landing, the process of reaching that goal can indirectly develop all sorts of useful tools applicable to other problems. As part of the Apollo missions, NASA engineers and contractors had to solve subproblems that ultimately proved useful elsewhere. The need for an onboard computer, for example, helped spark the nascent computer-chip industry. Perhaps more surprising, to ensure that astronauts did not get sick while in space, the Apollo program helped set food-safety standards that have since become standard in the industry.
Mathematicians hope that OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof will end up containing ideas that make it easier to study all sorts of other problems, inside and outside of pure mathematics. This has happened before. For instance, efforts to prove Fermat’s Last Theorem produced mathematical tools that now underpin the newest online encryption methods.
It’s still too early to tell what humans might be able to learn from OpenAI’s proof. The paper is 166 pages and “almost incomprehensible,” Dritschel said. Yet over the coming months and years, mathematicians will exert substantial effort to dissect and distill OpenAI’s proof until its central ideas are understood enough to (hopefully) be applied elsewhere.
Humans won’t be able to do that for most AI-generated math results, however. Already, there are AI proofs that no human understands, not because the ideas are impossible to grasp, but because no one has had the time to look through the solution carefully. It’s easy to imagine a future in which mathematicians use AI to prove ever more impressive results ever more quickly—but they don’t understand what they’re proving in much detail. AI systems can speed the rate of problem-solving, but they can’t make it that much easier for human mathematicians to grasp a proof.
So if the field as we know it is to survive, mathematicians need to figure out how to adapt. One idea is to give less credit for solving a problem and more credit for work that communicates the ideas behind a solution in a way that can benefit the broader mathematical community. Yet it’s hard to say exactly how that works in practice. Unlike solving problems, evaluating how well a mathematician has communicated with their peers has no clear metrics.
It will take time for mathematicians to figure out the best response. All the while, AI is continuing to develop incredibly quickly. In less than the time that it takes to complete a Ph.D., systems such as ChatGPT have gone from struggling with basic arithmetic to solving some of the most famous problems in the world. Math’s turbulent period, as Tao deemed it, isn’t ending anytime soon.
