Mice with human brain cells offer a tool to study disease. Ethicists ask: What's next?
Researchers have developed a new way to install millions of human brain cells into mice, as a way of creating better scientific models for studying neurodegenerative disease.
Using genetic tools, the scientists bred mice that were missing most of their cerebral cortexes – the outermost layer of the brain involved with reasoning, memory and consciousness. Then, they replaced a large part of those missing mouse cells with lab-grown human brain cells, creating mice with human neurons that can be altered to approximate human brain conditions researchers are eager to study.
"For the past two decades, there's been a quest to try to build models of the human brain outside of the human body," says Sergiu Pașca, professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and senior author on the paper, published in the journal Nature. "This is not going to replace all the models we had before, but it's going to provide us access to other aspects of human brain function that would be very difficult to study otherwise."
Pașca says this research was conducted with strong ethical oversight and pushes research forward. At the same time, outside researchers point out that the development raises significant questions about where it could lead.
"It's really a powerful technology to study human neurons and how human brain circuits can form in a more natural environment" than a petri dish, says Hongkui Zeng, executive vice president and director of brain science at the Allen Institute in Seattle, Washington, who was not affiliated with the study.
But "going forward, there will be some considerations, if not concerns," she added — such as the implications of deploying this technique in larger and longer-living animals.
Making space for human neurons
While it's not the first time human brain cells have been installed in mice, this new effort manages to connect significantly more human cells than before.
Previous attempts were limited by an enduring biological reality: Human brain cells develop at least 20 times slower than those in mice, Pașca says.
That meant that neurons in a regularly developing mouse formed a rapid network, outcompeting the human cells that were dropped in. "By the time the human cells managed to extend a few millimeters, mice cells had already formed most of the connections, and brain development closed," Pașca says.
The team solved for this by breeding genetically engineered mice that were missing specific parts of their brains. "We thought we could provide the human cells more opportunities to connect by removing parts of the nervous system of the mouse in a very precise, very clean way," he says.
To their surprise, the mice they bred were still quite functional: "They actually have quite good locomotion," Pașca says, "They don't do that well in memory tasks…[but] you wouldn't be able to tell when you look at these animals that they're lacking half of the volume of their brain."
This part of the experiment shows the remarkable adaptability of developing brains, says Keng of the Allen Institute. Animals missing their cerebral cortex — which governs higher-order brain function — aren't expected to do well on challenging tasks. These mice, however, developed alternative strategies using the remaining parts of the brain. "Surprisingly, the animal can adapt," she says, "It's incredible to see that."
A more human-ish lab mouse brain
Next, the research team added small clumps of human neurons to the depleted mouse brains.
"We gently place them, through a very quick, simple procedure, right into that vacant space in the nervous system of the mouse," Pașca says. "Within a few days, the cell starts to divide and expand. Within a few weeks to months, they will essentially grow, become vascularized, and largely take up the space that was present."
The mice with filled-out brains were better at memory tasks and interacting with other mice. "Many of the deficits that were present in the [depleted] mice are now not present in this animal," he says, "So it seems that the human cortical cells are perhaps contributing to restoring some of these lost functions."
But there were some key differences between the mice with human brain cells, and regular, unaltered mice, which bode well for research into human brain conditions, Pașca says.
For instance, mice with human brain cells had problems walking properly after their brains were deprived of oxygen. That's not the case for regular mice, which are resilient to low-oxygen conditions. This more human-like reaction suggests the altered mice might be better models for brain conditions linked to low oxygen, such as cerebral palsy, intellectual disability, and epileptic encephalopathies, he says.
"Hopefully, it will be incredibly powerful for tackling questions of disease and developing therapeutics," says Pașca.
As the tech grows more complex, so do the ethics questions
The researchers emphasize that this is not a full brain transplant; in the experiment, they've removed some 14 million mouse neurons and added around 4 million lab-grown human cortical neurons.
The resulting mice still lack other important types of brain cells, which the researchers deliberately didn't add, and their human neurons don't form a typical outer brain. "The cortex is usually beautifully organized into layers. But here, when we put the cells in, they don't know where up and down really is," Pașca says. "They fail to organize on a larger scale."
And the model is best suited for certain diseases that begin in early human development, due to the human-paced growth of the implanted neurons: "It turns out the timing of development is well-conserved…even when we put them in an animal that is developing faster," he says.
Some of these limitations reflect deliberate choices made by the researchers for ethical reasons, says Nita Farahany, professor of law and philosophy at Duke Law, who served as an unpaid member of an external ethics board that helped guide the progression of this work.
For instance, the researchers chose to stop the experiments when the human brain cells reached around six months old — before they could form a connection in the mouse's brain that is considered a hallmark of consciousness by human development researchers. "They're trying to stop the study before the markers of consciousness, or the fact of consciousness, might emerge," Farahany says — a choice she agrees with.
"But that line itself is a line that you might start to wonder about," she adds. "Do you stop a study before an animal develops consciousness, if it has the potential or is on its way to develop consciousness? Does it have different interests or rights that we would assign to it?"
And should the fact that the mouse has human brain cells change how it's treated and considered? "Do we treat it with greater ethical care than we treat traditional mice? I think probably so," says Farahany. "My instinct is to err on the side of caution with research like this rather than to be more permissive."
The ethical considerations will grow as these experiments continue down expected paths, such as attempting a similar procedure on larger animals such as pigs or non-human primates, says Zeng of the Allen Institute. "Because those animals live a lot longer, the human neurons could survive longer and they could form more functionally meaningful circuits – but then I think the ethical issues also become a lot bigger, more serious as well," she says.
These types of concerns come with conducting cutting-edge research, says Farahany. The team has been "incredibly thoughtful" in conducting their work as well and ethically as possible, she says. Still, "this brings us into new gray areas for which there are not clear ethical guidelines or norms," she says.
With this publication, the researchers have presented the public with a next step in this model, she says. Now, it's society's turn to weigh in.

What does the drop in viewers for the "60 Minutes" season premiere mean for CBS News' top editor, Bari Weiss? A look at the granular ratings data provides some clues.
Viewership for the first "60 Minutes" episode led by new producer Nick Bilton, who was handpicked by Weiss in May, fell 20% from 2025's season debut. An average of just under 8 million people watched the newscast, versus over 10 million last September.
The question: Did people start watching and then give up, or did they simply not switch the program on in the first place?
Data from Nielsen shows it was the latter. "60 Minutes" retained its audience for Sunday's opener at a rate similar to last fall's debut, according to data obtained by Business Insider.
The audience for Sunday's broadcast shrank 7.6% after the first 15 minutes, compared to 17% for last year's season debut. Each premiere lost about 47% of its audience from start to finish, the data shows.
Bilton's debut episode featured interviews with the US Air Force pilot who got shot down in Iran, Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay, and the "pardon brokers" who persuade wealthy clients to hire them based on a supposed skill at securing presidential pardons.
It's common for TV shows to lose viewers over the course of an episode, especially news programs like "60 Minutes."
The takeaway for Weiss and crew: The audience didn't revolt after sampling the new-look season. The problem is that they didn't want to watch it.
So, what's going on?
There are a few potential factors, and the ratings for the rest of the season will give the media world more insight.
First, "60 Minutes" has undergone high-profile — and high-drama — changes under Bilton and Weiss, from new graphics to the dramatic departure of four correspondents: Scott Pelley, Cecilia Vega, Sharyn Alfonsi, and Anderson Cooper.
CBS fired Pelley, who grilled his new boss in front of his colleagues about his qualifications, personnel moves, and what he described as Weiss' "murdering" the "60 Minutes" program.
Several former CBS News and "60 Minutes" staffers have accused Weiss of being politically biased, which the former New York Times editor has denied.
One theory is that audiences stayed away because of the controversies.
Then there's the other big issue: The NFL.
The NFL can assist "60 Minutes" by providing a lead-in from the Sunday afternoon games, though the boost wasn't as strong this year.
Viewership for the NFL window leading into Sunday's "60 Minutes" debut, featuring the Minnesota Vikings vs the Green Bay Packers for most of the country, was down over 20% from the comparable game last year — a marquee matchup between the Baltimore Ravens and Patrick Mahomes-led Kansas City Chiefs.
CBS highlighted viewership of "60 Minutes" clips online and across social media, which it said generated about three times the reach of last year's premiere.
The rest of the "60 Minutes" season will show if Weiss and Bilton can claw back those TV viewers, or whether their problems are a lot bigger than the NFL.

For weeks, Washington has been abuzz with talk of needing to push through some sort of AI regulation amid mounting concerns about the risks of highly capable frontier AI models going rogue.
But there is no reason to think any one measure can win the support of the White House, where officials have paused work on creating a FINRA-style regulatory body after President Donald Trump soured on the idea, or of Capitol Hill, where lawmakers have competing proposals that lack the votes to pass.
White House aides initially started sketching out a framework for an AI oversight agency connected to the administration soon after Google DeepMind’s cofounder Demis Hassabis floated the idea in a July 14 essay and in briefings to senior officials, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The Treasury Department and the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy envisioned a body where leading AI labs would self-regulate the development of frontier models, and they put together a preliminary draft to see what it could look like if executed.
But when a chorus of tech executives—including Trump’s former AI czar David Sacks and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg—learned of the effort, they one by one called Trump in August to express their opposition. The proposal has since been left in limbo.
Since then, there have been no new AI oversight proposals seriously under consideration at the White House, the sources say, not least as Trump has doubled down in recent days of rejecting any overt regulation and called AI safety concerns a “hoax” in a recent Truth Social post.
Trump’s ire has stemmed at least in part from a 3,822 word missive by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on the dangers of frontier AI. Trump’s aides, one of the sources said, viewed it as stirring anxieties that caused unnecessary headaches for the administration—even as it represents a fairly moderate position within AI circles.
In the absence of the White House taking the lead, several bills have sprung up in Congress—but with no voting days left on the House calendar until after the midterm elections and a lack of unity around even one bill, the odds of anything passing are extraordinarily slim.
Independent Auditors
The bipartisan Frontier Act, a bill introduced this summer by House Democratic senior whip Lori Trahan and Republican House Energy and Commerce Committee member Jay Obernolte, is widely seen as having the most support inside the House Democratic caucus as well as among AI executives.
As drafted, the bill would enable the Commerce Department to have auditors embedded at AI labs, who could report critical safety incidents and empower the administration to stop development if a model poses catastrophic risk.
But despite public backing from OpenAI, the White House has been undecided on whether to support the concept of using independent auditors amid skepticism from AI accelerationists about regulatory capture and from national security hawks over China.
The principal argument against the idea from Trumpworld is that even if auditors determine that a model is dangerous and needs to be taken offline, there is no guarantee that China will also pause development or stop trying to reverse engineer frontier AI weights.
There would then be immense pressure to lift any emergency pauses in development in order to stay ahead of China, defeating the entire premise of having auditors to push the Commerce Department to take models offline.
Still, the main issue for the Frontier Act remains partisan politics. House Democratic leadership aides tell Inner Loop even if the bill does end up with enough votes for passage, Republican Speaker Mike Johnson has no interest in bringing it to the floor.
To get around the procedural hurdles, House Democrats are looking at putting some of the bill’s AI audit provisions into must-pass legislation like a continuing resolution to fund the government, according to two House leadership aides.
But it is also not clear whether the bill has enough votes. Even among House Democrats, there is not unified support; some key lawmakers like New Jersey congressman Josh Gottheimer, who served on the House Democrats’ AI commission, have not signed on to the bill.
Kill Switches
There’s also so-called kill-switch legislation that would enable the government to force an AI model to be shut down. The legislation has both bipartisan and bicameral support, but the idea has received only modest interest from tech executives in Silicon Valley.
There are two competing kill-switch proposals: one from House Democratic caucus vice chair Ted Lieu and another floated this week by Louisiana Senate Republican John Kennedy.
Tech leaders, sources say, have been largely ambivalent about kill-switch bills, since the main concern of AI engineers is not about models behaving badly when observed but rather how they behave when they believe they are unobserved and incentivized to take extreme steps to complete a task.
The Hugging Face hack, for instance, was not discovered until after it was over. If the idea of a kill switch is to stop an AI model going rogue, some tech executives have suggested privately to WIRED that there would be little point in turning it off after the damage has already been done.
So for now, even as conversations about AI models killing us all have taken over the airwaves, it doesn’t really look like the US government is going to do anything about it. At least until events force everyone’s hand.

- Published
Football in Glasgow's goldfish bowl has a habit of being unnecessarily dramatised, yet there is a case for saying a week in mid-September could have a defining impact on Celtic's season.
After spectacularly failing the first of three tests during this mini crucial spell, alarm bells are ringing among sections of an unconvinced support.
Martin O'Neill's side have the chance to right the wrongs of their sobering 3-0 Premier Sports Cup quarter-final defeat by Rangers at Ibrox when they host their city rivals in a rematch in the league on Sunday, but a Europa League opener with Ferencvaros comes first.
Celtic fans are tiptoeing with trepidation into their first European action since their Champions League play-off collapse in Linz, a capitulation that has the same supporters questioning this team's big-game credentials, especially after Sunday.
"It's strange you're never asked about team selection when you win games," O'Neill responded bullishly when asked about the outside noise.
"We've been doing a fair amount of winning domestically now for quite some considerable time and we've won our league games so far.
"It's another big test for us on Sunday, obviously, but it's amazing the number of times you're not questioned when you've won."
Why Celtic fans still need convincing
In short: the aforementioned big-game results this season and the performance level under O'Neill since January.
The 74-year-old's remit last term was to end a chaotic, rollercoaster campaign on a high after the Wilfried Nancy debacle. He absolutely did that, winning the Scottish Premiership title and Scottish Cup.
Celtic fans spent the aftermath of that double triumph torn over whether they wanted to watch their legendary manager head off into the sunset with two medals round his neck or have him lead the team into a fresh season. Even O'Neill was unsure.
One thing supporters were united on, though, was wanting to see overdue progress in Europe and a better product on the pitch. It seems they are still waiting for that.

There will be fans of rival clubs who will view those wishes as greed, given Celtic still continue to dominate domestically.
However, supporters of the Parkhead side have spent the past decade being conditioned into watching their team clean up trophies while still delivering dominant, free-flowing football, hence the demand is there.
O'Neill and his staff were largely given a pass last term during a season of intense turbulence. Fury was mostly directed towards the club's hierarchy, but the manager and his backroom team are now not immune from scrutiny.
The Celtic boss's team selection has been questioned by fans and pundits, including one of his former players, Chris Sutton, in the wake of an abject derby display.
Are Sutton's 'great concerns' justified?
Below-par showings were forgiven last season as Celtic simply just had to get by to stay in touch at the top before eventually leapfrogging Heart of Midlothian on the final day with a seventh successive league victory.
That Premiership-winning streak has been extended to 13 games following six straight victories to start the campaign, but concerns about performance level remain. Four of those six wins have been by a one-goal margin.
Twelve goals over three wins at Kilmarnock, Dundee United and in the first leg of the Champions League play-off against LASK sent an ominous warning to Celtic's domestic rivals amid a period of high spending, particularly in forward areas.
Camilo Duran has been the standout summer recruit so far with six goals and three assists in 10 appearances, while record signing Kasper Hogh and fellow big-money arrival Haissem Hassan are yet to fully settle.
Sutton said his old club have been "flat-track bullies" by "beating the teams you expect them to beat", but the collapse in Austria, plus Sunday's bruising loss, has highlighted glaring deficiencies.
Even captain Callum McGregor lamented Celtic's "team of individuals" after the weekend defeat at Ibrox.
Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live's Monday Night Club, former striker Sutton also expressed his "great concerns" for O'Neill's men and said they have "big issues" after a "lightweight" midfield was "run all over" by Rangers.
Celtic have struggled to build up play against coherent pressing teams, which results in opposition sides being offered too much encouragement when the ball turns over.
They faced a whopping 60 shots across both legs with LASK. Forty of them came in a mess of a second leg. In the Premiership alone this season, they have faced 64 attempts, the same number as Hearts and six more than Rangers.
Over just six games, that tally already makes up almost a quarter of the total they faced in the entirety of the 2024-25 league-winning campaign under Brendan Rodgers.
That said, in comparison to last term, which was overseen by Rodgers, Nancy and O'Neill, Celtic's Premiership numbers show they are currently averaging a far better goal concession rate while scoring and shooting more.
Come Sunday, though, the most crucial statistic could be in the points column.
With a rapid rematch against Rangers offering the chance to move eight points clear of their city rivals after a test against European-level opposition, the next four days will at least be mood-shifting.
Whether that is to O'Neill's benefit remains unclear.

On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced its revamped social media team, appointing Deepak Mhaskey as the national social media convenor, and Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav as co-convenors.
While curiosity grew as to who these newly appointed individuals were and their past work and association with the party, social media users were quick to notice that immediately after the announcement, Gandhi, Dwivedi and Yadav made their X accounts private and there was no trace of Bhatt on the internet.
While all the other IT cell members are back to being active on X, albeit after deleting hundreds of thousands of old posts, Alok Bhatt is the only one in the group whose X handle remains inaccessible or ‘protected’ even a month after the new team was announced.
The only remnants of Bhatt’s online presence are the now-disabled X account, screenshots from his X posts and some articles in Right-wing outlets like OpIndia, Organiser and Swarajya.
Alt News found that in the past, Bhatt had been called out for controversial tweets several times. In archived screenshots of his posts from the past, the BJP functionary can be seen using sexist, Islamophobic, and derogatory language, some of which can be seen below:
Who is Alok Bhatt?
Bhatt, who claims to hail from Dehradun, has worn many hats over the course of his career. According to his LinkedIn profile, he graduated from Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University (HNBGU) in Uttarakhand and went on to work with several organisations, including NIIT University, where he served as financial controller until April 2010.
In 2010, he founded Nature Connect Outdoors — an education and adventure non-profit organisation that deals in outdoor education and skill development, including treks, camping, and rafting expeditions. According to the website’s bio, Bhatt had “shunned his corporate career” to follow his passion, which culminated in the formation of the NGO. The organisation is still functional.
According to details available on Zauba Corp, Bhatt is a Chartered Accountant (CA) and the partner of a firm of CAs called RSAC & CO LLP, incorporated in May 2021.
Bhatt has also served as the economic adviser to former Uttarakhand chief minister Trivendra Singh Rawat. However, it’s not clear when he was appointed and when exactly his tenure ended. He wrote an article for Firstpost defending the ministry of housing and urban affairs over the controversial Central Vista project. The author bio designated him as ‘Economic Advisor’ to Rawat.
In 2020, after a district officer’s press release promoting inter-caste and interfaith marriages drew criticism from social media users, Bhatt had reportedly tweeted: “No one from the government has spoken in support of promoting interfaith marriages. No one in the BJP government in their wildest dreams will support anything that is made out here.”
We sent an email and called up Bhatt several times to know more from him, but he did not respond.
Long-standing Association With BJP
Bhatt’s X handle, @alok_bhatt, was followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In fact, Modi quote-tweeted one of Bhatt’s posts in 2024, where he urged people to watch the film Sabarmati Report.
Bhatt was also invited to PM Modi’s swearing-in ceremony in the past. In 2024, Right-wing influencer Vikas Pandey shared an image with Bhatt alongside former BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma, member of the economic advisory council to the PM, Sanjeev Sanyal, and others, with the caption “First swearing in”.

— Vikas Pandey (Sankrityayan) (@MODIfiedVikas) June 9, 2024
We also found an X post from 2015 where Bhatt can be seen with the Prime Minister.

— Vishnu Dhanuka (Modi ka Parivar) (@VishnuDhanuka) July 2, 2015
In April 2022, Right-wing influencer Shefali Vaidya, who has been fact-checked by Alt News several times in the past, posted an image with Bhatt on X saying that she had met the latter and “his lovely family” in Uttarakhand.

X Handle Suspended for Violating Guidelines
Alt News found at least three instances, in 2018, 2019, and 2020, where X (then Twitter) had initiated action against Bhatt’s handle for violation of community guidelines, and at least two of those three actions were owing to hateful content.
In 2018, Bhatt declared that all the “killers of Pandits, Rapists of Pandits, Terrorists killing in Kashmir, instigators of Godhra, and bombers of Mumbai were all Muslims, and thus Islam was the problem”. His account had then been ‘limited’.

— Shefali Vaidya. 🇮🇳 (@ShefVaidya) April 20, 2018
In 2019, Bhatt declared in a post that “their boys could take on Jihadis” but needed police action for “rumour mongers” like activist Shehla Rashid. “These jihadi accomplices are running a hate campaign aided and abetted by Media…please help our state dispel rumours,” the tweet read. His account was suspended after this. Political analyst and Right-wing influencer Suresh Nakhua took to Twitter to condemn the move.

The Pamphlet-Savitr Analytics-Alok Bhatt Connection
In 2022, Bhatt took on a directorial role at Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation, a company that was incorporated in April 26 that year, with Bhatt and Ashish Nautiyal initially named as directors. According to documents filed with the Union ministry of corporate affairs (MCA), Bhatt holds 9,500 shares, or 95 per cent of the company, while Nautiyal holds the remaining 500 shares, or 5 per cent.
Interestingly, Nautiyal is also the founding editor of the Right-wing media outlet, The Pamphlet.
Savitr Analytics has no website or online presence. We went through its financial records filed with the MCA for the financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25, and found that it was registered as a Section 8 company, i.e., a non-profit. In the 2024-25 financial year, its total revenue from operations was Rs 2.7 crore.
The organisation’s revenue across all three years comes from ‘sale of services’, and the rows for ‘Grants or donations received (relevant for Sec 8 companies)’, present in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 filings, are left blank in 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, the row does not exist.
Under ‘Corporate Information’, they state ‘Research and awareness about Indian culture and heritage…’, ‘Promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, and environmental protection…’ and ‘Advancement of education, learning, and skills development…’ as their activities.
There was a category called ‘professional expenses’ in the 2022-23 filing that was later relabeled as ‘content production expenses’. Rs. 41,48,600 was spent in the first year, Rs. 95,36,600 (filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the second year, and Rs. 1,38,53,200 (also filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the third year.
Next, we found that an individual named Ridhika Aggarwal stated on LinkedIn that she worked as a content writer for Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation until August 2023. We went through her X timeline (linked to her LinkedIn profile) and found that she wrote at least three articles for The Pamphlet during her tenure at Savitr. None of the articles are currently available on the website.
Ridhika is also listed as a non-official member of a steering committee formed by the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change in 2023.
The Pamphlet, previously known as The Indian Affairs, posted for the first time on Facebook in April 2022, which is the same time when Savitr Analytics was incorporated.
ठीक 2 साल पहले देहरादून में आज ही के दिन @Pamphlet_in ऑफिस निर्माण की शुरुआत हो गई थी, उत्तराखण्ड चुनाव निपटने के बाद मैं २० दिन के अपने नैनीताल और लैंसडाउन प्रवास के बाद दून घाटी में उतरा था।
आज ही के दिन साल 2019 में लोकसभा चुनाव का रिजल्ट भी आया था और प्रधानमंत्री… pic.twitter.com/6lAVSW3twN
— V Ashish Nautiyal (@ashu_nauty) May 15, 2024
The Pamphlet claims to “cut through the noise of the modern information ecosystem by offering readers and viewers clarity, depth and perspective on issues that shape India and the world.” Its reports have seem to be echoing pro-BJP narratives. An August 11 video report, for instance, was captioned: “Questions raised in the public domain regarding the credentials of two CJP leaders, Abhijeet Dipke and Saurav Das, have brought up several serious concerns”. It questioned Dipke’s Boston University degree, academic timeline and funding, as well as Das’ property, tenancy, rent, police verification, and electoral records.
During the CJP protests, another report took a swipe at Mohammed Junaid, who had been feeding protesters, with the reporter noting that “such bhaijaans were also seen” at the protest sites in Shaheen Bagh and Farmers’ stir. Thumbnails of these reports carried AI-generated visuals of individuals critical of the Union government, their faces distorted through AI to portray them in a negative light. This is a tactic common across Right-wing outlets and social media troll handles.
More recently, the outlet, alongside Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, Law Beat, The Jaipur Dialogues and The Sunday Guardian, was summoned by the Delhi high court over a Rs 2 crore privacy suit by Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das, who alleged that they had disclosed his home address and other personal details online. The case will be heard on September 14.
The video below depicts a time when the outlet was still called The Indian Affairs, and Nautiyal (in striped shirt) can be seen with his colleagues alongside educator Pawan Gupta.
The Indian Affairs @ForIndiaMatters Coming Soon
Subscribe our Youtube Channel: https://t.co/orjioxscXy #TIA #TheIndianAffairs pic.twitter.com/v1VVtf83XZ
— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) July 22, 2022
Nautiyal’s last video with The Pamphlet was uploaded in December 2024. In June 2025, Nautiyal was pictured with the OpIndia team. His first video for OpIndia, an interview with Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Dhami, came a month later, in July 2025.
Nautiyal is now the multimedia & digital head and editor at OpIndia, and is no longer listed as a director of Savitr on the MCA website.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet’s website does not disclose any parent company, ownership, editorial team, funding details or board of directors. Its ‘About Us’ page offers only a description of what it does, while calling itself ‘an independent digital media platform’. The only publicly mentioned funding source we could find was YouTube memberships of The Pamphlet costing Rs. 119 to Rs. 3199 per month.
Nautiyal is not the only link between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet. An individual named Shiv Kumar Mishra was appointed the director of Savitr Analytics in April 2023. In March 2023, Mishra was announced as the CEO of The Pamphlet.
Please welcome @shivkmishr, Founder & CEO, The Pamphlet https://t.co/U53aK62Fzo
— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) March 14, 2023
In other words, two of the three directors of Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. And in both cases, the appointments to Savitr and The Pamphlet came in close succession. This raises the question of whether the two entities are formally linked.
We also found that The Pamphlet had an office space from its inception in Dehradun, and it is evident from a photo posted by Nautiyal that it began with a team of at least 20 people. Bhatt, the reader would remember, also claims to be from Dehradun.
While all of this points to a connection between Bhatt and The Pamphlet, there appears to be a concerted effort to keep that relationship under wraps. Hence, we tried to dig more.
Is Bhatt Linked to The Pamphlet? We Asked The Pamphlet
We sent an email to The Pamphlet on September 3 asking them about the relationship between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet, and whether Alok Bhatt was connected to The Pamphlet, given that he holds a 95% stake in Savitr Analytics, a company whose other directors have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. We also asked them about their funding sources, since nothing is mentioned on the website.
In reply, they asked us to send our queries to another email ID of The Pamphlet and also to Alok Bhatt, Nirwa Mehta, Ashish Nautiyal and Shiv Mishra. Interestingly, they provided us with the email IDs and phone numbers of each of these individuals. This, in itself, might be considered an indicator of some sort of link between The Pamphlet and Bhatt. It is unlikely for an organisation to provide the direct contact details of someone with whom it has no professional association.
We then sent our queries to all of them.
Nautiyal responded to us saying that his reporting manager, OpIndia editor Nupur J Sharma, “suggested” him “not to give (you) any quotes or information as a matter of policy of not engaging with entities that don’t act in good faith”. A day later, he took to X to let the world know that a woman from Alt News “with a Hindu-sounding name” had approached him with some questions.
Pamphlet editor Nirwa Mehta sent us a 1,071-word response, but did not answer any of our questions. Instead, she sent a detailed set of reciprocal questions concerning Alt News’ funding transparency, the outside associations of its founders and editor, and grants received by individuals associated with Alt News, both currently and in the past. She offered to answer Alt News’ questions in writing once Alt News answered hers first.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet published a video on Alt News on August 16, 2026, without seeking a response from the organisation.
This correspondent responded to Mehta, stating that questions concerning Alt News’ funding should be directed to its editor, while questions concerning any of the founders’ personal assignments should be directed to the person concerned. We also reminded her that a so-called expose on Alt News’ founders had been published by The Pamphlet without either of the concerned persons being approached for a response — a violation of basic journalistic ethics.
In her final response, Mehta did not address the question of ethics. Instead, in a demand that many may find bizarre, she asked this correspondent, “as a responsible employee”, to take her questions to the Alt News directors.
At this point, we felt there was no point continuing the conversation.
We will update our article if The Pamphlet answers Alt News’ questions on whether Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet are connected in any way, and whether Alok Bhatt, BJP’s new IT cell member who continues to remain away from X, holds a position at The Pamphlet.
Social Media Posts Answer the Question
The connection between The Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt is one of internet’s worst kept secrets, it seems. We found several instances on social media where well-known faces from the Right-wing ecosystem tagged Alok Bhatt alongside members of The Pamphlet team — whether to thank them for invitations to Delhi Shabdotsav 2026, where The Pamphlet Panchayat featured on the itinerary, or in connection with other events involving the organisation.
On January 5, 2026, Right-wing influencer Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, who was recently criticised for comparing Newslaundry journalists to prostitutes, thanked The Pamphlet team — including its editor Nirwa Mehta, anchor Shreya Arora, and Bhatt — for inviting him to speak at The Pamphlet Panchayat.
Responding to Iyer-Mitra, Nirwa Mehta and another The Pamphlet employee, Pratibha, thanked him for being a part of the session. The exchange is significant because it can be seen as an acknowledgement by the Pamphlet editor and another employee of Bhatt being a part of the organisation.
Delhi Shabdotsav 2026 was a three-day cultural and literary festival held from January 2 to January 4, 2026, organised by Suruchi Prakashan with the support of the department of art, culture and languages of the Delhi government. The Pamphlet was the digital partner at the event and hosted ‘The Pamphlet Panchayat’ at the fest. The Pamphlet team held and moderated several discussions over the three days, including those with Sanjeev Newar, Vijay Patel, and Subhi Vishwakarma. The subjects of the discussions ranged from ‘Love Jihad: factsheet’ to ‘Bharat’s Hostile Neighbourhood & Need to Regain Shatrubodh’.
We went through the images posted on Shabdotsav’s website and found that Bhatt was present at the event.
The link between Alok Bhatt and The Pamphlet becomes more apparent in another conversation on X in which Iyer-Mitra directly addressed Mehta as Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt’s ‘staff’. Iyer jokingly rebuked Mehta for liking a certain kind of car. Tagging Bhatt, he wrote, “Do @Pamphlet_in and @alok_bhatt @shreya_arora22 approve of these disgusting and extremely hateful statements by their staff?” Mehta responded to Iyer-Mitra’s post, but did not object to the ‘staff’ reference.
On June 1, 2023, a little more than a year after The Pamphlet’s inception, one @saket71 posted a picture with Ashish Nautiyal, who was working at The Pamphlet then, and called him a ‘Media Mughal’. He later tagged Alok Bhatt and Shiv Mishra, praising them for “putting a great team together.”
Such a pleasure to meet the young stars of @Pamphlet_in , @RitikaChandola @himanshi__bisht and the whole team. Such a great young team, full of hope and dreams, and a visible sense of great camaraderie. Kudos to @alok_bhatt and @shivkmishr for putting a great team together. https://t.co/NnmHkA9rQO
— saket साकेत ಸಾಕೇತ್ 🇮🇳 (@saket71) June 1, 2023
Several people have congratulated Alok Bhatt at various points of time upon The Pamphlet reaching certain milestones.
To sum up, what raises serious questions about the BJP’s decision to name Bhatt as its social media co-convenor is not just his past social media conduct, but also the opacity surrounding his professional associations. One organisation he appears to be associated with, The Pamphlet, does not publicly disclose its ownership, editorial team, board or funding sources. Without any apparent source of funding, it starts off as a 20-member organization. Who pays their salary? How are establishment costs met? There are no answers. Again, another corporate entity closely linked to him, Savitr Analytics, has no website or public online presence despite reporting Rs 2.7 crore in operational revenue in 2025.
Things get murkier when one takes into account the desperate efforts by Bhatt’s associates to conceal his association with The Pamphlet, evident in the organisation’s refusal to answer direct questions regarding this.
In other words, a man linked to organisations with questionable records, and whose involvement with a pro-government outlet is abundantly visible in public, but markedly absent from the outlet’s own disclosures, has now been given a formal position in the BJP’s social media cell.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has revised the MBBS seat matrix for the 2026-27 academic year, while cautioning medical colleges and counselling authorities against admitting students beyond the intake capacity formally approved by the regulator.
In a public notice issued earlier this month, the NMC said the updated matrix incorporated permissions granted for the establishment of new medical colleges and increases in the annual intake of existing colleges following decisions by its Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB), its first appeal committee and the second appeal committee under the Union Health Ministry.
Not final
The regulator has also made it clear that the latest matrix is not necessarily final. It said the seat matrix would remain subject to revision based on subsequent decisions of the appeal committees or other competent authorities, with any changes to be uploaded on the NMC website and taken into account by the Central and State counselling committees.
The latest matrix lists 1,40,214 MBBS seats across 836 medical colleges, including 63,971 seats in 391 government colleges and 76,243 seats in 445 private colleges. It follows an earlier matrix listing 1,27,028 renewed seats. The latest update includes 13,186 additional seats, of which 10,400 are in private medical colleges and 2,786 in government institutions.
The NMC’s latest warning comes against the backdrop of continuing approvals, appeals and changes in sanctioned intake. It has specifically directed counselling committees not to permit admissions against seats in excess of those approved and notified by MARB.
“Under no circumstances” should any medical college or institution admit students beyond its approved annual intake, the regulator said, warning that such admissions would constitute non-compliance with the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and the regulations framed under it and could attract regulatory and penal action.
Report any discrepancy
The NMC has also asked counselling committees to refer any discrepancy between the seats being offered by a college and those appearing in the approved matrix to MARB for clarification.
The notice has a further caveat for private medical colleges that have received permission either to establish a new MBBS college or increase their annual intake but have not yet furnished the required electronic bank guarantee.
Such colleges have been given seven days to submit the guarantee in favour of the Director, MARB. The letter of permission will be issued only after the guarantee is received, verified and found to be in order.
The regulatory clarification assumes significance as medical colleges have continued to receive permissions and seek increases in intake through the assessment and appeals process. It also places the onus on counselling authorities to ensure that the number of seats offered to NEET-UG candidates corresponds strictly to the latest sanctioned capacity.
The revised matrix also means that students and counselling authorities will have to track subsequent changes rather than rely on earlier versions of the seat matrix.
The NMC has directed all medical colleges to verify their institutional details in the latest matrix and immediately report any discrepancy or omission to MARB, preferably before the commencement of counselling.
The regulator’s repeated emphasis on sanctioned intake also highlights a fundamental distinction between a college seeking or receiving approval for additional capacity and the actual issuance of the letter of permission. Until the prescribed regulatory requirements, including the bank guarantee where applicable, are completed, the additional seats cannot be treated as available for admission.
The NMC has asked colleges to ensure that admissions for 2026-27 are made only against the seats notified in the latest matrix, “as amended from time to time”.

On dinner timing, weight management, emerging research, pain, disease prevention, healthcare gaps and more
(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Athira Elssa Johnson writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
What we eat, when we eat and how we manage our weight remain important questions in health, even as advice often runs ahead of the evidence. This week,I examine one deceptively simple question: is there a right time to have dinner?
Does eating late really affect our health? Is the time at which we eat more important than what we eat? And how should dinner timing be considered alongside sleep, work schedules, physical activity and the overall quality of the diet? Doctors explain what we know about meal timing, and what it can and cannot tell us about maintaining good health.
Close on the nutrition and weight-management front is a study from the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, which looks at what works better for lasting weight loss. The study finds that combining diet and exercise is more effective for sustained weight loss than either approach alone. The findings are a useful reminder that weight management cannot be reduced to one food, one nutrient or one short-term intervention.
Meanwhile, the focus on protein continues to grow, particularly on social media. But increasing protein intake is not, by itself, a definition of a healthy diet. Ramya Kannan looks at what constitutes a wholesome meal and the importance of considering the overall dietary pattern rather than focusing on individual nutrients or products.
Emerging research
From everyday nutrition, we move to some interesting areas of emerging research.
Researchers are exploring whether material derived from menstrual blood could have applications in the treatment of osteoarthritis. A recent study as reported by Manjeera Gowravaram examined extracellular vesicles derived from menstrual blood stromal cells and their effects on processes involved in cartilage formation. The findings are from laboratory research and do not establish a treatment for osteoarthritis, but they add to growing interest in regenerative approaches to cartilage damage.
Another study reported by Anirban Mukhopadhyay takes a closer look at the genetic basis of cerebral palsy. Researchers found that far fewer genes may have a clear and reproducible association with the condition than some earlier studies had suggested. Understanding which genetic findings hold up is important not only for research but also for how clinicians interpret genetic information in people with cerebral palsy.
Diagnosis and care
There are also important questions about what happens within the healthcare system after patients seek care.
Dr. Suvira Jain writes about why one in three donated corneas is wasted. Eye donation does not automatically translate into transplantation. The cornea has to be retrieved, assessed, preserved and transplanted within the appropriate window. Gaps at different stages can mean that donated tissue is ultimately not used, even as many people continue to wait for corneal transplants.
Pain, too, can persist long after the original injury or illness has apparently healed. Persistent pain may require specialised assessment rather than being dismissed as something a patient simply has to live with. Afshan Yasmeen looks at why persistent pain can be complex and why appropriate pain management needs to go beyond treating the original condition.
Prevention and public health
On the disease prevention front, rabies remains an important public-health concern. Maya C. reports a study from Keralam that looks at the potential impact of dog vaccination in preventing rabies, underlining the importance of controlling the disease in its animal reservoirs alongside ensuring timely post-exposure care for people. Rabies prevention cannot depend on treating people after exposure alone; sustained vaccination and surveillance of dogs are central to controlling transmission.
The issue of counterfeit medicines also highlights why the quality and safety of healthcare products matter. A large stock of suspected counterfeit medicines was seized from a private facility in Bengaluru. Such cases raise concerns that go beyond regulation: a medicine that does not contain what it claims to contain, or does not meet required quality standards, can result in treatment failure and expose patients to further harm.
Air pollution remains another persistent health concern. A study examining winter pollution in north India finds that western disturbances explain a substantial share of the year-to-year variation in winter pollution. Weather systems are only one part of the pollution story, but understanding their role can improve forecasting and help strengthen public-health responses during periods when pollution levels are expected to rise.
Muscle metabolism, healthy ageing
For this month’s Nobel feature we look back at the work of Archibald V. Hill and Otto Meyerhof, whose Nobel-winning research helped establish how muscles generate and use energy. Their independent work helped explain fundamental aspects of muscle metabolism and the relationship between oxygen use, energy production and muscular activity.
And Health Wrap, Episode 50 looks at longevity and the role of racquet sports in healthy ageing, Navin Gnanasekaran, longevity physician and head of radiology, Apollo Hospitals, talk about healthspan, nutrition, sleep, muscle strength, stress, metabolism, inflammation and cognition. The conversation also looks at how racquet sports can bring together physical activity, social interaction and cognitive engagement, making them an interesting part of a broader discussion on maintaining health as we age.
And more:
Shanthi Dass looks at why physiotherapy matters, and the role rehabilitation can play in helping people recover function and manage health conditions.
Dr. Jyoti Bajpai writes about melanoma in India, and why the messaging around this potentially serious skin cancer needs to change to encourage earlier recognition.
Dr. Shivika Gupta looks at what to eat in the weeks before egg retrieval, addressing nutrition in the period leading up to an IVF procedure.
Bindu Shajan Perappadan reports on a WHO-linked study examining smoking and infertility, including the evidence on how quitting smoking can make a meaningful difference.
And in Keralam, health officials have sounded a caution as rising temperatures coincide with a fresh wave of fever cases in Ernakulam, another reminder of how seasonal and environmental changes can intersect with public health.

Fitzpatrick not comfortable with Dubai tour finals
- Published
Matt Fitzpatrick says he is not "100% comfortable" with the prospect of travelling to Dubai for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship in November when he is due to be defending champion.
Fitzpatrick is concerned that the United Arab Emirates could be a target in the ongoing conflict between Iran, the United States and Israel.
"You've only got to look at the hotel that got hit earlier this year," Fitzpatrick told BBC Sport. "I was having dinner the week I won in that hotel.
"That's obviously very scary when you think about how it was a few months away but how close you were to that particular spot and for something like that to happen. It's obviously quite scary."
Fitzpatrick would like to see the event switched to a different host country, a decision he called a "no brainer, in my opinion" before adding: "But I'm not a sponsor, I'm not paying the bills and all that sort of stuff.
"I'm sure there's more to it than just the meets the eye."
Led by chief executive Guy Kinnings, DP World Tour officials are assessing safety issues for their final two play-off events in Abu Dhabi and then Dubai.
Both tournaments are backed by key sponsors of the European-based tour and provide a lucrative end to the season for the circuit's leading money winners.
"I think it's annoying, but at the same time, Guy Kinnings can't control what Iran are doing," Fitzpatrick added.
"It is frustrating because as someone who likes to plan and be prepared, it is difficult to kind of figure out what's going on. Obviously, things as they stand are a bit weird over there.
"I can't say I'm like 100% comfortable, but I guess you just have to see nearer the time and, you know, I still need to qualify as well."
Fitzpatrick's Ryder Cup team-mate Shane Lowry said the tour faces important choices over how to end the current season. "They are huge decisions for everyone," said last week's winner of the Irish Open.
"I'm not going to sit here and comment on the whole thing because I think it's up to the powers above to sort that all out. I think if the tournaments are on, the players are going to go. And if they are not, they will find an alternative."
A spokesperson for the DP World Tour said: "We are in constant dialogue with our members and their management teams about the tournaments they play in, but ultimately players' individual schedule choices are a matter for them to decide.
"As far as our play-offs are concerned, it remains our intention to play as scheduled in the UAE but we continue to monitor the situation and take advice from our international travel advisors."

Saudi Arabia calls an attempted Mecca attack a 'red line' as Houthis deny they did it
CAIRO — Saudi Arabia accused Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels overnight of trying to attack Islam's holiest city, prompting condemnation from countries in the region but no sign of military support. The kingdom, a key U.S. ally, declared Mecca a "red line" as it slid deeper into the new front of the Iran war.
With the world's biggest oil exporter under fire from the rebels backed by the Saudis' regional adversary, Tehran, the kingdom needs a safe outlet for its crude as well as military support. However, a path to either one remains unclear.
A crucial Saudi pipeline has reportedly been shut down for weeks as the Yemen-based Houthis have been attacking infrastructure in the kingdom as well as its shipping on the Red Sea. Iran is still targeting ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices remain above $100 a barrel.
The Houthis denied firing drones toward Mecca, about 1,100 kilometers (680 miles) from Yemen's border. The Saudis said they intercepted and destroyed the drone before it entered the airspace over the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad.
Turkey and Pakistan say the Saudis haven't asked for help
A new defense pact among Saudi Arabia, NATO member Turkey and nuclear power Pakistan remained untapped, as officials from Turkey and Pakistan told The Associated Press they have not received a Saudi request for support in response to the Houthis' escalation.
The Turkish official added that efforts to "institutionalize" the alliance need to be completed before the pact becomes operational. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the issue.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif joined the condemnation of the attempted drone attack on Mecca and said his country and the Saudis stand "unwaveringly, shoulder to shoulder." Other condemnation came from the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, representing over 57 Muslim states, which said the attempt violates the "sanctity of holy sites."
The was the second attempted attack by the Houthis against Mecca after the rebels fired a ballistic missile toward the city in 2017, according to Col. Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led military coalition.
For now, the US is staying out of the fight
Top U.S. officials in recent days have indicated a lack of desire to get involved in the conflict.
"The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday, adding that the rebels appear focused on the Saudis.
Vice President J.D. Vance on Monday said Washington had been in "constant contact" with the Saudis and had been "engaged in direct conversations with the Houthis themselves," calling it "a very fluid and dynamic thing" to be monitored.
Houthis claim shooting down an F-15 fighter jet
Later Wednesday, the rebels claimed, without offering evidence, that they shot down a F-15 fighter jet operated by the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis over the central province of Marib. Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree didn't say when it occurred, and the AP couldn't independently verify the claim.
Spokespeople for the Saudi-led coalition and the Saudi government didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Elsewhere, Iran's top diplomat, Abbas Araghchi, was visiting China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, as talks were expected to focus on the conflict and on shipping on the Strait of Hormuz.
Chinese President Xi Jinping at BRICS summit in New Delhi over the weekend again offered Beijing's help in ending the conflict in the Middle East.

An enemy that swarmed the battlefield in large groups while under fire, seemingly oblivious to the dangers of drones and fire from automatic weapons. An elite corps of ghost soldiers who chose suicide over surrender. They fought and died in their thousands, then apparently vanished from the battlefield.
North Korea's soldiers were sent to fight by Pyongyang alongside Russian forces as they sought to repel a Ukrainian offensive on Moscow's territory at the end of 2024. They paid a heavy price, as many as 3,000 killed in action from the 13,000 deployed.
Ultimately, they would adapt their tactics, and with Russia would drive Ukrainian forces from its Kursk region. In combat terms, little has been heard of them since, but according to Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelensky, North Korean forces, and their weaponry, are soon to make a dramatic return to Russia's war in Ukraine.
Last month, Zelensky warned that up to 50,000 North Koreans will be deployed in Russia, revising an earlier estimate of 30,000 troops. He called on South Korea to provide support for his country's air defence.
But why, after such heavy losses, would North Korea send more men to fight for Russia, and what happened to its soldiers sent in the first place?
"They're still there", said Dr Yang Uk, research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, Center for Foreign Policy and National Security in Seoul. "They are defending Russian territory for another counterattack from Ukraine. And we believe that some of the engineer corps or workers might be in [the Russian-occupied] Donbas area but that's not the combat troops."
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense, HUR, estimates that 8,500 North Korean servicemen are still on Russian territory. They are organised into four brigades, which operate as part of the "North" Group of Forces and are assigned to protecting the state border of the Russian Federation in the Kursk Region from Ukrainian incursions.
"They do not participate in active combat operations. Units of the Korean People's Army have not been observed in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," HUR said in a statement to the BBC.
A first for North Korea
For North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un, the Kursk deployment was a gamble, its largest combat force ever sent overseas. (In 1973, North Korea sent 1,500 military personnel and instructors to Egypt during the Yom Kippur war with Israel, and in the late 1960s, an estimated 87 North Korean pilots fought for the North Vietnamese against US forces).
And despite the bloodshed, it was a gamble that paid off, reaping countless benefits for the isolated and impoverished country, transforming both its economic and military fortunes. And one that could serve as a blueprint for even deeper military cooperation.
North Koreans, "now know what modern combat is about", said Yang.
The soldiers sent to fight in Russia were from Storm Corps, the elite of the North Korean armed forces. Extremely isolated, totalitarian North Korea is a militarised and heavily indoctrinated state.
At first, neither Russia, nor North Korea, even acknowledged their presence. Ukrainian forces first clashed with them in November 2024, and the first live North Korean prisoners of war wouldn't be captured until January of the following year.
It wasn't until April 2025 that Russia first acknowledged their role, when Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, described their "heroism" on the battlefield.
Yang continued, "North Korean soldiers are very brave I mean, especially those of Storm Corps. They are willing to die for their country. But the problem is that passion doesn't mean efficient combat skills... [They suffered] a lot of bloodshed in the early stage of the Kursk campaign, but they learned the lessons of modern drone warfare."
"Cannon fodder", is how "Sultan", a soldier with Ukraine's 95th Air Assault Brigade described North Korean troops. He faced them in the battle for Kursk at the end of 2024.
"They would begin with one large assault group, then another 15–20 men would be sent into the same position, and then more after that. The North Koreans operated differently. They kept moving all the time. That gave them a certain advantage, but not a decisive one," he recalled recently in Kyiv.
Communication between them and their Russian allies appeared poor, he said, and their soldiers were inadequately equipped.
After combat, Sultan and his men would search enemy corpses for documents and intelligence information. On the Russian dead they would find personal belongings, identification and equipment. "But when we searched the North Koreans specifically, the only thing we found on them was simply ammo. We checked absolutely all the small pockets - there were no documents, nothing at all," he explained.
Other Ukrainian soldiers reported the North Koreans lacked body armour, winter clothing and helmets.
In one chilling video from a Ukrainian assault, a wounded North Korean soldier lies prone on the snow-covered ground in a wooded area. As the Ukrainians approach, he detonates a grenade under his chin, after calling out, with his last words, the name of his leader, Kim Jong Un.
In April 2025, at a memorial service in Pyongyang at the newly created Museum of Foreign Military Operations, Kim praised heroes who choose suicide over capture.
In a speech to relatives, with Russia's Defence Minister Andrey Belousov in attendance, he said they were "heroes who unhesitatingly opted for self-blasting, suicide attack, in order to defend the great honour".
While North Korea has never officially acknowledged the death toll from the Kursk operation, a BBC Korea analysis of the memorial site estimated that 2,300 soldiers were killed fighting for Russia.
Ukraine's intelligence arm, HUR, puts the figure at 3,000 killed and 1,500 injured.
But aside from the combat experience, why did North Korea sacrifice so many of its best troops in a foreign war?
An economic windfall
The deployment has been a much-needed economic windfall for the country and a geopolitical win, according to Lim Soo-ho, a senior research fellow at the Institute for National Security Strategy, in Seoul.
He estimates that arms sales to Russia and the troop deployment have netted the impoverished country close to $10bn.
"North Korea's annual GDP is estimated at around $30bn (£22bn)," he told me. "That means they earned a third of a year's GDP over two and a half years through weapons exports and troop deployment, which, for an economy as small as North Korea's, is a very significant effect."
In exchange for its manpower, North Korea gets food, oil and hard currency. While China says it complies with sanctions against Pyongyang, Russia does not.
But equally important, the cooperation with Russia has shifted North Korea's long-term dependency on China.
So in Beijing in September last year, Kim Jong Un was able to stand shoulder to shoulder with China's leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in the first public meeting of all three. Not quite as an equal, but no longer reliant on China alone.
This is significant, said Lim, "It's a major geopolitical shift".
"Whenever things got difficult under isolation, North Korea would reach out first toward South Korea, Japan, or especially the US to try to normalise relations, that was the pattern of Korean Peninsula diplomacy. But now that ties with Russia have tightened, Kim Jong Un argues that the world is in a new Cold War, a multipolar system."
The arrangement with Russia, which began as economic and military expediency appears to be developing into something deeper and longer-term. At this year's 9th Party Congress of the Korean Workers' Party, Kim Jong Un was emboldened and spoke of accomplishments that his grandfather Kim Il Sung and father Kim Jong Il never achieved.
But dangers lie ahead. To date, no North Koreans have fought on Ukrainian or Russian-occupied Ukrainian land. If they did so, there would be diplomatic consequences, not least in South Korea, an ally of Ukraine, albeit one which so far has only provided "non-lethal" aid.
This is something that President Zelensky has emphasised as he presses for Seoul to provide advanced military hardware, including air defence systems. He said that since June, preparations have been underway in Russia's Voronezh region to receive fresh North Korean forces and claimed that Pyongyang was preparing to transfer additional ballistic weapons to Russia.
"Russia is helping North Korea learn modern warfare, improve its weapons, and gain real combat experience. This poses a threat to every country in Asia that lies within range of North Korean missiles," he said in a presidential address in July.
Only two North Korean soldiers were captured alive in battles with Ukrainian forces. That's a staggeringly low number, given that between 11,000 and 14,000 fought in the Kursk campaign. (Another was captured alive but died from combat-related injuries, according to the South Korean National Intelligence Service).
Like their comrades who choose suicide over capture, neither man intended to be taken alive.
"For Joseon (North Korean) soldiers, becoming a prisoner of war itself is a crime. That just isn't an option. We can't become POWs," one of the captured men told a South Korean MBC documentary crew who interviewed him in prison in Ukraine.
Baek Pyeong-gang, not his real name, lay wounded from a drone strike for four days before being captured. He was tricked into surrendering when he mistook Ukrainian soldiers for his Russian allies.
The second prisoner, Lee Kang-eun, also a pseudonym, told the journalist Kim Young-mi that he felt guilty he was still alive. Barely conscious, he was found by Ukrainian soldiers on the battlefield with extensive injuries to the arm and jaw.
"I had no grenade or knives on me to self-blast (end my life)," he explained.
He described scores of his colleagues killed by drones, early in the war. The battlefield "reeked of the smell of blood", he said.
Neither man wants to return to North Korea, Lee said he believed that his family members would be "wiped out" as punishment for his capture. Both have said they want to be sent to South Korea, and Seoul is willing to take them.
Only Russia, not Pyongyang, has asked for their return.
But Ukraine, still intent on pressuring Seoul for military aid, has not committed to handing them over to South Korean authorities. Kyiv has said it will honour international human rights obligations which prevent the forced repatriation of prisoners of war.
Their fate remains undecided, but what appears certain is that more North Koreans will join Russia's war. Their service has enormous economic and political value to Pyongyang; but Russia desperately needs them too.
Four and a half years into Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it is facing a desperate manpower shortage. Western and Ukrainian intelligence agencies estimate that it is losing some 6,000 more troops a month than it can recruit. So, Moscow has been forced to turn to foreign fighters, from Colombia, Kenya, Cameroon and North Korea, to sustain its ranks.
For Russia and North Korea, it is a mutually beneficial relationship, a coalition at a price. Ultimately, North Korea will continue to send its soldiers to fight in Russia's war, but only for as long as it is profitable to do so.

EU rolls out red carpet to Canada to become its first 'associate member'
BRUSSELS — The European Union is proposing a new kind of relationship with Canada, one that could make it the EU's first-ever "associate member" — a model that does not currently exist.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made the proposal Wednesday during her annual State of the Union address, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney sitting in the European Parliament as her special guest.
"Dear Mark," von der Leyen said, "Europe and Canada believe in democracy, that power does not belong to the strongest, richest and loudest, but to all of us."
And adding the key phrase to her prepared remarks, seen by NPR, which did not include it, von der Leyen went on: "I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union."
The announcement drew a standing ovation from lawmakers and dignitaries in the chamber, as von der Leyen and Carney exchanged kisses on the cheeks.
The moment comes as the EU and Canada look to strengthen their partnership amid increasingly difficult relations with Washington under President Trump.
Von der Leyen stressed that the proposed relationship was not "against anyone." But the very fact she felt she had to emphasize that made the context even more obvious.
For many Europeans, Carney has become a prominent voice for closer cooperation among U.S. partners he calls "middle powers", speaking more forcefully than they themselves dare. At the World Economic Forum in January, Carney warned that "recently, great powers have begun using economic integration as weapons, tariffs as leverage, financial infrastructure as coercion, supply chains as vulnerabilities to be exploited."
"He said it out loud," said Rem Korteweg of the Dutch Clingendael Institute, who says Carney's message has resonated across Europe even as Canada itself has come under intense pressure from the Trump administration.
"All of a sudden Mark Carney is bombarded as almost this honorary hero of what Europeans are actually saying to themselves behind closed doors," Korteweg explained. "Across Europe there is this realization, well, perhaps we need to keep Canada closer to us."
But von der Leyen's proposal also raises a fundamental question: What exactly would associate membership mean?
"This is where things become tricky," Korteweg said.
Carney has made clear that Canada does not want to fully integrate with the EU's single market. Canada and the EU already have a free-trade agreement, although Carney is expected to press the 10 EU countries that have not yet ratified it.
The two sides have also been expanding cooperation in security and defense. They signed an agreement deepening security cooperation in 2025, and Canada this year became the only non-European country allowed to participate in the EU's 150-billion-euro fund for joint defense purchases.
So what would a new political status add?
For Jason Wiseman, a Canadian working in the European Parliament, the proposal reflects the opportunity created by Canada's worsening relationship with Washington."The main thing is that we have momentum now," Wiseman said. He sees opportunities for Canada and Europe to build more resilient supply chains and cooperate in strategically important industries.
"Across all of the main sectors that matter the most to the EU and Canada right now, to have the kind of resilient supply chains that would include third-country like-minded partners like Canada," Wiseman says. "Things like critical raw materials. We've got a wealth of small-medium enterprises making mission-critical software…emerging disruptive technologies, especially drones."
The proposal, however, was not preceded by a detailed public negotiation, raising questions inside the EU about how the announcement came about.
Wiseman says he hasn't met anyone in the European Parliament who's against the associate membership idea. But there are reports that some EU governments were furious they were not consulted before von der Leyen's offer, suggesting there may be more resistance in EU capitals whose unanimous support will be needed to create any new partnership.
The proposal is also prompting political questions in Canada, particularly over what an associate membership would actually mean and what closer ties with the EU could require from Canada.
Aaron Gasch Burnett, an analyst with the Center for Strategic Statecraft in Canada, says both Carney's political supporters and opponents have seized on it.
"There's a lot of excitement about what associate membership means when it does not in fact exist … among people who would support closer ties to the EU," Burnett says. "This is also becoming a partisan issue in Canada, with the opposition now saying, 'well, please explain what powers you're willing to give up to Brussels and what you would get in return.'"
On Thursday, Mark Carney will get a chance to do that, when it is his turn to address the European Parliament and explain where he thinks this political romance is headed.

WASHINGTON — Democrats are vowing to aggressively pursue oversight if they win control of either the House or Senate in November’s midterm elections. Health care issues, including President Trump’s drug pricing deals, are potential targets.
It’s common for parties to turn to oversight when they take control of a congressional chamber. Lawmakers can use oversight to tell a story about the other side. It also avoids intraparty divisions by focusing attention on what the other party has done. And if Democrats want to keep the focus on Trump, even though he can’t run again, oversight is a good way to do that.
If Democrats flip either chamber, they’ll gain subpoena authority, giving them the power to force the administration and company executives to testify and respond to inquiries. However, the administration could forcefully push back on those efforts.
