The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

British tourists escape ‘wall of flames’ by fleeing into the sea as Croatia wildfire tears through holiday island
Dozens of tourists were evacuated from the Brač island on Croatian navy and fishing boats
Hundreds of people including British tourists have evacuated a Croatian island after a major wildfire broke out, with one recalling fleeing “as a wall of flames closed in”, according to reports.
Around 500 people were evacuated from the island of Brač near the popular coastal city of Split, firefighters told the Hina news agency, many of whom were guests at the Gava Waterman Milna Resort, including several guests.
Britons at the resort told how they were forced to flee into the sea on a paddleboard to escape the flames, with some alleging they were “abandoned” during the evacuation effort in an interview with The Times - an accusation the resort has denied.
Josh Robbins, 26, said he and his fiancée Shelby A’Court left their room to find the resort’s car park “surrounded by a wall of fire as firefighters tried to hold back the flames”. The pair had to “run for our lives as a wall of flames closed in as we were showered by burning embers”, he told The Times.
They first noticed something was wrong when the power went out. The hotel’s reception told them “everything was fine” but to pack their bags just in case, Mr Robbins told Croatian broadcaster RLT Danas according to net.hr.
“We went to our room, but about 10 minutes later the fire was already close to the room, maybe 20 or 30 meters away,” he said. “We went to the reception, but it was empty. There was only one member of staff left. The electric doors wouldn't open, and guests were trying to get out. We had to force them open.”
Boats were sent out to rescue those trapped on the island, including speedboats, fishing boats, and boats belonging to the Croatian navy and port authorities.
Ms A’Court gave more details of the harrowing evacuation effort: "It was terrible. We were in the water, on a stand-up paddleboard and trying to get to the boat that was leaving.
“We were screaming, crying, begging. Luckily, they stopped and we were able to get on board. It was a matter of life and death. We're safe now and that's what matters.”
She added in a separate interview with The Times: “Josh lost his shoes as we swam and I had to abandon stuff in my bag because it was soaked through and dragging me down. Others swam for it and it’s amazing no one was lost or drowned in the darkness.”
Electrician Steve Saunders, 57, from Kent, told the British outlet that he and his 52-year-old wife, Anna, were “abandoned and given no instructions whatsoever”.
Mr Robbins said the hotel “handled the situation very poorly”, adding: “They didn't give us any warning, they didn't tell us in time to evacuate.”
The Independent has contacted Waterman Hotels for comment, but a spokesperson previously denied that the staff abandoned guests in a response to The Times.
“This was an exceptionally fast-moving wildfire, driven by very strong winds. Power was lost across the resort, heavy smoke severely reduced visibility and conditions changed dramatically in a very short period of time. We completely understand why guests caught up in those circumstances were terrified, and we do not seek to diminish or challenge their individual experiences.
But the spokesman added the resort is “extremely proud of the responsibility and courage shown by our employees that night”.
The mayor of Milna, a village in Brač, described the wildfire as a “disaster”, adding that it was “simply impossible”.
Speaking to Net.hr, mayor Frane Lozic added on Sunday: "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly.
"We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9pm and out of nowhere, there is a monster.”
Authorities believe around 3,500 hectares have been burned by the fire, according to the AFP news agency, although a full damage assessment is still underway.
Croatia has suffered the its worst year for wildfires since 2022 in terms of burned area, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), the forecasting system for the EU’s Copernicus climate change service.
More than 20,800 hectares have burnt across 59 wildfires in the country so far this year, EFFIS data shows.
It is unclear whether this includes the Brač fire, but it remains short of the record of 67,666 hectares across 108 wildfires in 2017, the worst year for wildfires in the country since EFFIS started recording data.
It comes towards the end of a devastating summer for wildfires across Europe. Around 700,000 hectares of land were burned by wildfires across the EU in 2026, according to the bloc’s crisis management commissioner Hadja Lahbib, as back-to-back heatwaves scorched the continent causing tens of thousands of excess deaths.

Supreme Court directs ED, Delhi Police to submit details of cases against Unitech directors
SC told ED and Delhi Police to submit case details against Unitech directors to ensure speedy trial and said homebuyers should face no inconvenience.
The Supreme Court on Wednesday directed the Enforcement Directorate and Delhi Police to submit details of cases against directors of ailing Unitech Ltd to ensure speedy trial and said no inconvenience should be caused to the homebuyers.
A bench comprising justices JB Pardiwala and KV Viswanathan said law should take its own course but no further leeway should be given to the accused persons.
"Trial must commence and must not go for an indefinite period. We will create a special court to hear these cases exclusively but no further delay should be caused," the bench remarked.

The top court posted the matter for hearing on September 30.
During the hearing, the court asked where the monies deposited by the homebuyers had gone.
"Where has the money gone? Has it travelled beyond the country? What is the role of the investigating agency? Law should be lucid. Confusion created by law is benefitting the accused. We have skillful agencies which can find where the money has gone," the bench said.
The top court was informed that as far as criminal prosecution against directors of Unitech is concerned, it is in two parts.

While one set of cases is being investigated by the ED, the other is being probed by Economic Offences Wing which has filed charge sheet in 63 different matters.
The apex court had earlier said that its objective was to ensure that 22,000 homebuyers of Unitech Ltd get their dream homes and asked the new Centre-appointed board of the real estate group, banks and financial institutions to give suggestions for an amicable resolution of the long-pending dispute.
Around 22,000 homebuyers have been waiting for houses booked with Unitech for several years. A government-appointed board has since taken over the management of the real estate firm.
Earlier, the bench said it would take a serious view of non-compliance of its orders by any state authorities in matters related to the real estate group and cautioned them against creating hurdles in the completion of the stalled housing projects.
On January 16 last year, the top court came to the rescue of thousands of homebuyers and facilitated disbursal of their stalled loans for flats constructed by Unitech by granting exemption from registration under the RERA for different housing projects located in seven states.
It had said the order passed in the interest of justice would help in dispensing with the procedural requirements for releasing and advancing of loans to homebuyers of different Unitech projects.
Under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, every project measuring more than 500 sqm or more than eight apartments must be registered with the RERA.
The top court had also issued notices to banks and financial institutions, which has declared the loan accounts of homebuyers as non-performing assets (NPA) as the projects' completion was delayed, due to financial problems faced during the erstwhile management of Unitech Group and for non-compliance under the RERA Act.
It had issued the notices on a plea by Unitech, seeking directions for disbursal of stalled loan amounts of the homebuyers.
It was contended that the banks and financial institutions, which earlier sanctioned loans to the homebuyers for purchasing units in Unitech projects, had stopped payments of the balance dues on account of projects not moving forward.
Unitech further contended that now that the projects had been revived, directions be issued to the financial institutions for disbursal of loans of homebuyers.
On October 22, 2024, the top court permitted the Centre-appointed board of directors of Unitech to seek police assistance to deal with "impediments" created by third parties on properties of the embattled realty firm.
On January 20, 2020, the top court had allowed the Ministry of Corporate Affairs to take "total management control" of Unitech.
It had permitted the board of directors "to raise funds due from the homebuyers, and to sell the unsold inventory of stock and the unclaimed inventory available for reselling".
It had also allowed the board to monetise the unencumbered assets of the company for completion of housing units.
In 2017, the Centre had moved the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) seeking suspension of the current directors and taking control of the management of Unitech Ltd but had later withdrawn the proposal after a stay on its move from the top court.
In 2018, the apex court had directed a forensic audit of Unitech Ltd and its sister concerns and subsidiaries by Samir Paranjpe, Partner, Forensic and Investigation Services in M/s Grant Thornton India.
The forensic audit report said Unitech under its erstwhile promoters Sanjay Chandra and Ajay Chandra had received around ₹14,270 crore from 29,800 homebuyers, mostly between 2006 and 2014, and around ₹1,805 crore from six financial institutions for the construction of 74 projects.
The audit said that around ₹5,063 crore of homebuyers' money and around ₹763 crore of funds received from financial institutions were not utilised by the company and high-value investments were made in tax-haven countries between 2007 and 2010.

The Allahabad High Court has set Ayush Malik, a 31-year-old man from Shamli who said he had voluntarily converted to Islam, at liberty to live at a place of his choice, observing that an adult’s decisions regarding faith, residence and marriage cannot be overridden by family objections.
Justice Sandeep Jain passed the order on Wednesday while hearing a habeas corpus petition alleging that Malik, who changed his name to Mohammad Ali, was being illegally confined by his family following his religious conversion.
The court said Malik had categorically stated that he embraced Islam voluntarily and that his decision was not influenced by any threat, coercion, undue influence or pressure.
“Nothing has been brought on record which may persuade this Court to disbelieve the statement made by the corpus in the course of his interaction with the Court,” the Bench observed.
The court said there was no lawful justification for continuing any restraint on Malik’s personal liberty after he expressed his wishes before it.
It directed that he be allowed to reside wherever and with whomever he chose, profess and practise the religion of his choice, and take an appropriate decision regarding his matrimonial relationship in accordance with law.
Father opposed conversion
The court was informed that Malik had embraced Islam in 2014 and had been following the essential practices of the faith. He told the Bench that his decision was not acceptable to his parents and other family members.
Malik also expressed his intention to marry Chandni Qureshi, a Muslim woman, and alleged that he had been subjected to threats and unlawful confinement at his home since June 4.
His father, Devraj Singh Malik, disputed his son’s account, claiming that he had been influenced or brainwashed by certain persons and had not converted voluntarily.
The court noted that the father’s concern for his son’s welfare was understandable but said it could not override the constitutionally protected autonomy of an adult capable of making decisions about his own life.
Court cites individual autonomy
The Bench said a person who has attained majority is ordinarily entitled to determine their faith according to their conscience.
“Such a choice, being an expression of individual autonomy and freedom of conscience, cannot be displaced merely because it is not acceptable to his family members,” it observed.
The court also said the right to choose a person with whom one wishes to establish a matrimonial relationship is an integral part of the right to life and personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution.
It added that the mere fact that an adult’s choice may go against the wishes or expectations of family members cannot, by itself, provide a legitimate basis for restricting that choice.
“Once an adult person has unequivocally expressed his free will and choice before the Court, such choice is ordinarily entitled to be respected,” the Bench said.
Background of the case
The court had on September 9 directed authorities in Uttar Pradesh to produce Malik before it.
His conversion had earlier led to the arrest of Chandni Qureshi and her father under the Uttar Pradesh Prohibition of Unlawful Conversion of Religion Act, 2021, in a case registered by Shamli police.
Malik had previously told the media that he converted voluntarily. His father, a businessman, had alleged that the woman and her family coerced him in an attempt to gain control over their property. Malik had reportedly later returned to Hinduism.
The latest habeas corpus petition, however, alleged that he was being illegally confined by his family.
The court said that in exercising its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution, it was not required to substitute its own perception of what would be beneficial for the considered choice of an adult.
It accordingly set Malik at liberty to make decisions concerning his residence, faith and matrimonial relationship.

Maritime experts urge use of verified weather reports after kayaker capsizes in B.C. waters
Strangers rescue B.C. man from ocean after kayak flips in tall waves
Maritime first responders are advising against using AI chatbots for weather reports following a close call for a paddler on B.C.'s South Coast.
Jonathan Levine considers himself lucky to be alive after his kayak capsized in the ocean during what he thought would be a leisurely paddle in Howe Sound.
Levine and his wife Jane were eager to go for a morning kayak paddle on Sunday, as they’ve done many times, from their home in Furry Creek, about 35 kilometres north of Vancouver.
They tried to use an AI chatbot to determine the safest time to paddle after finding it difficult to get concise information online.
“We proceeded in the direction of Britannia Beach, as ChatGPT had suggested to my wife,” Levine said.
At first, it was sunny and seemingly calm, so the couple decided to stay out longer than planned.
That’s when they got into trouble.
“I hit these massive waves that came from nowhere. They were at least about five, six feet in height, and my kayak was rocking and rolling all over the place,” Levine said.
The Howe Sound commonly experiences strong winds in the afternoon on warm days due to the coastal fjords along and temperature differences. There can also be fairly strong currents due to the strong river outflow.
As the couple rounded the corner at Minaty Bay, Levine's kayak flipped, sending him plunging into the waves.
“The life-jacket was almost like trying to be wrenched off my body, basically because of the actual wave movement,” Levine said.
He tried over and over again to swim to the shore.
“Every time I kept swimming in one direction, [the waves] kept pushing me back,” Levine said.
Levine tried to stay calm while getting battered by waves for 15 minutes.
“I think as a human being aged 71, part of the advantages of being an old man is that you are probably quite clever in dangerous situations,” Levine said.
His wife, who was in another kayak, shouted to nearby boats and used her cellphone to call for help.
Strangers spot capsized kayak
Long-time sailor Adrian Ward and his friend, local firefighter Travis Welsh, were out for a boat ride near Minaty Bay when Ward noticed the bottom of the kayak floating amid the waves.
“As we approach, we're starting to see waves crashing over his head,” Ward said.
The conditions caught Ward and Welsh off guard.
“We were just getting lifted up and down, six feet at a time, and it came on really quickly,” Ward said.
Ward and his friend pulled Levine out of the water and onto their boat.
“He was really tired and a bit cold, not too cold, luckily,” Ward said. “Just really happy that it had a good outcome for the guy and that he got to go home.”
Levine was not injured and said the two strangers managed to get his kayak out safely, too.
“The two men were incredible, they calmed me down, they knew exactly what to do, they were so helpful,” Levine said.
His wife paddled safely to shore.
“She was a superwoman,” Levine said. “Without Jane, I wouldn't be alive.”
Staying safe on the water
Experts suggest checking multiple reports from verified sources for wind, tides and currents, rather than relying on artificial intelligence.
“Checking Environment Canada is important because they still have actual human eyes on those forecasts that understand thermal inflows and outflows,” said Scott Shaw-MacLaren, the coxswain with Squamish’s Royal Canadian Marine Search and Rescue.
“If you do, like, anything with AI, verify sources and read it for yourself.”
Shaw-MacLaren also suggests always having a marine VHF radio, as it’s the fastest way to alert other boaters if in trouble.
Brehnen Rowell, Officer in Charge at the Victoria Lifeboat Station with the Canadian Coast Guard, also recommends using multiple different sources and, in particular, the Government of Canada website.
“That’s really key for making sure you're staying safe out there, is making sure that you're aware of the currents and tides,” Rowell said.
Rowell said making a plan before heading out on the water and sticking to it is also important

The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has reportedly intensified its scrutiny of big tech giant Apple’s software warranty terms. This is part of the watchdog’s broader investigation into issues linked to the smartphone maker’s iOS 18 update, which allegedly damaged iPhone functionality and compelled users to pay “exorbitant” sums for repairs. As per documents accessed by Reuters, the CCPA, in June, told Apple that it had "escalated" the matter for a "detailed investigation" by its investigation wing. The iPhone is said to have responded to the regulator’s investigation. In a statement sent to Inc42, the company said that it primarily sells hardware, adding that software is something that goes along with the device. The company added that no tech company, including Apple, across the globe offers warranty on software Apple also said that it closely monitors user feedback after every software update, and that it did not identify any issues, safety concerns, or similar trends related to the launch of iOS 18 in India. The iPhone maker also noted that it is open to working with local authorities to provide clarity on the customer response to iOS 18. The development comes over a year after the CCPA issued a notice to Apple. This came after the watchdog received multiple complaints regarding performance issues of iPhones following the iOS 18+ software update. Notably, this is not the first time that the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) has come under the radar of Indian authorities. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) has already found Apple guilty of abusing its dominant position in the app store market. The big tech giant is already contesting the matter and has accused the CCI of “copy-pasting” allegations made by rival companies instead of conducting an independent probe into its App Store practices. Even as it grapples with issues related to the iOS18 software update, Apple began rolling out iOS 27 yesterday, which comes with Siri AI. However, critics have flagged that the new AI features are only available for its premium, higher-end devices, creating a two-tier model for its iPhone users. Despite this, Apple continues to double down on India. Earlier this month, the big tech giant launched its first foldable smartphone, called iPhone Duo, which will be available in India at a starting price of ₹3 Lakh for a 256 GB model. It also unveiled its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models. The launches came as Apple clocked record revenue in June 2026 quarter in India. At the time, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh also said India delivered strong double-digit revenue growth during the quarter, with Mac emerging as one of the standout performers. Besides sales, India continues to be a major manufacturing hub for Apple. Over the years, the company has significantly expanded local iPhone production, with iPhone exports from India crossing the ₹2 Lakh Cr mark in FY26.

NEW YORK — Pennsylvania officials have reported a fourth measles-associated death.
The latest death involved an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County, in the center of the state, the county coroner’s office said in a Facebook post. The cause was acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a rare and severe neurological complication of measles, it said.
On Saturday, a 40-year-old woman from Jefferson County, a rural area in western Pennsylvania, died of measles complications. And last month, two measles-infected infants died in Lancaster County, in the southeastern part of the state.
None of the four were vaccinated, according to the state health department. The infants were too young for vaccinations, according to current recommendations.
The U.S. is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991 and has seen seven reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak continues to grow, with nearly 700 illnesses reported so far this year across 38 counties, including about 100 cases in the last seven days. The measles-associated deaths are the first reported in the state in 35 years, state officials say.
“My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades,” the state’s health secretary, Dr. Debra Bogen, said in a statement Tuesday, referring to the two most recent deaths — those of the adults.
“We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the MMR vaccine, which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades.”
The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Meanwhile, measles infections have been surging in recent years.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.
The problem has been years in the making, as fewer kids get routine vaccines due to parental waivers, health care access issues and rampant disinformation. More recently, Trump administration health officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., have questioned and sown doubt about the established safety of vaccines at an unprecedented level while also defunding local efforts to improve vaccination rates.

After the U.S. commemorated the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, a claim (archived) circulated online that the Flight 93 National Memorial changed the time of its 9/11 observance to accommodate a visit from U.S. President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance but neither showed up.
United Airlines Flight 93 was one of four planes hijacked on 9/11. It was the only one that did not hit a building, instead crashing in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers attempted to retake control of the plane from the hijackers.
In sharing the claim about Trump and Vance, one X user wrote: "The 9/11 Flight 93 Memorial reportedly changed the time of their ceremony to accommodate a visit from Trump or Vance, but neither of them showed up. Trump traveled to a golf tournament instead."
The 9/11 Flight 93 Memorial reportedly changed the time of their ceremony to accommodate a visit from Trump or Vance, but neither of them showed up.
Trump traveled to a golf tournament instead. pic.twitter.com/SVhVbLaY6s
— Headquarters (@HQNewsNow) September 14, 2026
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
The claim is unproven. Though event pages for 9/11 observances at the Flight 93 National Memorial from 2020 to 2026 showed the 2026 event started around an hour and 15 minutes earlier than previous ceremonies, the program (archived) also was longer than in previous years.
We found no evidence that Trump or Vance were supposed to attend the event at the memorial but did not show. Trump attended a commemoration ceremony at the Pentagon with military leaders on Sept. 11, 2026, while Vance attended a commemoration event in New York City at the site of the former Twin Towers. Trump travelled to Dublin, Ireland, in the evening for a two-day visit that included attending the Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf club on Sept. 13.
We contacted the National Park Service, which manages the Flight 93 National Memorial, to ask why the 2026 observance started earlier than in previous years. We also asked the White House press office whether Trump or Vance were supposed to attend the Flight 93 National Memorial observance and await replies to our queries.
In the meantime, because the NPS had not confirmed why the 2026 event had a different start time than previous years, we leave this claim unrated.
Longer 2026 event also memorialized other 9/11 flights
According to event programs for the 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 events, previous 9/11 observances at the Flight 93 National Memorial started at either 9:45 or 9:50 a.m., which could be in order to coincide with the exact time Flight 93 crashed near Shanksville, at 10:03 a.m. Sept. 11, 2001. The 2026 event started at 8:30 a.m.
The event programs from 2021 to 2024 generally started with welcome remarks, the Pledge of Allegiance or national anthem, followed by a reading of the names of the 40 passengers and crew on board Flight 93 who died when the plane crashed.
The event programs then listed bells of remembrance, a moment of reflection and conclusion and a wreath-laying. Some events also featured speakers such as former President George W. Bush and then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2021 and then-first lady Jill Biden in 2022. Trump attended a smaller, live-streamed ceremony during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The 2026 program appeared longer than in previous years, and included remembrances for the three other hijacked flights on 9/11 that struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. The 2026 program added musical selections and also included bell tollings and wreath-layings for American Airlines Flight 11, which hit the North Tower on 8:46 a.m., United Airlines Flight 175, which hit the South Tower at 9:03 a.m., and American Airlines Flight 77, which hit the Pentagon at 9:37 a.m.
If the 2026 event intended to honor the other three flights at the times they crashed, it would have needed to start earlier than the previous 9:45 or 9:50 a.m. start times.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated a series of other rumors about where Trump was or what he was doing on or around Sept. 11, 2001.

Hague court to deliver verdict in war crimes trial of Kosovo’s former President Thaci
Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci will learn his fate on Wednesday as international judges in The Hague deliver verdicts in his war crimes trial
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci will learn his fate Wednesday when international judges at a court in The Hague deliver verdicts in his war crimes trial.
Thaci is facing multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity including murder, torture and persecution alongside three other former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army who fought Serb forces in the 1998-99 war. They are widely regarded as national heroes in their homeland.
Thousands of people rallied in Pristina over the weekend in support of the four men. The protesters filled a central square in the capital, many carrying red and black Albanian flags.
Portraits of the four former KLA fighters have been plastered across the city along with a huge digital clock counting down to Wednesday's verdicts.
“In the name of the people, declare them innocent," one banner read.
Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers court in The Hague have asked for a maximum 45-year prison sentence for Thaci and the other defendants, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi. They have all denied the charges against them.
“Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice,” Thaci told judges in February at the end of his nearly three-year trial.
According to prosecutors, the men targeted political opponents and civilians perceived as collaborators and traitors during their time in the KLA.
The staff at the European Union-backed court are largely international due to fears about witness safety and security. In 2022, the court convicted two leaders of a Kosovo war veterans’ association for intimidating witnesses by publicizing leaked confidential documents.
Thaci also faces a separate trial on charges of intimidating witnesses that will begin later this month.
He was a student who returned from what he described as political exile in Switzerland to join Kosovo’s struggle for independence. He earned the nickname “the Snake” for his ability to evade Serb forces during the conflict.
He was embraced by Western leaders, who invited him to the 1999 peace talks in France in his role as political director of the Kosovo Liberation Army, and was seen as a leader who could guide the country toward independence.
Thaci rose to political power after the war but resigned as president to defend himself before the court in The Hague.
Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians. A 78-day campaign of NATO airstrikes against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About 1 million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes.
In 2008, Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia, a move that Belgrade refuses to recognize. Ties between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense, despite years of negotiations mediated by the European Union and supported by the United States.

St. John's woman with 160 prior convictions, including for fraud and forgery, gets jail time in CERB case
Michelle Voisey has been handed a 10-month jail sentence
A former St. John’s housing advocate is returning to jail for the latest in a long list of criminal convictions.
Michelle Voisey was handed a 10-month sentence with 24 months probation for using her niece’s Canada Revenue Agency account to send $8,000 worth of Canada Emergency Response Benefit payments to her own bank account.
The federal program, known as CERB, provided financial support to people who lost their jobs during the COVID-19 pandemic.
- St. John's housing advocate pleads guilty to fraud, but legal aid request delays sentencing
- Sentencing of St. John's serial fraudster and former housing advocate delayed again
“The seriousness of the offence lies not only within the amount taken, but also its deliberate nature, the abuse of trust, the impact on the victim and Ms. Voisey’s extensive history of similar offending,” Justice Peter Browne said at Voisey’s sentencing hearing in Supreme Court in St. John's on Sept. 11.
Browne ordered Voisey to repay the $8,000 to CRA, and banned her from holding any job or volunteer position where she would have authority over another person's property or money for a period of 20 years.
Browne said Voisey’s decision to plead guilty was a mitigating factor in his decision, though he also considered her criminal history. Voisey has nearly 160 previous convictions, many involving fraud, forgery or theft.
“This record demonstrates a long standing and deeply entrenched pattern of dishonest conduct,” Browne said.
Voisey charged back in 2021
According to the statement of facts, Voisey's niece contacted police when her GST payment didn't arrive on time. She learned that $8,000 in CERB payments had been paid out in her name — even though she hadn't applied and didn't qualify for the benefit. Voisey was charged in October 2021.
In 2023, while the case was winding its way through court, Voisey, operating under the name Michelle Gushue, participated in the tent city protest on Confederation Hill. Voisey participated in media interviews and solicited donations of gift cards, cell phones, cash and more through social media.
Voisey’s latest conviction is unrelated to the tent city protest.
Voisey pleaded guilty in June 2025, but a last-minute request for a legal aid lawyer delayed sentencing until 2026.
- St. John's housing advocate pleads guilty to fraud, but legal aid request delays sentencing
- Sentencing of St. John's serial fraudster and former housing advocate delayed again
At Friday’s sentencing, Voisey’s lawyer, Dan Furey, submitted a letter he said is from her family doctor, indicating that she's been diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Browne declined to take the letter into consideration in sentencing, explaining that the defence would need to make an oral application and call in an expert witness, like an oncologist.
“I'm not prepared to entertain any of that without expert evidence and in this courtroom to know if incarceration would affect any type of [...] treatment,” he said.
Furey declined to make the application and the sentencing proceeded. After the sentence was handed down, Voisey asked if she could still make the application, but Browne said no. She asked for her sentence to be delayed for two days, but Browne denied that request too.
CBC News has asked Furey if Voisey intends to appeal her sentence.

Paediatric heart surgeries that can cost families anywhere between ₹5 lakh and ₹20 lakh each at private hospitals, were provided free of cost to children at the Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) in Hyderabad. As part of its fifth paediatric cardiac surgery camp, NIMS performed 19 complex heart surgeries on a cashless basis on children aged between two months and 13 years. The week-long camp concluded on Saturday (September 12, 2026)
The surgeries were carried out by the NIMS Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery in collaboration with Healing Little Hearts, with a specialist team led by paediatric cardiac surgeon Ramana Dhanapuneni from the UK. The NIMS team was headed by M. Amaresh Rao, Head of Cardiothoracic Surgery.
From screening to surgery
The camp’s impact extended well beyond the 19 operations. Around 1,000 children were screened as part of the programme. Of these, few were found to require minimally invasive intervention rather than open-heart surgery. The surgical team, meanwhile, selected a mix of complex congenital heart cases for the camp, prioritising children who required specialised cardiac surgery. More than 100 children who require surgery are still waiting, with dates already allotted for their procedures, said Dr. Amaresh.
“Congenital heart disease is common and the cost of paediatric cardiac surgery in private hospitals can be prohibitive for many families, ranging from ₹5 lakh to ₹20 lakh. Hope for the poor is public sector hospitals like NIMS,” said Dr. Ramana.
80 surgeries through five camps
The latest camp is the fifth such programme conducted through the collaboration between Dr. Dhanapuneni’s team and NIMS. The partnership began in 2023, when two camps were conducted. One camp was held in 2024 and another in 2025.
NIMS Director Rahul Devraj said the five camps had resulted in about 80 surgeries so far. “NIMS would like Dr. Ramana and his team to visit twice a year, assuring continued institutional support to the visiting specialists and the cardiac department,” he said.
Around 7,000 children in Telangana with critical congenital heart diseases
Dr. Amaresh said there are around 7,000 children in Telangana with critical congenital heart diseases, while NIMS currently performs around 400 paediatric cardiac surgeries annually. The department needs to reach 1,000 surgeries a year, he said.
ECMO support under Aarogyasri
Another significant development pertaining to the camp was the availability of ECMO services at NIMS under the Aarogyasri scheme for the first time. “No patient needed it during this camp,” Dr. Amaresh clarified. However, he said the significance was that ECMO would now be available to eligible patients free of cost for as long as it is medically required, subject to the scheme’s provisions.

Meta has removed several Instagram and Facebook accounts and content related to the Jantar Mantar protest that Alt News had flagged as AI-manipulated visuals.
On September 2, a Meta spokesperson confirmed to Alt News that following a review, all the accounts and content were found to be violative of the platform’s policies and had been removed.
These posts included several AI-generated and AI-manipulated photographs and videos of women protesting at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar during the Cockroach Janta Party-led students’ protest in July. Alt News flagged Instagram and Facebook accounts and posts to Meta, in which real visuals women had been altered using AI, purportedly in an attempt to outrage their modesty.
In these posts, women’s clothes, bodies and poses had been altered in such a way that they looked starkly different from the original videos or photographs. Alt News’ investigation found that many such visuals were either entirely AI-generated or altered using AI. In some cases, techniques such as face swaps or body swaps were used.
Targeting Women CJP Protesters
Women protesters who participated in the CJP protests in Delhi were particularly targeted on social media. For several days, women faced online harassment and trolling, doxxing, rape threats and the public disclosure of personal information. These AI-visuals formed part of this larger pattern of attacks against female protesters.
These fake visuals were shared on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, among other platforms, claiming that they were real footage from the Jantar Mantar protest. Users then mistook the AI characters for real women partaking in the protests which was followed by objectionable and misogynistic comments targeting their identities, physical appearance, clothes and character. A few of those comments are displayed below:
Alt News identified several Instagram accounts which circulated such malicious content, including @kauronfire, @sirfseerat, @tia_kaurr, @hey.siya_2.0, @kavya_homevibes, @annika0022, @divyankaha and @its_anushkaa69.
Right-wing Users Share AI Image
During the protest, several right-wing users, including RSS supporters Acharya Ankur Arya and Vikram Pratap Singh, shared an AI-generated image claiming that it was a real photograph from the Jantar Mantar protest.
The purported image showed a young woman wearing a crop top and jeans. Users who shared the post made objectionable comments about the woman’s clothing and character. Alt News fact-checked this viral image and found that it was entirely AI-generated.
However, in some cases that surfaced on social media during the final days of the protest, besides entirely AI-generated images, real photographs of women were being altered, making it difficult to determine its authencity.
Visuals Of A Woman In White Saree
An user, @divyankaha, shared a photo and video on their Instagram account and YouTube channel respectively. These showed a woman wearing a white saree and navy blue blouse, linking her to the Jantar Mantar protest. (Archive link-1, Archive link-2)
Alt News found the original video of the post uploaded on an Instagram page @khoji_reporter24news.
Comparing the viral clip with the original video, we found that the body and clothing of the woman were entirely different, thus confirming that the image had been altered using AI. The background and original footage of the viral video remained the same, but the appearance of the woman had been completely manipulated. After Alt News flagged this to Meta, they removed @divyankaha‘s account.
We found several such posts and videos on @divyankaha‘s page. In another post, a woman wearing a white saree is seen sitting on the road wit posters infront of her. Alt News found this photo was also an AI-deepfake. (Archive link)
Several different versions of the viral post, with a woman in a white saree, were also found circulating widely on social media. All of these were AI-deepfakes.
Visuals Of A Woman Standing With A Poster
Another photograph went viral showing different women near the stage at the Jantar Mantar protest, holding posters that read “Resign De De Bhai PUNE SE Aai hu..and Hum jeet gaye”.
In the different iterations of this photo being shared, the woman as well as the design of the poster kept changing. These photos were shared by right-wing handles and those opposing the CJP protest, with objectionable comments and captions. (Archive Link-1, Link-2, Link-3, Link-4)
We found that this photo had been altered using AI. The original photoe was posted on July 22 by an Instagram account named @nanddhini.
A comparison of the original and viral photos clearly showed the difference in the woman’s face and body. The design of the poster also appears to have changed across different viral versions. Thus, the face and body of the woman in the original photo were swapped using an AI editing tool.
Similarly, several AI-generated and manipulated photos and videos were shared on the Facebook and Instagram accounts of @sirfseerat. These posts either altered real visuals related to the Jantar Mantar protest or created entirely new AI visuals. Some of these posts, displayed below, were later deleted.

Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.
Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.
Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.
This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.
And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.
Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.
The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.
- 
  Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer alignment with “middle powers” since January in the face of recklessness in Washington.
But what should worry another middle power, the UK, is that it was Brussels that came up with Wednesday’s big reveal in Strasbourg.
To a standing ovation at her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first “associate member” in a push to forge new links among allies in “an openly hostile world“.
The European Commission president’s deal could be seen as an “earthquake” offer said Joel Reland, of UK in a Changing Europe, thought it remains “deliciously vague”.
But it also sets Canada apart from the UK, which could, once upon a time, have had some sort of associate membership with the EU were it not for the drive for a clean break Brexit.
The last time associate membership of the EU was mooted was in relation to Ukraine as an off-the-books novel way of bringing Kyiv closer to the bloc without become a fully fledged member state.
New partnerships, von der Leyen said, were needed “in the cold fragility of today’s world” and in the face of an increasingly assertive China.
Just moments earlier she spoke about the need for the EU to diversify urgently its supply of critical raw materials and rare earths currently dominated by China allowing it to follow Japan and stockpile said minerals needed for everything from the car to the defence industries.
It is not a new subject – after all the EU has been grappling with China’s export surplus since 2023 and it introduced the Critical Raw Materials Act as far back as 2024.
The prospect of an enhanced relationship with Ottawa is one that Keir Starmer might have dreamed of.
Canada has something the EU desperately needs – rich supplies of CRM and rare earths – and the EU has something Canada urgently wants: new market for products it can no longer sell into the EU in the face of a trade war with Donald Trump.
Speaking before von der Leyen’s speech, Tobias Cremer, a German social democrat MEP, said a new deeper relationship between the EU and Canada could be a blueprint for other countries, including the UK.
Bernd Lange, the influential chair of the European parliament’s international trade committee, said associate membership could “become a model for close transcontinental partnerships with democratic countries against the new model of the law of the strongest”.
After Iceland’s rejection of membership of the EU, Fabian Zuleeg, the chief executive and chief economist of the European Policy Centre, suggested it was time that the EU developed new models, beyond the European Economic Area, that might offer “partial, gradual or associated membership options”.
Reland said the vagueness of the offer extended to Canada could be promising for the UK’s hopes for a similar offer.
“Any deep Canadian integration into the EU market would take some very heavy work to negotiate a defined set of treaty-bound rights and obligations, and so it seems more likely that – at least in the short term – cooperation will focus on more vaguely constructed alliances for ‘prosperity’ and ‘security’,” which aligns with the UK government’s desires, Reland wrote on Wednesday.
In the current political climate in the UK, it is difficult to envisage a world in which Andy Burnham would encourage any associate membership of the EU. He has a steely focus on domestic issues and it keen to avoid going down any Brexit wormholes.
The UK is seeking a reset with the EU, but the goals in the first year were modest and have yet to be achieved.
The offer to Canada suggests the bigger ambitions for relations with the EU the better.
Additional reporting: Jennifer Rankin

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”

Painful endgame for Gray as stale Hibs slump
- Published
It was the strangest kind of farewell; more sadness than satisfaction, more 'thanks for the memories' than 'never darken our door again'.
After a dozen years as a player, a goalscoring and Scottish Cup-winning icon, a coach, an interim manager and, for the last two-and-a-bit seasons, the first team manager, David Gray exited Hibernian on Wednesday evening.
He left, not to the sound of euphoria from the fans, but to the sound of a support collectively exhaling in relief. Given what he did on an immortal day at Hampden in 2016, no Hibs supporter wanted to boo the man they called Sir David Gray, nobody wanted to call for his head. It was a painful endgame, for everybody.
Hibs have sacked many managers in recent seasons, but this was no Nick Montgomery, no Lee Johnson, no Shaun Maloney. Gray was altogether different. Driven, passionate, honest as the day is long, brutally so when talking about how things were going wrong, which he had been doing too much of lately.
Gray's big picture tells us this: he was the first manager at Easter Road to qualify for European football in consecutive seasons since the great Eddie Turnbull in the early 1970s. The kind of slump that Hibs are in right now is entirely in keeping with what's happened at Hibs over the last half century.
He's the only Hibs manager to win at Ibrox in three consecutive seasons. He won at Celtic Park last season, too.
The flipside is also clear. Six successive home defeats in the league equals a grim club record dating back to 1920. Two shots at European Conference League play-offs - and the finance that would have come had they completed the task - were wasted in the most self-harming way.
Six points from six games, ninth in the table, an awful loss to lowly Kilmarnock on Tuesday and a sense of drift did for him. Making the League Cup semi-final, against Hearts, wasn't enough to save him.
- Gray sacked by Hibs after six league games 
  - Published4 hours ago
The style of football wasn't easy on the eye, the lack of energy and entertainment was a problem that was only growing. Hibs just look a bit stale, a bit rudderless. Occasionally they can spark into life and show what they are capable of, but those moments have been too fleeting.
Jens Berthel Askou brought zest and enjoyment to Fir Park last season and Alfred Johansson, his successor, is trying to build on that. They both had bad nights on Tuesday but Johansson and Wouter Vrancken at Hearts are attempting to create something compelling and their fans are on board with them all the way.
Maybe Hibs fans want something similar, something shinier, something more exotic. There is the feeling that they have a decent enough squad of players but also a belief that these players should be delivering more than they are.
If there was a table for under-performance, Hibs would be challenging at the top.
Some of those same players must shoulder a chunk of the blame for Gray's demise, but they are a largely protected species, even if a number of them, weak-willed and unreliable, have no right to be protected. You can't sack a dressing room in one day, though. A manager and his assistants? Now that's different.
Gray goes but others must look in the mirror; the players, a sporting director in Malky Mackay, a chairman in Ian Gordon, a chief executive in Dan Barnett who could scarcely be more low-key if he lived in a bunker under Easter Road.
Gordon, presumably, will lead the search for another manager. It would be interesting to do a poll on the level of trust fans have in him and others to land the right man.
Gray took them to third in the league in his first season and fifth last season. There is an argument to be made that on the back of those bottom lines he deserved more time, but he hasn't got it.
He had a tumultuous beginning as Hibs manager; one league win in his first 14 games. In November he was bottom of the league. Hearts were second bottom. More than once Gray seemed to be in trouble only to pull out a series of wins that made him safe.
That first season was a prime example. From bottom of the table, he got them to third by the end. It was a fine achievement. Fifth last season was reasonable, but it must have felt nightmarish to Hibs fans as Hearts roared on and threatened to win the league.
The rise of Hearts adds significant pressure on whoever's managing Hibs. It's just the way it is.
Throughout his time, Hibs had a ruinous capacity to concede late goals that checked momentum and made the search for the holy grail of consistency all the harder.
In 2024-25 Hibs conceded late goals that cost them points against Kilmarnock, Ross County, Hearts, Dundee twice and Dundee United twice in minutes 88, 90, 90, 90, 86, 90, 87 and 90.
Last season that unfortunate habit of caving late on continued too often. They conceded damaging goals against Midtjylland, Legia Warsaw, Livingston, Dunfermline, Dundee and Hearts three times in minutes 119, 90, 98, 90, 90, 90, 88, 90 and 86.
This season they lost to Motherwell in the 85th minute and shipped goals in the 84th and 90th minute against Gent to exit the Conference League.
They salvaged a point, or three, on other days, but they were on the wrong side of the ledger on so many occasions. Gray will have regrets about that. What-might-have-beens. Plenty of 'if onlys' mark his time in the job. His players have cause for reflection, too.
They have no shortage of decent-to-good players at Hibs, but there is something missing, some steel, perhaps, some mentality, some leadership, some coaching nous.
Gray did his utmost to improve things. He always struck you as a manager who lived and breathed the job, who was terribly cut up by it when it didn't go to plan.
Most sacked managers think they could have improved things if they were given time. The betting is that Gray is one of those. He was in trouble in his first season and he found a way out of it to finish in a lofty position. He'd have backed himself to do the same in the months ahead, but that chance has gone now.
Hibs are back at the drawing board. Consistency there, at least. Meanwhile, Gray will start again somewhere else, hopefully strengthened by the experience of how brutal football management can be at times.

Disgraced former megachurch pastor Robert Morris seen with black eye in new sex offender registry photo
Robert Morris, who founded Gateway Church, was found guilty last year of sexually assaulting a young girl decades ago
Disgraced former megachurch pastor Robert Morris, who was once Donald Trump’s spiritual advisor, was seen sporting a black eye in a new sex offender registry photo.
The Texas sex offender registry’s website uploaded a new image of Morris on Tuesday with the prominent black bruise surrounding his right eye. The 65-year-old founder of Gateway Church pleaded guilty in October 2025 to charges of indecent conduct with a child after he was accused of sexually assaulting a young girl in Oklahoma more than 40 years ago.
“Last week, Pastor Robert was in his garage and leaned over to pick something up. When he raised up, he passed out and fell. He first hit a car door and then fell to the concrete floor. His wife, Debbie, was with him at the time,” Morris’ attorney, Bill Mateja, told CBS News Texas.
Morris was taken in an ambulance to the hospital, where doctors said he broke three bones in his face.
“Medical staff believe this might have been caused by the act of raising up coupled with him having recently taken his blood pressure medication on an empty stomach,” Mateja said.
Aside from the broken bones, Morris was deemed to be okay by medical staff, his lawyer added.
Morris led the Southlake, Texas-based megachurch, Gateway Church, for 24 years until he resigned in 2024. His resignation came after allegations that he sexually assaulted Cindy Clemshire starting in 1982, when she was 12 years old.
The abuse occurred at her family’s home in Oklahoma while he was there as a traveling preacher. Officials said the abuse continued for four years.
Even though Clemshire reported the abuse, charges weren’t brought against Morris until decades later. In October 2025, Morris was sentenced in Osage County District Court to 10 years, but only had to serve six months in jail under a plea agreement.
Clemishire, who was 55 at the time of Morris’ sentencing, said she reported the abuse to her parents and church leaders in 1987. She later attempted to pursue allegations in 2005 and 2007.
Morris’ Gateway Church grew into one of the largest megachurches in the country, pushing him into the national spotlight and leading to him becoming President Donald Trump’s spiritual advisor during his first term in White House in 2016.
After Morris was released from jail this past March, Clemishire told CBS News Texas, “The most important thing for me was that he plead guilty to all five counts, and that he’d served some amount of time.”
“While most people think it’s not enough, for me, it ensured that he would spend time behind bars,” she said.
Court records show that Morris plans to serve his probation at his $1.5 million lakefront home in Palo Pinto County in Texas.
While serving probation, he is required to report his whereabouts to a probation officer. He is also prohibited from drinking alcohol, carrying a gun or associating with other convicted felons.

A bipartisan pair of US lawmakers tell WIRED they plan to introduce legislation today that would strip federal funding from states that fail to restrict the use of Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers. The devices, which help police track the location of vehicles tied to crimes, have become the subject of nationwide backlash in recent months over more nefarious uses by officers.
The No FLOCK Act—for Federal License-Plate Observation and Camera Keeping—directs the US secretary of transportation to withhold 10 percent of annual financial support due to states for highways, roads, and bridges if it fails to ban Flock and similar devices for all but five use cases. Congressmen Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democrat representing Chicago suburbs, and Michael Cloud, a Republican whose Texas district includes Corpus Christi, are cosponsoring the bill.
The legislation says that Flock cameras could be used only for “enforcing toll systems, identifying stolen vehicles, missing or endangered persons, vehicles registered to persons with a warrant for a felony offense, or investigating a vehicle involved in a felony offense.” Notably absent are uses like conducting traffic studies, investigating minor drug crimes, and enforcing parking and speeding rules.
“Our investigation into Flock exposed serious gaps in oversight, and this bipartisan bill would put clear limits in place to prevent abuse while preserving legitimate public safety uses,” Krishnamoorthi said in a statement.
But the bill stops short of banning Flock systems altogether, which has been the number one demand from supporters of a global protest movement against the Atlanta-based company and its competitors. It also doesn’t stop Flock users from broadly sharing license plate tracking data with other government agencies, including immigration authorities.
Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the proposed bill.
If the legislation passes this year, states that fail to comply with it would begin losing out on tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars in annual transportation funding starting in October 2028.

As the US war with Iran drags on, the ranks of Republicans signaling the conflict is a liability for their party continues to grow.
When the House of Representatives on Tuesday evening considered its sixth war powers resolution intended to force Donald Trump to withdraw troops from the conflict, three Republicans who had not supported the previous efforts broke with their party to vote this one to passage. Earlier that day, a Republican who had lost his primary after repeatedly clashing with Trump proposed impeaching the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, alleging a variety of constitutional transgressions including prosecuting the war against Iran without congressional authorization.
The rebellions in the GOP are thus far mostly symbolic – Trump has ignored the sole war powers resolution to make it through both the House and Senate, and the prospects of Hegseth’s impeachment are unclear. But they underscore the growing nerves among both the party’s most vulnerable and most disobedient lawmakers over continuing a conflict that appears to have accomplished little other than play into the hands of Democrats, who have spent the entirety of Trump’s second term arguing that only they can be trusted to lower costs for Americans.
“I said it in March: the mission had to stay focused and limited, because Americans do not want another forever war. I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump,” said the congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks, one of the trio of Republicans who for the first time supported a war powers resolution.
She was joined by another Iowa Republican, Zach Nunn, who justified his vote by noting his state “has already paid a devastating price” in the conflict, with two Iowans among the US soldiers killed by Iranian attacks as the war began.
“Congress owes them, their families, and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight. With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” the congressman said.
“Having deployed multiple times and flown over 700 combat hours in the Middle East, I will not support another open-ended war. We can defend Americans, pressure Iran and pursue peace while ensuring Congress fulfills its constitutional responsibility.”
Since the US joined Israel in attacking Iran at the end of February, Democrats have wielded war powers resolutions as a cudgel to get Republicans on the record about a conflict that polls indicate is not popular with the public. Their first three attempts failed, but in June, the fourth passed with the votes of two libertarian-minded Republicans – Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Warren Davidson of Ohio – along with Tom Barrett of Michigan and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, both of whom occupy battlefield districts.
The Senate later approved that measure, but Trump refused to abide by it. In July, the same lineup in the House passed a fifth war powers resolution, before Nunn, Miller-Meeks and Nancy Mace of South Carolina expanded the ranks of Republican objectors to seven in Tuesday’s vote.
The two Iowans are among the Republicans considered most at risk of losing re-election in the November midterms, with Miller-Meeks having won her race two years ago by fewer than 800 votes. They also represent areas of a state where the market impacts of the war with Iran are pronounced, as Iowa farmers struggle with higher prices for diesel, gasoline and fertilizer, all of which have been compounded by Trump’s tariff regime.
Iowa has drifted consistently to the right over the past decade, but this year, Democrats believe the circumstances are right for them to oust not just Miller-Meeks and Nunn, but also to win a Senate seat, the governor’s mansion and potentially more congressional districts in the state.
It’s far from the only state where Democrats are on the offensive. The House vote took place on the same day the New York Times and Siena University released polling that showed likely voters preferred Democrats over Republicans for Congress by nearly nine percentage point, a finding that lines up with other surveys.
Democrats are helped in their quest to retake the House by the fact that Republicans control it with a tiny majority that may be exceedingly hard to defend in November, and has also enabled Republicans like Massie to seize on splits within the party to embarrass Trump and his ally the House speaker, Mike Johnson.
Last year, Massie banded together with Democrats and a handful of Republican dissidents to force passage of a bill requiring the release of files related to the disgraced financier and former Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein.
That intensified the president’s ire towards him, and Massie lost his primary to the Trump-endorsed Republican Ed Gallrein earlier this year. Now with even less to lose, the congressman appears to be trying to seize on splits within the House GOP to retaliate against Hegseth, who campaigned for Gallrein.
Massie proposed the resolution on Tuesday, and House rules appear to require it be voted on by Thursday. The chamber was scheduled to be in session that day for the last time before the 3 November midterm elections, but on Wednesday morning, House Republican leaders canceled votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home early to face their constituents.

Verstappen passes 100 amateur karters in 14 laps
