Max Verstappen needed just 14 laps and 35 minutes to overtake 100 amateur drivers in an exhibition go-kart race at Silverstone.
The four-time Formula 1 world champion had a maximum of 35 laps and 75 minutes to pass everyone on an adapted track at the grand prix circuit in Northamptonshire.
Red Bull's Verstappen, 28, was up to 37th by the end of a chaotic first lap in which many drivers crashed or span out, resulting in the race being briefly suspended.
The ruthless Dutchman, who warned participants "it's not a charity event" on the radio, moved into 10th by the start of lap six and was in fourth by lap 10, with each driver who he passed having to retire.
At that stage, the field - made up of TV, sport and social media personalities, with no professional racing drivers - consisted of just Dutch F1 journalist Jacky Martens, Red Bull engine builder Lewis Osler and YouTuber Zac Alsop.
All three were given an extra 'fast lap' where they could cut a corner of the track to try to hold off Verstappen for longer, but he inevitably reeled them in.
Martens, who was on pole position after qualifying, was the final driver to be passed as Verstappen completed his challenge with 40 minutes and 21 laps to spare.
Verstappen began his racing career as a junior in karting and won four consecutive F1 titles between 2021 and 2024.

Japan to charge rescue fee on Mount Fuji during off season
- Published
From next year, people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service, authorities governing the northern part of the peak say.
The fee is among a series of measures Japan's Yamanashi prefecture is introducing to deter reckless and poorly prepared climbers.
A similar fee of 8,000 yen ($51; £38) per five minutes is already in place in nearby Saitama prefecture for other mountainous areas and will be used as a reference.
Yamanashi authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season, which runs from early September to July the following year, to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We ask the general public to refrain from climbing during the off-season. We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Yamanashi Governor Kotaro Nagasaki said on Monday.
Officials in Yamanashi and neighbouring Shizuoka prefecture, which governs the southern part of Fuji, have seen a rise in off-season and unplanned climbs, some of which have left climbers stranded.
Shizuoka authorities say they will impose penalties on people who fail to register their off-season climbing attempts and strengthen efforts to keep climbers out of restricted areas.
They did not announce a helicopter rescue fee.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from July to early September, with about 200,000 hikers attempting the summit each year.
Climbing outside of those months is highly discouraged although permitted up to the fifth of ten stations.
However, most mountain huts and toilet facilities are closed off season. The weather and trail conditions also tend to be more severe.

The U.S. FDA is holding a public hearing on Monday to gather feedback on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelic drugs, the latest step in a months-long push by President Donald Trump's administration to speed up development of the treatments for serious mental illnesses.
The hearing is part of a broader push launched in April, when Trump ordered the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to focus on qualifying psychedelic drug programs for its priority-voucher program.
The order also directed the FDA to work with the Drug Enforcement Administration on a pathway for some patients to obtain investigational treatments under a law, which allows certain seriously ill patients to seek experimental therapies, and to increase collaboration with the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Since then, the FDA has issued priority vouchers to three companies developing psychedelic-based treatments, one for psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression, another for psilocybin for major depressive disorder and a third for methylone for post-traumatic stress disorder.
The hearing focuses on practical issues that could shape how psychedelic therapies are tested and delivered, including provider training and credentials, patient screening and monitoring, access and reimbursement, clinic capacity and the collection of long-term safety data.
The FDA said it was not seeking views on individual drug applications, the scheduling of controlled substances or the legalisation of psychedelics.
Doctors, veterans, pharmacists and therapists during the hearing urged the regulator to establish clear safety and access standards for psychedelic-assisted therapies.
Experts said any approved psychedelic treatment must include trained staff in the room during sessions, along with proper screening, follow-up care and community support.
Robert Barrow, CEO of Definium Therapeutics, which is developing an LSD-based therapy, told Reuters that the hearing offers "a nice opportunity for that continuing public dialogue" among regulators, clinicians and patients.
He said regulators and industry should treat psychedelics "like it's normal drug development, normal science, normal medicine," rather than as an unusually novel category requiring special treatment.
Just days before the hearing, senior FDA officials, including Michael Davis, head of the agency's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine outlining a framework for developing and approving psychedelic drugs and saying the agency was "meeting this moment" on hard-to-treat conditions such as major depressive disorder and PTSD.
The American Psychiatric Association said it "appreciates the FDA's public hearing and coordination with federal partners on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelics."
"The FDA's determination of safety and effectiveness... must remain the foundation for any future clinical use."
Jefferies analysts said the framework suggested the FDA was willing to consider flexible trial designs to address challenges including "functional unblinding," when a drug's noticeable psychoactive effects reveal to participants which treatment they received.
The administration's support has stirred fresh investor interest in the sector, with industry executives telling Reuters it could improve coordination between the FDA and the Drug Enforcement Administration and help reduce regulatory delays, even as researchers noted that approved treatments were still likely years away.
Continued alignment among regulators, clinicians and developers on a safe, supervised rollout should benefit AtaiBeckley, Compass Pathways, Definium Therapeutics, Helus Pharma and GH Research, analysts said.
Helus CEO Michael Halstead said "the science continues to advance, and continued thoughtful engagement among regulators, researchers and clinicians is critical to advancing these promising new treatments."

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian visited New Delhi on 11 September 2026 to attend the 18th BRICS Summit. During his visit, he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and participated in several engagements on the sidelines of the summit. On 11 September 2026, Iran’s Ambassador to India, Dr Mohammad Fathali, hosted an event in New Delhi where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met religious leaders, intellectuals and other dignitaries, including Jain monk Acharya Lokesh Muni and Jagadguru Swami Satishacharya Maharaj.
In this context, a video of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian bowing down is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows him touching the feet of Jagadguru Ramanandacharya Swami Satishacharya to seek his blessings. Several news outlets, including Times Now Navbharat and ABP News, also reported that Pezeshkian touched the feet of Swami Satishacharya during the event. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian touching Swami Satishacharya’s feet for blessings.
Fact: The video does not show Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian touching Swami Satishacharya’s feet to seek his blessings. Pezeshkian bent down to pick up something that had fallen to the ground, while Satishacharya also bent down at the same time. The Iranian Embassy and people present at the event confirmed that the video does not show Pezeshkian seeking blessings from Satishacharya. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords and found reports published by News18 Hindi and Moneycontrol, citing sources from the Iranian Embassy, which reported that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian bent down to pick up a piece of paper. According to News18 Hindi, the Iranian Ambassador and diplomats organised a special reception and interaction programme at The Oberoi Hotel in New Delhi, attended by Jagadguru Satishacharya Maharaj, along with several prominent Indian interfaith leaders, intellectuals and businesspeople. During the event, Pezeshkian bent down to pick up a letter that had fallen to the floor, rather than touching anyone’s feet. Moneycontrol also reported, citing Iranian Embassy sources, that the letter had been handed to Pezeshkian by another leader and accidentally fell from his hand, prompting him to bend down and pick it up.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to social media posts by INN News (archived) and Ismat TV (archived). An INN News post featuring Sahil Naqvi, who was present at the event, addressed the viral video, claiming that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had bowed to touch the feet of a Hindu priest in India. According to the post, Pezeshkian had bent down to pick up a pen that had fallen to the floor, while the priest also bent down at the same time, creating the impression that the President was touching his feet. The post described the viral portrayal as misleading and said the footage was being presented out of context.
Ismat TV shared a video from another angle, showing both Pezeshkian and Swami Satishacharya bending down to pick up the pen. According to the account, Pezeshkian first attempted to pick it up, followed by Satishacharya. The post said that the incident was a gesture of respect and courtesy and did not show Pezeshkian bowing to anyone.
We then contacted Ismat TV and spoke to Hussain Mehdi, a photographer employed by the organisation. Speaking to Factly, he said that the channel’s staff were present at the event and that the claim that Pezeshkian touched Satishacharya’s feet is false. He also shared another video shot from a different angle, showing both Pezeshkian and Satishacharya bending down to pick up a paper.
We found a Facebook post by Acharya Lokesh Muni, who shared pictures of himself at the event standing next to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. In the post, he said that he had invited Pezeshkian to host a first-of-its-kind peace summit in Iran, which the Iranian President accepted. He added that religious leaders and peace-loving groups from around the world would gather to promote peace through dialogue and discussion.
We contacted him, and speaking to Factly, he stated that the claim that the Iranian President touched the feet of a Hindu religious leader is false. He said that while he was showing Pezeshkian his magazine, Aahwaan, which is published by the World Peace Centre, an organisation he founded, the magazine fell from his hands. According to him, the video shows the Iranian President bending down to pick up the magazine for him as a courtesy, which was later circulated widely on the internet with a misleading claim.
We also contacted Maulana Taqi Haider Naqvi through the Iran Culture House, New Delhi, via WhatsApp. Naqvi, who was present at the event, also rebutted the claim that Pezeshkian touched Satishacharya’s feet. He also forwarded an Iranian Embassy statement regarding the matter, which reads, “The President bent down to pick up a letter that one of the leaders had given him and that had fallen to the ground.”
To sum up, this viral video shows Iranian President Pezeshkian bending down to pick up something, not to touch a Hindu religious leader’s feet.

Anna Nordqvist spoke in the build-up to the Solheim Cup about the European team being in a period of transition as she chose a line-up with four debutants.
Any fears about fielding rookies for the most pressure packed event in the women's game were proven unfounded in her team's thrilling 15-13 victory at Bernardus Golf last weekend.
Nastasia Nadaud (21), Julia Lopez Ramirez (23), Mimi Rhodes (24) and, eventually, Lottie Woad all delivered crucial points and gave an encouraging glimpse into Europe's future.
Three of the quartet were captain's picks, with the 22-year-old Woad the only debut automatic qualifier for the team that avenged defeat in Virginia two years ago.
"So many people said it was a bit of a risk having four rookies, but I was so impressed with them," Nordqvist said.

'I never felt like they were rookies'
Europe's skipper faced intense scrutiny throughout her captaincy, especially over her stubborn faith in Woad's partnership with fellow Englishwoman Charley Hull.
But she was ultimately vindicated, especially with her wildcard selections, which also included relative veteran Leona Maguire.
Between them they yielded eight and a half points, compared with five contributed by America's three captain's picks. Nordqvist's singles line-up also leant heavily on a willingness to trust in youth.
Of the youngsters tasting Solheim singles action for the first time only Rhodes failed to win and it took a brilliant performance from world number one Nelly Korda to beat her on the final day.
And the beaten Englishwoman had already contributed significantly alongside Nadaud with Friday fourball and Saturday foursomes wins that helped ensure 8-8 parity after the first two days.
In the singles Rhodes was sent out fourth, but it was positions six, seven and eight - Nadaud, Lopez Ramirez and Woad - that held so much significance to the final outcome.
All three delivered vital wins. "What people don't understand is they're so good when they come out on tour these days," Nordqvist said. "They just play fearless and they have so much personality.
"All of the four I had, I never felt like they were rookies. And the first day when I send out Nastasia and Mimi a lot of people questioned why would you send out two rookies, but I said why not. And they delivered.
"They delivered again on Saturday morning. And Sunday too. Mimi took Nelly down to 15. She's the number one player in the world, and she pushed her.
"Rookie Lottie making the winning putt. It's been really fun to have them and they bring out a fresh perspective.
"And I feel really old and I'm glad I'm retiring now because these girls are just so good."
'I said a few words' - Reid rallied Europeans
It fell to Woad to sink the putt that ensured Europe would win, with four matches still to be completed. Her 2&1 triumph over Auston Kim took Europe to 14 points with Carlotta Ciganda already unassailably three up on the 16th tee.
Europe were guaranteed to reach the magic number of 14½ points and there was nothing America could do about it. It should be noted, this was not a great US side with Korda, Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin being head and shoulders above the rest.
Nordqvist's persistent faith in Woad and Hull, playing her two highest ranked players together in the four opening sessions seemed a folly. She insisted stats justified the call, but the partnership never gelled, yielding only half a point.
It was all the more jarring because elsewhere Nordqvist had unmistakably fostered that famed European spirit which so often permeates through Solheim and Ryder Cup successes.
It was crucial in overcoming Jennifer Kupcho's hammer blow long range birdies late on the Saturday evening that allowed the United States to force an unlikely share of the foursomes and fourball spoils.
All the momentum was with the visitors on the Saturday night, but it was soon washed away as the rain drenched Sunday singles began.
"We were on the team bus, I said a few words," said assistant captain Mel Reid of the aftermath of Kupcho's heroics. "The team bus is a special place for Team Europe.
"I think it's where we really unite, we really get together. We put the music on and it's a special place. I'm just glad there are no cameras there.
"But we got to the hotel and we put on a song, and I felt like it changed the mood and united us. It was weird.
"We just forgot what happened, the disappointment, and we just got back on it."
Newcomers soak up Europe's unique bond
After a winless two days there was enormous pressure on Hull and Woad and the former barely missed a shot in an impressive 3&2 win over the tenacious Megan Khang.
The Englishwoman still could not buy a birdie putt on the slow greens but she never gave her opponent a sniff. Woad was equally strong and her decisive role at the end was in keeping with the spectacular start to her pro career.
There are no guarantees in golf, but in Woad, Nadaud, Lopez Ramirez and Rhodes Europe appear to have an exciting nucleus for the trophy defence at Valhalla in 2028.
America need to find something similar, maybe from their recent victorious Curtis Cup team. And, remarkably, that is the only one of the transatlantic trophies that now resides in US hands as the Solheim joins the Ryder and Walker Cups on this side of the pond.
In the Solheim, Europe's newcomers have soaked up the continent's unique bond. It has seeped into their bones and is best summed up by the irrepressible old stager Ciganda.
She might drive you mad with her glacial pace of play, but the veteran Spaniard knows as well as anyone what, for Europe, the Solheim Cup is all about.
"I just love it," Ciganda said. "I love beating the Americans. Yeah, winning for Team Europe, it's the best feeling."

St Leger win has removed Osborne's fear of failure
- Published
St Leger-winning jockey Saffie Osborne says the "fear of failure" has left her after she became the first woman to win a British Classic.
The 24-year-old said that despite wanting to achieve "so much more", her victory at Doncaster on Saturday means she will always be able to look back and think her career was "worth it".
Osborne said the sport can be "very lonely" - she estimates she drives 65,000 miles a year, often alone - and she has suffered some serious falls, breaking numerous bones.
But she told BBC Sport that winning one of British Flat racing's five Classics had been a dream since she was five. She has now fulfilled it.
While racing is a sport where men and women compete against one another, opportunities have not been equal.
Only six female jockeys have had rides in British Classics in 250 years, totalling 12 rides, according to the National Horseracing Museum.
They are Gay Kelleway (The Oaks, 1986; The Oaks, 1987), Alex Greaves (The Derby, 1996; 1,000 Guineas, 1996), Hayley Turner (The Derby, 2012) Josephine Gordon (1,000 Guineas, 2017), Hollie Doyle (The Oaks, 2021; St Leger, 2021; The Oaks, 2022) and Saffie Osborne (2,000 Guineas, 2024; 1,000 Guineas, 2026; St Leger, 2026).
"It has been a male-dominated sport for an extremely long time, and I suppose it's becoming less and less of a conversation, which is quite nice," she said.
"When people talk about the firsts of what women have done, I think to have my own one is quite special.
"I think it's also quite poignant because there's so few left of first things for women to do in this sport."
On Saturday's groundbreaking win, she added: "That sort of fear of failure has sort of disappeared. However much more I want to achieve, and I want to achieve so much more, it's kind of like I can always look back on my career and know that it was all worth it.
"I got to achieve what I always dreamed of achieving."
Osborne's ride on Highwayman in the St Leger was her first for trainer Joseph O'Brien, and only came about because of an injury to regular jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle.
She acknowledged that the success of a jockey is dependent on "being chosen", but is adamant that her gender isn't a factor in the opportunities she gets.
"I don't feel like in my position now that I'm ever looked at any differently because I'm a woman," she said.
"Any jockey, when you're starting out, it takes years to gain respect and be looked at as a person that people would want to use. And I don't think my gender at this point would have had anything to do with it.
"Hopefully Saturday will open more doors. But when it comes to me as a female jockey, I don't think I'm viewed any differently within the industry."
Osborne also said she is treated as "one of the lads" in the weighing room, and has never experienced sexism and misogyny unlike other female jockeys, including Bryony Frost.
Jockey Robbie Dunne was banned from racing for 18 months, with three months suspended, for bullying fellow rider Frost in 2021, which was later cut to 10 months on appeal.
Having ridden 60 winners since the start of May, Osborne is currently sitting eighth in the Flat Jockeys Championship, and is open about dreaming of being champion jockey in the future.
She would be the first female jockey to achieve that.
"You wouldn't be a jockey if you didn't want to be champion jockey one day. I think this is the first year that maybe I truly believe that I could one day," she said.
"It's been a phenomenal year that's been topped off by Saturday. But I'm very lucky. I have a very good agent [Tony Hind] and agents are so important in this sport. He's got an amazing book of jockeys, the likes of Ryan Moore, William Buick, Billy Loughnane. And I'm very lucky to be on his team.
"He makes champion jockeys, he's had a lot of them. And yeah, I would love to be the next one on the list."

Meet PitchFly, WIRED’s latest editorial recruit.
He has 165,112 neurons, and they’re all trained to generate story ideas. A sampling of his early output: “The Hidden Weather Problem Inside Surveillance”; “The Engineers Who Think Elon Musk Needs Less Computer Security”; and my personal favorite, “Everyone Wants Cooking. Nobody Has Solved Donald Trump.”
PitchFly uses a detailed map of the brain of a male drosophila—the common fruit fly. Developed by researchers from Google and a number of academic institutions, the map, known as a connectome, captures the way that 166,000 neurons and 125 million connecting synapses fire in response to stimuli. In essence, you can use it to simulate how a fly would respond to lots of stuff—it’s a very simple version of artificial intelligence based on charting real biological intelligence.
Because the researchers open-sourced it, you can easily use AI to import the connectome into a project with a little prompting. For PitchFly, I vibe coded a project in which the tiny digital drosophila brain generates story ideas. (I’m not sure why the fly has a little hat on, but I like its style.) This involved scraping together hundreds of the most popular story headlines from the site from the past year and feeding them into the connectome. I had Codex do the hard work, and it decided that the most efficient approach was to turn the headlines into words and phrases, then transform them into a representation that a neural network could understand. The connectome was fed the best-performing stories and told to generate its own ideas based on that.
In other words, this isn’t a fly-based language model—although someone apparently created one of those. The fly brain has no idea what any of the words mean, or if any of it makes sense. It’s just remixing the patterns it has seen in pleasing new ways. A cynic might suggest this is exactly how some journalists generate their own pitches, but I think that’s a bit unfair—and judging by its lunatic ideas, PitchFly won’t be replacing me anytime soon:
- The Tiny Shift in Agentic AI Is Rewriting the Rules of Food and Drink
- What Security News Is Quietly Doing to Donald Trump
- The Race to Reinvent Privacy Before Artificial Intelligence Breaks
- Is China About to Make Digital Syndication Obsolete?
In the future, perhaps I could have the program continue to learn by reading new WIRED headlines. For now, though, this seems like a decent proof of concept, not to mention evidence at last that the average WIRED writer is intellectually superior to a fruit fly.
After the connectome’s release in early September, dozens of other weird and wonderful projects powered by fruit-fly intelligence sprang up.
An X user called Lyra Bubbles, for instance, demo’d a project that involved training the virtual fly brain to play the VR game Beat Saber. Alex Wormuth, a software engineer at Coinbase, created StonkFly, which uses the fly’s tiny brain to decide how to trade stocks. (It’s losing money, but it’s doing surprisingly well, all things considered.)
“The fly brings lighthearted, humorous relief” at a time when everyone is worried about the existential risks of AI, Wormuth told me in a DM. He says he found playing with the fruit fly connectome philosophically fascinating, too. “It sparks questions about ethics of this and whether there is any consciousness [in the replication of fly’s brain],” he says.
Others trained the connectome to play Doom, Minecraft, and Pong. Some fly brains apparently learned to solve Rubik’s cubes. And someone also put the fly brain in charge of driving virtual cars—it turns out flies are terrible at parallel parking. (Then again, so am I, so I won’t pass judgment.)
I haven’t verified that all these projects actually use the connectome—they may just be fun animations. And some of them—like one that simply involves training the fly to take a well-earned break—seem like spoofs. But there are some serious science projects out there, too, including visualizations for exploring the connectome and tools for manipulating neural circuitry.
Mapping different animal brains may help neuroscientists decipher the biological foundations of intelligence. It isn’t possible—yet—to map all 86 billion neurons in a human brain, but peering into the brains of smaller creatures can provide useful insights. Neuroscientists can also test theories about how damage affects neuronal wiring—and how such damage might someday be repaired—by messing with the fly’s connectome.
As far as AI is concerned, all this fruit-fly frivolity also shows how easy it is now to train and deploy your own model. The best use for the giant LLMs run by big AI companies may be building specialized AI models for specific tasks (something I’ve written about previously). Sometimes even a tiny brain can do quite well.

About 70% of the year-to-year variation in winter air pollution across northern India may be explained by the frequency of western disturbances, possibly providing warning of unusually polluted winter months in advance, researchers said.
Western disturbances are storm systems that travel eastwards from the Mediterranean region towards South Asia by strengthening vertical ventilation and bringing precipitation that helps clear accumulated pollution, including PM2.5, from the air.
The team said winters with more frequent western disturbances tend to experience lower air pollution levels, while winters with fewer of these storms are more susceptible to persistent severe pollution.
"Currently, many of the most disruptive air-pollution measures are taken only after severe pollution is already developing," lead author Yuanyu Xie, an associate research scholar at Princeton University's School of Public and International Affairs, U.S., said.
"If scientists can anticipate the overall severity of the coming winter months ahead of time, governments, businesses, and communities will have more time to prepare," Ms. Xie said.
They also found that the frequency of western disturbances is linked to ocean temperature patterns already evident during the preceding autumn.
The team said the overall severity of winter pollution in north India may thus be predicted about a season in advance. Air pollution levels across northern India, including Delhi-NCR, spike during the winter season, increasing residents' health risks.
A combination of vehicle emissions, stubble burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and weather patterns that trap pollutants close to the ground is attributed to the seasonal spike in pollution.
Emergency measures, including pausing construction, restricting industries and limiting traffic, are implemented on severe pollution days, but may be a challenge if put in place on short notice.
The researchers said seasonal forecasts could indicate whether the coming winter is likely to have relatively severe or mild pollution levels overall, rather than predicting pollution levels for a particular day months in advance, thereby offering a more practical approach.
The information could provide a lead time, allowing authorities to strengthen enforcement before the pollution season begins, coordinate responses across jurisdictions, and give businesses more time to prepare for potential restrictions, they said.
"Emission controls will remain of paramount importance," co-author Denise Mauzerall, a professor of public and international affairs and civil and environmental engineering at Princeton University, said.
"However, we show that forecasts of winter pollution based on observations from the previous autumn can allow additional pollution controls to be arranged in advance of extreme pollution periods. This could provide time to plan and implement cost-effective controls that mitigate peak pollution concentrations in winter in northern India," Ms. Mauzerall said.
The authors wrote, "Nearly 70% of the inter-annual variations in winter PM2.5 pollution across northern India are explained by western disturbances (WDs) — prevailing extratropical storms originating from the Mediterranean region — through PM2.5 removal via enhanced ventilation and precipitation."

In the quest for a seam-bowling all-rounder, particularly when Hardik Pandya’s battle with injuries has resembled a long-running television soap opera, India has backed Nitish Kumar Reddy for the best part of two years. The 23-year-old from Visakhapatnam has himself had his tryst with injuries of late, but evenings like the one at the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Tuesday will go a long way towards boosting the youngster’s confidence.
Nitish, who has ramped up his speed in recent months, scalped three for 24 in his three overs as Shreyas Iyer & Co. restricted Afghanistan to 159 for eight and clinched a seven-wicket win in 14.5 overs. With it, India took an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match T20I series.
After conceding 30 runs in two overs in Sunday’s opener, Nitish needed a productive outing with the ball, especially as he was returning from a quadriceps injury.
HIGHLIGHTS - INDIA vs AFGHANISTAN 2nd T20I
If Nitish stepped up, so did Sanju Samson. With 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi watching from the dugout, the pressure on the 31-year-old to hold his own as opener is unmistakable in every outing. In the circumstances, Samson responded ably with a belligerent 22-ball 57.
Once again, Jasprit Bumrah set the foundation with a first-over maiden. Arshdeep Singh reaped the rewards in the next over. Off the left-armer’s third delivery, Rahmanullah Gurbaz’s desperation to get Afghanistan off the mark manifested in a hasty pull. The miscue was pouched by Ravi Bishnoi at mid-on.
After the second-wicket stand between Ibrahim Zadran and Sediqullah Atal accrued 51 runs, Nitish delivered the breakthrough as the Afghan skipper’s heave across the line found deep midwicket.
Bishnoi, who replaced the injured Varun Chakaravarthy, struck shortly after when Sediquulah holed out to Tilak Varma at long-off. More joy came India’s way as Gulbadin Naib skied Nitish to Samson.
A brisk 29-run stand between Azmatullah Omarzai and Darwish Rasooli was laced with lusty blows. Omarzai even had that tincture of luck that every batter needs, when Bishnoi spilled an easy chance off Axar Patel’s left-arm spin with the Afghan all-rounder on five. But when both batters departed in quick succession, the Afghans were back in a blind alley at 100 for six in 14.1 overs.
In getting to the total that Ibrahim & Co. ultimately did, Mohammad Nabi and Rashid Khan displayed their secondary skills. The spin duo, more than capable of chipping in with the willow, put together 48 runs for the seventh wicket.
Will such cameos suffice, however, against this Indian unit? Not on Tuesday’s evidence.

Alice Augusta Ball lived a very short life. In 24 years, she had remarkable achievements, and was predictably forgotten for a while, until the world was shaken up to her brilliance. Her work on distilling chaulmoogra oil for use as effective treatment for leprosy brought hope to a number of patients globally.
An African American woman born into middle class in the late 1800s, Alice Ball benefitted from an early exposure to chemical processes as her family was involved in photography. She went on to shine in science at school, and could hope to move on to university, a rare opportunity for a woman and a person of her race at that time. She lived up to her potential and at the University of Washington, racked up her skills in chemistry and pharmacy. She finished two degrees – a bachelor’s in pharmaceutical chemistry and a bachelor’s in pharmacy – thus arming herself for a career –short lived, but so sparkling, people are still talking about her, though subsequent innovations have transformed care for leprosy.
With a full scholarship, another rarity for the times, Alice moved to the College of Hawai‘i, and became the first woman and the first African American to earn a master’s degree in chemistry. We mention it because it is an achievement, but also because it was an achievement that attracted the kind of attention a career flourishes on. It is said that Harry T. Hollmann, a public health officer, thought her thesis research on extracting active compounds from the kava (awa) root might have implications for his passion – finding cures for leprosy.
Leprosy or Hansen’s disease is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, and was discovered by Norwegian physician Gerhard Armauer Hansen in the 1870s. While it is prevalent in people living in tropical regions, leprosy which affects the nervous system, also has the moniker of being the world’s oldest disease. Evidence of leprosy has been found in skeletons from back in 2000 BCE. Those affected develop visible skin lesions and extremities including fingers and toes malformed and misshapen fingers. Sometimes amputations were also performed on limbs that could not be salvaged. As a result of the disfiguration, the stigma surrounding the disease was so high, those with leprosy had to be sequestered in camps and asylums outside the community.
Alice did accept Hollman’s invitation and what she managed to achieve was to revolutionise the field of leprosy care in the very near future. Described as the Ball Method, Alice devised a method that would “convert the oil’s fatty acids into water-soluble ethyl esters that could be injected into patients. Until then Chaulmoogra oil was promising as treatment for leprosy, but it was thick, not soluble in water, besides difficult to inject and swallow. Soon the world adopted the Ball Method and the landmark contribution changed life for the better for people who were battling leprosy across the world, without hope until then. Alice was in her early 20s at the time of this achievement.
Records of the time say, since the new formulation dispersed in the bloodstream instead of pooling under the skin, patients for the first time celebrated as earlier, there was none of the severe local reactions and oozing oil that the injections caused. Used on patients at Kalihi Hospital in Hawai‘i, researchers managed to show that patients administered the new formulation, became ‘bacteriologically negative, their lesions resolved, and many were discharged from isolation to rejoin their families, without fear of infecting them.’ This injectable preparation remained the best available treatment worldwide until sulfone antibiotics, Dapsone, in combination with other drugs, replaced it in the 1940s, facilitating a future unimaginable until then, for those who were diagnosed with leprosy and condemned to social isolation.
However, Alice’s contribution never made it to the headlines thanks to a set of factors – her gender, age and race were primary. She died young, it is speculated that it could be a result of a laboratory accident, a senior male colleague, her department head Arthur L. Dean appropriated and published her work without sharing any credit, in fact, promoting it as the ‘Dean method’, accounts of that period list.
It went unchallenged until decades later, when researcher Harry Hollmann revisited the archives and credited Ball. Finally, the historical records were righted, and Alice Ball’s name was affixed to the method she had painstakingly developed. By 24, despite the disdvantaged circumstances she worked in, Alice Ball had changed the world, it is a matter of speculation how much she would have achieved had she lived longer, but a safe bet to say she would have left a deeper impact. For the punch she packed in her short life, and the revolution she managed in that life, it’s time we say her name, say “Alice Augusta Ball.”

Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara says he has "turned the page" and is focusing on the Ligue 1 season after his £47.1m move to Chelsea collapsed.
The 22-year-old had completed a medical but the deal fell through shortly before the transfer window closed.

Monaco have won their first three Ligue 1 fixtures of the season and sat second to Rennes in the table, with a game in hand, heading into the weekend.
"I can help the team a lot," Senegal international Camara said.

Trump chief of staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free
- Published
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis.
In a post on X, Wiles said her pathology tests "came back clear" after a visit to the Mayo Clinic earlier this week.
Wiles, 69, is considered among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president.
In her post, Wiles thanked Trump for his "unwavering support" and vowed to continue working to "advance his America First Agenda".
Wiles continued working virtually at the White House during the six months of treatment following her diagnosis.
In a March statement, Wiles said that one in eight women are diagnosed with breast cancer.
"Every day, these women continue to raise their families, go to work and serve their communities with strength and determination," she said. "I now join their ranks."
Her post on Wednesday did not reveal any more details about her treatment.
Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff - widely considered to be the most important role in the White House.
In her position, Wiles works to keep the president's agenda on track and serves as a gatekeeper to President Trump, as well as a policy coordinator and political advisor.
Before taking the job, Wiles played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.
Her tenure, however, has not been without controversy.
In December, Vanity Fair published interviews with Wiles in which she gave a blunt - and occasionally unflattering - assessment of her time working in the Trump White House.
For example, she described the famously teetotaling president as having an "alcoholic's personality" but added that there's "nothing he can't do. Nothing, zero, nothing."
She also provided candid thoughts about other figures close to the US president, describing Vice-President JD Vance as a "conspiracy theorist" and Elon Musk as an "odd, odd duck."
The US president, however, swiftly came to her defence and Wiles described Vanity Fair's reporting as having omitted "significant context" to create a "chaotic and negative narrative" about the administration.
President Trump and the White House have yet to comment on Wiles' announcement.

Beauty quick commerce startup Firi has raised $3 Mn (about ₹28.8 Cr) in a seed funding round led by 360 ONE Asset, with participation from Better Capital, CRED founder Kunal Shah, and other founders and operators. The startup currently offers deliveries in as little as nine minutes in parts of Gurugram through its first Beauty Studio. It plans to use the fresh capital to expand its assortment beyond skincare, haircare, and bodycare into makeup, fragrances, and other beauty categories. The startup said the latest funding will support its category expansion and continued development of its AI-led product discovery and fulfilment model. Incorporated in June 2026 following a pilot earlier this year, Firi positions itself as an “opinionated” beauty store that reviews and shortlists products instead of listing a wider catalogue. The startup claims to use AI tools to analyse Reddit discussions, YouTube reviews, ingredient lists, and other product information to identify products with high repeat-purchase potential. Firi said it has analysed more than 50 Mn reviews to shortlist around 3,000 products from more than 3 Lakh beauty products available globally. It was founded by former Uber India executives Karishma Rathaur and Vivek Madani. The duo was part of Uber’s early India team and worked on categories such as Uber Premier and Rentals, while Madani later worked on deeptech products at Flipkart Labs. Before launching Firi, the cofounders built Honestly, an AI-powered beauty search and discovery platform. Firi is targeting consumers who do not spend significant time researching beauty products or consuming beauty-related content and instead depend on recommendations from friends or family. The startup claimed that its AOV is nearly 2X the reported AOV of large online beauty retailers such as Nykaa and Tira, despite currently operating across only three product categories. It said customers are also purchasing products across multiple categories in a single order. Firi operated in a crowded Indian beauty commerce market dominated by players such as Nykaa, Reliance-backed Tira, and Purplle. Horizontal ecommerce platforms such as Amazon and Myntra, along with quick commerce players Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart, and Zepto, are also expanding their BPC offerings. India’s BPC market is expected to grow from more than $5 Bn in 2023 to over $28 Bn by 2030. BPC is also emerging as an important high-AOV category for quick commerce platforms as they expand beyond groceries and seek to capture a larger share of consumer spending.

With greater clarity around the monetisation of UPI payments following’ the introduction of a new Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) framework, Walmart-backed fintech PhonePe is set to revive its initial public offering (IPO) plans, which were put on hold earlier this year. Sources told Inc42 that the fintech startup is now targeting a public listing between February-March 2027. “They have an almost 45% share of merchant payments. With greater clarity on the MDR regime, PhonePe is now looking to revise its IPO plans and could target a listing between February and March 2027,” the sources said. PhonePe will look to file its updated IPO papers by the end of this year, seeking a valuation of $10 Bn, sources in the know told Inc42 on the condition of anonymity. Inc42 has sent questions to PhonePe to confirm the development. The story will be updated based on their response. Notably, the MDR framework was introduced by the Central government yesterday, bringing charges back on select UPI merchant transactions beginning October 15. The move marks a shift from the broad zero-MDR regime in place from 2020. The charges will apply only to select transactions, with merchant UPI payments above ₹2,000 attracting a 0.4% MDR. However, person-to-person (P2P) transactions up to ₹2,000 will continue to remain free. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month through UPI QR payments will also be exempt. A lower MDR of 0.02%, capped at ₹300, will apply to capital market payments, including transactions involving stockbrokers, securities dealers, mutual funds and investment platforms. The revised framework gives PhonePe, which has long been the UPI market leader, a greater clarity on monetising the service following years of no revenue. After filing for an confidential IPO in September 2025, PhonePe had filed its updated DRHP in March post receiving the SEBI’s approval for its OFS-only IPO. Existing investors including Walmart, Tiger Global and Microsoft were expected to sell shares. The IPO was earlier expected to value PhonePe at $9 Bn-$10.5 Bn, with the offering size estimated to be in the range of $900 Mn-$1.5 Bn. In its updated DRHP, PhonePe noted that UPI payments carried an MDR until 2020, allowing payment apps, aggregators and banks to earn revenue from transactions. The government later scrapped the MDR on UPI and RuPay payments to boost digital payment adoption. PhonePe’s DRHP also cited calls from the Payments Council of India to review the zero-MDR regime for large merchants and RuPay debit card transactions. The startup said a “carefully structured MDR regime” could support investments in infrastructure, innovation and merchant acquisition, while cautioning that changes to the MDR framework could affect its financial performance. PhonePe CEO Sameer Nigam has now welcomed the new framework, saying that the revenue generated from high-value merchant transactions could be reinvested in the UPI ecosystem. Speaking to ANI earlier in the day, Nigam said around 70-80 Cr UPI transactions take place every day and that about 96% would remain free under the new framework. He said the 0.4% MDR would help the payments industry recover some operational costs and invest in merchant digitisation, marketing, innovation and new use cases. “Now that a limited MDR has been introduced, we hope it will contribute to the further growth of the UPI ecosystem,” Nigam said. On the financial front, PhonePe’s net loss widened 62% to ₹2,792 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,727.4 Cr in the previous fiscal, as higher employee costs, marketing expenses, ESOP costs and one-time write-offs offset growth in revenue. Operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr from ₹7,105 Cr in FY25. Including other income of ₹467.4 Cr, total revenue grew 10% YoY to ₹8,387.9 Cr.

Cole Campbell, the breakout American star of the football season in Germany, has a unique advantage: his primary training partner is his mother, Rakel Karvelsson, a former pro in the U.S. and an Iceland international.
A “soccer mom”, Karvelsson is now sharpening Campbell’s game as he makes heads turn for small-town Bundesliga side Elversberg.
“My mom knows so much about football,” Campbell told reporters on Tuesday. “Having a mom also that played football, it’s great. I can also train with her, which is fun. She challenges me to a two-touch battle. She doesn’t win anymore but in the past, when I was younger, she used to beat me. That was, I think, maybe seven years ago when I was 13. When I was 14, 15, I started to beat her.”
ALSO READ: James Rodriguez announces retirement from Colombia national team
The 20-year-old joined Elversberg as the club’s record signing in July after his career plateaued at Borussia Dortmund, and the gamble on a promoted side paid off immediately: he scored on his first league start in a surprise win over former champion Bayer Leverkusen.
A proficient winger, Campbell and his young Elversberg side have shown they belong at the top level after pushing Bayern Munich in a 1-2 loss last week. Campbell had a goal disallowed for a teammate’s offside.
“I was confused because I turned and I didn’t see any of my teammates there (celebrating). So I was, like, ‘OK,’” he said.
From a town of just 13,000, Elversberg prides itself on its brand of “brave” football and refuse to be brushed aside as underdogs. “The bravery for me as an offensive player is to not be afraid of going one against one, going and trying something instead of being scared and not trying it because of the reputation,” he said.
While many players follow their fathers into the sport—think Erling Haaland, Tim Weah or Giuliano Simeone—the shorter history of professional women’s football means Campbell is among the first active players whose mother built a career in the game.
Karvelsson featured in the WUSA, the first all-professional women’s league in the U.S., when it launched in 2001; she won back-to-back NCAA titles with North Carolina in 1996 and 1997 and scored seven goals in 10 caps for Iceland. Campbell’s father also played college football.
His mother’s Nordic roots led Campbell to make his pro debut in Iceland in 2021, and he briefly represented Iceland at Under-17 level before switching allegiance to the United States in 2024—a move he says is final. “I’ve already made my decision to switch to the U.S. It was for a lot of different reasons, but my future is with the U.S., so that’s set. I have no second thoughts or anything, so that’s the thing for me that’s set in stone,” he said.

Campbell, a friend of U.S. midfielder and ex-Dortmund teammate Gio Reyna, says he has been in contact with the U.S. national team’s coaching staff for the last two years. After watching the “amazing” World Cup crowds while on vacation, he now hopes his Elversberg form can earn him an international debut, with Sunday’s match against fellow promoted side Schalke his next chance to impress.
“I’m just focused on trying to perform the best that I can and I’m praying that I get my first call-up, hopefully soon,” he said. That would be a dream come true for me to represent my country.” he concluded.

Asian Games chief defends 'functional' rooms after backlash
NAGOYA: Accommodation for Asian Games athletes in Japan is "functional" and efforts are being made to deal with numerous complaints from disgruntled teams, a chief organiser told AFP.
More than 17,000 competitors and officials are expected at the continent's biggest sporting spectacular, which opens on Saturday (Sep 19) in Nagoya.
In a bid to cut costs, organisers are housing athletes and officials in temporary accommodation ranging from a cruise liner and wooden containers to hotel rooms.
The plan has run into immediate problems, with South Korean officials branding the container huts the "worst ever" and saying the beds are too short.
An official from another team told AFP that he entered the facility, took one look at the arrangement and booked a hotel room instead.
Several countries have also complained about a shortage of accommodation.
Speaking ahead of the opening ceremony, organising committee president Hideaki Omura said efforts are being made to ensure athletes are comfortable.
"If there are different opinions then we will respond to them appropriately," said Omura, who also serves as governor of Aichi prefecture.
"At this point, while we are responding to individual opinions, we have been improving everything as issues arise and we will continue to respond that way."
Byeon Jun-hyeong, a player with South Korea's men's basketball team, posted a video on social media showing a leaking sink and soaked floor in his hut accommodation.
He posted the caption, "Please help us".
Hundreds of athletes were briefly evacuated from their accommodation last week as record rainfall lashed Nagoya.
About 2,000 people are supposed to stay in the huts.
CRUISE CONTROL
Omura said plans for the huts, which were built this year, had been given a favourable assessment by a committee of former athletes, including Olympians.
"We explained everything to them and had them take a look around, and they said it looked functional and good," he said.
About 4,000 athletes and officials will also stay on the Italian cruise ship Costa Serena, which arrived in Nagoya on Tuesday.
Cruise ships have been used previously as accommodation at international sports events but never on this scale.
The Asian Games are taking place at a time when typhoons are common in Japan, and Nagoya has experienced heavy rainfall in recent weeks.
Omura said the priority was to keep athletes and officials on board safe.
"We believe we can provide accommodation that guarantees athletes' safety and allows them to deliver their best performance," he said.
SLOW SALES
Athletes from 45 countries and territories will compete in more than 40 sports across over two weeks.
Omura said ticket sales were going "fairly well", especially for the marquee events.
But he admitted that lesser-known sports had yet to capture the Japanese public's imagination.
That includes cricket, which is practically unknown in Japan.
"India have a superstar cricket squad coming and Indian residents in Japan are saying, 'I can't believe we get to watch matches like this', but ticket sales haven't been very strong," said Omura.
"A lot of people in Japan have never seen cricket, so I really hope they take this chance and go and watch."
Events at the Games, including basketball and football have been underway since last week.
Omura said he was in attendance as the first action began when Qatar took on Iran in men's basketball.
After watching a physical contest, Omura said he hoped the Games would help Asia "reaffirm its bonds of friendship through sport".
"Iran and Qatar are in a situation where missiles are flying back and forth but they can still play basketball together," he said.
"Without the Asian Games you couldn't have a game like that."

Women’s cardiovascular changes may begin nearly 20 years before menopause: Study
A new study found that pulse pressure begins rising in women in their late 30s, about a decade earlier than in men, regardless of when menopause occurs.
Changes linked to future heart disease in women may begin nearly two decades before menopause, a new study suggests, challenging the long-held belief that menopause is the main trigger for age-related cardiovascular changes.
The research, published in Hypertension on September 14, found that pulse pressure — the difference between the top and bottom numbers in a blood pressure reading — begins rising in women in their late 30s, about a decade earlier than in men. This has traditionally been attributed to menopause and the decline in estrogen levels. However, the new research suggests the process may begin years before menopause starts.
The study’s authors analysed data from more than 6,500 women and more than 3,000 men participating in the Framingham Heart Study, one of the world’s longest-running cardiovascular research projects. Participants underwent three health assessments over a 14-year period.
Also read: Rethinking heart risk in Indian women
Researchers found that pulse pressure reached its lowest point and then began rising about a decade earlier in women than in men. Among women, the shift occurred in the late 30s, while among men, it occurred in the late 40s. The pattern remained the same regardless of whether women experienced menopause early, late or at the typical age. By around age 60, women consistently had higher pulse pressure than men, the researchers found.
“To our huge surprise, our results suggest that factors other than the timing of the final menstrual period were likely involved in the accelerated increase in pulse pressure in women after midlife,” noted Gary F Mitchell, an investigator with the Framingham Heart Study.
Pulse pressure is closely linked to the stiffening of the aorta, the body’s largest blood vessel. The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the rest of the body. As its walls become stiffer and less elastic with age, the heart has to work harder to pump blood through the circulatory system.
Also Read: Cardiac, respiratory ailments rise across age groups: Doctors
The study explains that widening pulse pressure is increasingly recognised as an important marker of cardiovascular health. Elevated pulse pressure is linked to a higher risk of heart disease, dementia and kidney disease. It may also make high blood pressure harder to control because some medications are less effective when arteries become stiff.
The findings of the new study suggest that changes affecting blood vessel health may begin much earlier in women than previously understood. Researchers said the results highlight the importance of paying closer attention to women’s cardiovascular health well before midlife and suggest that monitoring pulse pressure may help identify future heart risks earlier.

Chimpanzees are known to use rudimentary tools when foraging for food. According to a new paper in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, this learned behavior is passed down from adults to offspring through social learning. Specifically, adult chimps deliberately model the behavior, then turn their tools over to the youngsters so they can mimic the same motions.
“Receiving food and tools from experienced individuals, which we call food or tool transfer, may help chimpanzees learn to use technology to extract foods that are difficult to access,” said co-author Andreu Sánchez-Megías, a graduate student at the University of Barcelona and the Jane Goodall Institute Spain in Senegal. “Tool transfers thus appear to be a form of teaching, together with observation and supervised practice. It appears that mothers are the main models and teachers for young chimpanzees in this manner.”
As we have previously reported, tool use was once thought to be one of the defining features of humans, although Charles Darwin observed chimpanzees using stones to crack nuts in 1871. In 1960, the late primatologist Jane Goodall observed a chimp named David Greybeard bend a twig, strip off the leaves, and use it to spoon termites out of a nest and into his mouth. When he learned of the behavior, Goodall’s mentor, Louis Leakey, famously observed, “Now we must redefine ‘tool,’ redefine ‘man,’ or accept chimpanzees as humans.” Since then, chimps have been observed making sponges out of leaves to soak up liquids, shaping sticks to collect algae, and sharpening rudimentary spears for hunting.
Other examples of tool use have been observed in various species, although the behavior seems to have evolved more frequently among monkeys and apes. Dolphins can toss objects as a form of play, which some scientists consider to be a type of tool use, particularly when it involves another member of the same species. Potential purposes include communication, social bonding, or aggression. (Octopuses have also been observed engaging in similar throwing behavior.)

Small merchants may rethink accepting UPI over cash, says Retailers' body on merchant fee row
Retailers body warned that the UPI fee "could undo years of progress in digital payment adoption" among India's smallest retailers.
As the government moves to end free UPI payments after six years with 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate, the Retailers Association of India (RAI) on Wednesday reportedly said the move could reverse gains in digital payment adoption among small retailers ahead of the festive season.
This comes after the government introduced a 0.4 per cent fee on transfers worth more than ₹2,000 made to merchants through the platform from October 15, while explicitly ring-fencing everyday person-to-person transactions as well as small payments from any charge.
The MDR, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above, keeps consumers outside its ambit but places the cost on merchants, many of whom operate on thin margins, RAI said, news agency PTI reported.
Deep Dive
"For MSME retailers already running on thin margins, burden creates a straightforward incentive to steer transactions back toward cash," it said.
RAI also warned that the charge "could undo years of progress in digital payment adoption" among India's smallest retailers, just as the festive season gets underway.
"Small merchants will now think twice about whether to accept cash or UPI," said RAI CEO Kumar Rajagopalan.
RAI said the shift back to cash would also hurt the government's own formalisation push, as transactions that move off the UPI network no longer feed into GST reporting, the opposite of what a decade of digitisation policy has tried to build.
"This cuts against the government's own formalisation agenda. UPI acceptance should be incentivised, not taxed," Rajagopalan was quoted as saying.
The retail body also raised objection over treating all UPI transactions alike, as it argued that most such payments draw directly from a savings or current account and function as digital debit transactions, without the interchange cost or credit risk that justifies charges on credit networks.
"We do not see the case for charging a bank-to-bank UPI payment the way you'd charge for credit. Where UPI is linked to a credit line, a fee is easier to defend, because the cost structure genuinely resembles a credit product," Rajagopalan was quoted as saying.
RAI further argued that the cost of running the UPI network should not fall on merchants.
"NPCI keeps UPI running for the entire country, RBI or the government should be underwriting that cost, not merchants. The state gets a formal, traceable transaction it can tax out of every UPI payment. It should be paying for the enablement, not passing the bill down to the smallest retailer in the chain," Rajagopalan further said.
Similar concerns were raised by Clothing Manufacturers Association of India (CMAI) who said the MDR on UPI at the beginning of the festive season could not have at a more ‘challenging time for the industry’.
"This period is critical for merchants, retailers and consumer-facing businesses, many of whom are already working hard to revive demand and improve margins," CMAI President Santosh Katariya was quoted as saying.
He further said that adding another cost to digital transactions at this point risks putting further pressure on an ecosystem that is still finding its footing.
"UPI has been a powerful enabler of consumption and formalisation, and any move that increases the cost of acceptance needs to be carefully calibrated, particularly during the most important sales period of the year," Katariya added.
From October 15, merchants accepting UPI payments above ₹2,000 will pay a fee under the new framework, but customers will not have to pay this charge. However, if a person scans a shop's QR code and pay ₹500, ₹1,000 or ₹2,000, the payment remains free. Person-to-person payments also remain free.

Pennsylvania’s Measles Outbreak Is Enormous
The two latest deaths suggest that the true number of infections is much larger than reported.
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.
Following America’s recent measles deaths, anti-vaccine activists have cast doubt on the virus as the culprit. They’ve pointed to a victim’s underlying health conditions or, as they did last year in Texas, blamed hospital error. But the two latest measles deaths in Pennsylvania—bringing the state’s total to four since mid-August—have made the United States’ measles crisis undeniable.
Last month, the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-associated deaths; both cases were later revealed to be infants too young to have been vaccinated. In response, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—who was an anti-vaccine activist for decades before becoming health secretary—wrote on X that the deaths might have been “altogether fabricated.” (He later acknowledged a coroner’s conclusion that one of the deaths had been caused by measles.) Then, last weekend, an unvaccinated 40-year-old woman died in Jefferson County; immediately, people on Reddit and X insisted that her death wasn’t really caused by measles, because she’d had asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, both of which can make breathing difficult. Yesterday, state officials revealed that an unvaccinated 18-year-old died from a rare inflammatory condition of the brain and spinal cord that can be triggered by measles. Some commenters online deemed that death suspicious too.
What the armchair epidemiologists miss is that vulnerability to the infection doesn’t make a death less real. The two infants both tested positive for measles. The Lancaster County coroner’s office determined that one infant died of a ruptured spleen; however, when I spoke with that child’s parents, they told me that the mother had been extremely ill with the disease when she gave birth, the baby was not breathing when he was born, and they believed measles had killed their son. The other infant was born with a rare neurological condition, but the coroner found that measles was ultimately the cause of death. Greg Furlong, the Jefferson County coroner who investigated the 40-year-old woman’s death, told me that although the woman had conditions that made her vulnerable to measles, and was on supplemental oxygen, she was active before she contracted the virus. She cooked for her family and cleaned the house. Measles killed her in about a week. “If she wouldn’t have got the measles, would she still be alive today? I say yes,” Furlong, a Republican who is also the mayor of Summerville, said.
Four deaths in roughly four weeks suggest that the state is in the midst of an enormous outbreak. The Pennsylvania health department lists total cases at 693, with 99 in the past week. But considering that measles kills about one to three of every 1,000 children it infects, the actual number is likely much larger. Milder cases are going unreported. Many who fall ill, particularly in the Amish community, aren’t getting tested; the Amish parents of the infant who died with a ruptured spleen told me that their 13 living children had all caught the virus, but they never got swabbed.
These deaths are occurring after three unvaccinated people, including two young girls, died of measles in Texas and New Mexico last year. Those were the first measles deaths in the country in a decade. The last time the United States experienced four measles deaths in a calendar year was in 1992, at the tail end of a years-long outbreak that killed more than 100 Americans. That resurgence led to a recommendation that children receive two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, and prompted a nationwide push to increase vaccination rates. It worked, and measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. But overall kindergarten vaccination rates started declining during the coronavirus pandemic, and some areas, including Lancaster County, have fallen well below the 95 percent needed to maintain herd immunity.
Now, in the face of a new increase in measles deaths, Kennedy appears more interested in scoring political points than boosting national vaccination rates. He has accused Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, of “the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain”; Shapiro, in turn, charged Kennedy with “playing games with public health” after the CDC declined to update its measles statistics to include the deaths in his state. Kennedy’s stated reason for the omission is that the agency is “applying a consistent national standard.” But the delay marks a shift in policy: Last year, the CDC counted both Texas girls’ deaths and the death of the adult in New Mexico after the states announced them. (In a post on X, Kennedy wrote that the National Center for Health Statistics will determine if measles is the true cause of the deaths in Pennsylvania after examining death records; a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to questions about that investigation. In a statement, Pennsylvania’s health department said that its investigation had determined that all four deaths met the criteria for measles-associated fatalities.)
Tomorrow, Kennedy is scheduled to be the keynote speaker at the annual conference for Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization that he founded before becoming health secretary. Children’s Health Defense has a long history of ginning up fears about the vaccine for measles, mumps, and rubella while downplaying the seriousness of the diseases. Kennedy does, too. In July 2021, Kennedy told attendees at an Amish country fair in Pennsylvania, “The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A.” In fact, no known cure for measles exists; vitamin A has shown some promise in people with severe vitamin A deficiency, which is exceedingly rare in the United States. Since becoming health secretary, he has stated publicly that vaccination is “the most effective way to prevent measles infection,” but as I’ve reported, he also undercut that message by telling the father of a girl who died in West Texas that “you don’t know what’s in the vaccine anymore.” Kennedy has been a stronger advocate for measles itself, which he’s falsely credited with boosting resistance to cancer and cardiac disease, than he has for the vaccine that prevents it.
As cases and deaths rise, the reality becomes harder to ignore: Measles, a disease the country seemingly overcame 30 years ago, is once again killing Americans.

Stellar performance and cooling. Great battery life. Excellent and fun cameras with a customizable camera app. Bright, responsive screens with a smaller Dynamic Island.
TIRED
Pricier than ever. No base model (yet). Living in the iPhone Duo's shadow.
There is no iPhone 18 this year. If you were hoping to upgrade your smartphone right now, Apple is only offering the new iPhone 18 Pro models (and a very expensive folding iPhone coming next month). Don't let that be a reason to spend extra money on a phone you might not need.
Apple hasn't confirmed the next base-model yet, but the iPhone 18 is expected in spring 2027 alongside a mid-tier iPhone 18e. If you've historically been more than satisfied with the base iPhone model, you should absolutely wait to upgrade. Don't let the hype machine sway you.
That said, if you're a Pro connoisseur, the iPhone 18 Pro ($1,199) and its bigger sibling, the 18 Pro Max ($1,299), are very good phones, despite the $100 price hike over last year’s Pro models. No, you don't need to upgrade if you're coming from an iPhone 17 Pro, 16 Pro, or even a 15 Pro—hold onto your devices for longer!—but Apple's flagships deliver where it matters, even if they feel eclipsed by the spectacle of the foldable iPhone Duo.
Minor Refresh
Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro models have significant upgrades, but let's be a little more measured here.
Battery life has been stellar on the Pro models over the last few years, and that remains true here. The Pro Max is the more notable of the two because it packs a denser battery. With average use (around 5 hours of screen-on time), I hovered around 50 percent by the end of the day, and easily made it through day two on a single charge. I spent a little less time with the smaller Pro, but so far it has also comfortably gotten me through a day with around 40 percent left by bedtime. Safe to say, most people will very much enjoy the battery life, but the update doesn't feel drastic.
Next, there's the processor: the A20 Pro chip. I hardly run into problems with Apple's flagship silicon, and that hasn't changed. The phones run every app fluidly, and my benchmark tests show a surprisingly sizable leap over the A19 Pro in the 17 series.
It runs Control—a AAA game from 2019 ported to iOS earlier this year—decently well. However, aggressive upscaling makes the graphics look grainy, and character movements can feel a little sluggish. (I maxed out the graphics settings.) It's certainly not perfect, but I still can't believe I'm playing such a demanding title on an iPhone.
More impressive is Apple's thermal management on these phones. The company has expanded the vapor chamber's surface area by three times—the phone's cooling technology that helps spread heat around—meaning the entire phone felt toasty after close to an hour of gameplay in Control, with no uncomfortable localized hot spots. This larger vapor chamber also lets you game longer before phone’s thermal throttling kicks in and slows everything down.
The iPhone 18 Pro models come with iOS 27 out of the box, which features the all-new Siri AI. Yes, Siri AI is infinitely more capable than any version of Siri that Apple has offered before. It still doesn't quite have the spark or versatility of other AI assistants, but you might be fine with that. If you throw Siri AI a question, there's a good chance it can actually give you a satisfactory answer now. Remember that Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features aren't exclusive to the latest models, though you do need an iPhone 15 Pro or newer to access them.
The Dynamic Island, the pill-shaped bar housing the selfie camera and Face ID sensors, is noticeably smaller this year. To take full advantage of it, you can now view three live activities—like a DoorDash order status or your Uber ETA—simultaneously inside the Island, up from two. I was navigating in Apple Maps, chatting on a phone call, and had a DoorDash order en route to my home, and it spaced out all of these activities neatly.
Speaking of the iPhone 18 Pro design, I do like the new burgundy color, though I miss brighter, more playful options like last year's Cosmic Orange. But the real headline feature is almost invisible—embedded into the main camera on the back of the iPhone.
Aperture Priority
Apple is debuting a variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro models. This is by no means the first time we've seen a smartphone with a variable aperture—Samsung and Huawei both launched phones with the capability years ago. While Samsung abandoned the tech, Huawei and Xiaomi still ship it on their flagships.
What is a variable aperture? Simply put, the aperture is the physical opening that lets light reach the camera sensor. A wider aperture lets in more light and has a lower “f-stop” number, while a narrower aperture restricts light. Most smartphones rely on fixed apertures—the iPhone 17 Pro's main camera, for example, is locked at f/1.78. A variable aperture gives the lens mechanical blades that physically expand or contract in a circular shape, adjusting how much light hits the sensor. Apple gives you four f-stops to select from: f/1.48, f/1.78, f/2.8, and f/4.
Open the aperture to f/1.48 on the iPhone 18 Pro and more light floods in, delivering cleaner low-light shots and faster Night Mode captures. This also creates a real optical bokeh—the soft blurred background effect phone makers have spent years simulating with computational Portrait modes. Step it down to f/4, this blur recedes, keeping more of the scene and background in crisp focus. All of this can be very confusing for people unfamiliar with these camera terms, which is why Apple defaults the aperture to “Auto.”
I love it. I shoot manual on my mirrorless camera, so I immediately took to the new customization features in the Camera app to show Shutter Speed and Lens Aperture as easy-to-access settings. Shooting at f/1.48 delivers a nice bokeh effect—especially in low light—so I stopped using Apple's Portrait mode altogether. (Some parts of the image may look less sharp than on an iPhone 17 Pro because the plane of focus is narrower.) Apple will point out that Portrait mode is still useful, as you can always add more bokeh post-capture.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
iPhone 18 Pro Max, main camera with a one-second shutter speed.
Move to f/4 for group shots when you want everyone in the frame to be in focus. (Or if you want a very fun starburst effect with light sources!) As you change between the four aperture settings, you can see the blades moving on the main camera—it's very cool. In auto mode, the camera largely sticks to f/1.78, or f/1.48 in low light. It chooses the other two apertures for specific, usually brighter, scenes.
I have also enjoyed the ability to adjust the camera’s shutter speed. Yes, you can already do this with a third-party camera app, but now it's baked in! With a one-second shutter, you can capture some fun shutter drag to accentuate motion in a photo. However, you'll definitely need to buy a neutral density filter for super-bright scenes to balance exposure. It's fun to play around with.
I compared several of the 18 Pro’s photos with shots from Google's Pixel 11 Pro, and I do have to note that the iPhone tends to over-brighten scenes that should be very dark. So much so that it can misrepresent the dark mood you might be chasing. The Pixel tended to preserve more of those shadows, though it delivered more lifted blacks that made the image appear more matte. The iPhone can also struggle with backlit scenes, more so than the Pixel.
Apple has added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles, and this is a fun element to sink your teeth into and explore. Phone makers have realized that ultra-clean, sharp, “perfect” shots are perhaps not what most people want, and these stylings—like the new Camera Looks on Pixel phones—offer a new degree of “authenticity.”
The iPhone 18 Pro's camera system is fun without feeling overwhelming. You can pick and choose what degree of control you want, tweak Photographic Styles to your tastes, and add more depth after the fact, whether it's for videos or photos. Who knew people liked having more control? There aren't any sweeping improvements to the camera lenses or sensors, but this is a system that shutterbugs will love to experiment with, and that's what the Pro iPhone is all about.
